Andrea Shaw Resnick,  Coach, Inc. - SVP, IR & Corporate Communications: Good morning and welcome. We want to thank all of you for joining us for our 2014 Analyst and Investor Day. We have put together what we believe is an informative program covering our brand transformation strategy, including initiatives around our products, our stores and our marketing, as well as our financial outlook. And for those of you who provided content suggestions, we appreciate your input and tried to capture it in our speaking points.
 Despite being a bit fashionably late this morning, only typical, assuming everything goes to plan, we should conclude the program probably around midday. Before we begin today's program, please review the disclosure language regarding forward-looking statements that is on the screen. As all of you now have had an opportunity to read it, I will not delay our presentation by reading it aloud. Thank you. And now I would like to turn the podium over to Victor Luis, Coach's Chief Executive Officer. Victor?

Victor Luis,  Coach, Inc. - CEO: Thank you, Andrea and thank you, everyone, for joining us today for this very important investment community event. A warm welcome to the many familiar faces here in the room with us today, as well as to many who could not join us and are doing so via webcast.
 Our goal today is to provide you with a very detailed snapshot of our business, the challenges we are facing and our plan to reinvigorate growth at our great Company. You have heard us speak many times in the past of our four primary strategies  first, leveraging the global opportunity by aggressively growing our international businesses; second, tapping into the large and growing men's accessory category; third, harnessing the power of the digital world; and most broadly, growing our business in North America and throughout the world by transforming into a global lifestyle brand.
 Our focus today is on brand transformation with a specific emphasis on the North American handbag and accessories market where we have the biggest challenges, but the most significant opportunities. We have chosen to host an Analyst Day now because we are set to implement some very important initiatives as part of the next phase of our transformation plan and want to ensure you are informed as we move forward with this next phase of our journey. At the end of the presentations, we will provide ample time for your questions.
 Let me begin with some basic truths, truths that define who we are and that still resonate today. As many of you know, we are the leading player in a very attractive and growing industry and indeed, we created the accessible luxury category that we have led for over a decade. Our long history of success has been based on our track record of defining innovation, relevance and value to consumers in the many markets that we have developed. These attributes have remained central to our brand and our team's core proposition and there is no question that we design and bring to market beautiful leather products.
 However, we have now reached a unique moment for our brand and for our organization. After 12 years of growth, we are at a crossroads. The competitive landscape has shifted and we have not responded effectively. This has led to a number of challenges, especially in our North American women's business. We have to make some tough decisions and take charge of our destiny and choose the strategic path forward. Most importantly, we have to transform the Coach brand and we need to be bold and different in how we rewrite the Coach playbook for growth and leadership.
 Today, our discussion is about how we will accomplish these goals. Throughout the morning, we will share with you key elements of our long-term plan to reinvigorate growth and realize our vision for global modern luxury. First, we will explain where we are today and how we got here. We will also describe the key choices we are making and the benefits and costs of each. You will see that there are no sacred cows, that we have re-examined every aspect of our business through a new lens, ensuring that we are consistent with the broader brand proposition.
 Our analysis has been thorough and systematic and as a result, we have strong convictions about where we need to take the business. Among these is our very strong commitment to our multichannel strategy. One of the questions that we get asked most often is in relation to the balance of the number of retail stores versus outlet stores in our fleet. We believe this is not a problem for the Company or the brand; rather our issues have been more nuanced  an underinvestment in our full-price stores and too many promotional impressions in the marketplace. Our team will take you through this in detail, but you will see that our transformation plan aggressively addresses these past issues.
 You will be hearing more details about the plan throughout the morning, but first I'd like to take a quick step back as it is important to appreciate that while we face significant challenges, we are coming from a position of strength. We remain a leader in the accessories category at home and globally as the number one brand domestically and number two worldwide. We have over 1,000 directly operated stores across the world and have a growing global presence across five continents and 35 countries. And finally, we have over 400 million customer visits annually to our Company-operated stores and on our websites.
 In addition to our amazing brand and its iconic status as America's and New York's original house of leather, I am extremely proud to lead one of the best teams in specialty retailing both in the US and internationally. We have a very strong and seasoned global leadership team directing execution and I could not be prouder of how we have come together to understand our changing context, deal with our challenges and create a plan to return Coach to long-term sustainable growth. You will be hearing from several of these leaders today as they lay out the specifics of our strategic plan and I hope that you will see from their enthusiasm, their passion and their professionalism that we are an energized organization driven by a conviction to our brand and this sense of urgency to growth.
 Those of you who are familiar with our story and our team know that leading through change is part of our DNA and is indeed embedded in our culture. Throughout our history, we have consistently led our industry in driving innovation. We defined the leather good space in our US market. We were the leader in creating a global supply chain in our category and we were the first US brand in our space to bring international relevance to an American brand.
 This history of excellence and execution is important. It is a part of who we are and will help drive us to succeed again. But I also want to be clear that we do not consider today's challenges to be the same as prior generations. In many ways, they are more complex, but we have the confidence that we have built the robust plan that addresses these complexities. As we deliver our five-year plan to you today, you will see that, in Coach's next chapter, it is driven by a focus on defining what we are calling modern luxury. We will give you a definition of modern luxury and explain the steps we are taking to communicate it to current and new Coach fans and capitalize on the growth opportunity that we see in front of us.
 As I touched on earlier, there is no question that we operate in a very attractive global market. The global premium men's and women's bag and small leather goods market currently stands at $35 billion and is expected to grow at a 7% CAGR exceeding $50 billion during 2018. As the number two player globally in terms of marketshare and as a brand with a strong and unique DNA, we have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us.
 However, in order to fully unlock the growth potential of our brand on the global stage, we have to address a number of issues, especially in our North American business. Many of you know that the landscape has shifted dramatically and is populated with new players and governed by new dynamics. At the same time, we have not put sufficient investments and resources behind our brand and fleet and we have not demonstrated enough fashion innovation in an increasingly competitive category.
 In addition, sticking too long to our former playbook, we have suffered from an advertising focus that has relied on minimal fashion context to support the positioning of our bags and accessories. All of these issues have combined to weaken our position while competitors have aggressively built domestic marketshare in our category. The thorough long-range plan that our team has undertaken has given us all appreciation of these challenges and our transformation process is designed to address them.
 In recent quarters, we have made progress in laying the groundwork, but we have now reached an inflection point and have made some major decisions. Coach's transformation is about taking the tried-and-true attributes of our brand, committing to quality and reinvigorating our brand profile, all with the objective of evolving our competitive value proposition. And that is not just in handbags and accessories. We think our strategy offers significant growth opportunity in the broader set of categories that we have operated in for some time like footwear and outerwear. This will require an integrated holistic approach across product, our stores and our marketing and promotional activities. It will also entail the rollout of carefully crafted aspirational marketing campaigns to define our brand unlike anything we have done in the past to deliver a fuller and more consistent brand expression.
 While it is early in our journey, we have built some very important milestones. Over the past two years, we have demonstrated momentum in men's and gained increasing acceptance as a dual gender brand internationally. Our successful relaunch of footwear has been another key highlight. However, our leadership team's touchstone for the beginning of our transformation can be traced to the arrival of Stuart Vevers as our Executive Creative Director this past September. Stuart is already having a dramatic impact on how we tell our brand story and with the launch of his first collection in retail and the development of our new store concept, we are poised to begin our transformation in earnest. Therefore, we are now moving into the very important execution phase of our plan.
 There are several key strategic priorities that we are focused on and will implement across our distribution network in the months ahead. First, as you will hear in detail from Fran Della Badia, we will close our underperforming stores in North America and rebuild through flagships in our top 12 North American markets. In addition, we will broaden our presentation in US department stores, including moving to more open, accessible and fully branded displays, changing our product offering, driving relevance and making Coach more shopable. You will also learn that we will be further evolving our outlet strategy both to maximize product flow and leverage our new store concept. And finally, David Duplantis will share in detail how we will evolve our North American promotional strategies and continue to reduce the volume of our North American e-outlet store events.
 All of these activities and many others across product and marketing strategies are part of our holistic strategy aimed at communicating Coach as a global modern luxury brand and bringing relevance amongst the category drivers, as well as millennial consumers.
 You will be hearing more about what we mean by modern luxury today and in the future. But to explain in simple terms, modern luxury is our evolution from the accessible luxury positioning that we defined and have led. Let me start by saying that modern luxury is not about emulating traditional European luxury players or simply elevating our price points. It is about being authentic to ourselves, approachable, confident and original.
 From the viewpoint of our business, it is about quality, workmanship and the personal lasting relationships that we establish with consumers throughout all of our touch points, including our product, our stores and our associates. In short, it is evolving our view of luxury that differentiates us from the accessible luxury players who depend mostly on fashion and the traditional luxury players who depend mostly on exclusivity.
 These concepts will be evident in a lot of what we will show you during today's event. Our brand repositioning is at the foundation of our plan to reinvigorate long-term sustainable growth for our business and our Company. To achieve this, we will cut through the competition's messaging with consistent and disruptive messaging. And we will look to drive our share of voice across the most important touch points targeting the right message by medium to the right consumer. This will be a complete transformation in how we define our brand and as we move from the low context approach of the past to communicating the full expression of the Coach man and Coach woman.
 Today, I am extremely proud to lead the team that is writing the next chapter of Coach's incredible history. And in the next 12 to 18 months, as we move towards celebrating our 75th anniversary, you can expect to see Coach unveil a host of major initiatives aimed at defining our vision of modern luxury and resetting the agenda for our category.
 This morning, each of the senior executives with us will walk you through details of our strategic game plan beginning with Stephanie Stahl who will review our brand positioning and strategic transformation, as well as our related marketing strategy. Stephanie will be followed by Stuart who will present his vision of product and the evolution of Coach's modern luxury positioning. Stuart will be followed by Louis Minuto, our Head of Architecture, who will share with you our new store model. And Stephanie will then return with David Duplantis to discuss our marketing strategy, including our promotional approach and customer experience initiatives.
 Fran will then follow and will review our North America multichannel strategy and the steps we are taking to close underperforming stores and maximize our flagships. And Fran will be followed by Ian Bickley, who will provide an update on our international footprint and growth plans. And finally, Jane will wrap things up with an overview of our financial assumptions and guidance relating to our plan.
 Before handing over to Stephanie, I'd like to wrap up by summarizing what I see as the key headlines for our conversations with you today. The space that we compete in is an extremely attractive category and it is known that our playing field is changing dramatically. We are in a competitive environment with more players and a more fashion-driven focus.
 At the same time, we haven't invested sufficiently in supporting our brand and long-term success and there is no question that we have reached a crossroads. However, we have a clear vision and plan on how to address these challenges and we have the team and the resources to capture the great opportunity ahead of us. You will learn that we are taking bold steps to reinvigorate growth at our great Company while retaining the attributes that have made our brand so special to millions of consumers worldwide. And you will also learn that while we have laid the groundwork through the early stages of our transformation plan, we are truly now moving into the heavy lifting phase. We remain the leader in our space with a strong brand and while this will be a journey, the opportunities on the other side are compelling. Our market is attractive and growing and in many ways, it is indeed the best place to be in luxury retailing.
 As we continue the journey, we are committed to helping you follow and measure our progress. That starts with the context that we are providing today on our plan, the financial implications and our progress roadmap. All which we plan to share with you today. And now I'd like to turn over the stage to my partner, Stephanie Stahl. Stephanie?

Stephanie Stahl,  Coach, Inc. - EVP, Marketing & Strategy: Thank you, Victor. Good morning. I lead global marketing and strategy for Coach. I joined Coach in October 2012 and since then have been focused on creating our transformational strategy and plans and building our marketing impact and capabilities. Prior to Coach, I was the CEO of the Tracy Anderson method, the Chief Marketing Officer at Revlon and a partner at The Boston Consulting Group. I am excited to be here this morning to share the context around our strategy, including key market and consumer details, as well as some of the key strategic choices we are making to support our brand transformation.
 We participate in the large and growing global premium bag and accessories market, which has grown 6% per year since 2008 and is projected to grow at a similar rate for the next five years, reaching over $50 billion in 2018. Men's growth has been outpacing women's with the men's percentage of the category increasing from 15% in 2008 to 18% in 2013 and is expected to continue to slightly outpace the growth of women's to be 19% of the total category in 2018. Over the next five years, category growth will be strongest in Greater China and rest of world. Greater China includes both Mainland China and Hong Kong. North America is expected to grow at a 9% rate over the next five years.
 As Victor mentioned, Coach is the number two brand globally and the number one brand in North America. Coach has gained share most rapidly in Greater China over the past few years where we have advanced from the number eight share position in 2008 to the number three share position in 2013. Today, Coach offers products in all three key category price tiers  between $200 and $400, under $200 and over $400. We will continue to assort fully in the $200 to $400 price range and under $200 while taking advantage of additional whitespace in the over $400 price tier going forward.
 Footwear and outerwear are priority categories for Coach and are also large and growing. Both are expected to grow 7% over the next five years. Importantly, the footwear and outerwear categories are less concentrated competitively than handbags and accessories; whereas the top five brands represent over 50% of the total handbags and accessories market, the top five foot warehouses represent less than 25% of that total market and the top five outerwear, less than 40%.
 Coach has a rigorous consumer research agenda and approach. In our three largest markets, the US, China and Japan, we perform in-depth quantitative studies, including women's and men's bags and accessories annual brand tracking and women's footwear brand tracking in the US and China. In the past three years, we have surveyed or spoken with over 150,000 consumers across 13 markets. We also use qualitative research to understand emerging categories or new markets. Recent work includes outerwear product concept tests in the US and in China and footwear product concept tests in China and Japan.
 In sync with the increasing importance of social media, we also have begun using social listening tools in both the US and in China. We will be tracking our brand strengths on a quarterly basis in North America. We survey women aged 18 to 64 representing the age and income census. We ask about 40 questions ranging from demographics, awareness, purchase behavior, fashion and handbag engagement, as well as perceptions of our brand and other brands. We will use the learnings from this research to iteratively optimize our plans going forward.
 Today, Coach is the most loved handbag brand in North America and the brand that consumers would most recommend to friends and family. The Coach brand is well-positioned on three of the top five emotional attributes in the category, specifically confident, put together and complete. Our plans will reinforce that positioning while we strengthen the emotional attributes of fashionable and sophisticated. We will be tracking our progress on a quarterly basis.
 As Victor mentioned, Coach has built tremendous brand equity around our beautiful, classic, enduring leather products. We are building on that equity with Stuart's designs to add more uniqueness to our product, as well as enhance our fashion credibility with key customers.
 In the context of a changing competitive landscape, we are evolving and refining our product testing approach. We continue to seek and leverage consumer response to our products through testing and in-store piloting. The competitive landscape has shifted significantly and we have been slow to respond. We have underinvested in the Coach brand and created too many promotional impressions. Building off of the core strengths of the Coach brand with integrated efforts across product, stores and marketing, we will define modern luxury and take full advantage of the opportunities we have as a leader in the large and growing bag and accessories category.
 We have a clear strategic intent you will see reflected in all our plans and actions. Our core category is and will continue to be bags and accessories. We see opportunity in footwear and outerwear and have had initial successes in both. We will leverage our other lifestyle categories to reinforce our leadership in bags and accessories. We are the number two brand in the world and we will be represented in all domestic markets today and tomorrow and continue to lead in travel retail. We are fully committed to our multichannel distribution model and our plans call for growth across all.
 The Coach brand has incredible strengths. We have a heritage of outstanding quality, craftsmanship and design. We are loved and part of our customers' personal narrative. Our opportunity and focus is to add fashion relevance and emotion to our brand and product because, in this category, it is not about needing it, it is about wanting it.
 We have spent considerable time defining what modern luxury means to Coach. Essential in this process was delineating between what modern luxury is and what it is not. For Coach, modern luxury is authentic expression of quality and fashion at exceptional value. Modern luxury is inviting and approachable. It is the creation of a personal relationship with a trusted brand. Our transformation to a modern luxury lifestyle brand is driven by an integrated comprehensive plan of product, store environments and marketing initiatives. Product will have clear creative direction and deliberate investment in details and quality that reinforces what makes a Coach product Coach with a lifestyle offering to create context for priority categories.
 Our stores in the new modern luxury design will provide a unique-to-Coach special experience for our customers. The design will be brought into all channels and optimized by channel. True flagships will showcase the full breadth of the brand and store associates will tell our fashion, quality and heritage story. Our marketing will be consistent, disruptive, integrated and interesting. We will layer communications to reinforce seasonal themes and we will use innovative format and tailored messaging at competitive investment levels.

Fran Della Badia,  Coach, Inc. - President, North America Retail: Thanks, David. Stephanie and David have laid out how we will provide a holistic customer experience across all of our touchpoints. You have also heard about how we think about our strong commitment to a multichannel distribution model as the right positioning for Coach as a highly desirable global modern luxury brand. My goal for today is to take you through how we are implementing the transformation strategy in North America and show the way our real estate and wholesale strategies are tightly integrated with our brand repositioning and marketing initiatives.  Some guiding principles to keep in mind that have informed the process and decisions I will be talking about today. First, our overarching objective is to change brand perception. Key to this is creating more positive impressions in the mind of the consumer as we move from accessible luxury to modern luxury. Second, success in North America is about driving productivity across all channels. We are already in the best and most important locations in North America and there are limited new brand-enhancing locations available.
 We have lost productivity because we underinvested in marketing. We lacked distinctive product newness and haven't appropriately reinvested in the store base. This worked when we were alone and unchallenged in the marketplace. This isn't working today. Our competitors have successfully copied the Coach playbook. Today, we are rewriting the playbook, taking a progressive approach to optimizing our distribution strategy in parallel with our ambitions for the brand. As in all things Coach, behind the plan is a thoughtful, innovative, thorough and rigorous process. We have been systematic in our market analysis, store evaluation and designing the right mix of retail, outlet and wholesale to optimize the positive impressions we can make in key markets.
 As Victor stated earlier, multichannel is the right model for Coach and we are committed to it. It is a proven strategy in our category. Moreover, the Coach brand has always been and will continue to be strong and vibrant enough to support multiple channels of distribution. So our plan isn't to change our model; it is to make the right investments to drive higher levels of productivity. Today, I will focus on how we will achieve this across our retail outlet and wholesale locations.
 Brand impressions are created every day in every channel whether he or she walks into one of our retail stores, Macy's main floor or an outlet store. Given that reality and the size, scope and breadth of our business and distribution, as well as our extremely high brand awareness, we quickly realized that we needed to take a holistic approach. This means impacting all consumer touchpoints simultaneously in a given market. This contrasts with the more traditional retail rollout approach based on a top-door analysis by channel.
 Replatforming the brand in only one channel at a time would not be sufficient to cut through and tell a consistent and powerful brand story to change consumer perception. Our plan focuses on the 12 Metropolitan statistical areas or MSAs that represent the core of our North America presence. These markets are where roughly 50% of our total business happens and they serve as beacons for the brand message given their high traffic levels and tourist penetration.
 In each of these markets, we are focused on translating our global brand positioning into local market relevance. We will close unproductive retail stores in both these MSAs and throughout the retail base. At the same time, we will be investing; our investments won't be linear by market. We have made decisions by MSA to ensure that we have the right locations, the right mix of stores and the right wholesale touchpoints to optimize productivity.
 By the end of FY16, our actions will have a direct impact on 85% of the traffic that we see in these MSAs and we expect to impact 100% of the total North America fleet by the end of our five-year planning horizon.
 Now that you have the guiding principles of our plan, let me summarize the key strategic choices we have made in each of our North American channels.  In outlet, we expect to hold store count net neutral over our planning horizon, bearing in mind the changes David described in our largest source of outlet sales, EOS, where we will be significantly curtailing impressions. We will also be recalibrating outlet product as we align with the brand transformation. And in wholesale, we will be investing in an enhanced and more shopable presence in department stores.
 Now let's take a closer look at each channel starting with retail. Our retail store strategy is based on the thesis of culling where necessary and investing where appropriate. The 70 store locations identified were a result of a thorough analysis using a store evaluation lens that considered sales and comp performance, contribution, both dollars and margin, market density, in other words, sales transfer opportunity, brand positioning and cotenancy, making sure we are in the right neighborhood, lease renewal and the related cost of renovating to the new modern luxury concept. As we move forward, there may be additional closures beyond those planned for FY15. We will be opportunistic as leases come up, renewing where the economics and brand positioning are favorable and closing stores where that makes sense through our brand and productivity filters.
 The real estate decisions we are making are among the most visually impactful effects of our transformation plan. Changing brand perception is a softer concept, but real estate affects the impressions our brand makes on consumers in a very tangible way. Knowing that, leading with a stronger flagship presence in key MSAs is an important step in our strategy. We are prioritizing our investment focus on how our modern luxury positioning will translate in the market, starting with impacting flagships and aggressively rolling out our new retail concept. Of the closures, 13 are existing men's standalone outlets where we will transfer the business into existing women's stores in the same mall as we articulate a dual-gender brand positioning. We expect that we will recapture most of this men's volume, improving the existing store comps, productivity and profitability. Our strategy is to integrate both women's and men's product offerings into one Coach store wherever we can.
 The remaining outlet closures are in two of our 12 key MSAs, reducing our outlet footprint in these markets by a third. Our rationale for taking these steps is to learn more about consumer behavior as we transform. Some questions we are looking to answer are whether the consumer will shift to another channel, whether we can influence and guide her to shift through a targeted and segmented communication strategy, whether she will step up her purchase with a higher ADT. And in order to evaluate this, we will use consumer data that we have for these stores that track her address and her purchase behavior. Of course, we will track all comp metrics  conversion, traffic, ADT  to see performance in the impact market versus the balance of Company and we can also pilot direct marketing initiatives and consumer tracking. For example, pilot a program to capture names in wholesale to view crossover where today we don't have the ability to capture wholesale or department store activity.
 As we introduce new product, you will see us elevate the outlet experience. We need to bring more relevancy to our stores through innovative and compelling product. That means consumers visiting our outlet stores will see less logo, more leather, more lifestyle categories. We piloted this initiative in FY14 and were pleased with the sales lift that we have seen based on early reads. The number of dedicated shop managers is expected to triple by FY17.

This product, which will represent about 15% of the assortment, provides the channel high value and functionality at compelling price points.
 Now that I have covered the key strategic initiatives across our retail outlet and wholesale channels, I'd like to give a specific example of how we are implementing our plan focusing on the New York market. New York is an ideal example to profile our strategy because it embodies our multichannel model. The market includes the immediate tri-state area and represents roughly 10% of our North America direct sales, as well as being important to our wholesale business.

We are actively looking for a Fifth Avenue flagship. We are also rolling out our new retail concept to seven stores, including a flagship, as Louis discussed earlier, at Time Warner Center and in high-end locations such as Manhasset and Short Hills.
 We are continuing to think of our Bleecker Street women's and men's stores as design labs for our creative teams to test new ideas. This spring, we will be renovating and expanding our Harriman outlet store and in the greater Metro New York market, we will also be elevating our wholesale shop-in-shop locations such as Roosevelt Field and Garden State Plaza. The thoroughness of our New York strategy has been replicated across each of the 12 MSAs that we have identified and our actions will unfold over the next year.
 As we looked at the fleet, a key goal was to establish a consistent brand perception across the market, across all channels. That includes the marketing mix by market across prints, window and other media. We are, of course, looking to optimize sales pickup in impressions. Our plan allocates spending by MSA with a focus on how we can attract the most traffic.
 I will wrap up with a quick review of our aggressive near-term implementation plan. In retail, we expect to execute on the majority of store closures in the first half of the new fiscal year. Store investment activities will be timed to follow the launch of our product, marketing and customer experience initiatives this fall with our first new retail concepts debuting in November. In outlet, our store closures will take place throughout the fiscal year with Stuart's product for outlet launching in the second half. Reductions in our EOS event cadence will begin in Q1 and will be ongoing. And in wholesale, we are quickly moving to more open, accessible displays and rolling out the shop manager program.
 Our new playbook will change brand perception. We are not waiting to get started. To support all of these initiatives, we have a clearly articulated financial plan, which Jane will speak to in a few minutes. Now here is Ian Bickley to talk through our international strategy.

Ian Bickley,  Coach, Inc. - President, International: Thanks, Fran and thank you all for participating in today's presentation. In fact, I have been involved at the start of our business in every one of the more than 30 countries we operate in today. I served as President of Coach Japan from 2001 to 2006, President of Coach International from 2006 to 2013 and was appointed President, International Group one year ago. I have been here for chapters one and two and could not be more excited than I am today about the next chapter of Coach.
 Today, I am going to provide a concise overview of our international business, including our current marketshare, our distribution footprint and our growth strategy. Our international growth remains robust and we have got a number of terrific opportunities in front of us. I hope you will share our enthusiasm regarding the direction our global business is headed.
 As Victor shared, the global market opportunity for Coach is significant. It is currently $35 billion and we expect it to grow 7% annually to reach $50 billion during 2018. We believe this is the most attractive place to be in the global retail and apparel sector.
 As we also shared, Coach is the number two brand globally and has a strong position in most of the world's largest markets. We are number one brand in North America and the number two brand in Japan. And in China, we have rapidly gained share moving from number eight to number three between 2008 and 2013. We believe China has the potential to become the next geography in which Coach gains a leadership position.
 We are also a top five brand in most Asian countries where we directly operate our business and we are now moving forward in building out our footprint in Europe, a key market for our brand. Our international sales have been growing robustly, exceeding $1.7 billion at retail in 2013. They have grown at a compound annual rate of nearly 30% over the past decade and we are seeing continued robust growth in 2014.
 Coach's international sales now account for over 30% of Coach's total sales and we expect the share to expand given our growth momentum and the size of the opportunity in front of us. Through our brand transformation, we expect to expand marketshare by reinvigorating growth in our mature markets, solidifying our position in the fastest-growing markets and entering new markets with a very clear positioning.
 In addition to our excellent product, which is resonating with our global audiences, our success is based on a very robust global multichannel distribution strategy. Today, we are represented in 35 countries and have over 1,000 directly operated locations with over 200 additional locations operated by our international distribution partners. Over half of these more than 1,200 locations are outside North America.
 Our flagship locations around the world are also a very important part of our distribution strategy. In line with our plan, over the next two to three years, we will be making significant investments in building new flagship stores and renovating existing flagship locations with a focus on key international cities. New flagship stores are planned in Paris, Milan, Beijing, Tokyo, Bangkok, Jakarta, Sydney, Melbourne and Dubai and we will renovate existing flagship stores in London, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Singapore and Kuala Lumpur.
 China represents the largest single market growth opportunity outside North America. Already our third largest market, we see China as the next $1 billion business for Coach. The Chinese consumer loves Coach, evidenced by our continued strong comps and we have an extremely high repurchase intent of over 80%. We are also the number one fashion brand on [Cinowavo] with over 1.25 million fans and on WeChat with over 200,000 fans with both growing rapidly. And we are already recognized as a dual-gender and lifestyle brand with more than a third of our sales coming from men's and lifestyle categories.

We anticipate that the China market will grow 60% to over $8 billion by 2018. Although women's will grow faster than men's, men's will continue to grow at a double-digit pace and already represents close to 40% of the total market.
 As you can see, we are growing rapidly in China. Our sales have increased at a compound annual rate of 70% over the past five years and we are on course to deliver sales of $540 million in our directly operated business in China this year. Today, we operate 147 locations in 52 cities, including the Mainland, Hong Kong and Macau. In addition, our partners manage an additional 18 Coach locations, primarily in airports and downtown duty-free. E-commerce, which launched more than a year ago, is in the early stages, but also growing. Internet consumers are shopping from over 250 cities on the Mainland, including 200 with no bricks and mortar locations. Clearly the opportunity for future distribution is significant.
 We have built a solid foundation and enjoying double-digit growth and we still have only 16% unaided brand awareness compared with about 64% in Japan and 78% in North America. Macro changes are also playing to our favor with a rapidly emerging middle class and a consumer shift from status to value. At the same time, we are planning conservatively for several reasons. First, we are building off a business with a much larger base, now more than $0.5 billion. Second, we are seeing the need to aggressively review our fleet given changes in the retail landscape. With the emergence of many new large-scale shopping malls, there will be clear winners and losers and we may need to close a few stores. We are planning 25 to 30 new openings, but could have as many as 10 closures resulting in 15 to 20 net openings.
 Given these shifting market dynamics and the rapidly evolving competitive environment, we are fine-tuning our growth strategies and investing in brand transformation to solidify our leadership position. We cannot be complacent and must build a sustainable growth platform. Through our product, we will build fashion relevance, leveraging Stuart Vevers' collection and lifestyle categories and reinforce value through our core product offering.
 Through our stores, we will develop high-quality multichannel distribution. We will accelerate fleet renewal in Shanghai and Beijing, impacting 80% of traffic by FY16 and 100% by FY17. We will open regional flagship doors and reinforce tier 1 and tier 2 city distribution. We will continue to capitalize on tier 3 and tier 4 opportunities that are ready and we will be highly selective with our outlet openings. Through marketing, we will build awareness and desire, leveraging our new marketing campaign and promotional model to build brand awareness and drive traffic.
 Turning to Japan, this is the largest market outside North America and currently represents 15% of total Coach sales. We are the number two brand and number one in units with around $700 million in sales, 15% share of the market and 200 locations. This is a mature market and our goal is to drive further marketshare gains. We will leverage our brand transformation to positively impact brand perceptions, re-engaging our core consumer while appealing to the category-engaged and millennials and we will focus on building men's, which represents 25% of the category spend.
 Led by retail, our brand transformation plans include renovation of key doors in Tokyo, representing over 70% of traffic by FY16, including flagship stores in Ginza and Shibuya and a new flagship store in Shinjuku set to open in October, which will be our first modern luxury retail store in Japan. We will also renovate key locations in other important cities throughout Japan.
 Outside of China and Japan, the Asia region has a market size of $4 billion and is expected to reach $6 billion by 2018. We are consistently a top five brand in these markets with a combined share of about 6%. We directly operate close to 100 locations in Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia and Singapore and through our distributor partners, there are an additional 70 locations in these countries plus Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and Australia.
 Moving to Europe, which is a large and fragmented market representing about 18% of the total global category, it represents the largest whitespace for Coach. We entered a little over three years ago and now directly operate 26 locations and 55 wholesale locations. While our business in Europe is still small with sales at retail of about $60 million, we see a big opportunity for accessible luxury brands who are gaining marketshare. Our current design direction resonates with the European consumer. Our price points and quality offer compelling value and our heritage linked to New York fashion creates a differentiated positioning. We see brand transformation as an opportunity to provide consumers in Europe with a clearer and more relevant positioning.
 In FY15, we expect to grow our business to over $100 million, adding about 15 directly operated locations and more than 100 wholesale locations, achieving operating profitability. Our goal is to achieve $500 million in retail sales, representing a mid to high single digit share of the $7.5 billion premium men's and women's bag and accessory market by 2018.
 Lastly, I would like to touch on the opportunity in global travel retail. For context, Chinese outbound travelers are expected to grow from an estimated 100 million in 2015 to 175 million by 2020. We also expect similar rates of increase for other Asian travelers over the same period. Today, we have over 90 global travel retail locations, including key airports globally and through our international distributor partners and focused travel retail operators, we plan to rapidly expand in this channel. Specific nationalities we expect to be important include Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Indonesian, Russian and Brazilians. Positioning ourselves globally means penetrating other markets and building a strong brand position with these key consumer groups.
 In summary, the Coach brand is exceptionally strong at the global level. We see a particularly attractive opportunity in China where we are growing robustly. We are also pursuing a strategic plan to grow our business in Europe. We will benefit from our brand transformation initiatives, including our new approaches on product and marketing, as well as our new store model. This is a very exciting time and I will look forward to talking with you in the future regarding our progress. Now let me introduce Jane Nielsen, our CFO. Jane?

 As we expect our strategy to impact key metrics first, followed by a turn in our financial results, from a performance perspective, we anticipate five areas of business metric improvements  North America comp improvement, North America wholesale share growth, international growth given the substantial category opportunity, better sales productivity resulting from our re-platforming investments and share growth in our men's category.
 Judging our performance as we move through the early stages of the journey is best achieved by looking at some leading indicators. In terms of comps, we expect retail to lead the recovery and that should be first evident by improving conversion and ADT. Traffic will be more of a lagging indicator. Outlet is expected to follow retail as consumers respond to our new offerings and brand positioning. We should see ADT improve first in part due to lower reliance on promotions.
 Our wholesale strategy is largely about enhancements in the shopping experience and making it more approachable, particularly through our case line strategy, which we expect to positively influence conversions. International is a straightforward story given our strong positioning and our focus on key growth markets such as China. Our fleet productivity initiatives will ultimately impact two-thirds of our North America store traffic and 60% of international traffic in new or renovated stores. Finally, men's should be positioned to show comp growth as we realign distribution and continue to position Coach as a dual-gender brand.
 Let me bring it all together in our financial outlook. FY15 is the invest and reset year. Largely as a function of our reduced promotions and store closing activity, we expect to see low double-digit revenue declines with high teens comp declines in our North America stores with EOS pressuring the aggregate North America comp by an additional 10 points. Gross margin should hold steady through our plan while operating margins will move to the high teens as we invest across the Company.
 CapEx will total in the neighborhood of $400 million. Our actions should lead to sales resuming growth in the low single digits in FY16. Comps should inflect as we move through the year. FY17 is when we return to sustainable growth with both revenues and comps in solidly positive territory. Operating margins should recover to about 20% to 25% and CapEx should decline to about 7% of sales. This performance will position us by the end of the five-year planning horizon to return Coach to best-in-class operating performance.
 As we aggressively invest in our business, it is important to keep in mind that we are embarking on this journey from a position of financial strength. We plan to fund investment activities from current cash flows while also maintaining our dividend. We have a strong and flexible balance sheet with about $1 billion in cash and investments and low leverage. We can continue to access the capital markets at attractive rates as needed to fund our headquarter investment.
 We get a lot of questions about the buildings, so I thought I would use this time to review our investment strategy. Beginning in the fall of next year, we will move from our space in three locations into one central headquarters in the Hudson Yards development. We believe we have gone about this in a strategic way, negotiating a good price in the context of today's New York real estate market and achieving an operating cost per square foot that is in line with our current level. At the same time, we are obtaining a centralized and more efficient space that carries the added benefit of being a magnet to fashion talent in the city that is our home and home to our brand and our legacy.
 Moreover, we are approaching the building expense flexibly. We expect to fund the cost with debt while preserving cash to fund our business transformation and our dividends. And we will have both the ability to sublet excess space and to monetize the building via potential sale-leaseback option.
 We have many transformation priorities ahead. So in that context, it is useful to review our capital allocation priorities. Reinvestment is the number one priority over the next several years. We have a compelling opportunity to drive sustainable growth and value creation and we are putting our capital against this opportunity.
 Our second priority, strategic acquisitions, is also about growth. While we have nothing planned imminently, there is a broader competitive landscape in place in our industry today and we do believe opportunities could arise. We want to have the flexibility to act if and when it is in Coach's interest and our shareholders' interest to do so.
 And third, capital returns. As I have stated before, we are committed to our dividend and we have a strong track record of capital returns. Underpinning all of the three of these priorities are our guardrails for allocating capital effectively, maintaining strategic flexibility, strong liquidity and access to the capital markets. We are proud of our track record for delivering additional value to shareholders through capital returns. In fact, since our IPO, we have returned over $8 billion via dividends and share repurchases. As we move forward, we remain strongly committed to our dividend and as our transformation takes hold, we expect to resume growing our dividend at least in line with net income growth. I am sure I don't have to remind anyone here of our 3.5% current dividend yield. Excess cash flow beyond this and our cash needs for preserving flexibility will be available for future potential share repurchases.
 In closing, I'd like to give a bit of a historical perspective. When we talk about transformation, we have often been asked if anyone else has done what we are about to do and done it successfully. And the answer is yes and it is us, Coach. In the late 1990s, after more than a decade of double-digit growth, we faced intensified competition, changing consumer preferences and a lack of fashion innovation. And we reinvented ourselves, broadening our offering, increasing our fashion innovation and updating our retail concept and reengineering our supply chain. Yes, we were only a $500 million brand, but we really competed in only one market that was about $2 billion in size and we reinvigorated our business, resulting in more than a decade of profitable and sustained growth.
 Today, we are facing similar challenges as a $5 billion company participating in a $35 billion category. But we have done it before and we have a plan and a new playbook all our own to do it again. Thank you and I would like to turn it over to Victor for closing remarks.

Juan Esteban Calle Restrepo,  Cementos Argos S.A. - CEO & President: Thank you, Indi, and good morning, everyone. During the current market situation, I would like to start by giving you an update of the status of our operations today. The U.S. region that represented last year 39% of our cement volumes and close to 55% for our consolidated EBITDA continues to operate under regulatory standards. Market demand behaved normally and in relation to when we started to experience a slowdown in the regions segment mainly related to cement dispatches from our Martinsburg plant. On the Caribbean and Central America, we are dispatching cement from all of our facilities except from Panama. That is still closed by governmental instructions.
 In most of these countries, the demand continues to be affected by the COVID-19 crisis with the exception of Haiti, which exceeded a satisfactory market performance. The Colombian quarantine was lifted on April 13 for infrastructure and April 27 for the residential and commercial sector, allowing us to gradually restart our operations ever since.
 At the end of April, the retail segment had experienced a recovery of 50% on its daily volumes. The industrial segment, on the other hand, started much slower given the higher complexity of restarting its operations.
 In light of this challenging market conditions, we have restructured and launched RESET, a comprehensive action plan to operate the company during the next months. RESET, which stands for restart safe and healthy to boost the economy, bring hope and transform lives, is a program that helps the company to face the pandemic and the later gradual market recovery.
 RESET tackles 3 dimensions: health and safety, liquidity and operational excellence.
 The health and safety dimension was built on our I Promise program to design and put in place all the health and safety protocols that are being implemented to protect our employees, clients, supporting communities and suppliers to be able to operate under the COVID-19 outbreaks. We are ready to safely restart operations in those facilities that are still closed or that are gradually going back to regular production standards while maintaining and improving the current safety protocols in countries such as the Honduras and [Haiti], where we have not experienced any halt in production.
 The liquidity I mentioned includes cash preservation and the construction of an operational model, built with a zero-based budget methodology for the rest of 2020. To improve our cash position, Argos disbursed around $160 million in short-term credit lines and consolidated payments-related decisions from its local operations to have a more efficient use of liquidity. As a result of these measures, the consolidated cash position of the company stood at approximately COP 615 billion as of April 30, an amount significantly higher than the amount we held at the start of the year.
 Our new zero-based budget captures efficiencies that amount between $75 million to $90 million on 2020, of which 84% will be obtained from fixed cost and 16% from SG&A. On top of that, the company has decided to reduce $40 million in CapEx from the current year on projects that are not necessary to operate under the existing market conditions. The initiatives related to operational excellence aim and ensuring the optimal mix of assets, products, services, manpower and logistics to be deployed according to the evolution of demand in our different markets. In this context, we expect a further integration to our technological tools in the future such as Argos ONE that enables our clients book contractors cement and ready mix dispatches through our digital platform.
 During March, Argos ONE accounted for 70%, 41% and 23% of the cement dispatches of Colombia, the U.S. and Panama, respectively. And for 49%, [3%] and 33% of the ready mix dispatches in these countries. In relation to the divestitures announced to the market on our last earning call for $400 million, we would like to mention that after careful analysis, the transaction has been postponed based on the uncertainties surrounding the short-term impact of COVID-19 on the worldwide economy, but maintaining our commitment to carry them out as soon as the market returns to better conditions. We are aware of the impact that the decision has on leverage ratios of the company. And in that sense, we have been in constant discussions with both our rating agency, our lenders to make sure that they fully understand and support our decisions.
 Given the strong cash position of the company, savings initiatives within RESET, the support from our stakeholders and the passionate commitment of our more than 10,000 employees, we firmly believe that Argos is fully prepared to face the current market conditions to continue building dreams that promote development and transform lives.
 Now moving to our consolidated results, I would like to start by mentioning that all comparisons on this call will be made on the results including IFRS 16 as we now have comparable figures for the present year. Percentage changes in ready mix dispatches and EBITDA are calculated based on the pro forma numbers of 2019, which exclude the operations from the ready mix divestitures carried out in the U.S. region during 2019 as well as the land appraisals registered in Colombia last year.
 Cement dispatches reached 3.6 million tons during the first quarter of 2020 decreasing 6.1% when compared to the same quarter of 2019, and ready mix dispatches reached a 2.1 million cubic meters , posting a 10.7% decrease on a like-for-like basis. These results were affected mainly by the lockdown measures in Colombia and some countries of the Caribbean and Central America and to a lesser extent, to the adverse weather conditions experienced in some regions of the U.S.
 Revenues closed in COP 2.2 trillion with an increase of 0.2% on a year-to-year basis driven mainly by the devaluation of the Colombian peso. The EBITDA, on the other hand, it is 1% on a like-for-like basis in line with the declining volumes experienced in both segments during the quarter as a result of the shutdown of operations in Colombia and most of our markets in Central America and the Caribbean.
 Now to start with our results in each region, I would like to invite Bill to explain the performance of the business in the U.S. and our view for the market.

The way I look at it, there were really three highlight areas for the quarter, operating cash flow, high-speed data, and the rollout of the advanced High-Def DVR boxes, and let me talk about each of those three. 
 In terms of operating cash flow, I think it was a superb quarter. We were about $95 million ahead of our budget for the quarter, which is a record for us. We had 15.9% year-over-year cash flow growth versus about 10.5% that we had projected in our budget. 
 Our margin was 39.1% for the quarter. As those of you who follow the industry know, the margins tend to build during the year, the first quarter is traditionally the lowest margin quarter for any cable company. So we were happy that the first quarter got off to such a strong start, it is particularly important because the first quarter tends to set the run rates, or it is the first time when you can see the run rates that go throughout the year. So if you are ever going to have a quarter that you want to exceed budget, you would want it to be in the first quarter. And the real stars in terms of operating cash flow were high-speed data, programming where we continue to see excellent scale results, and High-Def DVR boxes. 
 Moving on to high-speed data, we had a very strong quarter. We now sit at about 7.4 million customers, and this is now a $924 million revenue business in the first quarter, which is a 32% jump versus the quarter, same first quarter last year. Every year, when we sit down and do budgets, in the late summer and fall, we wonder when our net adds are going to peak, and every year for the last couple years, just in the interest of conservatism, we have assumed that our net adds are going to be slightly lower than the year before, but the answer clearly this year, is that our net adds have not peaked the first quarter we had 414,000 net adds, which was up 5% versus the first quarter last year, when we had 394,000 net adds. 
 And as important as the net adds, and we constantly talk about this internally, and try to make the point externally as well, is ARPU. And our ARPU was $42.83 for the first quarter, which was actually up from 42.46 last year, which is really important. As this business gets bigger, a dollar in ARPU is unbelievably important, and in some ways more important than really knocking the cover off the ball in terms of units. While our ARPU is up, our network costs per unit continue to decline. So the financials of this business look better and better. 
 We sit today at about 18% penetration of the 40 million homes passed that we market high-speed data to. And we think sitting at 18% leaves us lots of upside, in that this business is going to be one that is going to continue to fuel our growth for many years to come. We also think that our pricing and promotional and positioning strategy of positioning our product as a faster, more interesting, better portal, more  just a better overall product is working very well, and that's a key part of fueling our growth, and maintaining that ARPU. 
 Moving on to High-Def DVRs, Brian mentioned the great success we're having with VOD, but we're also having great success with High-Def and DVRs. We used to think going back a couple of years ago that digital would plateau at about 40%, and we picked 40%, because traditionally that was the level at which the premium business had plateaued, and we figured there is just about 40% of people who are willing to pay extra for a differentiated and more robust television experience. We have now gone beyond that 40%. And I think because of VOD, High-Def, and DVRs, we now should be able to take digital subscriptions into the mid-50s, maybe 55% penetration rate over time, so we think there is more growth in this business, as we pass the 40% penetration level.

On average, these advanced boxes cost about $250 per box more than low end boxes. So let's assume $250 is the incremental investment, and we get back 9.95 a month. So that's an IRR well in excess of 40%, and you're putting a service into the field that our customers love, and when they get will make them much more sticky to us. 
 So basically, we look at this as a business that we should accelerate, not decelerate, and what's happened is we installed about 200,000 more high end boxes during the quarter than budget, at $250 incremental each box, that equates to about $50 million in capital. Given the recent trends in the way we feel about the importance of this business, we would assume this would continue, maybe accelerate slightly, maybe decelerate slightly, but assuming it continues, that is a big part of raising our capital guidance by 200 to $300 million for the year. Which we think is an excellent trade-off to make. Basic subscribers for the quarter declined slightly by about 28,000 subscribers. This sub loss was almost exclusively from low-end analog-only customers, and it really had a minor impact on our financials. 
 Moving on to telephony, we made very good progress during the quarter, as we start expanding our IP-based phone business. Which we call Comcast Digital Voice. As of today, we have about 10 million homes passed for circuit switched, and a little over 1 million homes passed for IP phone. We have 1.2 million customers in total, almost exclusively circuit switch customers, and a 10.9% penetration.

You can see on slide 14 that the unit costs at Greens Creek were quite low, $16 per ton less than a year ago and cash costs after byproduct credits of $1.58 per ounce. Planned expansion at the Greens Creek tailings facility continues to work its way through the permitting process.
 On slide 15, you can see the quarterly rampup back to full production at Lucky Friday and the corresponding reduction in the costs over the past five quarters since the mine restarted. We have increased Lucky Friday's full-year cost per ounce by $0.75 to approximately $9.75 per silver ounce after byproduct credits to bring our full-year expectation in line with our first-quarter result of $9.60.
 On #4 Shaft, on slide 16, we have excavated below the 6,500 level and are over 2,000 feet deep. We believe the project risks have declined significantly with the focus primarily on the sinking of the shaft and development of operating stations outfitting the shaft with steel and services and commissioning. The higher risk projects such as design, fabrication, procurement, commissioning of the centralized refrigeration plant and hoist room construction are complete. We are on track for completion of this $215 million budgeted project in Q3 of 2016. The #4 Shaft project is designed to access higher grade ores zones, potentially increasing silver production at Lucky Friday to the 5 million ounce per year rate as soon as 2017.
 On slide 17, you can see Casa Berardi's production and cost. This brings the mine production to about 94,000 ounces of gold production since we acquired the mine. Since then, we have been busy integrating the asset by rebuilding the long-term mine plan, improving the ground control program to improve safety performance, ensuring consistent operations and optimizing our cost per ounce margin. I think we have come a long way so far and we are now moving beyond integration and into optimization.
 The advanced engineering work to optimize Casa Berardi operations is detailed on slide 18 and targets increasing metallurgical recoveries, better controlling dilution and reducing the amount of development necessary to maintain production. Let's look at these projects for a minute. We are working to increase metallurgical recovery by adding a flash flotation circuit, grinding the concentrate and then leaching it. The target is an 8% improvement in recovery on two ore zones. With about $15 million of required capital, this project is worth about $70 million life of mine.
 Due to permitting, the investment and benefit should occur in 2015. The second optimization project is to reduce development costs by reducing the drift cross-section. Basically what we are doing is having dedicated loading bays so we can reduce the size of ramp and drift cross-sections throughout the mine, reducing waste and improving stability. Every 1% reduction in waste is worth about $3.5 million life of mine, so our goal of reducing waste by 10% could result in a $35 million pickup to our life of mine.
 The third project is a reduction of dilution. Basically the mining method at Casa has changed over the years as the ore zones narrow going to more longitudinal, long-hole stoping, which can have large dilution variability. The dilution depends on the stability of the hanging wall, the length of the stope cut and the thickness of the vein and the irregularity of the mineralized zone. We plan to optimize dilution by reviewing our minimum mining widths and reviewing our blasting practices. We are targeting a 5% reduction in dilution, which could mean $35 million in savings life of mine.
 These initiatives should positively impact revenue, cash cost, as well as reduce capital with an expected benefit of $140 million over the life of the mine. Additional information on these programs can be found in the April 9, 2014 Investor Day presentation on the Company's website.
 On slide 19, you can see some images from the shaft deepening project at Casa. The project that was originally started by Aurizon to deepen the West Mine Shaft by 340 meters requires approximately another 38 meters of shaft construction and shaft loading facilities to be completed. This project is expected to provide additional access to the 118 ore zone and to enable deeper exploration. We continue to expect the shaft work and loading pockets to be finished late in the third quarter. I will now turn the call over to Dean for exploration and predevelopment.

It was caused by the signing of the final Kashagan agreement, on which I will be happy to answer your questions at the end of the presentation.
  We are pleased to be reporting a very strong set of numbers today. In a minute, [Sandro] will take you through those in details. Looking ahead, we are currently working on our plan for 2009-2012, and we will update you on our strategy presentation next February. But given the turbulence that we are seeing, both in the wider financial markets and in the oil market itself, I thought it might be helpful to give you my perspective on how this affects our future plans.
  The first point to make is that Eni's strategy is devised on the basis of a conservative oil price scenario. Indeed, our 2008-2011 strategy was built on the assumption that the average oil price would be $64 a barrel in 2008 and would then fall to $57 a barrel in 2009, $56 in 2010, $55 in 2011, and $50 in the long term.
  This is the scenario that we used last year in the rigorous assessment process to determine our investments and, actually, I would expect the new scenario to be very close to it. Therefore, the four-year capital expenditure plan that we presented in February is robust in the current market conditions and the upstream acquisitions that we've completed to date are cash generative and solid, below the long-term assumption of $50 a barrel oil price.
  Having said that, we are obviously monitoring our CapEx closely, with particular attention to the time to market and risk profile of each project, and I can anticipate that we have the flexibility to respond appropriately to changing market perspectives.
  Our conservative scenario also governed our thinking on cash priorities and distribution. As we said last February, we are firmly committed to maintain a leading dividend yield, also, leveraging on the resilience of our gas and power division, which enables us to remain highly cash generative, even at a time of falling oil prices.
  With that, I would like to hand over to Sandro to take you through the numbers, after which, together with Claudio, we will be happy to take your questions.

Sandro Bernini,  Eni - CFO: Thank you, Paolo, and welcome to everybody. This is something of a landmark for me, as this is my first presentation as Eni's CFO, and I am pleased to start with a strong set of results that provide solid support in this uncertain time.
  Going to the results, adjusted net profit in the third quarter amounted to EUR2.9 billion, an increase of around 53% compared with a year ago. This was largely due to a 46% increase in the adjusted operating profit that totaled EUR6.2 billion, as a result of the good operating performance and the strong trading environment on the exploration and production division, on which I will comment in a minute.
  Moving now to our business segments, in the exploration and production, hydrocarbon production in the third quarter increased by more than 6% compared to the same period of 2007. This strong performance is the result of the startup, buildup, and better performance in Angola, Congo, Egypt, Pakistan and Venezuela, and the contribution from the Baron Energy acquisition, which totaled 24,000 barrels per day. These improvements were partially offset by the impact of the production shedding agreements that accounted for 60,000 barrels per day. Net of this effect, growth would have been of around 10%.
  The PSA impact is based on the new 2008 sensitivity of around 1,500 barrels per day for each US dollar change. The lower sensitivity resulted from the recovery and the screening of our PSA contracts, which proved to be less sensitive to changes in oil price. Having said that, assuming an average oil price of around $100 per barrel, our full year production will reach a record level, increasing by approximately 3%, one of the highest growth rates in the industry.
  The third quarter adjusted operating profit amounted to EUR5.3 billion, up 60% compared to one year ago, mainly as a consequence of high realization prices denominated in US dollars and higher production sort. These improvements were partially offset by the appreciation of the euro versus the US dollar and the higher depletion depreciation and amortization. In dollar terms, third quarter adjusted operating profit increased by 75% versus the corresponding period of last year.
  As far as the gas and power division is concerned, overall, gas volumes sold slightly declined in the third quarter of 2008, as a result of lower sales in Italy, partially compensated by the growth in international sales. The gas and power adjusted operating profit amounted to EUR564 million, down 3% over the same period of 2007. Gas and power adjusted pro forma EBITDA for the third quarter of 2008 amounted to EUR781 million. This compares to EUR797 million in the third quarter of 2007.
  Marketing segment result decreased by 9%. This reduction was primarily due to the lower volumes sold as a consequence of the stronger competitive pressure in Italy, as well as to lower electricity sales. This negative elements was partially offset by the favorable scenario in terms of both the [yusa] appreciation versus the US dollar and the trend in energy parameters to which gas purchase cost and selling price are indexed.
  The regulated business generated EUR228 million, up 6% versus the third quarter of 2007. The increase is due to the improved operating performance and to the recognition in tariff of expenditures incurred for new investments and for the upgrading of the existing transportation network. Finally, international transportation showed a 6% increase versus the third quarter of last year, thanks to the increase in transportation capacity.
  Turning now to refining and marketing, adjusted operating profit of this division increased by around 56%. The higher refining margins in dollar terms were partially offset by higher maintenance activities and the appreciation of the euro versus the US dollar. Marketing segment benefited from the higher volumes sold due to the higher market share in Italy and the full contribution from the acquisition in Eastern Europe. Furthermore, marketing margins showed a positive trend.
  As far as the other businesses are concerned, in the third quarter of 2008, the petrochemical business, represented by Polimeri Europa, posted an adjusted operating loss of EUR59 million compared to a EUR30 million profit in 2007. This loss is due to the negative base chemical margins resulting from the higher feedstock costs. In the engineering and construction sector, third quarter adjusted operating profit amounted to EUR276 million versus EUR211 million in 2007. The increase is attributable to higher results across all business lines.
  Turning now to cash flow, this slide compares our sources and uses of cash in the first nine months of 2007 and 2008. Operating cash flow increased to EUR16 billion, up 20%, and disposals provided a further EUR500 million. The strong cash generation fully covered the EUR9.9 billion CapEx and the EUR5.9 billion of shareholder distributions, which included a payment in September of the 2008 interim dividend.
  Net financial debt as of the end of September increased to EUR17.8 billion and our net debt-to-equity ratio declined slightly to 0.37. Assuming $100 per barrel for the full year, on the basis of planned outflows, which means EUR14.4 billion of technical CapEx, the acquisition of the majority stake of Distrigas and the total acquisition of First Calgary leveraged at the year end is expected to be lower than that of the end of September.

Our short-term debt amounts to EUR9.3 billion, of which EUR3.1 billion are euro commercial paper. The market for euro commercial paper has always been open for Eni, even in these severe financial market conditions. From a strict liquidity perspective, we can rely on more than EUR7 billion of cash and committed undrawn facilities.
