Bill Burke,  Ametek, Inc. - Treasurer: Good afternoon. I'll go through the normal cautionary statements that we use any forward-looking statements, please refer to the risk factors in our 10-K filings. As well, we may be using some non-GAAP measures through this presentation, and we refer you to our website to see the reconciliation of the appropriate GAAP measure.
 By way of overview, Ametek is a diversified manufacturer with annual sales of $2.5 billion, a component of the S&P Midcap 400, Russell 1000, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange with the symbol AME.
 We've built what we feel is a very strong record of earnings growth over the last five years with a compounded growth rate of 25%. If you go back and look over  take that back through the last economic downturn; you'll see a strong growth pattern in earnings as well.
 I'll touch a little bit on fourth quarter and full-year results. Despite the weakening environment, economic environment, as well as a slow in core growth environment, we still posted very strong results. Sales were up about 7% minus 2% on the core plus acquisitions was really the driver to the growth in earnings  or in sales.
 Moving down through the other elements of the income statement  operating income, up 18%; net income and diluted EPS, up 15% and 16%, respectively; operating margins increased about 180 basis points.
 For the full year  similar story  18% growth on the top line; 4% from core growth; 1% from FX; and then the balance coming through acquisitions; and then the operating metrics all north of 20% illustrating our ability to leverage top-line growth through to the net income line.
 Both the fourth quarter and full-year numbers exclude a fourth quarter restructuring charge, which I'll talk to in a second.
 Moving on to how are we dealing with the current economic environment, weakening core growth environment, we did announce in January, in the fourth quarter, a restructuring of our operations. We took a $40 million or $0.25 restructuring charge to cover headcount reductions, facility closures, as well as some asset writedowns. The net result of that is we will be reducing headcount by more than 10%, closing or significantly reducing 10 manufacturing facilities, and implementing spending cost reductions across the business. This will yield about $75 million in annual cost savings, about $25 million in the first half, $50 million in the second half, exiting the year therefore in 2010 with north of $100 million of operating income improvement.
 As a company, we are very focused on margin improvement, even before the fourth quarter downturn. We were proactively cutting costs throughout 2008. We've got a number of programs to help drive margin improvement and dealing in a negative core growth environment, maintaining margins, including moving production to low-cost locales. I'll touch on that a little bit later in the presentation.
 As well, we have strategic procurement initiatives including the global sourcing office in China, which yielded about $21 million in savings in 2008 and would expect a similar type of number in 2009l. And we've got a very strong track record of margin improvement. I think if you go back and look at the last economic downturn, we were one of the few industrial companies to actually improve margins through that timeframe.
 The second key strategy for us in dealing with the current economic environment is to remain focused on acquisitions. The acquisition pipeline is good now, and we will continue to be a disciplined acquirer through the downturn. We've already closed one acquisition this year. We acquired High Standard Aviation, a third party MRO business with about $30 million in revenue. We closed that in January.
 We have a strong new product development focus in the business. Sales from new products was 18% of revenue  that's products introduced within the last three years. And, importantly, with all of the restructuring that we've done, we've not gutted our new product development focus. We expect RD&E expenses to be up 3% this year versus 2008, meaning when the economy does return, we are going to continue to make those investments required to keep the product portfolio fresh.
 We continue to focus on international expansion. Russia, China, the Middle East and Japan are important areas, especially for our analytical instrumentation businesses, and we're going to continue to stay focused on expanding in those parts of the world.
 So at the end of the day, we believe our strong portfolio of businesses, proven operational capabilities, the lower cost structures as a result of the restructuring, and a successful focus on strategic acquisitions will enable us to outperform in 2009.
 I'm going to spend a few minutes now going through the different parts of the business; talk about products, markets, and then we'll move on to the strategies for the Company. Essentially, we produce two types of products  electronic instruments and electromechanical devices, fairly well balanced between the two. Instruments is a little bit larger both in terms of sales and even moreso in profitability. That's not a stated strategy. We are very focused on growing the differentiated component of the business, and all other things being equal, I would have told you five years ago the instruments group would have been much larger, but we continue to find good acquisitions on the electromechanical groups side.
 The next number of slides  we'll take each of those two groups and look at them in a little more detail. On the electronic instruments group, we are a leader in the development and manufacturing of monitoring, testing, and calibrating instruments. Essentially, we measure physical phenomena  pressure, temperature, flow, elemental composition, and do it in a variety of settings, process and analytical, aerospace, power and industrial.
 We are not trying to be the process control house, we want to be the measurement supplier, and we look for the most difficult types of applications you can find to be able to provide that level of measurement capability.
 Looking at the sub-platforms, if you will, within the electronic instruments group, we have the process and analytical instrument segment with about $930 million in revenue. We do analytical in a mission monitoring instrumentation. We'll measure combustion efficiency; we'll measure oxygen; we'll measure hydrocarbon contents; a number of physical parameters for the process.
 As well, we'll do drilling and completion instruments that are used in down hole oil and gas and sort of middle technology world  little measurement pressure gauges, transducers and seal, and then we do a lot of work in elemental analysis and radiation measurement for elemental composition.
 If you look at the markets here, about one-third of the revenue is in the oil and gas stream, if you will, from down hole transmission refining, chemical, petrochemical, and the other two-thirds are used in research and laboratory applications, whether that be government research, universities, industrial research, or on the factory floor in terms of high-end quality control types of applications.
 Our aerospace business on the instrument side is about $225 million in revenue. We'll talk about a broader aerospace exposure when I get onto the electromechanical group side, but it will probably be helpful if I size the whole thing for you now. About $700 million of revenue is related to aerospace and defense, about 40% to 45% of that is military, about 40% is in the large commercial aircraft arena, and then the balance of 15% to 20% is in business and regional aircraft. Again, that covers the whole exposure, both on the EIG and the EMG side.
 On the instrument side, we do airframe and engine monitoring systems, so we're going to measure physical parameters on jet engines or elsewhere on the airframe, so pressure, temperature, flow, and the like. We do work in avionic systems for small aircraft and do a lot of work in fluid gauging, whether it be potable water, hydraulics and the like, throughout an airframe. As well, we do pressure transducers and accelerometers. So, again, carrying that theme of measuring physical parameters on an aircraft and then feeding that back into whether it be the cockpit systems or other flight data recorded information.
 The final part of the instruments group is the power and industrial business, a little north of $300 million in revenue. About two-thirds of that business is power-related. Products that we produce here would include uninterruptible power supply systems. These will be very large ruggedized, industrialized types of applications not for server farm but for an offshore oil-drilling rig or powering the safety systems in a nuclear power plant  that kind of a type of application.
 We also do power quality monitoring instrumentation and then with a couple of acquisitions we did over the last year, we do programmable power systems where we will simulate power for the testing of electronic devices.
 And more industrial part of the business, we do dash panel instruments for class 8 heavy vehicles as well as military vehicles. We do some food service instrumentation as well as  we have a small business. It's a [total] compounder of plastics.
 The second half of the Company is our electromechanical group. Here we do differentiated  a set of differentiated products as well as a legacy business in floor care and specialty motors. Looking at the differentiated products with about $900 million in revenue. We've already talked about a little more than half of that business would be aerospace applications where we do AC and brushless DC motors that are used in electronic cooling and large-sheet exchanger systems that are used on aircraft and military ground-based vehicles.
 As well, we do highly engineered, hermetically sealed connectors with both aerospace applications as well as non-aerospace applications. As well, we do some metal powders, metal strip and specialty wire. So, again, about half of this revenue is related to aerospace and defense, but then these same types of products are used in a variety of niche applications in the industrial world  petrochemical, electronic components, as well as medical and business machines and computers.
 The final part of the electromechanical group is our floor care and specialty motors. This is our legacy business. This used to be what Ametek was and what it was known for, but it's now only about a little more than 10% of the Company's revenue. We are still the world's largest producer of vacuum cleaner motors. We produce about 25 million motors a year; do it in plants in China, Mexico, and in Eastern Europe. We do similar types of motors that are used in commercial floor care equipment, outdoor power equipment, and small household appliances.
 That wraps up the businesses, products, that we produce. I'd like to take a moment and take a different view of Ametek and move into the strategies we're pursuing for the business.
 We've taken another view of Ametek and looked at the business as a set of differentiated businesses and a set of cost-driven businesses. The differentiated businesses are going to compete primarily on product features, much higher engineering content, tend to be niche-focused and have higher margins, lower capital requirements, whereas our cost-driven businesses, price is the most important thing to the customer for us than cost has to be the most important thing to us in terms of how we manage those businesses. They tend to have higher capital requirements and lower margins.
 If you take that same view of the businesses that we talked about before, our differentiated businesses make up about 88% of Ametek's overall revenue, and it's the electronic instruments group that engineered materials and technical motor systems, the differentiated businesses, if you will, within EMG, and then the cost-driven businesses are floor care and specialty motors business.
 And we're taking the good cash flow out of our cost-driven businesses and deploying that to grow our differentiated businesses. So the plan has been working in terms of making those differentiated businesses a much larger component of the overall mix, and we continue to see that, going forward, to where the cost-driven businesses will become a smaller and smaller part of the Company.
 Our vision is to double the size and profitability of the Company in five years. That implies a 15% compounded growth rate. It's going to be over the business cycle. Obviously, we're not going to double if it stays like this for the next five years, but the key thing there, and I think if you go back to our earnings chart at the beginning of the presentation, you can see we've done that and more over the last five years and over the business cycle, that will be our goal, going forward.
 Our commitment to the Street has been double-digit earnings growth over the business cycle, and we certainly have achieved that, and we're employing four growth strategies to make that happen. Three internal strategies  operational excellence, global and market expansion in new products, and then the external strategy is obviously acquisitions.
 Looking at those individually, for us, operational excellence is the cornerstone strategy for the Company  very focused on cost and asset management and really underpins the success that we've had in growing the earnings of the Company. It's absolutely essential for the cost-driven business. It's how you continue to survive and thrive in that business.
 For our differentiated businesses, it adds value, and I think we earn higher margins for many of our businesses than our peers do, and I think it's in large part due to this operational excellence capability. And then we'll talk about the acquisition strategy in a few minutes, and this operational excellence capability is very important for to be able to drive value from those acquisitions through both expense and asset reductions.
 This slide shows the strong margin performance. You can see operating margins have grown significantly from a little less than 18% to nearly 20.5% in 2008. And if you extend this chart backwards several years, you'd see a continued growth path that wasn't just during good times. We were able to grow the margins through some tougher economic times in the earlier part of the 2000s. As well, working capital performance is very important, and we rank near the top of our peer group for those metrics.
 I mentioned how operational excellence is important in the acquisition integration process. To give you an example  a company we acquired in Germany in 2005, a company called Spectro  very high-end technology; do atomic spectroscopy instrumentation for elemental composition of solids and liquids; great, great strategic acquisition for our high-end analytical instrument business. But it was a 10% business based in Germany, but we saw, given the technology, market position that they had, that that could be a 20%-plus business, and we were able to get that there within the first couple of years of ownership through global sales channel, rationalization, headcount reductions, and other expense reductions. So just an illustration of  and we'll come back to this point a little later in the presentation  but, for us, the ability to integrate acquisitions is a core competency for the Company.
 Global market expansion is the second strategy. Today, about 48% of our sales 2008 were from markets outside the US. Given where our opportunities and where our products are sold, this number should probably be 60% to 65%, so we're going to continue to move in that direction; continue to penetrate new markets with our differentiated products. We'll add international acquisitions where it does make sense and continue to expand our distribution networks in all parts of the world but particularly in Asia and Middle East and Russia.
 The second part of the strategy is our best-cost strategy. We are aggressively moving manufacturing to low-cast locales. We've been doing this for about 10 years  actually, almost 12 years now, so something we're very  we've gained a lot of expertise at. This year we expect about $330 million in revenue to be produced in these low-cost locales  Reynosa, Mexico, the Czech Republic and Shanghai; very important for us to maintain both competitive position as well as to improve the profitability of the products.
 And the final part of the global market expansion strategy is leveraging existing technologies into new markets. The example we have here is taking our process instrument work that we do in terms of mass spectrometers and analytical instrumentation that's used in the process industries, and applying that to the pharmaceutical world.
 There is something called PAT, which is process analyzer technology, that the FDA is pushing to take process technology, put it all online in the pharmaceutical manufacturing process to improve productivity, efficiency, and efficacy of the production process, and we're making some good inroads with a number of the pharmaceutical manufacturers here.
 As this initiative gets further rolled out, we think it's going to be a good marketplace for us, and I think it's just an example of the types of things that we look to do with our technology  always looking for new end market applications for those products.
 In terms of new products  a key strategy for generating internal growth, continued strong funding of R&D. I mentioned earlier, even with all the other cost-cutting that we're doing throughout the organization, we're going to continue to fund this initiative. We will expect to see this go up about 3% in 2009; RD&E totaling nearly $120 million, a little less than 5% of sales.
 There is no blockbuster new product introduction for Ametek. Given the number of niche markets we serve, it really is a lot of singles and doubles, and that's how you win the game. We think we are very well positioned with new products that meet the demands of the marketplace.
 The next few slides are just a few examples of what  of new products that we have outstanding. The first one is a gas analyzer that's used in commission  continuous emission monitoring, again, measuring the combustion efficiency and the amount of pollutants that are [culling] in a stack  again, simple, robust design; powerful data processing, and, really meeting the needs of our customers in the marketplace.
 The next product is a metal analyzer from our Spectro Division. It uses something called optical emissions spectrometry. And, again, this is used in element  high-accuracy trace element and metal analysis. This might sell for more than $100,000 apiece  so high-end instrumentation.
 And then the final one is from our Cameca business, which we acquired in August of 2007. This is literally the highest technology business within Ametek. We are measuring metals and other materials, literally, down to the atomic level. This is used in geochemistry, metallurgy, microelectronics, and an instrument like this will sell for about $2 million apiece  so very, very high-end technology.
 Final strategy is our acquisition strategy  our business model is really predicated on  given the markets that we serve, over the business cycle, we would expect that our businesses should generate GDP plus a couple of points in terms of internal growth, and then we're going to look to get one-half to two-thirds of our growth from acquisitions. So another 5% to 10% of growth in order to get to that 15% top-line growth bubble the Company in five years. So it's a very important strategy for us, and, really, the largest use of our free cash flow.
 Our program is targeted at businesses between $30 million and $100 million of revenue for a number of reasons. We want to do multiple smaller acquisitions in any given year. You reduce the risk, and we haven't messed any of these up, but the odds are that we will someday, and when we do that, we don't want to bring the company to its knees. Less competition, lower multiples, and higher opportunities for synergies are the other reasons for focusing on the smaller deals. And referencing what I said earlier, we're going to focus on adding differentiated businesses and making that a larger part of the overall Ametek portfolio.
 The slide here lists all the acquisitions we've done, going back through 2004. Again, you can see the sizing of the acquisitions is in that arena that I talked about, just to show the adherence to the strategy and very happy with all the acquisitions we've done and really opened up a lot of opportunities for us in a number of different platforms.
 The strategy is not capital constrained, it's managerial constrained. We want to make sure that we've got the right amount of effort put into the due diligence in the integration to make sure that we don't trip. But, furthermore, that strategy is supported by the strong free cash flow levels in the business traditionally north of 100% of free cash flow as a percentage of net income, and the ability that we've shown to prudently expand our debt levels, over time.
 A very strong record of success in making and integrating acquisitions and, in fact, we go back and report to our Board on how we've done with those acquisitions, and if we look at the last 31 acquisitions we've done through December 2007, in our first year of ownership, the pretax profit of those businesses is up 35% over the prior year. So, again, bringing that operational excellence capability to bear in terms of increasing the profitability of those acquisitions.
 So, in summary, we think we have a very strong foundation, a clear vision, solid strategy. We've got a proven management team. The top five executives have, on average, 23 years with the Company  so a seasoned management team that's worked together for many years in creating shareholder value, and we are committed to creating shareholder value through these four growth strategies.
 So, with that, I'd be happy to take questions.

 On our last earnings call in July I spoke to the diversity of Under Armour: the diversity in having our revenues spread more evenly across product categories and geographies; the diversity in whom our brand is now reaching; and the diversity in how we reach both our existing and new consumers across the globe.  But more importantly, it illustrates the Under Armour brand's ability to thrive beyond our core North American apparel business and help feed our diversification. The best evidence of that is in the performance of our footwear and international businesses over the first nine months of 2014.
 We've detailed how we've continually invested in both of these growth drivers over the past few years, building the infrastructure needed to grow and adding talent to supplement the team. So let me provide some detail that confirms the return on the investments we've made in these two key growth drivers. Let's begin with footwear.
 As we cited in our release earlier this morning, our footwear business grew 50% in Q3, while our international business was up 94%. In terms of the contribution to the overall revenue growth, footwear and international have added nearly $200 million to our growth through the first nine months of this year and together accounted for 35% of our total growth year to date.
 What's more encouraging than the actual numbers is the strength of the platforms we are building in these businesses that will lay the foundation for sustainable growth in 2015 and beyond. Let me talk first about our growth globally and the investments we are making in all corners of the globe. To reinforce our focus on building that global organization, I am dialing into this call today from our office in Hong Kong on one of five stops I'm making throughout Asia as part of our continued focus on bringing the Under Armour brand to that global audience.
 Whether it's business to our newest retail doors in Chengdu, China, Tokyo, and Singapore, or conversations with potential partners about next-generation technology, visiting these markets reinforces the opportunity that we have to grow the Under Armour brand. Ensuring we bring the right balance of Under Armour culture and international experience to our global leadership team has been a major focus for me over the past 24 months. We've done a great job of using our own team to build and establish the Under Armour culture in any market we do business in, especially Europe and China.

 And with that, I'll turn it over to Brad.

 I would now like to spend some time discussing our third-quarter 2014 financial results, followed by our updated outlook for 2014 and our preliminary thoughts on 2015.  Our accessories net revenues during the third quarter increased 32% to $85 million from $64 million last year. Growth during the quarter was primarily driven by headwear offerings and gloves. Our direct to consumer net revenues increased 35% for the quarter, representing approximately 26% of net revenues.
 Square footage in our North America factory house channel grew 18% year over year. On the full price side we remained at five brand house stores in North America.
 We continue to see strong momentum in our eCommerce channel, where we are driving strong traffic gains through efforts such our I WILL WHAT I WANT women's campaign.  International net revenues increased 94% to $86 million in the third quarter and represented 9% of total net revenues. In Europe our strong results throughout the year have been driven by a combination of higher brand awareness and a more focused in-country strategy around our three key markets of the UK, Germany, and France.
 In Asia Pacific we continued to build both wholesale distributor relationships, including accelerated partner store openings throughout greater China and Southeast Asia. Finally in Latin America our business benefited from the conversion of our Mexico distributor to an Under Armour subsidiary at the beginning of 2014, as well as our recent market entries into Brazil and Chile.
 Moving on to margins, third quarter gross margins expanded approximately 120 basis points to 49.6%, compared with 48.4% in the prior year's quarter. Three primary factors contributed to this performance during the quarter. First, we lapped higher US import duties from the year-ago period, contributing approximately 90 basis points for the quarter.
 Second, we experienced a favorable sales mix during the period, primarily driven by a more profitable product mix across our factory house channel, contributing approximately 70 basis points for the quarter. Finally, liquidations negatively impacted gross margins by approximately 40 basis points driven by the shift in footwear liquidations into the third quarter that we highlighted on our last call.
 Selling, general and administrative expenses as a percentage of net revenues deleveraged 230 basis points to 34% in the third quarter of 2014, from 31.7% in the prior year's period. Specific details around our four SG&A buckets are as follows: first, marketing cost increased to 10.6% of net revenues for the quarter from 10.3% in the prior-year period, primarily driven by higher year-over-year sports marketing sponsorships across our international businesses.
 Second, selling costs increased to 8.9% of net revenues for the quarter from 8.1% in the prior-year period, primarily driven by higher variable costs tied to the growth in our North America direct to consumer business, as well as increased investments to support our global retail store strategies. Third, product innovation and supply-chain costs increased to 8.5% of net revenues for the quarter from 7.3% in the prior-year period, primarily driven by higher product innovation costs, including our connected fitness efforts as well as higher personnel costs in footwear and international.
 Finally, corporate services held steady year-over-year at 6% of net revenues. Operating income for the third quarter increased 21% to $146 million, compared with $121 million in the prior-year period. Operating margin contracted 110 basis points during the quarter to 15.6%, compared to 16.7% in the prior-year period.
 Interest and other expense for the third quarter increased to $5 million, compared with $1 million in the prior-year period primarily reflecting the negative impact of foreign currency. Our third quarter tax rate of 36.9% was favorable at the 39.4% rate last year, primarily driven by lower year-over-year losses across international markets in aggregate.
 Our third-quarter net income increased to 22% to $89 million compared to $73 million in the prior-year period. Diluted earnings per share increased 21% to $0.41 compared to $0.34 in the prior-year period.

 Inventory increased 28% year-over-year to $637 million, compared to $497 million at September 30, 2013, below our net revenue growth rate for the period. Our investment and capital expenditures was approximately $26 million for the third quarter compared with $23 million in the prior-year period. We continue to plan 2014 capital expenditures of approximately $150 million, primarily driven by incremental investments to support our direct to consumer and international businesses, further develop and expand our global office footprint, and increase capacity at our distribution centers.
 Now moving onto our updated outlook for 2014, based on current visibility, we expect 2014 revenues of approximately $3.03 billion, representing growth of 30%, and 2014 operating income of approximately $348 million, representing growth of 31%.  We will provide further color on 2015 during our earnings call in January. We would now like to open the call for your questions.

Gerald Gleeson Van Riet,  SilverBow Resources, Inc. - Executive VP & CFO: Thanks, Steve. In my comments today, I'll highlight our fourth quarter financial results as well as our operating costs, hedging program and capital structure.
 Production for the quarter averaged 177 million cubic feet of gas equivalent per day, which represents a 13.6% increase from the third quarter, driven by strong base performance in Artesia, including contribution from a 3-well pad that came online late in the third quarter. Fourth quarter production also benefited from turning 4 wells online on or ahead of schedule, including our first well in Uno Mas.
 Fourth quarter revenue was $58.7 million, with natural gas representing 79% of our production and 63% of our reserves. Our average realized natural gas price, excluding hedging, was $2.88 per 1,000 cubic feet compared with $3.01 in the third quarter. Our differential was a $0.05 discount to Henry Hub and illustrates why the Eagle Ford is such a great market for selling gas.
 Turning to liquids, our average realized crude oil selling price, excluding hedging, was $57.64 per barrel compared with $46.93 in the third quarter. Our differential was $2.23 above WTI due to the fact that we sell off LLS, which currently trades at a significant premium to WTI. Our average realized natural gas liquids selling price increased $2.70 in the quarter to $24.37 per barrel, or roughly 44% of WTI.
 Turning to hedging. We added significantly to our hedge book in the quarter and have since then even added a few more hedges. Using our 2018 guidance midpoint of 185 million cubic feet equivalent per day and assuming that same level through 2020, we are 63% hedged in 2018, 41% hedged in 2019 and 23% hedged in 2020.
 A disciplined hedging program is integral to how we manage risks, so we plan to continue to systematically adding additional hedges to further protect our cash flows. As mentioned on our last call, we entered into some NGL hedges in the fourth quarter, and in addition, we are now hedging both our LLS and gas differentials to lock in favorable pricing.
 Turning to costs. LOE was $0.34 per Mcfe compared to $0.41 in the third quarter, driven by continued compression optimization, labor force reductions at the field level and other cost initiatives that Steve discussed.
 For the first quarter of 2018, we're expecting LOE expense of $0.35 to $0.36 per 1,000 cubic feet equivalent, which represents a slight uptick to fourth quarter levels, primarily due to lower volumes. As a reminder, our first quarter cost guidance assumes 2 full months of AWP Olmos in our financials, so we'd expect further reductions going forward as these higher LOE wells exit our portfolio.
 The AWP Olmos sale is expected to close today, and has a sales price of $28.8 million with an effective date of January 1. As such, we will recognize all the production, revenues and cost in our financial statement until the end of February, and adjust the final settlement payment downwards by the amount of net cash generated by those assets during these first 2 months.
 This divestiture represents 491 wells, with approximately 60% of our well count and 6% of our fourth quarter production, so removing them from the portfolio goes a long way towards cleaning up a lot of noise around our reported results and allows us to leverage our existing personnel across our core Eagle Ford footprint.
 Additionally, this patch of wells has significantly higher lifting costs on a per unit basis. As such, our full year 2018 LOE guidance of $0.25 to $0.28 is significantly lower than the $0.39 we reported for the full year 2017.
 Transportation and processing costs for the fourth quarter were $0.32 per Mcfe. Adding our LOE and T&P together, we have a total OpEx of $0.66 per Mcfe, which we believe compares favorably to our peers.
 Production taxes came in at 3.1% of oil and gas revenues for the fourth quarter, which was a significant decline from the prior quarter, primarily due to onetime credits. Cash G&A of $5 million was up slightly compared to third quarter levels, primarily due to $1.7 million in severance costs related to the replacement of our COO and other adjustments to our officer group.
 We're guiding for cash G&A of $4.7 million to $5.1 million in the first quarter of 2018 due to the timing of our annual bonus payments, which always occur in the first quarter. In total, our strong production growth and continued cost focus drove a $0.35 quarterly increase in adjusted EBITDA to $42 million.
 Cash interest came in at $3.2 million for the quarter, an increase from the prior quarter primarily due to higher borrowings under our credit facility.  Our all-in cash operating expenses, including G&A, came in at $1.08 per Mcfe in the quarter compared to $1.24 in the prior quarter. We spent approximately $50 million on capital expenditures in the quarter, including $22 million for leasing and acquisitions.

This [BEC] transaction reduces our ARO by $20.9 million, which is split between $7 million of current liabilities and $13.9 million in long-term liabilities. We record a $16.3 million payable for our obligations under the sale contract, split between $11.3 million in accounts payable and $5 million in noncurrent liabilities.
 Under full cost accounting, we do not recognize any gain on the $4.6 million difference between the transaction price versus the ARO liability removed, and instead, we recorded a $4.6 million decrease to our capitalized oil and gas properties.
 Additionally, our AWP Olmos sale will remove another $6.2 million of ARO from our balance sheet during the first quarter of 2018. As such, on a pro forma basis, our ARO at December 31, 2017 would be approximately $5 million, which compares very favorably to our 2015 ARO liability of over [$16 million]. We view this low level  this low liability level as extremely favorable for a company of our size, which further highlights the benefit of our streamlined portfolio.
 Our 2018 capital program of $245 million to $265 million provides for 30 to 32 net operated wells to be drilled compared to approximately 18 net operated wells in 2017. Approximately 70% of our budget is allocated towards drilling and completion capital, driven primarily by 13 net wells drilled in Fasken, 7 net wells drilled in AWP and 5 net wells drilled in Oro Grande.
 Since our second rig is just getting started and we won't finish completing any wells from this rig until late in the second quarter, we plan to bring 25 to 26 net wells to sales in 2018 compared to approximately 22 net wells in 2017. That said, since the second rig will have a typical startup lag between spudding its first wells, completing them and then turning them to sales, we expect to end 2018 with an increase in DUCs from 6 at the end of 2017 to 10 to 12 at the end of 2018.
 We are forecasting average production of 175 million to 195 million cubic feet equivalent per day for the full year 2018. Additionally, we provided first quarter 2018 guidance of 156 million to 162 million cubic feet equivalent per day on an as-reported basis, and 150 million to 156 million on a pro forma basis to reflect the AWP Olmos sale. Our corporate presentation includes updated first quarter and full year 2018 guidance, so please refer to it for our latest expectations.
 While the timing of the 6-well Fasken pad and commencement of the second rig lead to some lumpiness on our production for the first half of the year, they set us up for strong growth in the second half of 2018 and well into 2019.
 Our liquidity of approximately of $260 million as of December 31, 2017, consisted of $7.8 million in cash and $252 million of availability on our bank credit facility. As previously announced, our fall redetermination concluded with an increase of our borrowing base from $330 million to $370 million. However, our borrowing base was subsequently reduced to $330 million in connection with the grind associated with the issuance of the second lien notes.
 The proceeds from our second lien notes significantly increased our liquidity and enhanced our balance sheet flexibility and attractive cost of capital. This flexible capital has relatively benign prepayment penalties, with some minimum hedging requirements which are in line with our prudent hedging strategy and have already been taken care of.
 Our strong liquidity and solid balance sheet are a testament to our entire team's efforts, and I'd like to thank our banking syndicate for their continued support during our fall redetermination as well as the second lien transaction.
 We expect to fully fund our 2018 capital program with cash generated from operations and borrowings on our credit facility. At the end of the fourth quarter, we were in full compliance with our financial covenants and had significant headroom.
 And with that, I'll turn it over to Sean to wrap up our prepared comments.

  In the Haynesville, we not only have pricing advantages based on the location of the play in comparison with other major US natural gas plays, but Petrohawk specifically as advantages in infrastructure and local knowledge. I hope you have had a chance to go over the press release we issued earlier today, covering the details of our strong performance and, as usual, I will walk you through some details for the quarter. Then Adrian will discuss the financial results and at the end we will be happy to answer any questions you may have.
 First of all, let me give you an overview of the second quarter. As in the first quarter, the excellent performance was shown across all regions and segments.
 We continue re-enforcing our market leadership and we were able, again, to capitalize on the favorable climate and economic growth, thanks to the actions we have been taking to streamline all of our operations, from procurement to final delivery, while strengthening our product portfolio to meet the different consumer needs and occasions.
 Launching new products and creative promotions, combined with state-of-the-art technology and great people to assure excellent execution in our marketplace and a more precise supply chain co-ordination. This outstanding top line growth, coupled with productivity gains, resulted in a 22% rise in operating profit in the second quarter year-on-year, a 200 basis points margin expansion and 41% increase in earnings per share.
 Free cash flow after CapEx for the first half of the year reached approximately MXN1.4b - a similar amount generated for the full year of 2005. We distributed roughly MXN683m in dividends during the second quarter and finished with nearly MXN2.7m in cash in this year.
 Now, let me mention the main market initiatives and development during this period. As we have informed, we grew across all regions and segments, with Colas and Diet Drinks posting a robust volume growth of 9%, primarily as a result of the strength of the Coca-Cola brand.
 Other actions that were major contributors to our success in these segments include the different packages and price point alternatives, effective advertising campaigns, product innovations such as Coca-Cola Caffeine Free and the Spacio Leve concept, and our improved execution to guarantee coverage of CSD use by cluster.
 Regarding flavored CSDs, we grew by an outstanding 10%, strongly supported by advertising and promotional campaigns aimed at youngsters, driven mainly by Sprite and Fanta, while Joya continued performing well as a regional multi-flavor brand combined with other leading national flavor brands.
 Additionally, Topo Chico mineral water delivered another extraordinary increase of 20%, as a result of its expansion and greater coverage in all the territories of Arca, as well as advertising campaigns aimed at better positioning mineral water among younger consumers.
 Topo Chico exports increased significantly by 23% during the second quarter. This strong performance was driven by a greater presence in the West Coast in the U.S. and the introduction of new presentations. Additionally, to better serve the California market and reduce freight costs, we are now bundling some Topo Chico flavored products in our Mexicali plant.
 We have also launched new products in the export markets, including the 20 pack Topo Chico mineral water with 6.5 ounce bottles and the 2.5 liter Topo Mexican flavor.
 Single serve purified water volume increased nearly 21%, thanks to an improved coverage, new ways of displaying the product at the point of sale, including “out of the cooler” exhibition and also due to incentives to clients, while the rest of our Non-Carb portfolio grew by an impressive 61%, driven mainly by Ciel Aquarius, the flavored water, and recently introduced Minute Maid juices and Nectars.
 In the second quarter we continued protecting the value of our single-serve product portfolio. We see this as a major contributor to our continued profitability, with initiatives such as the installation of additional vending machines and also more than 10,000 coolers in our customers up to now. Focus also innovative promotions and the extension of 500 milliliter one-way, as well as the 1 liter non-returnable to more of Arca’s territories.

We saw these as major drivers to our growth this quarter.

With this completion we will have five of the six zones operating on this platform. The last one left is the South Pacific region which is underway and will be completed by the end of this year.
 We are also working on new ways of placing orders  creating ways of placing orders, by allowing certain customers in certain channels to request products through the Internet or through telephone, which should result in a better service and improved productivity to routes in the near future.

Dr. Adrian Wong,  Embotelladoras Arca S.A. de C.V. - CFO: Thank you Pancho. Good morning everyone and thanks for joining us today. I’m happy to report the financial situation and results of Arca for the second quarter, as well as for the first half of 2006 versus 2005.
 During the second quarter of 2006 net sales increased slightly over 12% in real terms over the same quarter of 2005, due to an increase in sales volume of almost 10%. As you can see, our selling price per unit case also increased, in real terms, 2.1% from $34.2 to $34.9 per unit case.
 During the first half of 2006 net sales increased, in real terms, more than 12% when compared to 2005 as a result of the combination of an increase in volume of 10.4% and an increase in selling price per unit case of 1.6% in real terms.
 Cost of goods sold for the second quarter of 2006 increased 12% as compared to the same quarter 2005. Similarly, during the first half of 2006 cost of goods sold increased 10.7% as compared to the first half of 2005.
 In both periods the increases accounted mainly by the increase in sales volume and, to a lesser degree, to the shift in mix towards more non-returnable products, because of the main raw material explained a very small portion of the variation in cost of goods sold.
 Although the absolute amount of our operating expenses, excluding non-recurring items, increased almost MXN45m, which represents a 4.1% increase, on a percentage of sales basis operating expenses decreased from 27.4% during the second quarter of 2005 to 25.5% during the second quarter of 2006.
 The main reason for the increase in absolute amount is due to the fact that our selling expenses increased 4.7% as a result of higher sales volume, which translated in higher sales commission and trades, graded expenses for launching of new products, as well as new promotions and more advertising expenses.
 As for the first half of 2006 versus 2005, operating expenses mirrored the behavior of the second quarter of 2006 already mentioned. Consequently, operating income, excluding non-recurring items, for both the second quarter and the first half of 2006, increased 22.3% and 28.4% respectively.
 The operating margin percentage increased 200 basis points during the second quarter of 2006 from 22.2% to 24.2%. For the second half of 2006 the operating margin increased from 19.1 to 21.9% when compared to the same period of 2005.
 Our comprehensive cost of financing increased significantly, mainly during the second quarter of 2006 as compared to the same period of 2005, as a consequence of gains on exchange rates and an increase in interest revenue. Our combined income tax and employee profit sharing rates went from 39.3% during the second quarter of 2006  excuse me, 39.3% during the second quarter of 2005 to 33.9% to the same period of 2006. The combined rate for the second half of 2006 and 2005 was around 35% in both periods.
 Arca’s net income for the second quarter of 2006 increased 41% to MXN717m or MXN0.89 per share and, for the first half of 2006, net income increased 32.5% compared to the first half of 2005 to MXN1.122m or MXN1.39 per share.
 To conclude on the income statement, our EBITDA margin, excluding non-recurring items for the second quarter of 2006, was 28.2% as compared to 26.5% during the same quarter of 2005.
 EBITDA margin for the first half of 2006 was 26.4% as compared to 24% for the same period of 2005.
 On the balance sheet as of June 30, 2006 our cash and temporary investment position is almost MXN2.7b. Our cash position exceeds that by MXN1.147b. Our capital expenditures during the first half of 2006 were almost MXN413m, representing 45.3% on sales, allocated mainly towards transportation equipment, coolers and installation of additional capacity.
 As far as to the relevant topics concerning our financial situation, we continue with our share repurchase program. Our goal here is to help increase our stock liquidity. As of June 30, 2006 the balance of shares repurchased by the Company was 4.5m shares.

Donald Lang,  CCL Industries, Inc. - Executive Chairman: Thank you, operator, and welcome everybody. As we have always done in the past, we will be referring to a presentation. The presentation is on our website, and hopefully everybody has been able to access that at cclind.com, the Investors tab. And you'll see in the top right corner the analyst slides which you can review as we go along. We'll identify the pages and you can also print it as well.
 As you know, joining me is Geoff Martin, Gaston Tano, and Steve Lancaster. Before I just turn it over to Gaston for the financials, which will be followed by Geoff and the operations and we will open it up for questions, just a couple of comments. Obviously, everybody has seen our announcement. It has been a difficult quarter. But from a sales and operating income standpoint, the results we believe are not that different than many other packaging companies that we have seen that have been releasing over this past quarter, especially those that have a European component where we have seen a much tougher market than our other markets around the world.
 However, there are many really good points that we want to discuss and we'll highlight in our conversation. There's a lot  as you know, we are very well-positioned. We have a lot of good things going on. We still continue to have a very strong cash flow. We have a number of new business awards which we talked about last quarter that are coming into play going forward, and some new exciting things happening going forward.
 We still have  we are still seeing some good solid growth in Asia, some solid performance in our healthcare Latin American businesses, and we're also announcing some encouraging signs in the US in some of the categories as well. So, yes, it has been a tough environment, but I think we are very well-positioned.
 We have a leadership position globally, and we're going to continue to capitalize on those around the world, and I believe it puts us in a very good position, a preferred position against our suppliers who are all having the same type of challenges out there. We have a strong balance sheet and a very preferred  good preferred position with our customers. So I think the future still holds very, very good promise for us despite these tough, difficult times.
 So with that, I will turn it over to Gaston to get some of the financial details. Gaston.

Now if we move to slide 3, the statement of earnings for the second quarter.  The second-quarter comparatives have been impacted by acquisitions, Eltex and Ferroprint. And if we look at sales now, sales for the second quarter were CAD301 million, down 4% compared to CAD313 million recorded in the prior-year quarter.  The largest contributor to the organic decline was our battery and beverage business in Europe. And you will hear more about that from Geoff when he talks about the operations.
 Operating income for the quarter was CAD29 million, down by CAD14 million or 32% from last year's strong comparable period, which benefited from better economic conditions and the timing of the Easter holidays. Excluding foreign currency effects, operating income for Label and Container divisions were significantly lower, while Tube was marginally higher.
 Corporate expense was CAD5 million for the second quarter compared to CAD4 million in the prior-year quarter. The increase was due to higher legal claims in the current year and the prior-year comparators being favorably affected by a reduction in self-insurance claim reserves.
 Interest expense increased to almost CAD8 million due to higher long-term debt levels, lower rates on our cash deposits, and the unfavorable foreign exchange impact on the interest of our US dollar denominated debt. Restructuring in the second quarter reflected a loss due to foreign exchange on a capital dividend from a foreign subsidiary.
 The effective tax rate excluding restructuring items increased significantly in the quarter to 41% from 27% in the prior-year quarter. This increase is primarily due to the Company's continuing ability to tax benefit certain losses in certain countries, and to a lesser extent from the unfavorable mix of income earned in high tax jurisdictions versus low tax jurisdictions.
 This increase is primarily an accounting exercise, I'd like to remind everybody. It doesn't mean the Company is actually paying additional cash taxes. Although we expect the tax rate to continue for the rest of the year, if the current country  income mix continues, we are implementing certain restructuring initiatives by the end of the current year that could reduce the effective tax for 2010.
 Net earnings were CAD9 million for the second quarter, down 63% from CAD24 million in the prior year, reflecting the items discussed above, while EBITDA was CAD49 million a quarter, down 18%, reflecting lower operating income and higher corporate expenses.
 Slide four, statement of earnings, six-month results. The six-month results reflect a similar picture. Sales excluding currency translation were down 7%. Organic growth accounted for a reduction of 8%, partially offset by a 1% increase from acquisitions net of a disposal. Operating income declined 20%, reflecting the organic decline in sales. Corporate expenses were higher, mainly due to prior comparator results benefiting from a foreign exchange gain in the UK relating to the movement of the proceeds from the sale of the Colep joint venture and by a reduction in self-insurance claim reserves that I mentioned earlier.
 Interest expense is due to the same reasons as the quarterly interest expense I mentioned earlier, higher long-term  higher debt levels, lower rate on cash deposits, and the unfavorable foreign exchange impact on the US denominated debt.
 Restructuring and other items. In 2009, we have the loss due to the settlement of pension obligations to certain members of the UK pension plan and the additional closure costs for Avalon that we had in Q1, and then the foreign exchange impact on the capital dividend from the foreign subsidiary in the second quarter. The prior-year number includes a gain due to foreign exchange on the receivable related to the sale of Colep and the sale of the ABS product line, offset by restructuring costs.
 The effective tax rate for the six months was 36% compared to 28%, reflecting the reasons I discussed earlier. Net earnings for the six-month period were CAD26 million, down 50%, while EBITDA was CAD108 million, down 9%.
 Slide 5, earnings per share. Basic earnings per Class B shares were CAD0.28 in the second quarter compared to CAD0.75, a decrease of 63%. Restructuring and other items in the second quarter reduced EPS by CAD0.01, while the prior-year quarter benefited by CAD0.01. Adjusted EPS for the quarter was CAD0.29 compared to CAD0.74 in the prior year, down CAD0.45 or 61%. This is reflecting lower operating income which accounts for the CAD0.33 negative impact, and also negatively impacted by higher corporate expense, interest expense, and effective tax rate.
 Basic earnings for Class B shares of the six-month period were CAD0.80 compared to CAD1.60, a decrease of 50%. And excluding restructuring and other items, adjusted EPS for the six months was CAD0.85 compared to CAD1.54 in the prior year, down CAD69 or 45% driven by the same reasons of the quarterly results.
 Slide 6, impact of changes in exchange rates. As you know, our results are impacted by foreign exchange rates in both translation and transactions. The transaction effect results from our Canadian container operation, which sells the vast majority of its product in US dollars. Foreign exchange for the quarter had a positive impact on EPS of CAD0.04, with CAD0.01 coming from translation and CAD0.03 from transaction. This basically reflects the 16% appreciation in the US dollar, 1% appreciation in the euro in the second quarter, partially offset by the UK pound being down 9%.
 On a year-to-date basis, foreign exchange had a positive impact of CAD0.10, CAD0.06 from translation and CAD0.04 from transaction. Based on the current rates which have just changed with the continued weakening of the US dollar, basically the US dollar right now is $1.07 for US dollar and EUR1.54 for the euro. Foreign exchange will have a negative impact on EPS for the balance of 2009.
 If we now move to the balance sheet, slide 7. The balance sheet as of June 30, as you can see we still have a strong financial position. And all the balance sheet items here have been affected by the currency translation due to the higher US dollar and euro FX rates.
 Net working capital remained stable at CAD40 million. It's actually decreased to exclude foreign exchange. Property and plant equipment reflect our capital additions of the past 12 months. And the decrease in intangible assets and goodwill is due to the write-down of the two goodwill that we booked in the Q4 of 2008.
 Net debt, we're going to talk about that in the next slide. And then shareholders' equity and book value per share are in line with the prior-year comparators.
 If we move now to slide 8, debt summary. Net debt as of June 30 was CAD441 million, up CAD85 million from CAD356 million in June 2008. Net debt to capital was 36% compared to 30% in the prior year. The increase in long-term debt is due to the $130 million private placement that we completed in September of '08, and the impact on the strengthening of the US dollar on a US dollar denominated debt.
 Foreign exchange basically represents CAD53 million of the CAD85 million increase that you see in net debt. Cash and equivalents have also increased to CAD120 million, up CAD16 million from CAD104 million in the prior year. And as communicated in previous quarters, other than the annual repayment of $9 million on our 1997 senior notes, we have no other payments due unto July 2010.
 Slide 9, the cash flow highlights. Despite the challenging economic conditions, normalized cash flow, if you exclude the impact of the Colep receivable in the prior year, has improved to CAD22 million outflow in the current year compared to CAD57 million outflow in the prior-year comparative. The increase is due to our lower planned capital spending and improvement in working capital, partially offset by our lower net earnings for the six-month period.
 If we include the impact of the Colep receivable, the repurchase of the shares, acquisition dispositions and long-term debt, cash and equivalents decreased by CAD16 million in the six-month period compared to an CAD8 million increase in the prior-year period.
 At this point, I would like now to pass on to Geoff Martin, our President and CEO, who will discuss the operational results in more detail.

 Best estimate we have at this time is capital for the year will come in something below CAD100 million.  Same picture really in slide 12 that is the results for half-year. So those two things are really the cause of all of the EPS drop from operational effects.
 Just a quick summary on slide 13 about our revenue line, and I think the organic one is the one to focus on here. So down 7%, and it's pretty typical for many companies in this segment. Both suppliers who supply materials to the label industry and the one or two public companies, really, pretty much everyone is reporting organic declines. This is probably at the higher end of performance. I mean there's been declines well into the mid teens, so I think we feel quite good about the revenue line.
 Very soft conditions in the Container business, no real change from the first quarter there. Probably the surprise really is our Tube business where a lot of companies in this segment have had difficult revenue comparisons, partly driven by resin costs and just the very soft conditions in the US postal care market. So that is probably the one real highlight on a revenue basis for the quarter.
 And the year-to-date position looks slightly different. There are some calendar effects in there, which I will talk about when we get into the division discussions which I think is where the meter is buried. So without further ado, I will come on to that.
 So slide 15 is the second-quarter picture for CCL Label. I'll start with the good news first. We had a pretty soft start to the quarter in April and May, but certainly in the month of June  and that's for sure continued in the month of July  we did see quite a pickup in both order intake levels and sales and margin performance in the business.
 So it was a sort of quarter of two pictures really, April and May which looked like difficult times continuing. And then in June, we did see some improvement which, if anything, continued to improve and get better in the month of July.
 Same picture down in Latin America on the sales side. We did have a mixed picture there between Mexico and Brazil, with Mexico improving significantly and Brazil going the other way. A lot of that has to do with what is going on with the currencies down there, and I will talk a bit about that later on in the call.
 So as you might expect, given everything you are reading about in China, our sales there continues to do well and our margins improved actually pretty significantly in the quarter. So the whole issue really comes down to what has been going on in Europe. And just before I start on that, just a quick comment about the comparisons.
 We had  in 2008, we had the Easter period dropped into the month of March and that really swaps around our best-performing month of the year quarter to quarter, just because of the timing of the Easter vacations. And I can give you some more color on that during the Q&A.
 So just a picture of the operational impacts in Europe in the quarter. Our home and personal care business was flat on the top line. We had a loss in the quarter. We also had a loss there last year, but it was a wider loss this year, really driven by some issues at a new plant we started up in Paris, and I will answer some questions about that in the Q&A.
 Our shrink sleeve business, we did see a drop-off in sales. Again, I think that is more calendar related than anything else. Actually, this business is pretty much on budget for the quarter. And we had a couple of one-time issues in the P&L, one positive event last year, one negative event this year, more or less non-operational. So the underlying results from this business were pretty much as we expected.
 Health care and specialty was down, but the margins again in this business are still at or above average. So nothing really to worry about there. It was just a soft quarter. The main issue was really in the battery and beverage business. And we have a couple of plants in Europe that make these products on big [reveal] presses, and the beverage business in particular declined pretty significantly this quarter against a very strong prior quarter last year.
 And you have to remember in Europe in the second quarter of 2008, the global recession was then seen as an American problem.  Our durable goods business which services the automotive and engineering sector in Germany, as you might imagine, has continued to have a difficult time.  Russia is still very difficult. That affects our beverage business. Our largest customers are actually in Russia.  Turning now to North America, this is the more positive story, particularly in the norm of home and personal care product lines. Suzanne H. Wood,  Vulcan Materials Company - Senior VP & CFO: Thanks, Tom, and good morning to everyone.
 While we faced some challenges in 2021, it was a year of significant accomplishments, including the completion of our acquisition. Our most notable financial achievements were the growth in our unit profitability and adjusted EBITDA. Full year Aggregates cash gross profit per ton rose by 5%, while adjusted EBITDA increased by 10%. The ability to generate numbers like this while incurring $93 million of higher energy-related costs across the segments demonstrates the strength, flexibility and resiliency of our aggregates-focused business model.
 It also points to the contributions of our 4 strategic disciplines which help us make the most of any economic environment. Aggregates prices increased by 3% as compared to the prior year, and we held our cash unit cost growth to less than 2% through efficiency improvements and general cost controls. This allowed us to offset inflationary pressures and improve our unit profitability.
 With respect to the balance sheet, we quickly reduced our net leverage to the top end of our target range, ending the year at 2.5x. Given our ability to generate strong cash flows, there is capacity and liquidity to invest in other opportunities, whether organic or inorganic. But as always, we will be disciplined in doing so.
 Certainly, we'll continue to prioritize sensible leverage and financial flexibility in order to support our capital allocation priorities and maintain our investment-grade ratings. Our debt structure is sound with long maturities that make sense for our business. Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged and have led to an improving return on investment profile. On a trailing 12-month basis, our ROIC was 14.2%. While investing in growth and overcoming inflation and the pandemic, we have improved our ROIC by 160 basis points over the past 3 years.
 Now turning to our outlook. Let me make a few comments before turning the call back over to Tom. Following a strong performance in 2021, we expect 2022 to be another good year of earnings growth. In terms of our guidance, it incorporates the full year contribution of U.S. Concrete. Given the level of integration and change going on in our business, we are providing guidance on a consolidated basis.
 We expect adjusted EBITDA of between $1.72 billion and $1.82 billion. The midpoint of this range represents a 22% increase over 2021.  With that as a backdrop, I will turn the call back over to James.

Despite weakness in our international businesses, we increased revenues domestically and maintained strong margins in both polyester POY and DTY; had strong results in our dyed yarn, beam yarn, and nylon businesses; and saw continued strong shipments into the CAFTA region. In the longer term, we are taking action to ensure we are well positioned to profitably grow, as the economy improves and the textile consumption increases in the years ahead.
 I remain confident in our China business model and am encouraged by the any new PVA sales opportunities in the pipeline, as well as increased activity and opportunity in Europe that Roger mentioned.
 Turning to our balance sheet, we have seen a temporary increase in working capital related to timing in our accounts payable, as well as an increase in inventories. Some of this inventory increase is driven by one-time preproduction purchases related to a new high-value PVA business. In addition, we reacted slowly to the loss of some low-end commodity business, and produced beyond demand for a short time. We expect inventories to reduce through the current quarter and expect to be at goal levels by December.
 Despite the increase in working capital, we generated sufficient cash to fund $5.7 million in capital expenditures, including the purchase of nine texturing machines from a recently closed competitor. These machines, now being installed in Yadkinville, will increase our capacity, flexibility, and efficiency. We also committed $5.8 million to purchase nearly 250,000 shares of our stock, as James mentioned, while maintaining our net debt and liquidity at better-than-target levels.
 Over the past few years, we have discussed on this call the recent stabilization and growth of the US and Americas region textile industry. I feel it may be helpful to delve into the details for a few minutes to better explain our continued commitment to this region.
 As I'm sure most of you are aware, over 70% of our revenues come from sales into the NAFTA/CAFTA region, and we have invested in growth here over the last few years. However, as the industry shrank under the onslaught of cheap Asian apparel imports over the last decade, there have been misconceptions about the demise of this industry in this region.
 I feel it's important to clear up these misconceptions with some facts about our industry. The US textile and apparel industry employs over 500,000 people, mostly in manufacturing jobs, providing better pay and benefits than many service industries such as retail and food services.
 In addition, we estimate there are from 1 million to 1.5 million jobs in support industries  like trucking, packaging, and chemicals  that are directly dependent, here in the US, on the US textile industry. Compare this to about 800,000 jobs in the US auto industry  which includes auto-parts workers  and 150,000 jobs in the US steel industry, and it becomes obvious that the US textile industry is still large and important.
 In Mexico and Central America, we estimate there are an additional 1.5 million textile workers. And the industry is an important engine of growth in many emerging economies, like Honduras and El Salvador, while providing well-paying jobs and adding political stability. Textile and apparel exports are often, far and away, the largest export commodity of many countries in Central America, and supply much-needed income and capital to their economies.
 NAFTA and CAFTA sourcing share of US synthetic apparel has remained stable, at 18% for the last five years. And supply in units has grown by 5% to 7% annually over the last two years, as US retail has grown. In the US over the past 12 months, there have been about 20 new textile plant openings and expansions. And many large new investments have recently been announced for 2014. In CAFTA, over the past 12 months, an additional 10 new plant openings or expansions have occurred.
 Apart from apparel, regional production of items consumed at US retail is important in many textile segments. For instance, 60% of pantyhose is still produced in this region; 32% of socks; 60% of upholstery for furniture; 90% of mattress fabric; and 80% of light vehicle upholstery are all produced in this region. The US textile and apparel industry generates over $70 billion in revenue, exports $23 billion worth of goods, making the US the third-largest textile exporter in the world, and has invested over $16 billion in new equipment in the last 10 years.
 As wages increase in major Asian textile-exporting countries, as safety and environmental standards there increase in response to some horrific tragedies in their garment industries, and as costs and efficiencies improve in this region through growth in production capacity, we expect to see continued competitiveness and growth here in NAFTA/CAFTA.
 Now, one potential threat to this region's industry is the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade pact currently being negotiated, which includes Vietnam. Vietnam's state-supported  and, in many cases, state-owned  textile industry has significantly grown exports to the US over the last few years, primarily at the expense of China and other Asian exporting countries.

The US industry has been working closely with the United States trade representative and the Commerce Department to assure a strong set of trade rules, including a yarn-forward rule of origin; reasonable market access conditions; strong customs enforcement; and strict, fair, and consistent industry standards for all participating countries.
 Our aim for this agreement is for an agreement that does little damage to the growing textile industry in this region and provides export opportunities for all participating countries, including the US. As negotiations move forward, we will continue to provide updates.

As we expect our domestic business to remain strong, and should see improvements in our international businesses as the fiscal year goes forward, our annual guidance remains in the mid- to high-50s.

Our innovative composite solutions enable our customers to achieve faster time to market, require lower upfront investment and provide enhanced thermal protection and weight reductions.
 We closed a $400 million financing with Oaktree and have $200 million potential follow-on investment committed. The financing enabled us to shore up our balance sheet and position ourselves for additional growth when market demand recovers.

 On slide 12, we summarize our pro forma financial position.  With that, I'll turn it over to Ross.

Ross Craft,  Approach Resources Inc - Chairman & CEO: Appreciate the question. What we've been focusing on since mid-2015 is reducing stage spacing. Obviously we started out in our new completions in 2015 at around 200 feet, and then we gradually decreased it roughly 20 to 30 feet at a time, with our lightest well down around 150 feet that we completed.
 So what we are looking at on sand loading, is somewhere  right now  around 1,600 pounds per foot if you average over the last five wells. But we are steadily moving up to that 1,800 and 1,900 pounds. And we think that's, right now, will be an appropriate level.
 But more importantly I think is a combination of our sand sizes we are running. We are also running 100 mesh, a fairly large chunk, 55% of our sand loading is 100 mesh. That we ramp up pretty high.
 We ramped up to 2.5 pounds per gallon. Followed by a stage flush, and then we saw our [40/70], and we bring that up to a high concentration at 2.5 pounds per gallon as well. We think that does a lot for the microfractures and we think that's giving us some positive results as well.
 So going forward, I would say that our stage spacing is going to average somewhere between 150 and 175 feet on these wells. We think that's going to give us an optimal position. We are also looking at playing with the initial fluid loadings.
 The pad stage, and possibly running some different types of sand particles starting at the beginning of the pad. But that's kind of the outline. I think it mirrors what a lot of folks are doing in the industry, and we are seeing positive results from it.
 One thing to point out during this downtrend, even though we've increased our stage spacing  we've decreased our stage spacing, which results in more stages, we have been able to keep the cost of these wells pretty flat.
