Mike Ahearn,  First Solar, Inc - Chairman of the Board, Interim CEO: Thanks, David. Welcome to our Q4 2011 earnings call. As discussed on our recent call, traditional solar market subsidies are declining  continuing to decline and significant non-subsidized markets are not yet developed.
  Last week, the German Environmental and Economics Ministers released a proposal that would significantly reduce or potentially phase out the German solar market. The fate of this bill, which will be presented to the Cabinet tomorrow and still needs to pass through Parliament and the Chambers in the Federal States, remains unclear. However, it is likely that even if less draconian measures are ultimately adopted, Germany, like other feed-in tariff markets, will continue to be challenged in 2012 and beyond.
  The key to First Solar's success is to develop new markets that do not depend on subsidies, and we believe we can do this by focusing on regions in the world that are blessed with a lot of sun and need more peak electricity. Our superior module technology, combined with our ability to design, engineer, construct, and maintain large solar and electricity generation plants and integrate them with the grid should enable us to reduce solar electricity prices to good parity levels in these markets, while still making an attractive profit. Our demonstrated success in selling solar electricity and solar generation plants to leading US utilities will provide targeted customers in these new markets with important validation of our capabilities.
  Solar electricity has never been deployed without subsidies at the large scale we envision. And local utilities, regulators and politicians will need time to understand how to plan and integrate solar electricity into their local grids. But fortunately, our existing US project pipeline provides a level of continuing demand while we work on opening the new markets that will drive our future growth. However, it is important that we begin taking steps in 2012 to create these new markets, in light of those long lead times involved.
  We have been busy working on our three-year plan over the last several weeks. As an out growth of the planning process, we have decided to idle four lines in our German plant for up to six months this year, postpone the commissioning of our proposed facilities in Mesa, and discontinue work on our proposed plant in Vietnam, which is expected to result in an impairment charge of up to $100 million this year. We've also begun the process of eliminating unnecessary operating expenses, which will continue over the course of 2012. At the same time, we have begun to add resources in targeted markets where we expect to derive significant growth in coming years.
  The impact of these and additional actions will be rolled up in a three-year plan, which we had hoped to share with you today, but is now scheduled to be discussed in our Q1 earnings call in May.
  This quarter we incurred $125.8 million in additional warranty reservesto reflect an updated estimate of costs related to the manufacturing excursion that occurred between June 2008 and June 2009. As previously disclosed, a small percentage of product manufactured during that time period may experience premature power loss once in the field. First Solar identified and addressed the manufacturing excursion in June 2009, and later initiated a voluntary remediation program that goes above and beyond our standard warranty obligations.
  The remediation program includes module removal, testing, replacement and logistical services, and additional compensation payments to customers under certain circumstances. A large volume of claims made under the remediation program were processed in the fourth quarter, and we identified a significant increase in remediation costs under the terms of our voluntary program.
  Our estimates now benefit from having processed over 95% of the total claims submitted under the life of the program. The total cost of remediating the manufacturing execution that occurred from June 2008 to June 2009, now stands at $215.7 million, including $145.6 million above and beyond our standard warranty.
  There are approximately 4% of the claims submitted for which we have not yet been able to determine if remediation is required. If it is determined that these claims should be remediated, there is at least a potential for additional cost of much as $44 million. While the cost of the program has been much higher than we would have liked, we believe we have done the right thing in demonstrating our commitment to our customers beyond our product warranty.
  Also, our analysis of hundreds of PV systems and modules returned under warranty as part of this program, combined with analysis of system-level performance for sites under O&M agreements, has given us unique insight into the real-world performance of our products in a wide range of PV systems. That knowledge has contributed to the continuous improvement of our technology and refinement of our product development roadmaps.
  Briefly turning to the markets; in North America, we continue to make progress with projects in our pipeline. At Agua Caliente, we had completed approximately 60% of the balance of system and installed 2.9 million modules by the end of the fourth quarter, and we energized the first 30 MWs in Janurary of this year.
  Construction has started at Desert Sunlight, and while we cannot recognize revenue under GAAP, we have received net cash received of $77 million as of the end of the fourth quarter.
  AVSR One has yet to receive funding for the loan guaranty, but Exelon and First Solar are pleased that the Los Angeles County has approved changes to the construction permit for the project, satisfying a requirement for the funding of the initial loan advance for the project. The companies have extended their deadline for receiving initial loan advances to April 6th to allow sufficient time for the funding to be received. In the meantime, the project construction continues to move forward.
  While Topaz did not receive a loan guaranty, we nevertheless completed the sale of the project to MidAmerican Holdings Company in January, and we'll begin recognizing revenue in the second half of 2012.
  We're pleased to include on our growing list of customers MidAmerican, one of the leading investors in renewable energy, which also purchased 49% of the interest in Agua Caliente from NRG in the last month.
  In China, we recently executed small demonstration projects with two strategic partners, one was a ground-mounted project, with Guohua Energy Investment Company, one of the largest [GenCos] in China, and a subsidiary of the Shenhua group, which is the largest coal-mining company in the world. The other project was a roof-top project in Beijing, with BOE Energy Technology Company. Mark Widmar,  First Solar, Inc - CFO: Thanks, Mike, and good afternoon. We'll start with operations on slide six. In Q4, our production was 540 MW, up 37% versus the prior year, but down 2% quarter-over-quarter. The year-over-year increase was driven by capacity expansions in Germany and Malaysia.
  Sequentially, in order to better align our supply with market demand, we (inaudible) our Malaysia facility over the year-end holiday season. This downtime reduced our capacity utilization for the quarter to 94%, or 600 basis points below the third quarter. Malaysia now, though, is currently running at full capacity.
  At our 2012 guidance call in December, we stated that we will be running our manufacturing plants at 80% utilization in 2012. As demand in Europe is more challenging than expected, we will be reducing our utilization rate further, to a range of 60% to 70%, which will reduce our production in 2012 to a range of 1.5 to 1.8 GWs.
  As part of this process, we are suspending four production lines for up to six months in (inaudible), and accelerating our [go-fast] efficiency roadmap by idling and retooling each line, sequentially, in Malaysia. These actions might not be sufficient to reduce production to a level that aligns with demand, so additional options might be neccessary as we continue to adjust production capacity to match expected market demand.
  Because we will not be running at full capacity, we will be not be disclosing our line run rate on a quarterly basis. That said, we continue to make improvements for our line throughput, held by our advancements in model efficiency. Thus we are increasing our goal for our line run rate from 80 MWs per year by 2014, to over 90 MWs by the end of 2015.
  Our average line conversion efficiency for our modules was 12.2% in the fourth quarter,which was up 0.6 percentage points year-over-year, and up 0.4 percentage points quarter-over-quarter. This is our largest sequential increase since 2007. Our best plant improved to 12.6%, which is up from 12.4% last quarter, and 11.6% last year.
  We continue to make significant progress in conversion efficiency. At 2012 year-to-date, our average conversion line efficiency is 12.4%, up 200 basis points from the end of the year. And the current efficiency rate of our modules produced on our best line is 13.1%. We expect sustained improvements in efficiencies as we continue to invest in our technology.
  Last month we announced that we received confirmation from the National Renewable Energy Lab, or NREL, that First Solar achieved a record 14.4% efficiency, for cad-tell thin film modules, which eclipses the prior record of 13.4%, also heldby First Solar. The record performance comes just six months after First Solar announced that it had achieved a record 17.3% efficiency for cad-tell thin film cell.
  Both the cell and module record setters were constructed using commercial-scale manufacturing equipment and materials that can be implemented across our existing line, for a capital spend of around $100 million for each of the next three years. The achievement supports our module efficiency roadmap, updated last month. And underscores the tremendous, on-going potential of cad-tell.
  Module manufacturing costs per watt for the fourth quarter was $0.73, which is down $0.01 quarter-over-quarter. This cost includes a $0.01 impact from the increase in warranty accrual rate, and a $0.01 headwind from plant under utilization.
  Had our plants run at a full utilization, as we historically have, then our module manufacturing costs per watt would have been $0.72 or $0.03 below the third quarter, on a comparable basis.
  Our best plant is manufacturing modules at a cost of $0.69 per watt,excluding the impact of under utilization.
  Moving on to slide seven; we show our updated view of available capacity and anticipated production utilization. This updated slide no longer includes Mesa. In our guidance call for 2012 in December, we noted that production in Mesa would be delayed until 2013. As we further evaluate market demand and our capacity requirements, we have now decided to put Mesa on hold until market demand justifies additional capacity. First Solar will retain ownership of the building associated with the site and we expect to relocate various engineering and administrative work rigs to the office space there. Some of the space on the main floor will also be used to store product and equipment in transition.
  Moving to manufacturing  to our systems business, on slide eight. In 2011, we added approximately 650 MW AC of contracts to our pipeline, and installed approximately 425 MW of DC. Our pipeline stands at 2.7 GW AC, which represents the sum of the contractual MW of the projects in our pipeline.
  As of the end of the fourth quarter, we have recognized revenue for approximately 180 MW equivalent. The remaining pipeline will either be constructed in the future or is currently under construction. But all revenue recognition criteria have not been met. MW equivalence is calculated by taking total cumulative revenue recognized, divided by the total contracted revenue for each project, multiplied by the MW for such project.
  Mike also discussed the solid progress we were making on our four large projects; Agua, AVSR, Topaz, and Desert Sunlight. In addition to these large projects, we continue to advance the balance of our systems pipeline. In the first quarter 2012, we began construction on Copper Mountain 2, and received initial funding under the contract. In addition, outside of the four large projects previously mentioned, we have completed the financing of one of our projects, subject to certain conditions  which we anticipate announcing the closing of the project in the next couple of weeks.
  Moving on to the financial portion of the presentation, on slide nine. Net sales were $660 million, down from $1 billion last quarter. The decrease was primarily due to lower third-party module volumes and lower module and balance system buyings in our systems business.
  Our EPC revenue mix decreased from 39% of total net sales in the third quarter, to 30% of net sales in the fourth quarter.
  Our solar power systems revenue, which includes both our EPC revenue and solar modules used in the systems business, decreased slightly from 65% of sales in the third quarter, to 64% of sales in the fourth quarter. Aggregate modulated SPs increased 2.9% quarter-over-quarter, including the impact of currency, or 4.1%, excluding currency.
  Modulated SPs in the systems business increased sequentially, whereas third-party modulated SPs declined 4%, excluding currency. We expect the largest sequential decline in third-party module ASPs from the fourth quarter of 2011 to the first quarter of 2012, as higher-priced, legacy contracts expired at the end of 2011. On a year-to-year basis, fourth quarter module ASPs decreased 2% and third-party ASPs declined 24%.
  Gross margin was 20.9%, down 16.8 percentage points from the prior quarter. The decrease was due to an increase in incremental warranty charges, primarily related to our previously announced manufacturing excursion. Absent these one-time charges, gross margins would have been 36.1%. Module gross margin was 19.5%, down from third quarter module gross margins of 41.4%. Excluding the impact of incremental warranty charges. module gross margin would have been 35.5%.
  Operating expenses were up $467 million quarter-over-quarter, to $623.4 million. The primary reasons for the increase were a series of charges that we considered non-recurrent, namely a $393.4 million goodwill impairment, $31.8 million in lost power compensation related to the manufacturing excursion, and $60.4 million of restructuring charges, which consisted of $53.6 million for asset impairment and associated decommissioning, and $6.8 million in severance. These restructuring charges were previously announced in our 2012 guidance call last December, where we said the total charges could be up to $85 million.
  The goodwill impairment is a non-cash charge that does not affect our cash position, or cash flows from operating activities. The goodwill was primarily related to acquisitions of OptiSolar in 2009, and NextLight in 2010, representing benefits from expected synergies, economies of scale, and vertical integration. We allocated most of the goodwill for these acquisitions to our components business, consistent with our historical view of the systems business function as being an enabler for the components business to drive module through-put. We believe that the acquisitions of OptiSolar and NextLight have provided tremendous value to First Solar, far in excess of the acquisition costs, including goodwill.
  As a result of these acquisitions, First Solar has announced the sale of and is currently constructing four of the largest solar power plants in the world. This impairment charge does not change the value of the acquired project pipeline, nor does it change the Company's view of its business prospects or future results, as discussed later in this call. It is primarily triggered by the fact that the market capitalization of our stock was trading below the book value as of the end of the fiscal year 2011, and the related pressures on the industry as a whole.
  In order to provide a comprehensive view of the manufacturing excursion and warranty charges in Q4, a break down is provided on slide ten. In the quarter, we expensed $163.5 million. Of this amount, $125.8 million was for the manufacturing excursion. As Mike mentioned previously, a large volume of claims made under the manufacturing excursion program were processed in the fourth quarter, and we identified a significant increase in remediation costs under the terms of our voluntary program.
  The Q4 costs associated with the manufacturing excursion is composed of three items. The first item is the cost to remove, replace and provide logistical services related to the manufacturing excursion. In the fourth quarter, we expensed $23.9 million for these efforts, and have expensed $99.7 million to date.
  The second item is expected payments to customers, under certain conditions, for power loss prior to the remediation of the customer's system. In the fourth quarter, we expensed $31.8 million for this compensation, and have expensed $45.9 million to date.
  The third item, $70.1 million, is due to an increase in expected number of replacement modules above our standard warranty rate required for our redmediation efforts.
  Finally, we recognized a $37.8 million charge to increase our warranty accrual. We believe our PV modules are potentially subject to increase in cellular rates in hot climates. As our geographic mix of sales has shifted to hot climates, we have increased our warranty accrual. Our experience has shown that our warranty rates for hot climates are slightly higher than the return rates for temperate climates. With this change, our standard warranty accrual rate has been increased by one percentage point to account for the potential returns, going forward. We will continue to review our warranty accrual rate in the future and we'll adjust the rate as appropriate to reflect our actual experience.
  Due to the charge for goodwill impairment, additional warranty accruals and restructuring, we recorded an operating loss of $485.3 million for the quarter, compared to an operating income of $222.7 million in the third quarter.
  The fourth quarter net loss was $413.1 million, or $4.78 per share.
  The effective tax rate was 14.2%.
  Before the non-recurring charges mentioned above, that is;goodwill impairment, additional warranty accrual and restructuring, earnings per share for the quarter would be $1.26 on a fully diluted basis, and the effective tax rate would be 19%.
  Overall, our fiscal 2011 net sales grew 8% from 2010, to approximately $2.8 billion. On a GAAP basis, operating margin was negative 1.3%, and earnings per share was a loss of $0.46.
  Excluding the full-year impact of the items listed above, the full-year diluted EPS would be $6.01. Slide 11 presents a walk from our GAAP EPS to our non-GAAP EPS for the fourth quarter of 2011 and for the fiscal year 2011,calling out the three non-recurring charges related to warranty, goodwill impairment and restructuring. The complete reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP numbers can be found in the slide at the back of the presentation.
  Turning to slide 12; I'll review the balance sheet and cash flow summary. Cash and marketable securities were $788 million, down slightly from $795 million as of the end of the last quarter.
  Accounts receivable trade balance declined quarter-over-quarter, due to improved collections and lower shipments. Our unbilled accounts receivables increased $208 million due to a $224 million increase in unbilled receivables at Agua Caliente.
  Inventories increased, mostly due to higher inventories in our systems business, both for modules and balances systems equipment, partially to help secure the economic benefit of the 1603 program for our projects.
  Project assets increased as we proactively developed projects that we have not yet sold. Deferred project costs  also increased  sorry, I lost my page  also increased, as we constructed projects that we have sold but for which we cannot yet recognize revenue. As a reminder, when we sell a project, the project assets turn into either revenue or deferred project costs, depending on whether the applicable revenue recognition criteria have been met.
  Our debt level increased by $55 million from the end of last quarter, primarily to fund working capital increases on our systems business, as certain projects anticipated to close were pushed out of the year.
  Operating cash flows for the quarter were $11 million. And free cash flow was negative $76 million.
  We spent $118 million for capital expenditures,down $106 million from last quarter.
  Depreciation was $67.9 million, compared to $60.8 million last quarter.
  This brings me to our updated guidance for 2012. We are reaffirming our guidance for net income and earnings per share, excluding any impairment and restructuring charges that we may be taking this year.
  While earnings guidance is the same, the assumptions behind the guidance has changed, as shown in slide 13. As we mentioned earlier, the Europe market will be more challenged than we initially expected. Our third-party sales are expected to be in the range of 300 to 500 MW, down from prior guidance of 720 MW.
  To accommodate lower sales, we will further reduce our manufacturing utilization rate to a range of 60% to 70%. This will include our module manufacturing cost per watt from $0.67 under fully utilized to $0.74 under utilization rates of 60% to 70%.
  Note that our costs, excluding under utilization, is the same as we had guided in December, despite incurring a $0.01 headwind due to higher warranty accruals going forward. The reason is that we continue to accelerate our efficiency improvements. We now expect to average a module efficiency of 12.7% in 2012, up from the prior guidance of 12.6%.
  Turning to our guidance on slide 14; we are reducing our 2012 revenue guidance from a range of $3.7 billionto $4 billion, to a range of $3.5 billion to $3.8 billion, to account for the lower third-party module volumes. Offsetting the impact of lower third-party module sales and higher module manufacturing costs due to our lower production volumes, its favorable balance of systems costs productivity associated with our systems business, where we plan to install 1.2 GW of modules.
  Our operating cash flow guidance declined due to the 2012 cash impact associated with the incremental manufacturing excursion charges accrued as of the end of 2011. Our operating cash flow guidance for 2012 includes approximately $75 million of net cash receipts from Desert Sunlight.
  To summarize, on slide 15; overall our operating performance for the quarter and year end were solid, given the challenge from challenging market conditions. We expect challenges in the subsidized markets to intensify in 2012, due to uncertain and in some cases collapsing FiT regimes. Cash flow generation should accelerate in 2012, as working capital turns into cash flow. We are accelerating module efficiency and cost road maps to increase our competitive advantage. We are developing a three-year plan to aggressively enter the sustainable markets, the details of which we will unveil in the first quarter earnings conference call.
  With this, we conclude our prepared remarks, and we'll open the call for questions. Operator?

During the fourth quarter of 2021, freight rates remained firm following a strong Q3 driven by augmented demand for raw materials and an improving coal trade, solid iron ore volumes and a continued fleet-wide reduction in productivity. Spot freight rates remained on the uptrend in early October with Capesize rates exceeding $85,000 per day and Supramax earnings approaching $40,000 per day. Towards the end of 2021 and into early 2022, Capesize and Supramax rates pulled back from these decade-plus highs due to various seasonal factors. These include weather-related cargo disruptions impacting Brazilian iron ore volumes, which were down 13% year-over-year in January and front-loaded newbuilding deliveries as we saw annualized net fleet growth of nearly 6% in January.
 Additionally, the timing of the Lunar New Year in China together with the Beijing Olympics resulted in steel mill utilization declining by approximately 5%. These seasonal factors are beginning to subside which are being reflected at spot earnings with Capesize and Supramax rates are up approximately 200% and 50% respectively versus earlier year lows. On the demand side in 2022, we anticipate China to continue to shift towards more accommodative policies to support economic growth. We have seen the shifts commence last December through a series of interest rate cuts and continue into early this year with increasing lending growth following a year of contraction.
 The trajectory of lending growth tends to be a leading indicator of metals demand. The timing of policy accommodation and its potential impact is expected to coincide with improving drybulk trade flows in the coming months and a ramp-up of China's steel production driven by spring construction season. We've already seen an uptick in work on construction projects in many parts of China that have restarted sooner after this year's Lunar New Year than in years past, partly as a response to the central government on for quick progress on new infrastructure projects to help boost the domestic economy. We believe these developments are positive for iron ore trade, particularly as seaborne volumes rise in Q2 and Q3.
 Regarding trade flows, we expect coal demand to remain firm given tightness in energy markets. On the grain side, the South American grain season has had an early start, which has been supportive of minor bulk earnings. Overall, we believe we are in a cyclical uptrending market. Our positive go-forward thesis for the drybulk market is underpinned by the historically low order book. The order book as a percentage of the fleet is 6.6%, which compares to 7% of the fleet, which is greater than or equal to 20 years old, implying fleet renewal rather than material net fleet growth in the coming years. Encouragingly, newbuilding vessel orders have been relatively low despite the strong market conditions in part due to uncertainty around go-forward future propulsion and tightness and shipyard capacity. Overall, we believe these positive supply side dynamics provide a solid foundation for the drybulk market and we do a low threshold for demand growth have to exceed in order to improve fleet-wide utilization freight rates.
 This concludes our presentation and we'd now be happy to take questions.

Despite these achievements, I confirm again that we never will be satisfied until all our operation units run fatality free.
 Looking at the tonnage milled and the yield into matte, we again had an exceptional operating year and we broke all previous production records and increased mill tons by 26% over the previous year while maintaining stock piles at over 1m tons of ore. Underground production increased by 280,000 tons in the open cast section contributed an additional 2.7m tons - making a total of 14.2m tons mined and milled. We concentrate recoveries on the operational section on the open cast section, while lowered into the underground ore actually exceeded our expectations.
 That resulted in total pgm production including gold, an increase of 20% to 1.758m ounces. Of that, Impala treated some 300,000 ounces. Included in the 933,000 ounces of Platinum were 30,000 ounces of what I call non-repeatable production, which is mainly sourced from historical stocks. We sold 903,000 ounces of Platinum and 405,000 ounces of Palladium, which is rather less than the production because we decided to use that opportunity which was provided by the significant production increase to add to our finished metal stocks. That enables us to better manage the future contractual and the [spot] sales over the current year.
 Just touching on the furnace incident, the furnace explosion in the smelter, which you know about on December 26 last year. The extensive investigations into the cause of that furnace explosion have enabled us to make design improvements, which should significantly reduce the risk of a similar incident in the future. These design improvements together with the rebuild costs will total some $20m and negotiations with our insurance brokers are continuing.
 We expect re-commissioning to take place probably late December, early January and the first matte to be produced towards the end of January 2004. Following the explosion the contingency plans we had were put into place. These included the re-commissioning of the Merensky and Pyromet furnaces and the signing of a toll treatment agreement with Impala Platinum and the additional costs of both of those amounted to some $34m.
 Leading on then to the unit costs. Processing and toll treatment costs increase substantially due to that smelter incident, and the yield into matte decreased mainly as a result of the increased open cast throughput. The satisfactory increase in production, however, partly negated the knock-on effects of these additional costs. The cash cost per pgm ounce excluding royalties, rose by only 12% to 1,996 Rand per ounce. I think this we can safely say was a pleasing result, particularly given the combined effects of the smelter explosion and South African mine inflation.
 The marked strengthening of the Rand against the US Dollar resulted in an increase of 51% in the dollar cash cost per pgm ounce, again excluding royalties from $168 last year to $254 equivalent this year.
 Just look at our expansion profile for a second. Starting with the Pandora GV. We are still awaiting a Section 9 Mining Authorization Permit from the Department of Minerals and Energy, so that project has not commenced. We continue to discuss this with both the Minister and the people in her department.
 Looking at the vertical shafts. As you know most of our growth is destined to flow from three new vertical shafts, all of which are currently under construction. The first of these is the Saffy shaft at Eastern Platinum, that is 825 meters deep and a 8-meter diameter vertical shaft. It provides access to an ore reserve of some 50m tons of [UG2] reef. [Complex] made very good progress during the year and we now expect production to commence some 18-months earlier than planned, and that around July 2005.
 The Karee 4 shaft and the Karee Mine, the largest of the three shafts is an 8.6-meter diameter shaft, 1.3 kilometers deep and it provides access to an ore reserve of some 126m tons of both UG2 and Merensky Reef. Progress during the year has also exceeded expectations and the first production here is now expected some 15-months early and that in the first quarter of the calendar year 2007.
 Finally, the Hossy shaft that is located between Western and Eastern Platinum and it is on the middle [indiscernible]. It is a 6-meter diameter, 410-meter deep vertical shaft and it provides access to an ore reserve of some 14m ones of UG2 reef. This shaft has no production levels but it hoists rock from its linked seven level sub-incline and first production here is expected during the first quarter of 2005.
 Looking at future production - the CAPEX profile, we spent $161m in the year under review, which was in line with our forecast. During the course of the year we undertook a detailed review of the capital expenditure for the 11-year period from the year 2000. This was obviously considered necessary given the strengthening of the Rand. The overall CAPEX profile and our current view of our growth profile are actually shown here. You can see there is actually no change.
 We remain confident in our ability to achieve 1m ounces of annual production of Platinum by the year 2008 and that despite the delays in the Pandora project which I referred to earlier, and due mainly to the very satisfactory progress on the major shafts which I have just touched upon.
 I would just like to say a few words about HIV/AIDS. It goes without saying that the impact of the HIV/AIDS pandemic on our company and our employees has always been a great concern to us. During the year, we completed one of the world's largest voluntary prevalence testing programs, which involved some 11,000 of our employees or about 60% of the workforce. The purpose of this was to establish the magnitude of the pandemic within the company and the results showed that around 25% of our employees are currently HIV positive.
 This result, together with statistics that we had already compiled on absenteeism, medical costs, retraining and productivity were fed into a very well tested actuarial social of South Africa who have a model. This was done in order to undertake a detailed impact assessment on our operations, both current and in the foreseeable future. The realistic view of the future medical cost was also fed into the model, and as a result of all of this the model now shows that as far as Lonmin is concerned, our HIV prevalence will peak around the year 2006 and that is 26% of the payroll. That prevalence will drop below 20% once again, around 2011 as a result of our interventions, of which I will talk in a minute.
 The AIDS deaths will peak somewhat later at 2011, as later in the prevalence because of the delay period between the HIV infection and the onset of sickness and ultimately AIDS related death. Finally that the additional cost of HIV/AIDS including the provision of anti retroviral drugs is expected to peak around the year 2006.
 So we are now satisfied that we have fully and accurately evaluated the threats which HIV/AIDS pose to our business. Therefore, from December 1, 2003, which is World AIDS Day, we propose to include anti-retroviral treatment in our overall healthcare arrangements. This is clearly a significant intervention and it will improve the quality of health and will extend the lives of those workers who are already infected. We are also investigating the feasibility of extending ART as part of our healthcare benefit schemes to the dependants of the employees.
 As cost was never really an issue in this case, the model nevertheless shows that the additional cost of HIV/AIDS, which includes the provision of the ART, will be about $6 per pgm ounce, or 1.5% of a basket price of metals, say $12,000 per kilo of [indiscernible] metals. The provision of ART in that extra cost is actually very minimal.
 Looking now at the Empowerment Charter. This screen, which I think you are familiar with, shows the representation of our current position, regarding the scorecard requirements of the Mining Charter and summarizes the key developments. The equity box on the top left I will deal with separately. So I am just going to concentrate now on just the other three boxes and I am not going to spend too much time on the detail because it is covered very fully in our Corporate Accountability Report for the year 2003, which will be published shortly.
 I can therefore confine myself now to just a few examples of progress in each of the boxes, which I think will adequately describe our commitment and progress thus far. On the first one, the Employment, Equity and Skills Development, during 2003 we invested some $8m or just under 6% of our wage bill on education, training and developing across all our operations. This includes bursaries and scholarships.
 Our budget for the current year is $8.5m, excluding learner's salaries and if you include the learner's salaries in that cost, it rises to about $16m. Most of this expenditure is aimed at the historically disadvantaged South Africans.
 The Mining Charter caused for a 40% HDSA participation in management within five years. By September 2003, HDSAs will comprise 47% of our junior management and 18.6% of our senior and middle management as defined by the Act. We are confident that these numbers will rise to 51% and 24% respectively during the current year, thus already far exceeding the scorecard target.
 Dealing now with the Corporate and Social Investment, Lonplats has invested and donated more than $15m in various housing projects for HDSA employees and other community HDSAs in the last three years. We anticipate funding a similar amount over the next five years.
 Finally on procurement, we directed approximately $75m of our total spend, 19% of our total spend, on affirmative HDSA procurement in 2003. So in summary then I am quite confident of being able to say that we will be able to meet the non-equity requirements of the scorecard well within the envisaged timeframe.
 I am going to say a few words now on the markets and start with Platinum. The market price trend for Platinum which you I am sure know, rose steadily throughout the year and it ended on a 23-year high of around $720 per tr oz. Some of this increase could be attributed to the speculation, which followed the tension and uncertainties surrounding the events in the Middle East. The very tight balance between supply and demand however, in my view, is by far the dominant feature.
 Some of the announced major expansion plans have fallen behind expectations and demand has lived up to, if not exceeded, expectations. Cleaner air is becoming an increasing priority in the world and this is reflected in the far reaching emission control legislation already on the statute books in the United States, Japan and Europe and which now requires catalyses to be applied to the diesel engines used in both light and heavy vehicles. In general it is said that diesel catalyses favors Platinum.
 China and India are both significant newcomers to the introduction of emission control legislation and both for obvious reasons represent a huge potential for pgn consumption.
 As Platinum prices rose, the demand in the jewelry sector decreased. The manufacturers margin is obviously been squeezed as a result for jewelry. So I think we already said clearly now becomes a swing demand for Platinum. You will have noticed the increasing publicity I think regarding the use of hydrogen, now widely regarded as the next generation's potential alternative source of clean renewable energy, producing only water as an emission. In my personal view, hydrogen could ultimately compete with fossil fuels as a primary source of energy, thus clearly creating a long-term market for Platinum.
 The Palladium price, slightly different here, and it previously benefited from the - we could call euphemistically the somewhat erratic delivery pattern with Russian supplies and it fell steadily through the year before settling at the more traditional level now at between $115 to $100 an ounce. That the widening gap between price of Platinum and Palladium could lead to substitution in ore catalysts, I think is greatly over-emphasized.
 Generally speaking, Palladium works best in a closed [indiscernible] environment and that is to say near the exhaust manifold because of the higher temperatures. But elsewhere, any substitution requires to up to three times as much Palladium to do the same work as the Platinum equivalent. This is because Platinum is inherently more mobile and therefore has a lesser tendency to oxidize in service.
 As I have mentioned during previous presentations, a combination of production and inventory allows the Russian suppliers a considerable capacity to influence the price, but in their most recent announcements, they have demonstrated a wish for stability. Finally Rhodium, which previously had a variety of end uses, because of the high prices of the recent past, it is now almost exclusively used in auto catalysts. Demand therefore remains sound with consumption in this sector continues to increase. Only the overhanging inventory levels at both supplier and consumer level that prevented the price from rising from its current level of around $500 an ounce. But as this overhang is drawn down, it is reasonable to expect that the Rhodium price could return to the more traditional levels of around $1,000 an ounce.
 I am going to pause here and ask John Robinson if he would just take you through the financial results and then we will return and talk about the strategy.

 We can see in summary that the group has achieved a material increase in free cash flow per share. It has maintained the overall dividend for the year at 72 cents per share despite the reduction in reported earnings and has maintained a comfortable level of gearing.
 We can see from this slide, that despite a 26% appreciation of the average Rand rate during the year, the EBITDA margin at 44% continues to remain strong whilst being somewhat lower than the 53% achieved last year. Depreciation at $46m shows an increase over 2002 as further assets are brought on stream in South Africa.
 Net interest in similar items at a charge of $28m reflects both a higher level of borrowings and the effective of the appreciation of the Rand on working capital facilities borrowed in South African Rands. The resulting profit before tax and exceptional items is $269m.
 Looking in a little more detail at the operating profit. We can see that the affect of the 26% depreciation in the average Rand/Dollar exchange rate has been to reduce operating profit by $110m. This has been offset by the growth in revenue of $137m, which arises in itself from a combination of the increase in average prices realized of 7% and the material increase in the volume of metal sold.
 In addition, the other marked feature of these results is the $34m of non-recurring additional costs from the smelter incident, which Ed referred to earlier. Overall then, the decrease in operating profit was only $34m.
 Moving on down the P&L account. We can see that here there have been two marked features in the year. Firstly, the exceptional profit on the sale of the land at Brakspruit, which realized a profit of $24m. Secondly, the very significant increase in the tax rate from 23% in 2002 to 63% in 2003. The net result of these movements has been a reduction in the overall attributable profit to $74m or 60% when compared to last year and a reduction in EPS of 57% to 52.5 cents from the 121.5 cents achieved last year.
 We can see from this slide the analysis of the tax charge as we have previously discussed. The reason for the increase in the overall rate to 63% noted above, can be seen to derive from the exchange rate movements with the underlying tax rate excluding exchange and exceptional items moving only marginally from 37% to 35% in the year.
 The unrealized exchange loss on deferred tax of $82m represents the translation adjustment arising from the 34% year-on-year appreciation in the Rand measured at the financial year-end and clearly is very significantly higher than the affect of the depreciation in the previous year.
 Looking forward, the reported tax rate in 2004 would obviously continue to be highly dependent upon the movement in the Rand/Dollar exchange rate.
 In order to look at the underlying earnings from operations, we can see from this slide how the earnings figures are adjusted to eliminate the effects of exceptional items and the net affect of exchange primarily being unrealized on the deferred tax. The resulting underlying earnings of 87.2 cents are only 11% below the 98.5 cents achieved last year, which in itself broadly reflects the reduction in operating profit.
 Turning now to the all-important cash flow of the group. We can see that in terms of trading cash flow per share, there has been a 35% increase from 118.9 cents in 2002 to 161 cents in 2003. This results from a reduction in cash inflow from operating activities being more than offset by the reduction in the tax cash payments, where you will recall there were exceptionally high payments in the first-half of last year.
 The interest costs, reflect the level of borrowing throughout the financial year as compared to 2002 when the group had significant cash resources in the first-half of the year.
 We can see from the free cash flow analysis, there has been a significant improvement in the overall generation of cash, with a free cash flow per share of 48.2 cents, as compared to a small outflow last year. Capital expenditure at $161m was somewhat ahead of last year, and $25m was realized from the sale of Brakspruit. There was a reduction in minority dividends resulting from the short-term working capital requirements of the business.
 In terms of net cash flow, disposals on the financial investment essentially comprised the sale of our assets in Zimbabwe in 2003, whereas in 2002 it represented our investment in the Ashanti MENS.
 The overall cash flow of the group shows that the free cash flow paid for the majority of the cost of the shareholder's dividend of $101m, with only a small net cash outflow of $23m.
 Exchange losses of some $19m were realized during the year on Rand borrowings as a result of the appreciation of the Rand, whereas there was relatively little Rand borrowings in 2002.
 We can see there has been little movement in the equity of the group during the year and the increase in borrowings to $197m results in a comfortable level of gearing of 23% on equity and minority interest. The issue of a $216m 3.75% convertible bond on the September 30, 2003 represented a significant step in the efficient management of the balance sheet. The return on operating assets based on underlying earnings and excluding the investment in Ashanti from capital employed was 32%, compared to 24% last year.
 Given the level of gearing at the year-end, and in the context of the underlying earnings and cash flow outlook for the group the board has decided to recommend the year's dividend at 72 cents. This is covered 1.2 times by underlying earnings.
 Finally, as we can see from the slide, the overall enterprise value has grown by 17% in the year under review.
 In summary, therefore, we can see that the operating assets continue to return a commendable underlying 32% despite the market depreciation of the Rand. Free cash flow at 48.2 cents, reflects a strong underlying cash generation. Gearing at 23% and equity and minority remained at a comfortable level and overall the enterprise value has been enhanced by 17%.
 I will now hand you back to Ed to take you through the strategic developments.

Jarrod David Ritchie,  Palla Pharma Limited - Founder, MD, CEO & Executive Director: Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Thanks for joining us to discuss Palla Pharma's results for the half year ended 30 June 2020.
 I'm Jarrod Ritchie, Managing Director and CEO of Palla Pharma. And I'm joined today by our CFO, Brendan Middleton. This morning, I will take you through the 2020 half year results presentation. I will touch briefly on the company overview, a summary of our results and an update on our progress with the marketing authorizations. Brendan will then take you through the financials, after which I will provide a further update on our strategic initiatives and outlook for the rest of the year. We can then take questions at the end.
 Before moving through the slide pack and starting at Slide 3, I would like to just give a brief summary of where we are. This year's sales and earnings will have a different profile to 2019. The results will be heavily skewed towards the second half due to our transition from a lower-margin non-opiate contract manufacturer to one selling high-margin opiate-based products via recently acquired marketing authorizations. The second half, as a result, will see an increase in gross profit as the product mix changes and a reduction in indirect overhead costs from the planned early exit from a non-opiate contract manufacturing business. I'll explain this in more detail through the rest of the slides.
 Turning to Slide 3. If you are new to Palla Pharma, this slide provides an overview of our company. There are only 3 fully integrated opiate manufacturers from farm gate to tablet production in the world, and Palla Pharma proudly is 1 of them. We utilize our competitive advantage as a low-cost producer of narcotic raw materials and active pharmaceutical ingredients to offer competitive pricing and win market share from our peers. Recently, we have done this through gaining contracts to manufacture opiate-based tablets for others. Increasingly, we will do it directly to farmers and wholesale distributors through our own marketing authorizations, giving us significant earnings uplift.
 Moving to Slide 4, our fully integrated supply chain. Moving from the left of the slide to the right, you can see the entire supply chain of our operations and how we increase gross margin as we move from raw materials to tableted pain medications. Our vertical integration allows us multiple channels to market our products and diversify revenue streams. Our diversified raw material supply chain from both sources in Australia and various locations in the northern hemisphere allow us to derisk supply of our crop compared to our competitors. A good example of the benefits of this happened last growing season, where we had a reduced growing area in Australia due to adverse weather events in New South Wales but could increase our poppy straw supply from growers in the northern hemisphere.
 We have secured additional aggregator supply agreements, and we continue to focus on improving local expertise with increased farmer and aggregator engagement through the company's on-the-ground agricultural expertise in Europe. This raw material of crop is then processed into narcotic raw material at a facility in Melbourne. From here, we sell poppy seed externally, and we sell narcotic raw material such as morphine and codeine to both external customers and our own API manufacturing facility in Norway. We then produce API for external sales and contract manufacturing tablets. Importantly now, we have geared our business up with the purchase of 7 marketing authorizations to manufacture and sell directly to pharmacies and wholesale distributors. This will allow us to increase gross margin threefold compared to 1 kilogram of NRM and rapidly increase our earnings growth.
 Moving on to Slide 5. Slide 5 shows what milestones we have achieved since 2015 and our transition to higher-margin opiate-based products going forward. I will cover the 2020 progress in the third column in more detail in later slides, but a key thing to take away from this slide is that the company now has all of the parts required to deliver on our cost-competitive potential and complete the transition to value accretion in the supply chain. We are making good progress with the approval of 2 of our main MAs that were recently acquired for the supply of opiate-based tablets into the United Kingdom. Sales are on track to start in the last quarter of this year and will significantly improve our path to long-term earnings growth. Furthermore, with the early planned exit from the low-margin non-opiate contract manufacturing business, we have made significant changes to our business which have streamlined production capability, and it will enable us to diversify our customers and product revenue based on opiate-based products.
 Moving on to Slide 6. While the disruption in 2020 to business has been unique in living memory, Palla's Victorian and Norwegian facilities have continued to operate under the permitted industry exemption as a manufacturer of essential products. In March, Palla Pharma implemented strict COVID-19 safe operating procedures at its Melbourne facility, including provision of additional PPEs, staggered shifts and breaks and adherence to physical distancing requirements in shared working areas. To date, this has proved effective in keeping the workplace safe and keeping operations functioning. We have also ensured we have had higher inventory levels to mitigate risks from supply chain interruptions. These inventory levels, however, will decrease in the next 6 months, freeing up working capital. We remain in close contact with the Victorian, Australian and Norwegian governments, ensuring uninterrupted supply of an essential medicine.
 I'd like to now turn to Slide 8, the first half results overview.
 An overview of our results for the first half demonstrates the transition for Palla Pharma from lower-margin contract manufacturer to high-margin opiate tablet sales via marketing authorizations. Revenue as a result of this transition is down 54.9% on our first half '19 results. This was primarily due to the early exit of non-opiate-based supply agreement, lower API volumes from a major U.K. customer losing its license. We expect revenue to significantly accelerate in the second half from the sale of opiate-based products via our own MAs that I outlined earlier. Gross profit decreased 82% on the prior corresponding period due to the timing of the exit of the non-opiate-based supply agreement, reduced poppy seed margin contribution due to a reduction in domestic growing area and reduced API volumes due to the prolonged manufacturing license suspension of a major API customer. Margins will improve significantly in the second half '20 as we start producing under our own MAs.
 Indirect overhead costs were 19.6% lower than in the previous corresponding period, following the early exit from the contract manufacturing agreement, allowing us to reset the business' cost base. The reported operating EBITDA was a loss of $6.7 million, impacted by the decline in revenue and gross margin. However, it was partly offset by indirect overhead cost reductions.
 Net debt increased with the MA acquisitions; and additional inventory to avoid COVID-19 supplier disruptions, which I will talk more about that shortly. However, the standby debt facility will provide sufficient headroom to execute the current strategy.
 Moving to Slide 9, the half year trend results (sic) [results trend]. The next slide shows the temporary decline in revenue and profitability due to the non-opiate-based finished dosage formulation supply agreement termination, loss of license of a major U.K. customer and decreased API volumes in the first half. As we start up sales of opiate-based products through our MAs and significantly increase tablet production in the second half of the year, these figures will all trend sharply upwards. On the next slide, I'll explain how the revenue mix will also change.
 Slide 10. This slide shows how we are transitioning the revenue mix from the start of last financial year to the end of this financial year. We are currently in the middle column. We have reduced revenues due to the exit from a legacy non-opiate CMO supply agreement and major customer license loss. The purples in the first 2 bars shows the planned exit from the non-opiate finished dosage formulation, while the green dotted box in the center shows the impacted (sic) [impact] of the contracted U.K. customer who lost their license to manufacture. However, the gray area in each column shows the revenue from opiate finished dosage formulation and our own new marketing authorizations and how MA sales will take off dramatically in the second half of this year once approved. We are on track for Q4 sales for our codeine phosphate tablets. And API sales have already reached 50% of first half sales in July and August.
 Slide 11. You can see that our transition from API to MAs rapidly increases earnings faster than revenue. Over the next few years, we will rapidly see an increase in our gross profit percentages and our revenue will increase dramatically, allowing for significantly faster earnings growth than would otherwise have been possible without the MAs.
 Slide 13. Critically is the explanation of where we are with the approval of our MAs. And in simple terms: They are on track. Our 7 MAs are key to the journey from low-value to both high-value and high-volume business. Stages 1 and 2 are complete. We have completed the 3 validation batches in our Norway facility, which have all met required specifications and are now being processed through stability studies. Sales can commence once approval from the MHRA has been obtained, which are expected to enable us to start commercial sales in the last quarter of 2020.
 Moving to Slide 14. On the right, you can see the 7 products we will supply to the U.K. market. We are currently completing the validation and submission process for the 30/500 milligram tablet and caplet, as they provide the most significant market opportunity. This is the product that will start sales later this year. Following successful validation and approval from the MHRA, Palla will then shift its focus on to the remaining 5 marketing authorizations that have been acquired earlier this year. While the U.K. is our initial focus, the next 2 biggest markets in the U.K. will follow in FY '21, which will be France and Spain.
 I'd then like to move to Slide 15. Slide 15 gives a very good example of how our strategy can harness retail market changes to greater effect. We have been, in the past, isolated from these advantages. The sale price of a 100-tablet packet of codeine/paracetamol 30/500 milligram has increased significantly in the last 2 years from approximately GBP 2.50 to over GBP 4 per a 100 pack. As a marketing authorization holder, Palla will receive 70% to 75% of the retail price. At the full packaging capacity of our Norway facility, the expected monthly revenue is to exceed AUD 4 million at the historical GBP 2.50 level. There is the  exists the opportunity to increase monthly revenue to AUD 12 million a month following an approximate CapEx spend of $4 million. As you can see, once approval from the MHRA is granted, Palla expects earnings generated from codeine phosphate sold in tablet form to be a significant contributor at greatly improved profit margins moving forward.
 Slide 16. This slide looks to demonstrate the market opportunity in Europe. Thinking of the products we showed a few slides ago and the current capability I just mentioned, Slide 16 demonstrates how big the EU codeine phosphate market is. Palla believes it will rapidly gain access to these markets over the coming years. And by far, the largest which we have purchased the marketing authorizations for is the U.K. market, which is currently valued at EUR 278 million. We will use these MAs to target the next largest markets, France and Spain, respectively.
 Slide 17. On Slide 17, we put this extra MA detail back into the revenue mix that I mentioned previously. Revenue in the first half has been significantly lower than the previous comparative period. This is due, as highlighted, to product mix [having changed] this year. This occurred from the early termination of the non-opiate CMO contract in the first half and the loss of license of one of our major customers. Therefore, revenue and earnings will be heavily skewed to the end of the year with the start of the MA sales in the fourth quarter and a much stronger expected sales of API in the second half overall. This will enable FY '20 revenue to be modestly down compared to FY '19 but with significantly higher gross margins. There will also be indirect overhead cost savings from the early exit of the non-opiate contract manufacturing business, which we expect to carry forward in the coming years. This higher-margin product mix will see gross profits increase faster than revenues in the coming years, with exciting opportunities further ahead.
 I'll now hand over to our CFO, Brendan Middleton, to cover our financials in greater detail.

 The credit loss provision of $1 million was recognized during the half due to slow payment by a major U.K. customer, but we are expecting to recover the amount owing in full. I would like to once again start thanking the Petro Rio team. We are living difficult and challenging moments. But we have been performing really well amidst all of the difficulties that we are all facing on a day-to-day basis. So I would like to start thanking my team for their perseverance and discipline.
 Now moving to Slide 3. We have the highlights after period. The first highlight that I think it is important to underscore is our EBITDA. In the first quarter, our EBITDA totaled BRL 428 million, 12x higher than the first quarter of 2020. Of course, in 2020, we already felt the early COVID effects. The pandemic started in March 2020. So we have a little bit of an effect there.
 As part of this EBITDA, we have to take into account 2 important things this year. First, a higher production, most likely, a record mark in the company's history. And a Brent oil price that is also higher. We took an average, and it was higher than $60 per barrel. It's been a while since we have seen this happen.
 A second point about this first quarter that is important to highlight was our follow-on offer. We raised $370 million, approximately BRL 2 billion in January. We had a capital increase. We had a book that was more than 3x oversubscribed. Meaning we had 3x more orders than the size of the book. So it was very successful.
 And here, I would like once again to thank both our new shareholders and the shareholders already in our base at the time. We always had a lot of support from all of them. This follow-on prepared the company for growth, either organic growth via investments in the fields that we already have or preparing for inorganic growth through acquisition of new fields.
 We also had the approval by ANP, the regulatory agency of the 30% stake of Frade Field, that we had acquired from Petrobras in 2019. And this was finally approved in February of 2021. We also acquired the working interest belonging to Total in the Wahoo Field, 28.6%. As we mentioned in the past, we were interested in acquiring that, so we finalized that deal. And we also had a stratification of reserves and resources, adding 92 million barrels of 1C resources and reserves for the company. This was very interesting because we already included Wahoo field.  Now moving to Slide 4, please. Here, I'm going to address some items in perhaps more detail, and then I'll turn the floor to Francilmar. Well, the first point on Slide 4 was a reduction of our lifting cost. We have here $14.3, reducing the lifting cost a bit quarter-over-quarter. It's still a little below what we would like. The main reason why it fell a little below our expectation was some downtime at Polvo, given a problem we had in the boiler of the FPSO operated by BW. This cost us a little bit, although the number is a little lower than in Q4 '20 at $14.3. So a very good lift in cost, we could have done even better.
 The next item here is increased production. The main reason explaining this increase in production was the approval of the 30% stake belonging to Petrobras. We increased from an average production of 29,900 to 31,300. As we mentioned in the first quarter, we had the stoppage of the Polvo FPSO, a downtime of 10 days on account of the boiler and had a stoppage of 1 pump in the TBMT field, Tubarão Martelo. And here, it's important to differentiate the issues. Of course, the FPSO performance is something that we have to address, and this will be addressed. It is being addressed as we will keep this FPSO until July of this year.
 Now the Pump, ESP, that's the day-to-day of an oil company. We'll continue to have pumps that fail. This is our day-to-day. These things will continue to happen. It's not a surprise. But the FPSO, yes, that was a little surprising, and we are taking measures and addressing that topic.
 Well, our cash position increased to BRL 3.370 million, almost $600 million in cash. So when I said that the company is prepared for what's coming in the future, that's what I meant. In addition, the company also had the follow-on top of this good performance. That make the company completely prepared and ready for the next challenges. And for the next steps, we'll take to drive organic and inorganic growth.
 With that, I will turn the floor to Francilmar to discuss our operations, and then Milton will speak about the financials, and I will be back at the end to talk about the next steps. Thank you very much. Francilmar?

Thank you for joining us here this morning at the CSR results presentation for year ending March 2016. Thank you to JP Morgan and Keith Chau for hosting us, very much appreciated, thank you.
 So just quickly on the agenda, the usual double act between Greg and I, about 25 minutes for the presentations. I'll give you an overview of the results, Greg will give you a little bit more detail in the financial numbers by business unit and I'll come back and give you some perspective of business unit performance, plus also some comments on the outlook for 2017, YEM17.
 So on to the first slide, which is the main drivers and the headline result. We can see another very pleasing result for CSR earnings this year. In fact, these are the highest earnings since the divestment of Sugar in 2010.
 It's been driven by three key factors: building products earnings are now at record levels, I'll talk to that in a moment, supported clearly by solid market activity, but also improving margins and very good growth in new products and new categories by the team.
 Secondly, recent transactions, including the consolidated results from the PGH Bricks joint venture, has flowed through to very solid earnings. We've also posted another very good result in property and our aluminium division. The lift in earnings has driven strong cash flow and enabled us to increase the dividend by 18% to AUD0.235.
 So before I let Greg talk you through the results in detail, I just wanted to highlight the improvement in returns over the last five years. Slide 5 shows the return on funds for the Group and each of our main operating divisions.
 While we should be mindful of past write-downs in Viridian, the charts illustrate the combined effect of the sustained earnings growth, the increased margin in building products and the good performance from recent acquisitions. Pleasingly, Viridian's return on funds continues to steadily improve.
 So in summary, from a Group perspective, we are pleased with the progress being made in each of the operating businesses and the 20.7% return on funds for the Group is obviously a very strong number.
 So a couple of comments on just looking back over the last few years and it's worth noting the key issues we faced as we developed our strategy for building products and how this has actually played out in the market.
 Our forecast growth in multi residential has actually been much stronger and has accelerated as we've seen in the last 12 months. We identified this as a key opportunity due to our lower relative share in this segment. That's, of course, compared to our traditional high market share in the detached market.
 The main drivers of growth in multi residential included the increase in cost of land, combined with a desire by young people and  for everyone to have a higher proportion of inner city living. So combined with increasing labour costs and trade shortages, this meant that the industry needed to develop smarter, faster and easier ways to construct buildings, less reliant on the traditional construction trades.
 So we've developed our strategy to help solve these issues, particularly with the growth in Hebel, the acquisition of AFS and with new products like the Velocity offsite walling system.
 We've developed a slide there that pretty well illustrates our strategic progress over the last four years. You can see that by fixing bricks and Viridian and through growth in our other products, we have fundamentally improved the spread of earnings within our buildings products business.
 The red bar is Gyprock and fibre cement, or Cemintel earnings, which has seen earnings growth consistent with the market. In contrast, the pink bar represents growth across all our other businesses, including PGH, AFS, Hebel, Monier and Bradford, which is combined to deliver growth four times the relative growth in Gyprock and fibre cement.
 So our key message out of this slide is that over the last four years we've developed a much more resilient, more balanced building products business.
 So with those comments, I'll hand over to Greg to give you some detail, a breakdown of the results for the year.

Greg Barnes,  CSR Limited - CFO: Well thanks Rob and good morning everyone. As you know, this is the first year where we're presenting the bricks joint venture on a consolidated basis, so that just confuses comparisons a little bit.
 So where I can, I'm going to refer to both the headline result, as well as to the results net of the minority share in that joint venture, or the minority portion in that joint venture and Rob has a slide later which just presents the bricks JV separately for your information.
 If we look at slide 9, it summarises our profit and loss for the year and as Rob just mentioned, you can really see the progress we've made on our strategy and how it's played out in the profit and loss this year.
 A combination of operational efficiencies, the bricks joint venture, growth in Hebel and in AFS have all contributed to the best net profit after tax result since the divestment of the Sugar business.
 In terms of revenue, it was up 14% to AUD2.3 billion this year. The consolidation of 11 months of trading of the bricks joint venture represents 5% of that growth, so underlying revenue growth was approximately 9%. Strong residential construction activity also contributed with detached commencements up 6% during the year. Pleasingly, Viridian revenues were also up 8%.
 The benefit of this revenue growth, together with some operational performances flowed to earnings. EBIT was AUD276.8 million, up 18%. Excluding the minority portion of the bricks joint venture, EBIT was up 11% year-on-year.
 Our effective tax rate was 27%. That was broadly in line with the guidance we gave last year and at the half and it's also a good indication of what to expect in the future. So with all that, NPAT was up 13% to AUD166 million.
 We did report significant items this period of AUD23.7 million after tax. The largest component of this was the transaction costs and integration costs associated with the bricks joint venture, as well as the discount unwind linked to the asbestos liability. As a result, NPAT, post significant items, was AUD142.3 million and that was also up 13% year-on-year.
 If we look at the EBIT performance by division on slide 10, building products was actually up 40% for the year and up 28% adjusted for that minority interest in bricks. Essentially all businesses grew year-on-year. AFS, bricks, Gyprock and Hebel were standouts and Rob's going to talk to that in more detail in a moment.
 It also allowed us to invest further in long term growth initiatives such as CSR Connect, which is our digital platform, Velocity, which is an offsite wall construction system, as well as AFS and Hebel. We saw further improvement in Viridian, with an EBIT of AUD8 million.
 Aluminium EBIT was steady at AUD104 million. Operationally, the business performed extremely well, with increased output and tight cost control. However Australian dollar prices was down 4% for the year, with volume, hedging and a weaker Aussie dollar helping to mitigate the fall in US dollar pricing in particular in ingot premiums.
 Property EBIT was AUD23.3 million and that has exceeded our long term guidance of AUD15 million to AUD20 million of EBIT per annum and Rob will get into specific transactions when he comes back.
 Just looking at asbestos on slide 11, the table at the top reconciles the movement in the asbestos liability over the last 12 months. As you can see, claim related costs were AUD27.6 million and that's down 11% year-on-year. After adjusting for the discount unwind, the provision reduced to AUD334.5 million.
 That's the lowest level we've seen in that liability for 11 years. The provision includes a prudential margin of AUD65.2 million, or 24%, above the central estimate. So all in all, we've seen further good progress in the United States and Australia remains relatively stable.
 Just finally from me, on cash flow on slide 12. We're actually really pleased with our cash performance this year. Underlying operating cash was up 12% for the year on strong earnings.
 The bricks joint venture does impact balance sheet comparatives, but we have seen really good progress in working capital, in particular in our debtor collections where overdues were only 5% of total debt outstanding. That's a very good performance on the back of a good performance last year.
 Looking beyond operating cash, our property business generated net inflows of AUD15.9 million and that compares to an inflow last year of AUD40.5 million. So that delta, given our cash position, highlights a strong performance and is purely related to timing of transactions, both development and proceeds.
 In terms of CapEx, we spent AUD72.8 million during the period and that excludes property and acquisitions. This represents 88% of depreciation. It does include 100% of the bricks JV spend.
 It includes investment in the ready-wall factory, which is our PVC structural wall solution for AFS and the Viridian commercial double glazing line. We actually expect CapEx to be at similar levels next year. So as a result, we exited the year with AUD73.1 million in net cash.
 So look, I might stop there. I'm going to hand back to Rob and we'll come back to questions at the end. Thanks very much.
