Jean-Jacques Gauthier,  Lafarge - CFO: Thank you, Bruno. As Bruno said in his introduction, the unprecedented economic crisis in 2009 significantly impacted our results. That being said, the signs that the pressure on volumes is starting to ease. In Cement, volume declines on the like-for-like basis slowed to minus 4% in the fourth quarter as compared to minus 7% in Q3 and minus 8% in Q2. Emerging markets also remained solid with earnings continuing to rise in the fourth quarter, with the exception of Central and Eastern Europe.
  It is important to note the resilience of the Group's margin during this period. In our largest division, Cement, EBITDA margins remained over 30% for the full year despite the overall fall in volumes. Cost cutting and improved pricing were the main drivers of this achievement.
  In terms of financial structure, the Group outperformed the action plan put in place to deal with the impact of the prevailing crisis. Free cash flow increased by 34% to EUR2.8b, divestments came to over EUR900m and net debt declined by more than EUR3b, EUR3.1b. Looking forward, these achievements strengthen the Group as we enter a still challenging 2010. Solid liquidity, a lower structural cost base and strategically-placed assets in emerging markets, are the key elements which will give Lafarge an ongoing advantage.
  Let's now take a look at some of the key figures for the quarter and year to date. As the table shows, both the year and fourth quarter were impacted by lower volumes resulting from the global economic slowdown. Also playing a much larger role in the fourth quarter, in addition to more adverse weather conditions, was the negative impact of foreign exchange and scope.
  On the like-for-like basis sales in the fourth quarter declined 11% versus a growth decline of 22%. Similarly, current operating income declined 27% in the fourth quarter on the like-for-like basis versus the reported minus 34%. That being said, as you know, Lafarge continues to diligently adapt to the current environment through closely managing costs, reducing production and lowering working capital.
  This helped slow the decline of current operating margins, down only 260 basis points in the quarter. Again, these actions also underpinned our significant 34% improvement in free cash flow year to date, to EUR2.8b, although EBITDA fell close to 20%. Given these efforts, the Group is pleased to announce a EUR2 per share dividend for financial year 2009.
  The clearer focus on the Group's cost cutting is seen here. As the chart shows, the cost cutting in the Group has gained strength over the years. With the launch of Lafarge's Excellence programs in 2006 the Group has achieved EUR650m of structural cost savings up until the end of 2009. These savings are permanent thanks to a structural change of our cost base, and will remain in effect even when volumes return to higher levels. In 2009 alone the Group exceeded its target and achieved EUR230m in structural savings. In addition, Lafarge forcefully acted to limit the impact of declining volumes by shutting down Cement capacity, closing Ready Mix and Aggregate facilities and extending factory downtime in weaker markets.
  Let us now review our different activities, starting with Cement. Cement results declined in the quarter and year to date, marked by significant contrasts between regions. Our operations benefited from positive trends in the emerging markets of the Middle East, Africa and Asia, while significant declines were posted for Central and Eastern Europe, Western Europe and North America. The quarter also reflected tight cost control across all regions and firm pricing. EBITDA margins remained above 30% for the year and edged down only 30 basis points in the quarter.
  This table shows the solid results posted in most emerging markets as well as the progressive stabilization in mature markets. In Western Europe, North America and Central and Eastern Europe declines in volumes negatively impacted operating income and margins, yet cost controls were tight and overall pricing remained solid. In Middle East and Africa, Latin America and Asia, like-for-like earnings increased throughout the year. Rates of growth did inch lower in the fourth quarter, particularly in Asia. This reflects a higher earnings base in Q4 2008 when our China operations picked up speed after the impact of the earthquake in Szechwan.
  Moving to the Aggregates and Concrete division, our Aggregates and Concrete business, which has a far greater presence in developed markets than our Cement business, was impacted by lower construction demand in Western Europe and in North America. We have taken aggressive actions to cut costs, reduce capacity and improve working capital in order to offset these lower volumes. In our Pure Aggregates business actions to reduce inventory negatively affected operating margins by close to EUR25m, but significantly helped cash flow generation. Also important is that prices remained solid, 3% above last year's level.
  Similar measures have been taken for Ready Mix Concrete. Tight cost control, higher prices and increased market penetration of value-added products partially offset the significant impact from volume declines.
  Now looking at Gypsum, as you can see, the opening results were relatively stable compared to last year. Current operating margins slightly improved thanks to lower costs in an environment that continued to see volume declines.
  Now moving further down the income statement, excluding one-off items net income stood at EUR98m for the quarter and at EUR829m for the full year, reflecting the impact of the severe economic downturn. Other expenses in the fourth quarter include asset write-offs of approximately EUR100m and restructuring costs of around EUR80m in the quarter. This reflects the actions taken by Lafarge to permanently close capacity and react to lower volumes in mature markets.
  Finance costs in the quarter were down, reflecting the drop in debt levels and the lower average interest rate thanks to the decline of floating interest rates. Income tax expense decreased in line with the lower net income with an effective tax rate of approximately 20% for the year, in line with last year.
  Let us now take a look at the cash flow highlights. As mentioned earlier, the strong focus on cash generated EUR2.8b in free cash flow in the year. The 34% improvement was driven by actions taken to reduce working capital, EUR1b, and to lower capital expenditures. Based on all the actions implemented, including the rights issue in early 2009, net debt levels, again, are down EUR3.1b.
  Let us take a further look at the Group's debt structure. We have a strong liquidity and a balanced debt maturity schedule. Lafarge not only reduced net debt by EUR3.1b but also improved, during the course of the year, the maturity profile with EUR3.3b in bond issuance during 2009 between May and December. This balanced debt maturity, in combination with EUR5.6b of cash and unused credit facility, fully committed, provide the Group with strong liquidity over the coming years.
  As usual, I would like now to give you an update on our outlook for 2010. Here we have provided estimated volume and price trends for all markets in 2010. Based on where we stand today, we are forecasting, as Bruno mentioned earlier, in Lafarge markets to grow between zero and 5% overall. The growth will continue to come from Lafarge emerging markets in the Middle East and Africa, in Latin America and in Asia. I will begin the presentation with an overview of the quarter, before I turn the call over to Tom to discuss the financial results and the outlook for the remainder of the year. Then, as usual, we'll close with Q&A.

 Operationally, our efforts are being acknowledged by nationally recognized surveys. JD Power and Associates ranks our gas utility the second highest in residential customer satisfaction in the Midwest. The gas utilities improvement from the prior-year study makes it the most improved utility in the nation. Sustainalytics, which looks at a number of sustainable factors, ranked Consumers Energy number one among peers. These recognitions are evidence that our Company is getting better every day.
 Looking back over the last few years, we have consistently grown 7% each year. This is our 12th year of predictable financial performance. Each year, we grow earnings off the prior year's results. Today, we are pleased to provide 2015 guidance of $1.85 to $1.89, consistent with our 5% to 7% growth rate. We are confident in next year's plan and our ability to execute it. We have many upside opportunities that will keep us on track to achieve our long-term organic growth.
 Election Day is less than two weeks away. We have been watching the local and national races closely. The race for Michigan's Governor has remained, as we have envisioned, focused on a number of non-energy issues. The challenger, Mark Schauer, is supportive of an increase in the renewable energy standard, as is Governor Snyder. We will work closely with either administration on making Michigan's energy policy one of the best in the nation. The latest polling results show that Governor Snyder leading by 4% over Mark Schauer.
 The Michigan senate is reviewing energy policy and beginning to construct legislation. Senator Mike Nofs is coordinating two work groups. One is focused on energy efficiency, and the second on renewable energy. An important issue for Senator Nofs is defining clean energy sources, rather than just focusing on renewables. This definition may allow us to capture the 300-megawatt upgrade at our Ludington pumped storage facility.
 As we look around the corner, we see opportunities to continue to grow the Business. The election will be behind us shortly, and we can begin focusing on Michigan's energy future. Next year, we should see improvements with the passage of the 2015 energy law.
 Our competitive industrial rate structure will take effect late 2015. In time, we may see a final order in our upcoming electric case. As we continue to monitor the capacity markets, we also see opportunities for capital investment that are not included in our current plan.

 The largest energy-intensive industrial customers could see base rates drop up to 15% with the new rate design. And including fuel savings, these rates could drop 20% in the next 15 months. These structural changes, rate changes, and fuel savings will improve price competitiveness for all customers, and make Michigan more attractive for large businesses.
 I receive a lot of questions about how we can continue our performance for our customers and our investors. We begin by increasing customer satisfaction, and adding customer value, the foundation of our business model. Every year, about 400 employees leave, and about 300 full-time employees are hired at lower cost, including benefits. With fewer employees, we continue to do more work and improve productivity.  Here is a look at two major construction projects: Crosswinds, located in the east side of the state, will begin commercial operations by year end. With this investment, we are able to meet the state's 10% renewable energy standard 1 year ahead of schedule and at a cost less than planned. In the southwest part of the state, a 24-mile, 36-inch pipeline has been installed, eliminating a bottleneck and completing a 90-mile span. Jari Rosendal,  Kemira Oyj - President and CEO: Thank you, Olli. Good morning. Looking at the full year of 2015, I'm pleased how the outcome came. We hit our own internal targets and were able to improve our operating EBITDA.
 But when I look at the year how it started, we had really low visibility going into the year. We all know how the oil price was coming down. No one knew in the beginning how fast, how low it's going to go and what impacts it has in various industries.
 We had also FX rates going drastically last year. Some of them were positive to us. Some of them were negative to us. But mostly we experienced positive gains from FX.
 Raw materials were strongly on the move also and we didn't see how  quite how that will impact the industry. For us, we had mostly benefits from that. But there are some negative impacts from raw materials also last year.
 There were geopolitical upsets going on. Directly those didn't affect Kemira, but it could have been that it affected our customer base and the markets much more they ended up doing.
 And in the beginning of the year, we were not sure when our AkzoNobel paper chemicals M&A deal would close. We saw that there were no major issues, but we didn't know the timing of the competition official final decisions. Finally, we were able to close in May 1.
 This volatile environment was adverse in some areas of our business, but beneficial in other areas and I think our operational execution went well.  If I now look at about the numbers and go forward from here. So full-year basis we grew top line by 11% and got close to EUR2.4 billion and operative EBITDA grew to EUR287 million and grew by 14%. So we were able to leverage our fixed cost.
 I would like to point out that we guide and we measure ourselves operative EBIT margin. As we are investing to our business through M&A and organic investments, our depreciations go up and with the structural integration of industry, we have some one-times when we do the integration work. So that's why we focus on operative EBITDA and the margin of operative EBITDA.
 So we had some small organic growth in pulp and paper, also municipal and industrial grew organically. Naturally, oil and mining industry came down with the drastic drop of oil price. But all-in-all, we feel that the progress was good in these volatile markets.
 Strong cash flow in the second half of the year. So we built up some net working capital in the first half of the year.  The integration of the former Akzo business is going very well. I'm really pleased at that.  Our new China site called Nanjing, we got it up and running full capacity.  Looking at our competitive situation and looking at the integration in the industry that we are doing with Akzo, we have won a great deal of new machines, especially in APAC. There are four new machines starting up during this year, one started late last year and we won all of those total chemical management packages for the wet-end of the year machine.

Pulp and paper we want to grow double the market growth and we continue to look at selected bolt-on acquisitions. We did a small one also second part of last year. I feel it's also competitive because it's above 5% yield on the share price, so that way above chemical industry average and quite competitive in the Helsinki Stock Exchange.

 We drive both organic and inorganic growth. We drive to improve profitability by operating improvement, leveraging growth and capturing synergies. And I believe on a bigger picture we are on track to deliver that growth also in the future.

 We reported an adjusted EBITDA of $269 million during the quarter, during the fourth quarter, which is 102% higher than the fourth quarter of 2017 and 17% higher than the previous quarter in 2018.  During the quarter, our Iowa Fertilizer Company was one of the main drivers of our growth. Nassef Onssy Naguib Sawiris,  OCI N.V. - CEO & Executive Director: Thank you, Hassan. I will first give an update on recent developments, followed by the outlook for 2019.
 I'm pleased that we ended 2018 on a strong note. We generated strong free cash flow, reduced our net debt by almost $300 million during the quarter and made excellent progress on our deleveraging. We are now clearly starting to see the real benefits of our investments and also benefit from our disciplined commercial approach. We were able to capture healthy selling prices as we stuck to our commercial strategy. Our industry has been plagued by the practice of selling large quantities forward of product during growth seasons, which we see as value destructive. This results in producers making significant commitments that restrict them from fully participating when prices rise. It also allows traders to purchase product at typically seasonally low prices and then become a competitor to producers when the season kicks in. This is why we have invested heavily in on-site and off-site storage capabilities and retained significant working capital flexibility to weather market fluctuations and help realize better value for our production facilities.
 In Europe, we are close to our customers, and we have facilities in North Africa that can efficiently export product to [keep them under use.] In the U.S., we have significant trade and logistical advantages, and we expect this to be especially beneficial at times when there are bottlenecks for product to be transported into the Midwest. Our team has established excellent transport capabilities by truck, rail and barge for our products, with  which, coupled with our very flexible plan, allow for just-in-time production and delivery to respond to customer needs.
 For example, we will have 1,100 lead railcars in season this year from about 400 in 2017. We have global storage capabilities of almost 2 million tons and have invested in a network of strategically leased or owned warehouses in both Europe and the U.S.
 For example, in Western Europe, we have strategically located off-site urea storage, allowing us to position our product close to the customer for in-season usage in Netherlands, Belgium, France and Spain.
 In the U.S. alone, we have almost 0.5 million tons of storage via on-site and off-site storage that give us meaningful flexibility. Our significant on-site ammonia storage allows us to comfortably keep tons that are not taken to [forward] for our customers and achieve a step-up for our spring pricing. On UAN, we have over 150,000 tons of off-site storage in places across the Corn Belt shared between 10 facilities.
 Of course, I  the N-7 joint venture bolsters our storage and adds additional local marketing capabilities for urea in the Dakotas and Minnesota, the biggest consumption region for the product in the US, providing synergies, not only with our U.S. production facilities, but also for value-creating opportunities with our global production base. N-7 is a successful example of value-creating consolidation without any dilution to OCI shareholders.
 I firmly believe that we can maximize netback prices and outperform as a result of our logistics, coupled with our disciplined [techniques].
 As I look ahead first at nitrogen products, in the short term, we expect some shift to fertilizer sales from the first into the second quarter as seasonal demands start picking up at the end of March or in April. Our sales approach will result in some inventory buildup during the low season, which we replaced in our key locations near our customers.
 We are particularly bullish on the outlook for the U.S. for the second quarter of 2019. Here, we expect the catch-up in spring from a poor fall application season, and the USDA is expecting a significant increase of 3 million additional acres of corns. Both factors are very supportive for a strong second quarter in the U.S.
 If I look at our industrial nitrogen products, we expect to continue to capture healthy margin for our melamine business. This is a significant contributor to our Dutch operations. We also expect some growth in our DEF business. This market is growing at rates of more than 15% per year, and we have invested in our logistics to capture this growth. Because of these investments and our N-7 joint venture, we have already signed contracts that represent more than double our 2018 sales volumes.
 If I now look at the methanol market, the supply-demand fundamentals continue to look favorable with very few new capacity coming into the market. We saw some price weakness at the end of the fourth quarter, but in the past few weeks, prices have rebounded, markets in Asia have picked up with an increase in MTO operating rates to above 90% after Chinese New Year.
 Looking ahead, firmer oil prices and the expected addition of 2 new empty MTO facilities in China in the next few months will be supportive for methanol prices and demand. The 2 new MTO facilities will create combined demand of 3 million to 4 million tons of methanol, the equivalent of 2x the capacity of Natgasoline.
 Gas prices are lower than the highs reached in the last quarter. In Europe, we expect to see the full benefits from the second quarter onwards when our European winter exposure hedges will have expired.
 In the U.S., we benefit from hedges at 242 million MMBtu at IFCo for most of our gas needs in Q1, and we have secured prices below $2.30 for Q2. Moreover, we believe both fertilizers and methanol prices have recently been negatively impacted by U.S. sanctions on the Iran, which has resulted in Iranian products being sold at significant discounts into the market.
 Finally, looking at OCI's outlook for 2019. Specifically, we expect our low-cost operations in the U.S. to be a key source of growth in 2019, with tailwinds from fundamentals of our end markets. We are excited that IFCo reached record production levels in the fourth quarter. For 2019, we're looking forward to the full effect of 2 increases in allowable operating rates and from the DEF expansion. We also expect the full income from  impacts from Natgasoline, the doubling of capacity at BioMCN and the 13% capacity increase at OCI Beaumont, which is earmarked for startup this summer.
 As we continue to ramp up our volumes into 2019 and 2020, we expect additional step-ups in free cash flow, which bodes well positively for our future value creation. We will now open the line for questions.

Toby Z. Rice,  EQT Corporation - President, CEO & Director: Thanks, John, and thanks to everyone for joining us today.
 I am humbled to have this opportunity to lead and transform EQT into a modern, digitally enabled E&P company that will create significant value for shareholders. Being the largest gas producer in the U.S. comes with an inherent responsibility to do what's best for our employees and contractors, our landowners, our shareholders and the environment, without compromise. I expect the turnaround that we are executing will lift the company to new heights as it relates to our overall corporate citizenship.
 Before I continue, I would like to take a moment to recognize and thank our employees. EQT has undergone a lot of change in recent years, but I am impressed with our employees' enthusiasm and dedication to the company. Their openness to our new plan is encouraging and their participation will be one of the most important factors in our near and long-term success.
 Getting back to my remarks. My team and I got to work immediately following the annual meeting and have made great progress in assessing the business. We've had some quick wins along the way, but I want to focus my remarks on sharing my vision for EQT.
 Let's first start with a snapshot of where EQT is today. EQT is the largest gas producer in the U.S., with 660,000 core acres in Southwestern PA and Northern West Virginia and 64,000 core acres in Southeastern Ohio. We believe EQT has the deepest inventory of economic locations in the basin and with the right leadership and approach, we can deliver superior shareholder returns in any commodity price environment. Unfortunately, EQT has not yet realized the potential of its asset base. Throughout the proxy contest, we communicated to our fellow shareholders that we believe EQT's legacy performance was the result of poor project planning due to underutilized technology and a disconnected organization. In our first 72 hours on the job, we were able to confirm our diagnosis was accurate. The employees are working tirelessly to improve current operations, but the organization has limited visibility on future development projects.
 Planning in Appalachia is extremely difficult and perhaps more difficult than anywhere else in the lower 48. Our plan is specifically designed to leverage technology to connect the entire organization to improve development planning. A well-designed development schedule planned 36 months in the future is the key to consistent operational execution that will drive lower well costs and more free cash flow.
 Before I talk to the details of our plan, let's look at an example that shows the importance of planning. Please turn to Slide 5 of the presentation we posted this morning.
 What we are looking at here are 2 sets of pads developed by EQT in 2019. The pads on the left represent a poorly planned development run and on the right, a well-thought-out development run. The example gives us the opportunity to isolate the impacts of planning on efficiency and costs, since the same drilling team developed both projects in the same service cost environment. The development run on the left is clearly not an efficient set up. The new wells were squeezed onto pads with multiple existing producing wells. Our drilling team was forced to use complex well geometries to avoid wellbore collisions. The fractured rock down hole caused mud losses while drilling. And the poorly planned wellhead layouts required time-consuming rig maneuvers between wells. These factors led to inefficient and costly operations.
 Adding the fact that these wells had an average lateral length of less than 8,000 feet, and the result was a drilling cost of $325 per foot, which is 80% higher than our targeted cost. Further, because these new wells were offsetting producing wells, approximately 30 million cubic feet of gas per day had to be shut-in for an extended period of time, which contributed to EQT's legacy curtailment issue. And finally, because of parent-child relationships, these newly drilled wells are expected to underperform our type curve by 10% to 15% once they are brought online. We just hit on many of EQT's legacy issues: elevated costs, curtailments in wells that underperform type curves, all explained by a poorly designed development project. So what happens when this team is given a properly designed developed development project?
 On the right side of the page, we're looking at 12 wells developed simultaneously from 2 adjacent pads. This development was initially designed by Rice Energy back in 2017 as part of what we call combo development. This project is currently being drilled by EQT today by the same team that executed the development run on the left.
 Through the first 6 wells, EQT has drilled at a rate of 1,500 feet per day, a 50% improvement versus the previous pad. Drilling costs are trending to around $200 per foot, a 40% reduction in costs versus our prior example. I'll pause here to make this clear. When EQT's operational teams are given properly designed development projects, they are nearly at our targeted well cost goals, which for drilling are $190 per foot. With some additional leadership, improved engineering practices and the right pad layout, these cost goals are well within reach. Rounding out this development run, because we planned these wells so far in advance, curtailment issues are minimized and we expect all 12 wells to perform at or above type curve once turned online.
 This example is focused on drilling, but we are seeing the same thing on completions. When our completion teams are given poor projects at the last minute, their efficiencies are half of what they are on properly planned projects. You may ask, "Why would EQT develop the pad on the left?" The answer is simple. EQT did not have a better location to send the rig and the teams were given orders and incentivized to hit production targets. Unfortunately, less than 50% of EQT's future schedule is currently set up for efficient development, as illustrated on the right. This is why we are here.
 Our jobs as leaders of this organization is to align the workforce to march towards these large-scale development projects so our operational teams can execute. Our vision in path to well costs of $735 per foot ends when 80% of our development looks like what you see on the right. This is what we're simply calling the end state.
 The end state is where all planning tasks are completed at least 12 months before spud, giving our execution teams the opportunity to succeed every time they step onto a pad to drill and complete a standardized well design with the lowest possible cost, on budget, on schedule and for maximum value. To give you a sense of how achievable this is, by the end of our time at Rice Energy, we had definitive and detailed development planning 3 to 5 years into the future.
 Combo development represented more than 80% of our planned activity. That type of visibility becomes very powerful for decision-making, particularly around capital allocation. Planning further out in time also provides for better oilfield service contracts, lower well costs, greater leverage for commercial arrangements, ample freshwater pipe to the site for completion operations and sufficient midstream and downstream capacity for new production. This is how we get well costs to $735 per foot and hit type curve for each and every pad.
 I realize this sounds simple, it is not. That said, it is our job as leaders of this company to take complicated tasks, such as master planning, and simplify them for our employees to execute.
 Our first step towards the end state was the creation of our Evolution Committee. This committee is comprised of EQT's Executive Team as well as Danny Rice, Derek Rice and Kyle Derham. The committee will serve as the primary liaison to the Board with respect to the execution of the 100-Day Plan. Under the oversight of the Evolution Committee, we are going to transform EQT to our planned end state in 3 key areas. First, we're going to restructure the organization to be function-based. Employees will have clear roles and priorities that facilitate efficient project planning and execution. Over the last 130 years, EQT's org structure has morphed into more than 50 departments that has led to a lack of accountability. We'll reorganize the business into 16 departments with roles that better match the life cycle of a well.
 Second, we're going to bring new technology to this organization to foster the level of inter-departmental collaboration and real-time decision-making that the end state requires.
 The company currently operates in a very silo-ed manner. Data and workflows are trapped in e-mails and each department is acting on predetermined department goals, even when the goals of the organization may demand adjustments. The solution here is to implement a digital work environment that has been customized to run an Appalachian E&P business. This platform, which we used at Rice Energy with great success, will break down silos and bring transparencies to data and workflows to enable more value-driven decisions.
 Third, we have high-graded leadership where needed to execute our vision. I'm happy to report that we have hired all 8 Evolution leaders mentioned during the campaign. On the operational side, we've added a VP of Operational Planning to oversee proper planning and coordination of future development; a VP of Asset Performance to oversee management of the optimal well design for each of our operating areas; a VP of Drilling and a VP of Completions to ensure well designs are consistently executed. On the technology side, we've added a Chief Information Officer and a VP of Digital Technology to oversee the buildout of our key digital solutions and change the way we work. On the organizational side, we've added a Chief Human Resources Officer to create a world-class culture and a Director of Evolution to ensure the transformation remains in compliance with established audit, governance and risk controls. These 8 leaders previously worked together in the same end state at Rice Energy and are currently marching on the 100-Day Plan we outlined.
 And finally, we'll achieve the end state by properly aligning, valuing and supporting our people. EQT's employees are motivated and hard-working, but they have not been allowed to reach their full potential. In addition to the benefits of the operational, technological and organizational changes I discussed earlier, we are to challenge our employees with proper goals, recognize them in real-time and align them through incentives. This will allow them to see how they contribute to the company's mission: achieving the end state and making EQT a better business for all of its stakeholders. I'm committed to making EQT the best place to work in Pittsburgh, and these steps will get us there.
 Stepping back, how long will it take before EQT is executing at well costs of $735 a foot? As we laid out in Slide 10, we expect a gradual improvement of well costs as best practices are implemented and efficient development  inefficient development is removed from the schedule. Master planning takes time, but we expect our schedule to be predominantly combo development-runs by mid-2020, which will lead to a step change in well costs to $735 per foot around that time.
 With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Jimmi Sue to share our second quarter results.

 Second quarter 2019 adjusted operating revenues were approximately $958 million, down 6% compared to the prior year as a result of weaker pricing, partly offset by the higher sales volumes.
 Average realized sales price for the quarter was $2.59 per Mcfe, $0.22 below the average price in the second quarter of 2018. The decrease in average realized price was primarily due to a decrease in higher-priced liquid sales and Btu uplift as a result of the 2018 divestitures and lower NYMEX net of cash settled derivative.
 Total operating revenues for the quarter were approximately $1.3 billion, up roughly $360 million, as the second quarter of 2019 included $408 million of gains on derivatives not designated as hedges, compared to a $54 million loss last year. This reflects the increase in the fair market value of our NYMEX swap and options due to declines in forward prices during the quarter.
 Now moving on to operating expenses. Second quarter operating expenses were down approximately 5% as $118 million impairment charge recorded in the second quarter of 2018 and lower production expenses in 2019 as a result of the 2018 divestitures more than offset increases in SG&A, proxy cost and lease impairments in the period. The increase in SG&A was a result of royalty and litigation reserves of $38 million recorded during the quarter. The lease impairments primarily relate to acreage exploration, mostly outside of our current development plan.
 At the unit cost level, second quarter 2019 total cash unit costs were $0.02 higher than the second quarter of 2018. Of note, EQT's transmission costs per unit was $0.54 per Mcfe, which was $0.02 higher than the second quarter of 2018 and $0.03 above the high end of our guidance range. This increase was primarily due to higher unreleased Tennessee Gas Pipeline capacity. As a reminder, we have unused capacity on this pipeline in Northern Pennsylvania. We typically either release this capacity to others or, depending on market conditions, purchase gas to sell off the pipeline.
 When released, the cost of this capacity is netted against the released revenue in net marketing services. When we move gas from the pipeline, our gas or third-party gas, the cost is reported in transmission expense. We have increased our guidance range for transmission costs for the year to reflect our current expectation for the use of this capacity in 2019.
 As noted above, SG&A was impacted by royalty and litigation reserves this quarter. Adjusting for these items, SG&A was $0.13 per Mcfe, which is within our annual guidance range.
 Now moving to cash flow items. Second quarter adjusted operating cash flow was $386 million, compared to $529 million in 2018. As noted in our press release, second quarter adjusted operating cash flow and adjusted free cash flow included the impact of approximately $38 million of royalty and litigation reserve and $22 million of proxy, transaction and reorganization-related expenses. Excluding these 2 items, operating cash flow would have been $445 million and adjusted free cash flow would have been a negative $21 million, which is slightly better than the favorable end of the range that we provided in June.
 Our second quarter capital expenditures of $466 million were better than internal expectations for the quarter, primarily due to continued efficiency gain.
 Looking forward, we are guiding to third quarter volumes of 365 to 385 Bcfe at an average differential of negative $0.55 to negative $0.35, and we reiterate our full year capital expenditure guidance of $1.825 billion to $1.925 billion.  With respect to free cash flow, we have updated our annual guidance for the strip price as of June 30. At this level, our net debt to trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA leverage is at 2.1x. When reduced for the value of our investment in Equitrans Midstream using quarter end pricing, it's 1.7x.
 With that, I will pass the call to Kyle.

Kyle Derham,  Rice Investment Group - Partner: Thanks, Jimmi Sue. I've had a chance to get to know many of our investors over the last few months. I'm currently a member of the Evolution Committee. And I'm working alongside the team to execute certain finance, corporate development and investor relations initiatives as well as helping form our general capital and allocation strategy. To help set expectations, I would like to lay out our guidance plan for the next few months.
 Jimmi Sue walked through some of the changes to 2019 guidance, but we are suspending our outlook in 2020 and beyond as we develop our revised plan. We expect to come back to The Street with longer-term guidance in the next 60 to 90 days, but I will spend a few minutes providing some directional color on where we expect things to shake out.
 We will be taking a different approach to capital allocation to many of our peers. In today's commodity price environment, there's a high bar to allocate capital to the drill bit, especially given the opportunity to improve our leverage profile and buy back stock at 10-year lows. We believe EQT trades at a significant discount to its intrinsic value, and while we recognize many E&Ps share this trait today, net asset value will always be an anchor for us to make the right capital allocation decisions. Fortunately for shareholders, EQT also has the potential to generate substantial near-term free cash flow per share even at current strip pricing, and that will be our focus going forward.
 As Toby mentioned in his comments, EQT's legacy capital and efficiency was a function of poor development planning. Our near-term strategy will be to remove high-cost development from the schedule and focus our land, permitting and planning teams to transform that development into a combo development run that we can drill in 12 to 24 months.
 This disciplined approach to development has several benefits. First, the capital efficiency of our program improves because we are only deploying development dollars when we know we can execute highly economic projects. Second, we generate more near-term free cash flow that can be used to repay debt and buy back stock. Third, we put less near-term supply on a soft gas market. And lastly, we give our midstream service provider a chance to catch its breath and provide water and gathering services at the lowest cost possible, greatly improving their capital efficiency and free cash flow.
 The ultimate level of our development capital spend will be determined by the number of economic projects we have to drill measured against the opportunity to buy back shares and achieve our leverage targets. Production growth, if any, will be an output of that decision, not a target. We will be driven by growing free cash flow per share, which we believe is the key to driving shareholder value.
 In making these near-term decisions, we have maximum flexibility as all of EQT's rig contracts roll off by the end of the year and we have minimal long-term commitments to other services. We will use that flexibility to design the most efficient program possible with services procured in the soft service cost environment.
 Stepping back. Over the last 3 months, the forward gas strip has weakened, bringing significant pressure to the balance sheet to both public and private gas-levered E&Ps. There are approximately 75 rigs running in Appalachia today and 50 in the Haynesville. We believe the vast majority of these rigs are subeconomic at strip pricing. The equity in gas markets are sending a clear message to operators to cut growth to maintenance levels and some will need to go further than that.
 While we have started to see a pullback in activity, more is needed to balance the market. We believe the marginal cost of supply is well above strip and the market will work itself out over the long term. That said, all of our efforts are geared towards transforming EQT into the lowest-cost operator in the basin to weather what could be a challenging 2020 and position the business for long-term success when prices normalize.
 Turning to the balance sheet. In general, our policy will be to target forward leverage of less than 2x net debt-to-EBITDA at the lower of strip gas prices or $2.50. Free cash flow and any potential divestiture proceeds will be used to achieve this leverage profile and any additional cash flow will largely be returned to shareholders via stock buybacks. We are committed to the investment-grade rating and believe access to low-cost financing will be a strategic advantage over the next several years. We believe this policy will allow us to maintain investment-grade metrics. And we look forward to engaging with the agencies over the coming months after we have finalized our long-term development plan.
 One lever we can pull to manage debt is our retained interest in Equitrans, which is worth approximately $900 million as of today. While we are evaluating a divestiture, it is not part of our immediate plans. Any potential exit will be done responsibly, and we have several options at our disposal. For now, we are benefiting from the 10% dividend yield and see several positive catalysts for Equitrans as we transform EQT.
 First, while there may be a reduction in our volume forecasts in the near to medium term, we expect that our ability to hand Equitrans a fully baked schedule that plans combo development 12 to 36 months in advance will greatly reduce their capital needs and boost free cash flow. We saw this happen in 2017 at Rice Midstream Partners following Rice Energy's upstream transformation, and we expect it to happen for Equitrans as early as 2020.
 Second, we are working together to simplify our services contracts. While we all recognize the gathering fees are on the high end of the market, our strategy allows for other levers to be pulled that will be a win-win for both parties, including increasing utilization of freshwater systems and the construction of produced water disposal systems. These opportunities should lower our overall cost mix, while providing incremental revenue sources for Equitrans. We have already engaged with Equitrans management, and both sides are thrilled to start working together to develop this world-class resource and deliver gas to market at the lowest cost possible.
 Regarding asset sales, we're in the process of reviewing all of EQT's assets and remain open to divesting acreage or production as it fits within our capital allocation framework of maximizing free cash flow per share and NAV. To summarize, we are taking a differentiated approach to capital allocation. We are in the process of rationalizing EQT's development schedule and we will come back to The Street with a revised long-term outlook that reflects the potential of this world-class asset while also respecting the current commodity price environment.
 With that, I'd like to open up the call for Q&A. Operator?

Bill Urich,  The Boston Beer Company, Inc. - CFO and Treasurer: Thank you, Jim and Martin. Good afternoon, everyone. We reported net income of $25.4 million, or $1.88 per diluted share, for the second quarter, representing an increase of $5.7 million, or $0.42 per diluted share, from the same period last year. This increase was primarily due to shipping increases partially offset by increased investments in advertising, promotions and selling expenses.
 Core shipment volume was approximately 1.1 million barrels, a 25% increase compared to the second quarter of 2013. We believe distributor inventory levels at June 28, 2014 were at appropriate levels. Inventory at distributors participating in the Freshest Beer program at June 28, 2014 increased slightly in terms of days of inventory on hand when compared to June 29, 2013. We have over 65% of our volume on the Freshest Beer program, and we believe participation in the program could reach up to 70% of our volume by the end of 2014.
 Our second-quarter 2014 gross margin decreased to 53.1% compared to the 53.6% in the second quarter of 2013. The margin decrease was a result of product mix effects and increases in packaging and ingredients cost, which were only partially offset by price increases.
 We are currently maintaining our full-year gross margin target of between 51% and 53%.
 Our second-quarter advertising, promotion and selling expenses were $15.7 million higher than costs incurred in the second quarter of 2013. The increase was primarily the result of increased investments in media advertising, increased costs for additional sales personnel and commissions, point of sale and local marketing, and increased freight to distributors due to higher volumes.
 General and administrative expenses increased $1.8 million compared to the second quarter of 2013, primarily due to increases in selling and benefit costs.
 Based on information which we are currently aware, we have left unchanged our projection of 2014 earnings per diluted share of between $6.00 and $6.40, but actual results could vary significantly from this target.
 We are currently planning 2014 shipments and depletions growth of between 20% and 24% and national price increase of approximately 2%. Full-year 2014 gross margins are currently expected to be between 51% and 53%.
 We intend to increase investments in advertising, promotional and selling expenses by between $37 million and $45 million, an increase in the range from the previously communicated estimate of $34 million to $42 million. This does not include any increases in freight costs for the shipment of our products to our distributors.
 We estimate increases of between $3 million and $5 million for continued investment in existing brands developed by Alchemy & Science, which are included in our full-year estimated increases in advertising, promotion and selling expenses. These estimates could change significantly, and 2014 volumes from Alchemy & Science brands is unlikely to cover these and other expenditures that could be incurred.
 We believe that our 2014 effective tax rate will be approximately 38%.

These estimates include capital investments for existing Alchemy & Science projects of between $7 million and $9 million.

 Now to the proposed federal regulations for coal-fired power plants. The Canadian federal government has outlined its proposed regulations regarding the reduction of carbon dioxide emissions from coal-fired generation. It was released last Friday and the draft is to be published in the Canada Gazette on August 27. A 60-day comment period will follow. There are no surprises in the draft regulations from Maxim's point of view and, of course, we'll be commenting to the federal ministry. If adopted without revision, the regulations would allow us to continue to run M1 commercially and profitably until the end of 2019 and commission M2 as a supercritical, pulverized coal-fired power plant before July 1, 2015. Pending carbon policy has not impacted any of our project development plans.
 On a related note, similar moves in the US by the EPA to reduce emissions through the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule should reduce the availability and energy from conventional coal-fired plants in the US and is expected to increase the capacity and energy values for gas-fired assets. You may recall that Maxim owns and operates 4 such plants in the northeast US with a total of 383 megawatt's of capacity. In terms of Maxim's development projects, all of our development projects remain on track and can be advanced on our timelines without dilution and this is rationale, in part, for having layered in part year hedges to protect cash flows and that is to support a non-dilution financing strategy. As Mike pointed out, our CFD hedges are somewhat unique and offer more upside than as realized by many.
 Turning to M2. On August 10, 2011, the Alberta Utilities Commission issued their final decision approving the Milner Expansion Project. Maxim did not consider the appeal of the interim decision to have any merit and that shall certainly remain the case in the event that the final decision is appealed by any party. Maxim has been working on the M2 Project since 2005. Our public consultation process has been to the highest standard and our facility's application was complete in all respects, including all environmental matters. The application to construct M2 and the AUC approval, after what the AUC describes itself as a complete and exhaustive review has been anything but a rush to beat proposed carbon dioxide regulations, which until June 2010, were not even on the table. M2 is a reliable, low-cost generation supply option that will meet the needs of Alberta's consumers. It will reduce per unit CO2 emissions by 20% by replacing old and retiring conventional coal facilities in the province and is part of the solution in achieving the federal and provincial emissions reduction targets for 2020 and beyond.
 Turning to Mine 14, we continue to believe that Mine 14 offers not just significant value but extraordinary value as a fuel source for Maxim's existing Milner Plant, the Milner Expansion Project, and for sale of metallurgical coal. Unfortunately, I don't think M14 is well understood outside of our Boardroom and I apologize for that. M14 had always been primarily a future physical supply option in contemplation of the expiry of our coal-supply contract at the end of 2013 but it is also a high-grade metallurgical coal resource. Now as we were developing this project, metallurgical coal prices rose dramatically in 2008 and 2009 and they have remained very strong. Met coal is a very valuable commodity and M14 is our most attractive development project with an extremely rapid payback.
 We have received significant interest in M14, so in 2010 we tested the market in terms of a potential sale or joint venture. During that period, international thermal coal prices also strengthened very significantly and varying materially relative to our coal-supply contract which was signed in 2004. That is why our existing coal-supply contract even with the new price indexation factors remains very much in the money today. There are very few alternatives, other than Mine 14, that are more attractive than our existing fuel supply arrangement. So our strategy is as follows  until such time as we can arrange an appropriate call on residual fuel or tailings from M14 in a dialogue with any other party or secure a low-cost supply of coal for the years 2013 and beyond, we've elected to preserve our options on both the self-supply and the met sales options which would commence in years 2012 and 2013, just to be explicit.
 The construction and completion of Mine 14 will allow us to start producing run-up mine coal, non-washed coal by the end of 2012 and ultra-fine washed product by the end of 2013 putting us in a position to have no-supply risk in terms of fuel at Milner 1. Now, if thermal prices fall, which they may very well do given the prospects of conventional coal-fired facilities being retired in North America, we would happily contract for supply and monetize M14 in some other fashion. Both options remain open to us at this date.
 So you may want to know what we have achieved during the quarter in terms of advancing and derisking the M14 project while preserving these options. Well, there's 4 areas; one, we've confirmed the project attributes. We've extracted and tested unoxidized coal from both seams which has improved our yield assumptions. The yield of metallurgical coal is now a better assumption or a better scenario.
 We've prepared detailed metallurgical specifications of a low volatile resource and we're finalizing the wash plant design and we've confirmed the marketability and desirability of the met coal. We've received a bankable feasible study which is an update of our previous feasibility study from our independent mining engineers, and we've incorporated Summit Coal Inc., which will be the general partner that will manage all of our coal marketing and operating activities. Those are the project attributes.
 In terms of reducing the execution risk, we have refined our CapEx estimates through a comprehensive competitive tender process. We have a very narrow range of contingencies and we are very confident with the capital that's required to either construct the self supply or the metallurgical or ultra-fine wash scenario. We've built a team with coal marketing, underground mining and project management expertise, and now I want to talk about our just-in-time capital investment model. We have structured the CapEx on this project such that we can continue to fund the project without dilution.
 And then lastly, and this is item four, we've preserved the project timeline. Construction activities such as mine, site portal construction and temporary construction access will commence this fall. Maxim continues to anticipate that Mine 14 will be fully commissioned and producing run of mine coal by the end of 2012 and met coal by the end of 2013. Now, of course, various options to capitalize or monetize Mine 14 will be preserved and considered dynamically but we are going to continue to derisk this project on a non-dilution financing strategy. So, in summary, what I would like to say is that we think our outlook for 2012 and beyond looks very good. We're reaffirming our guidance and we think that we're in relatively good [step]. That concludes our remarks. Thomas, to you for any questions.

 With us on the line today are Mr. Assi Bartfeld, President and CEO; and the rest of the management team. Following a summary of the results, management will be available to answer any questions. I note that an English translation of the results are available on the Delek Group website.

And in 2017, there has been a decrease in the production costs at Ithaca to around $19 per barrel compared with a production cost of around $23 per barrel in 2016. In September 2017, the company's floating production facility FPF-1 was connected to the oil transmission pipeline. Connection of the facility to the pipeline allows the transportation of the oil from the reservoir via pipeline rather than using tankers, which was the case until now. We expect this will lead to further improvement in efficiencies and lower operating costs. In addition, the company's floating production facility was chosen as the facility of the Vorlich reservoir, of which Ithaca holds 34%. Mark Ferguson,  Renovo Group - Co-Founder, CEO: So thank you very much and thank you for the opportunity to speak about JUVISTA. I'll begin by saying that Renovo is a biotech company and we were outlicensing JUVISTA. We had a lot of interest in JUVISTA. We had a lot of competition for the deal and we chose Shire for a number of reasons, not just because of the finances of the deal, but because we believe that they will make an excellent partner in the commercialization of the drug in a new market.
  And I think it's a mark of the strength of that that they've invited me here to talk to you so you should see this as a very serious partnership between Renovo and Shire and from Renovo's perspective, that we are delighted with it.
  So what I want to tell you about is the market for an anti-scarring drug and a little bit about JUVISTA itself.
  So first of all, this is a drug for the prevention and reduction of scarring. So just think about it. Any time you have surgery, you have an accident, emergency, trauma, you cut yourself, you get a scar. This is a drug that prevents or improves the scarring.
  There are no approved pharmaceuticals in this market. I'll tell you something about the size of the market in a moment. But unlike new pharmaceutical markets, this is a highly primed market, so if you think about it, when you go into a new area to begin with, you often have to spend a lot of money in educating doctors, telling them about the disease and so on. That's not the case here.
  Surgeons discuss scarring with patients routinely. If you're going in for an operation you'll typically ask, 'What's the scar going to look like?' 'What are you going to do to minimize it?' And surgeons will very rapidly identify for you those patients where they have a high concern for scarring. And that's about 46% of patients, and it's really quite obvious. Women, children, scars on the face, scars on the hand, colored skinned individuals who scar worse and so on.
  So there's a lot of discussion; there's a highly primed market.
  What's currently available? Good surgical technique. Our drug improves upon good surgical technique.
  JUVISTA is not a miracle. It does not turn a butcher into a plastic surgeon. It is actually a drug that improves incrementally on the surgery that you're doing. So aesthetic surgical technique is very good. There are a whole series of over-the-counter products, vitamin E, aloe vera, onion skin extract, whatever, that you can purchase. In double-blind, randomized trials, these products do not work but they sell very well. They're over the counter therapies. That tells you that patients are very interested in scarring.
  So a typical comment that we get from plastic surgeons is they will advise the patient that they viewed over the counter products and they don't work and they will also say the patients buy them anyway because they want to try and improve their scar.
  And then finally if you have a bad scar, the way that you would improve it is have a plastic surgeon cut that scar out. That's scar invasive surgery. Use his or her fine surgical technique to try and improve upon the existing scar that was there.
  So what does the market look like in the US? We have obviously licensed all of the world apart from Europe to Shire. The big piece of that is the US so I will focus for the purpose of the Shire shareholders on the USA.
  So what we did with the Mattson Jack Group, basically said go on out and analyze the ITD codes, the hospital discharge codes and ask the simple question, 'How many Americans every year go in the hospital either to be cut electively or an accident and emergency?'
 And remember when you go into surgery; I used to be a clinician so I joke with my colleagues and I tell them, surgery is trauma by appointment, okay? You make an appointment and somebody cuts you. So that's where you go in the hospital and you can do that. There's 42 million Americans every year that roll up to a hospital to be cut. That's a big number.
  You know I put that in perspective of the number of potential patients who are perhaps depressed in the United States or have osteoporosis or asthma or diabetes. That's a bigger potential market than any of those. It's right up there with the big markets that support blockbuster drugs but there is absolutely nothing in this market for this.
  How does that break down? Look at the pie chart and ignore the numbers just to begin with. I know you'll find that difficult but just ignore the numbers and think about the pie chart.
  So the red bit is plastic and cosmetic surgery. That's people who are having face lifts, tummy tucks, breast augmentations, abdominalplasty, that's plastic surgery for cosmetic purposes.
  The small piece in black labeled 'Moles' is minor lesion removal, moles, warts, lumps and bumps, typically what dermatologists do.
  In yellow, reconstructive surgery. That's plastic surgery that doesn't have a cosmetic element, so that's for example reconstruction following trauma, following major excision; a mastectomy for example, a woman following breast cancer.
  Elective minor surgery in the office in the US, that's exploratory surgery say for your joints or what have you.
  Elective surgery in the hospital, Caesarean section in a woman, laparoscopy and then trauma and injury.
  So since there are no drugs in this market place, then you might think how big is the potential market place for sales. So since we are a UK company we take a very conservative view. Think about the most analogous product and the most analogous product in our book is BOTOX, because almost certainly a good segment of JUVISTA sales will be self-pay.
  BOTOX is for wrinkle reduction, wrinkle removal. That is not as high a medical need as JUVISTA. Remember, scarring, burned children, traumas, is one big medical need, as well as cosmetic surgery. But just take that as a comparator. BOTOX you give every six months. Our drug you only give once, and on average BOTOX costs about $400.00 US per treatment given every six months.
  So let's assume that we price JUVISTA $100.00 cheaper than that. This is simply for the purposes of illustration. I am not saying that's where we'll price it. The dosing of the drug is every linear centimeter of wound margin. So you inject every linear centimeter of wound margin. Most wounds are five centimeters long. There are very ones that are longer than that. That's the average size of the wound. So that's about $50.00 US per linear centimeter of wound, average price at about $300.00, $250.00, $300.00 US.
  Now you look at the penetration. On this slide are the weighted average penetrations in these various sectors. If I was that determined, the Mattson Jack Group talked to 150 US surgeons, plastic surgeons, dermatologists, general surgeons and so on and they said, 'Where would you use a drug with the profile of JUVISTA generated from our clinical trials?' So this is not some abstract airy-fairy nonsense. This is the actual data that comes out of JUVISTA.
  And they would obviously be children, you know who go over the handlebars of bicycles, a woman, lesions on the hand and so on and you can see the penetrations are quite conservative. Even in cosmetic surgery, only 56% penetration assumed, gives you a weighted average of 40%.
  So you run the numbers. $300.00 US, 40% penetration into this 41 million operations every year in the United States and you come out US peak sales $4.1 billion. Now that's just in the United States peak sales.
  Is the purpose of this slide to tell you that the US market is $4 billion or $3 billion or $5 billion? The purpose of this slide is to tell you that even with conservative pricing, even with conservative assumptions about penetration, this is a multi billion dollar opportunity.
  There were a lot of companies who were interested in licensing JUVISTA. I can safely tell you that none of them, but none of them, had price projections or sales projections that weren't in the multiples of billions. This is a big opportunity even with modest pricing.
  What's very interesting about anti-scarring is that it spans everything from serious medical need; that's burned children, major trauma, accident and emergency, which would be reimbursed, all the way through to the medically trivial but commercially very attractive cosmetic and aesthetic surgery, which would not be reimbursed, which would be self-pay.
  And we, and I think Shire, see that as a big advantage in the competitive landscape that currently exists. Self-pay is really important. And I can tell you, I do not know any patient who is having cosmetic surgery who wants to have a bad scar. And equally, I do not know any plastic surgeon in the United States who claims to have worse scars than anybody else. I know plenty who claim to have better scars, but I don't know anybody who claims to have worse scars.
  So that tells you that this is a highly primed market in terms of patient need and also in terms of doctors wanting to prescribe the drug.
  There's also a big upside; you don't need any upside, but there is a big upside in scar revision. Scar revision is one of the areas of our clinical trials. That's where you have a bad scar and a plastic surgeon excises that scar, uses his or her fine surgical technique to try and get a better result.
  Of every ten patients that go into the doctor's office in the US for scar revision, the doctor will only offer it on one or two of them. And those are the numbers that are in our projection, about one or two.
  The reason is that in the other eight or so patients they do not believe they can improve the existing scar using their fine surgical technique alone. If you have a drug that significantly improves scarring, you might imagine that a larger number of people with existing scars might request scar revision and you might imagine that a lot of doctors might increase the performance of that operation and that's what the bottom bullet says. Large upside for latent scar revision market. That's in none of our numbers. That's in none of our projections. It's icing on the top of the cake.
  Okay, so how do we measure scarring and what does the drug do? So we have reached agreement with the regulators. Obviously this is a new area. We are the first people to bring a pharmaceutical along to try and get it approved. And what we do is we take photographs of the scars and most importantly all of our clinical trials are with in-patient controls. That means it's the same patient having drug or placebo, typically bilateral surgery done at the same time by the same surgeon, double-blind fashion. One wound site gets drug, the other gets placebo.
  And that's the most demanding task of the drug because you're not comparing placebo or drug in different people. By the way it also reduces the variation and it cuts down the numbers that are required in our clinical trials.
  So what we do is we take standardized photographs of these scars, typically 12 months after the surgery has been done, and we show them to a panel of plastic surgeons, eight plastic surgeons under standardized fashions, and then they use a visual analog scale, which is a ten centimeter line; zero is normal skin, ten is the worst scar. They make a mark on the line where they think it is.
  So if you look at the example that I've got here under the thing where it stays standard care, VAS 7.32. This is one year after surgery. This is the scar. You can see it's red, it's pigmented, it's elevated, and the plastic surgeons thought on average that scored about 7 on the VAS score.
  On the other side of this patient was the drug treated. This is after the blind is broken. You'll see that score is 3.23, significantly lower. It's a lot better. You can see that for yourself. It's not as red. It's not as elevated. It's paler, blends into the surrounding skin.

Chris Beckett,  Pacific Drilling SA - CEO: My name is Chris Beckett. I am the CEO of Pacific Drilling. Pacific Drilling is a relatively new entrant ultradeep water drilling contractor. We are NYSE-listed. Market cap of a little over $2 billion, although it's somewhat volatile in today's market.
 We have about 1,100 employees to date and the fleet of eight Samsung-built ultradeep water drill ships of a consistent design. Contract backlog of about $3.2 billion.
