Over the last two years, that pace of growth has ramped up appreciably as we've brought the newbuild  first of the newbuild rigs into the market.
 If you look back to the first quarter of 2011, we had four rigs on order, none of them operating, two of them contracted. About $1.5 billion of backlog and about 500 employees, and we were listed over the counter in Oslo. Fast forward a year and we have migrated our listing to New York, almost doubled the size of the Company in terms of employees, ordered two incremental rigs, delivered three of them and put them to work, and increased our backlog to $2.1 billion.
 Today we have eight rigs  four on order, four working. The fifth one will be delivered in the next month or so. We have the first six contracted. We have two available rigs that will be delivered in 2015 late 2014, sorry, and 2015.
 We have increased the contract backlog to $3.2 billion and grown the Company again to 1,100 employees. That will continue to grow to a target of about 1,800 by the end of 2015.
 So we continue to grow the Company. We are doing so with very much a strong focus on developing a sustainable competitive advantage. We believe that will come to us through the combination of performance excellence, measured growth with the right assets, and a very strong focus on capital management.
 Now there is no golden bullet in this business. You have to be able to deliver what the client wants. We are a service company at the end of the day, we just happen to use very large assets to provide that service. And our ability to differentiate hangs on our ability to deliver to the clients that which they are looking for.
 We believe that there are really four cornerstones to our ability to do that. The first is the quality of our assets. As I said, we have eight rigs either in operation or under construction, all built at Samsung Heavy Industries, who are recognized as the premier constructor of drilling rigs.
 It's a very consistent fleet. We believe that it's right-sized, that there is an optimal size to be a drilling contractor and we are approaching that now. And that we have brought the right technology to bear.
 We have taken a very targeted approach to both the geographies we work in and the clients that we work for and we have developed a very strong operating team to run those assets and deliver to the clients the service quality they are looking for. All of that is driven by a very strong focus on functional excellence that drives both our desire to not be the biggest but to be the best. And, in fact, we think being the biggest is actually contrary to being the best.
 You need to have the right resources, the right focus on performance, the right ability to oversee the details, and the right processes in place to do so. So we have built the Company from the ground up with a very specific focus on some of the areas that we think the industry tends to be weaker on — supply chain, human resources management, and financial management. These are the cornerstones that will allow us to reach our goal of a sustainable differentiation.
 So when we look at our asset base, it is today the youngest and most capable fleet in the industry. This chart shows average age on the vertical axis and water depth on the horizontal, but you can replace water depth with mud pump capacity or mud capacity or top drive capacity or lifting capacity or bed space or any of the other metrics you want to use. We plot out in the same places the benefit of having the newest fleet.
 Others have similar rigs, but nobody has the same consistency across the fleet.
 Those new rigs have always been preferred by clients. We look back over the last five years at the level of utilization and you can see a very clear distinction by generation. The newest rigs are the most sought after and the rigs that get marketed and contracted first and stay working.
 But, increasingly, we are seeing a drive from the clients not only for newer rigs to go to new areas, but for newer rigs as replacement for older rigs. The first five generations of rigs were built to go toward new market or a new area, to go ever deeper in the water.
 The last two generations, the sixth and seventh gens as we are now delivering, are about doing the same job better or about drilling the same wells faster or about drilling better wells for the same amount of money. So that the per barrel cost of developing fields and, frankly, finding those fields and appraising them is lower for the client.
 These new assets are able to operate in locations to drill deeper and longer offsets, to use more complex completion technology, to operate in more demanding environments, high pressure, high temperature very deep wells, and do so in a much more demanding regulatory environment than we used to face. When you look at today's fleet, over half the fleet is more than 10 years old, and those rigs are the rigs that are going to find it increasingly difficult to compete with the modern assets, even paying a premium for modern assets.
 So we think we've got a great fleet and it's in the right part of the market. We also think the fact that it's a standardized fleet gives us a fundamental advantage in terms of maximizing our revenues and minimizing our costs. We train people on one rig; we can take them to any other rig in the fleet. It's effectively the same place.
 The carpet might change color, but that's about the only variance. They're running the same equipment. They are living in the same sort of accommodation. They are doing the same job.
 So we can apply lessons learned on one rig to the rest of the fleet very quickly. We can train our people once and not have to retrain them. We can share fleet spares and inventory much more effectively across the whole fleet.
 Then interchangeability of resources across the fleet allows us to deliver consistent service quality declines, irrespective of which vessel they take. They know if it's a Pacific Drilling rig it's the same, irrespective of which rig it is.
 We are also bringing some new technology to market. Dual gradient drilling is a technology that was technically proven 10 or 12 years ago in a joint industry project, but it was never commercialized because at the time it wasn't necessary. We weren't drilling 35,000-foot wells in 10,000 feet of water. But today it is necessary and it brings significant benefits.
 It brings benefits in terms of the safety of the drilling process. The fact that we have a closed circuit allows us to have much more rapidly  identify any kind of pressure change in the well and any kind of incursion into the well of hydrocarbons and respond to it much more quickly. We get to much more closely map the pressure gradient in the well bore to that in the surrounding rocks, which allows us to drill the well with fewer casing streams or fewer casing points.
 Every time we have to stop and put a casing string in place it takes us 10 days of otherwise nonproductive time. In today's spread cost environment, that's $10 million. So if we can reduce the number of times we do that in a given well, and our belief is in the Gulf of Mexico we can reduce that by 2 to 3 casing points, that saves the client anywhere up to $30 million or $40 million on a $100 million well. That's pretty significant potential value to them and low-hanging fruit.
 The real benefit of this, though, is that the number of casing point you have or the fact that you have to put a new casing string in place is the limiting factor for how deep you can drill. So by using dual gradient technology we can drill reservoirs that previously couldn't be drilled and, ultimately, the clients can book reserves that they couldn't previously booked.
 So this has a huge potential value. We just loaded up the last piece of equipment onto the Pacific Santa Anna, which is the world's first dual gradient rig, and it will start using that equipment in anchor for the first time on the well that it's due to start in the next couple of weeks.
 It won't be a full dual gradient well. We are still field testing the equipment, but we expect to be drilling the first dual gradient well end of this year, early next year. So we're getting pretty close to proof of commercial concept.
 So this sort of focus on bringing the right technology that will help us build the relationships we target with clients. In the case of dual gradient technology, it's a joint project with Chevron. Chevron, as you can see, is our largest client.
 They have contracted four of our drill ships. They took two fairly early in the process and they've recently contracted two more, which shows that they are both satisfied with the service we are providing and look to us as a partner at this point. We will be their largest provider of ultradeep water rigs for the next couple of years.
 We have also got Total on board as a client and Petrobras, so a $3.2 billion backlog with premium clients and pretty well laddered. We have got availability, though, in the fleets with the newbuild Pacific Meltem, which will be delivered in the middle of next year. Pacific Bora was due to rollover and will have repriced to market rates in the middle of next year as well. That should happen sometime in the next couple months.
 Pacific Scirocco has fixed-price options, so that's going to almost certainly be exercised by Total because, frankly, they are well in the money and they've already told us they intend. The Pacific Zonda will be the eighth rig that we add to the fleet in the first quarter of 2015. That leaves us with an eight-rig operating fleet and a goal to continue growing but at a measured pace.
 Now we haven't bought those contracts. We have earned those contracts through our ability, the quality of our assets, and our people. Pretty much all of our contracts have been in the upper half, if not the market-leading rate, at the time at which they were contracted.
 Now in today's market, some of them look kind of low, but that is because the market has moved a long way in the last couple of years. We are pretty pleased and proud of our record for contracting rigs at premium rates.
 So even though we are a new company, we didn't have to buy our way into this market. We were accepted on the strength of the quality of the Company and the assets that we have.
 We have delivered on our operational performance to back that up. Now starting up a new ultradeep water rig is always a challenge and, as you can see, we've had some volatility in the first six months of operations on each of our rigs. Some of them have come out and done exceptionally well straight out of the gate. Pacific Scirocco delivering 95% revenue utilization.
 Others have had more challenge. The Santa Ana we had some BOP issues that were fairly well made clear at the time and they are behind us. But if you look at the second six months of operations once we've been through that shakedown period, got the rigs to the operating status they should be at, we have delivered exceptional performance averaging 95% revenue utilization in the second six months of operation. That's pretty unusual and we are pretty proud of it.
 We've also done that very safely. Our safety record exceeds that of the industry by a margin and we continue to focus on safe operations as a key basis. We don't operate safely as an addition. It is the only way we operate.
 We have know had  the first three of our rigs have now passed two years without an LTI and we intend to keep delivering that quality of service to our clients.
 I think a lot of the time you can tell the quality of overall operational performance of any rig as easily through its safety performance as you can through anything else. Invariably, if a rig has safety issues, it also has operational issues in other areas. So this is something we watch very carefully, not just for the safety, but also because it's a leading indicator for overall performance on the rigs.
 So as I said, our focus is on delivering a sustainable differentiation through the combination of performance excellence, measured growth, and very strong capital management. If you look at growth as an opportunity in this space, the entire market has continued to grow very attractively.
 It's a global market. The Atlantic Basin, which is where we operate, the Gulf of Mexico, South America, Nigeria, Ghana, are the core areas. They happen to be the largest growth areas in the immediate future, but there's a lot of other growth within the ultradeep water and expansion into new parts of the world.
 Our view of the world tells us that in aggregate the market will stay undersupplied through the end of 2015. We don't have an explicit forecast beyond that, but we don't see any reason why supply is going to able to catch up with demand in 2016 either. So we think it's a very robust market going forward and we are extremely comfortable that this gives us a great marketing ability to put the rigs to work at premium rates.
 Now I think there has been a lot of confusion in the world of drilling over  at least of investment in drilling over the last couple of months, because this is not an industry that historically has a very stable pricing environment. If it's not going up, it's going down and we have bucked that trend for the last 12 to 18 months.
 We've had a market that has basically been range bound plus or minus 5% around $600,000 a day for the best part of six — of 12 to 18 months. And that's unusual, but it's also true. I think it's driven by a number of things.
 This fundamental undersupply means that there is more than sufficient demand to use [up all the] assets, but there's also a ceiling on how much premium clients are willing to pay for prompt availability or shorter-term when they know that they can order a rig to be built into the future by one of the drillers at a significant discount. Just as Shell did with Transocean.
 So that caps the premium they are willing to pay. We will see rates in that same range, I think, for the foreseeable  the next couple of years, because there's nothing that is going to drive the rates down that we see. But there is also not — there's enough of a cap provided by that alternative of building to order that we won't see $700,000 day rates either. Except in exceptional circumstances where prompt availability is a requirement and maybe shorter-term, difficult work environment.
 But that sort of rate, $600,000 a day, is an extremely healthy return for us and you've seen these rates remain pretty solid for an extended period now. There was a lot of noise about how the market was slowing down earlier this year. Frankly, it didn't happen.
 If you look the average contracting rate, i.e., the number of rig years contracted each quarter for the last five years, it averages out to somewhere around 26 rig years per quarter. And we've delivered right around that for the first two quarters of the year, so there really hasn't been this dramatic slowdown that people were worried about in the pace of rig contracting.
 I think you'll find that by the time we get to the end of Q2, this will be — Q2 will look like a very strong quarter again and Q3 is shaping up to be equally strong. So the markets continue to be robust, both in terms of rates and in terms of the level and pace of activity.
 I know that tends to confuse people because everyone is expecting to see it move in one direction or the other. And, frankly, it's staying as a very strong, robust market that we are very happy to be part of and that we intend to keep growing into.
 We have a target of a 12-rig fleet. We have eight rigs on order or in the water today. The pace of that growth will be dictated by market conditions, but also by operational constraints of the pace at which we want to add new rigs to ensure that we can both construct them properly and introduce them into the markets so that we get them up and running and generating revenue as quickly as possible.
 Now that for us is a pace of about one rig a year, so today our eighth rig will be delivered in Q1 of 2016 — 2015, sorry, and if we were to build a ninth rig, we would not be looking for delivery before Q1 of 2016 or maybe Q2. That means we don't have to order that rig until the end of this year/early next year, and so we will make that decision as we get closer to that date. But we don't intend to order any more rigs until then.
 When we do, we will go through the same process we have with the others, which is a turnkey contract with the shipyard to remove the construction risk. We will make sure that we don't have any more than two uncommitted rigs on the fleet at the time. That means that we want to get a contract formally announced on the Meltem before we go ahead and do that.
 We are going to build at one of the premier shipyards. It may not be Samsung next time because we think we can maintain the synergy and equipment irrespective of who builds the hull and, frankly, we want to go to market make and make sure we get the best pricing we can from the constructors. Defense sales, which represented 48% of Aerospace, increased in the half. Civil business weakened beginning with the business and regional jet markets.
  Filton is solidly on track. Sales of GBP169m with trading profits of GBP18m were recorded in the first half. Margin on a normalized basis was around 9%, ahead of our expectations.
  OffHighway sales declined through the first half. Quarter two was down 47% on prior year versus quarter one down 21%. Broad-based weakness was evident in agriculture, construction and mining.   Net interest of GBP30m was up GBP4m from 2008 due primarily to the absence of balance sheet translation cover. The Group's overall borrowing increased due to the Filton acquisition. Lower borrowing rates had a favorable effect.
  Other net financing charges relate mainly to our pension. The combination of the return on scheme assets, offset by an interest charge on our liabilities, resulted in a GBP23m non-cash charge. The change year over year was driven by the fall in value of the scheme assets during 2008.
  Our one financial covenant, EBITDA to net interest, stood at 5.2 times for the 12 months ended June 2009, well clear of the minimum of 3.5 times in our bank facilities.
  On the next slides, I will review the progress we've made on cash generation. Despite seeing trading profit fall significantly year over year, operating cash flow of GBP45m was only GBP15m lower than 2008. I will discuss in more detail the actions we have taken to deliver cash on the next slide.
  This chart highlights the details of our cash performance between the halves. As the EBITDA red bar shows, the dramatic fall in profit presented a challenge in our efforts to generate cash. Since December 2008, the cash flow benefit from inventory movement was GBP95m, a major contributor to the fall in average working capital levels.

Len Schleifer,  Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc. - Founder, President and CEO: Ying, thanks for having us. I know you have a lot of questions and there may be some questions from the audience that you want to get into. But let me just make a couple of initial observations about what's going on in our industry and how it affects Regeneron's operating in this environment.
 As we all know, this is a brand-new environment over the last several years, where an industry which has cured terrible scourges, which has brought breakthroughs for blinding diseases, which is making advances in cancer, which has been unthought  never thought could be possible a mere decade ago, is one of the most hated and reviled industries in the world. And how do you square that circle? And how do you operate in such an environment?
 And I think the problem is that many of the wounds really are self-inflicted. That is, rather than getting the credit for doing all the great things that the biotechnology and biopharmaceutical industry does, the headlines, of course, are all the bad things we do. Whether it's we promote off-label  not we, Regeneron, but as an industry people have been  paid all sorts of fines for that. People have bought up drugs and raised prices by astronomical multiples in an unconscionable way, frankly. If not illegal, certainly unconscionable.
 But even reasonable companies have derived growth over the last decade or so largely from price raises. If you look at one of the most important classes of drugs, one we are going to be entering, rheumatoid arthritis, there had been drugs that were initially $10,000 a year as their initial price are now $40,000 a year. So obviously, the public is balking back at this. It's really important that we get this right. And how do we operate in this kind of environment?
 I think that the secret to operating in this environment plays well to our strength, which is innovation, innovation, innovation. If you can't grow your business by price increases  and mind you, our biggest drug, EYLEA, which has now got a global run rate of close to $5 billion  has never had a single price increase since we launched it. If you operate in an environment where price increases are not really going to be possible, in fact discounts are going to be the rule, you have to be innovating like crazy and bringing lots and lots of products to market as quickly as you can.
 And it's going to have to be more of the old-fashioned way. You're going to have to keep bringing new products. And so that's how we think of things, with 13 products in clinical development, with getting  in the midst of a launch for PRALUENT, our drug for hypercholesterolemia. And hoping to launch two more products over the next 12 months. That's our answer to the environment is to keep innovating.
 So with that, I'll be happy to answer your questions, Ying.

Len Schleifer,  Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc. - Founder, President and CEO: So, under the Affordable Care Act the Medicare has some broad authorities to do some tests and implementation and perhaps a test that implements the entire market. And in their desire to try and control costs. I think it's important to remember that  let's talk about Part D before we get into Part B for a minute. Part D are the normal drugs that are outpatient drugs not administered by doctors, such as PRALUENT. And it is a myth that there's no negotiation of price, by the way, because the Medicare carriers who provide the Part D coverage all negotiate with us on PRALUENT, and lots of rebates were given. So I just wanted to make that clear.
 But now the Part B, where Medicare covers drugs that are given  bought by doctors and then administered to patients, such as EYLEA. They are looking to ways to control costs. And of course it's not just the eye drugs they're focused on, although EYLEA is a big one, but there's lots of oncology drugs, etc. We have looked at this pretty carefully and we've spoken to lots of people in Washington about this. The notion that some rule could mandate that seniors somehow use a cheap version of an anti-VEGF such as Avastin, and use Avastin in place of EYLEA  you would be forcing Medicare patients, rather than based on their doctor's choice but based on price, to take a drug that has never been approved for this indication by the FDA, is not manufactured by conventional manufacturers, is repackaged.
 And there have been lots of issues associated with that. And in the government's own testing, independent testing, Avastin was an inferior product to EYLEA. But in the government's own evaluation. So, it is hard for us to imagine, and there are a lot of people, a lot of organizations  the retinal physicians, a lot of congresspeople, senators and so forth on both sides of the aisle  that feel that, particularly in this setting, that would be a huge disservice to patients, which I don't think CMS wants to do.

 And I think it has to do with EYLEA perhaps being a longer-acting agent, and in that study being given a bit more consistently. So I think the easiest way to make sure that we're doing the right thing for patients is to make sure that we are not systematically undertreating them. Adding something, we hope PDGF  and as Mike mentioned, I think you mentioned ANG2 as well  is another agent we're testing in single-injection combinations. And that's going to be user-friendly to the doctor, the patient, and frankly, to the cost system because we don't have to worry about charging for two separate injections.

Len Schleifer,  Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc. - Founder, President and CEO: Some of the psoriasis  anti-TNF drugs and others that have been developed have been  they've got a theme on their direct-to-consumer advertising that it's not just a rash. I don't know if you've seen it. It struck home for me, even greater with atopic dermatitis, which in my opinion can be even more severe to patients than psoriasis. Because psoriasis, many view  although that's not the only view  many view it as a cosmetic problem. Atopic dermatitis is a terrible problem.
 People are truly debilitated both physically, by having moderate to severe covering of their body, frequently almost their entire body surface. These people can be suicidal. There is an increased rate of suicide in this population. These are people who have dropped out or tried all of the healthcare system, or are offered very powerful, unapproved and somewhat dangerous, I believe, systemic immunosuppressants to try and deal with this. This is a disease that causes super infections, it can cause sepsis.
 And we think we have a transformative approach here. We call it transformative; the FDA calls it breakthrough, based on our data. And so far, remarkably enough, it has been a drug that's generally very well tolerated. There was some conjunctivitis in our study, some other low-level things. But for the most part people just continued to take the drug because anything that was happening was not severe enough or worrisome enough for them to stop. So we are pleased with that. We've got important, longer-term data coming out. We hope to get filed sometime in the third quarter and get it to market just as quickly as possible.
 Now, who is the market right now and how big is it? When you are creating a new market I think it's just impossible to know. I know I love  every time somebody asks me how big is the market going to be for dupilumab, I remind them of what their estimates were for EYLEA, which was $80 million in the first year, and we did $800 million. And then I remind them what the estimates for PRALUENT were, which were $10 billion or $100 billion class, which we are struggling to do millions.
 So, predicting these things is not the easiest thing in the world. And so I would rather think of it  is there a medical need out there? Absolutely. Are these underserved? No question. Are these patients really ill? Is this a serious problem? Absolutely. Do we have something that could be a breakthrough? So far it certainly looks that way. Obviously, if you start to look at people who have been treated with systemic immunotherapy and a suppressive therapy, even though it's unapproved, those people  and there are lots of those. Those are the kind of people who would be natural. And obviously we're going to go to dermatologists initially who are familiar.
 You could save us some money, by the way, Ying. Do one of your surveys so we don't have to do them. Go talk to the dermatologists who prescribe biologics for psoriasis and tell me how many patients that have that they would prescribe  somebody must know that at the Company, but I would rather you did it than we spend the money on it, which would be handy. But that's the kind of patient population we would try and address.

Mike Crews,  Peabody Energy  - EVP and CFO: Thanks, Vic. Good morning, everyone.
 Peabody's second quarter results reflect ongoing cost containment actions that are yielding significant benefits, lower capital spending, and additional debt reduction in line with our previous expectations. We are executing well in these focused areas as we continue to navigate the current coal markets. Let's review the quarterly results in more detail, beginning with the income statement. Second quarter revenues totaled $1.7 billion on sales of 61 million tons. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $254 million and includes a $21 million charge from an adverse court ruling dating back to a 2006 issue and a $12 million impact related to a voluntary employee separation program in the US.
 Adjusted EBITDA from US mining operations was largely in line with last year, as lower revenues were offset by cost reductions. Year-over-year Australia contributions continued to be affected by sharply lower prices; the effect of which was partially mitigated by lower operating expenses.
 Moving down the income statement, you'll note that we took a $21.5 million impairment charge to write down a minority equity investment in Asia to its current trading value. You'll recall that we exclude impairments from our adjusted EBITDA definition. We also had $7 million of higher interest expense associated with the court judgment, as well as our early debt extinguishment. And we recorded a $148 million income tax benefit related to our revised annual earnings outlook. Diluted earnings per share totaled $0.39, with adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.33.
 Now, let's turn to additional details in our supplemental schedules. In the US, volumes were in line with the prior year with the modest mix shift toward more western tons. Revenues per ton declined 5% from prior-year levels, reflecting the roll-off of legacy contracts in line with our expectations. US unit costs were down 6% on average with improvements in both regions, where we continue to focus on maximizing margins through cost reductions and shifting volumes to the most productive operations. We continue to target full-year costs 2% to 3% lower than the prior year.
 Turning to Australia, volumes rose 5% on the prior year on increased output from several mines, including the PCI operation. This was offset by more than $200 million [in effect] from lower settlements from both seaborne met and thermal pricing.
 During the quarter, we shipped 4.1 million tons of met coal at an average price of $123 per short ton and we sold 2.6 million tons of seaborne thermal coal at average price of $77 per short ton. Our Australia team continues to advance our cost containment initiatives, reducing costs by 6% from 2012 levels to $73 per ton. The team also worked through impacts from geologic issues at two operations during the quarter.
 Cost benefited from improved productivity at the remediated PCI mines and the recent owner-operator conversions. For the first time in a number of years, we would note that the Australia dollar is also providing some relief to our cost position. Based on the progress of first half cost cutting, we are again reducing our Australia cost targets to the mid-$70 per ton range for the full year. Now in trading and brokerage, half of the quarter's results were driven by the court judgment I discussed.
 The remaining $20 million loss was largely associated with $14 million of unfavorable mark-to-market movements on economic hedges that will reverse at delivery of the related fiscal shipments in the third quarter. Trading results also continue to be affected by lower market volatility and reduced structure transactions. Resource management turned in a very strong quarter that included a sale of undeveloped reserves in the Midwest for prices in excess of book value. We will continue to seek opportunities to monetize surplus properties in the portfolio.
 That's a review of our income statement and key earnings drivers. You'll note that operating cash flows totaled $60 million during the quarter, which includes semi-annual interest payments and a payment in Australia to preserve our tax position during an ongoing audit. During the quarter, we reduced debt by more than $100 million, while still retaining $518 million of cash at quarter end. Capital expenditures totaled $93 million, less than half prior year levels and we are lowering our capital targets for the full year by approximately 20% to $350 million to $450 million by continuing to trim our sustaining capital needs and reduced project spend.
 Looking ahead to the third quarter, we're targeting adjusted EBITDA of $210 million to $270 million and adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.16 to earnings per share of $0.09. These ranges reflect expectations for increased US volumes, lower pricing, and carryover impacts from geologic challenges as we work to improve production at the North Goonyella and Burton mines. I also refer you to our Reg G schedule in the release for additional details regarding DD&A, taxes, and other line items. That's a brief review of our second quarter performance and outlook.
 For a discussion of the coal markets and other updates, I'll now turn the call over to Greg.

Greg Boyce,  Peabody Energy  - Chairman and CEO: Thanks, Mike, and good morning, everyone.
 I'm proud of the work of the Peabody team in removing some $130 million from the cost structure in the first half. We view these cost reductions as sustainable and believe more improvements are coming. As Mike noted, in addition to cost controls, we continue to reduce capital and pay down debt. I'll first review the market indicators and outlook and then discuss Peabody's actions as we continue to take the necessary steps for these market conditions. Within global markets, both elements of the supply and demand equation have been at play during this period of market softness. Demand growth has been lower than originally expected, reflecting economic conditions both in Asia and Europe.
 While at the same time, the overhang and seaborne supply represents follow-through from projects that were initiated in recent years when prices were higher and projections of demand greater. Still, we've seen favorable changes to both the supply and demand picture globally and we do not believe the current prices are sustainable in the long term.
 Within the global coal demand, both China and India imports have risen year-to-date and are on a pace to increase 15% this year to new record levels, as the trends to urbanize, industrialize, and electrify continue. Japanese coal use is climbing and in Germany, coal market share's back over 50% as nuclear use declines and natural gas prices remain high. We expect seaborne thermal coal demand to increase some 50 million tons in 2013; the fuel existing plants, as well as the approximately 75 gigawatts of new generation that start up during the year. Metallurgical coal demand is also increasing with Chinese and Indian met coal imports expected to rise 10% this year.
 Now, in regards to global coal supplies, output reductions are occurring in the two largest coal-producing nations, China and the United States. Industry reports note that some 45% of the Shanxi producers are unprofitable at current prices. US coal exports declined 30% in June, as contracts continue to roll-off. The Indonesian government is again discussing steps to limit coal exports and increase domestic use. Mongolian exports to China remain below prior year levels.
 In longer term, the lag effect of reduced project capital may set up a sharp rebound when demand accelerates. That is the historic trend that often follows periods of significant underinvestment. Within the US coal markets, we continue to see improvement in both supply and demand fundamentals as we move through 2013. Natural gas generation is down 15% year-to-date as natural gas prices are up 50% over year-ago levels. Meanwhile, US coal generation is up 11%, with industry shipments down 5% this year.
 These trends come despite a summer that has started in earnest only in July, with cooling degree days down almost 10% versus normal so far this season. What does that mean? It leaves customer inventories for Powder River Basin coal more than 25% below last year, at a bit over 60 days of supply. We think this should move into 50s on days use later this summer. Longer term, we continue to see a significant growth in Powder River Basin and Illinois Basin coal demand during the next five year period.
 This occurs as some plants retire, primarily in the eastern US. At the same time, recovery continues from low gas prices, some new coal plants are coming online, basin switching is occurring and most coal plants can run at higher average operating levels. We believe these factors will combine to continue to boost US coal demand from the Southern Powder River Basin and Illinois Basin; the two regions in which Peabody leads in both sales and reserves. Now, looking to the second half, we continue to expect US markets to improve as stockpiles normalize and uncompetitive production is removed from the system.
 That's a summary of market drivers affecting both metallurgical and thermal coal fundamentals. Against this market context, we believe that Peabody is well-positioned to succeed. At the beginning of the year, we said that we were focused on operational performance, cost improvement, capital savings, and debt reduction. And I'm pleased to say that we have had major successes in each of these areas.  At our PCI operations, we reduced costs by more than 20% after major work to boost productivity, increase overburden removal, widen benches, improve equipment availability, and implement multiple process enhancements. While we clearly are not pleased with the changes in coal prices since our acquisition, the operations are running very well and the asset base is better than expected. And our owner-operator conversions are also exceeding expectations with costs now down more than 20% at the mines we converted.
 Overall, in Australia, our productivity and cost initiatives will allow the team to reduce the contractor and employee work force by more than 20% since the beginning of the year, without affecting our production target ranges.  One of the major benefits to our capital program in our owner-operator conversions in recent years, is a modern equipment fleet and significant base of installed capacity. These allow us to increase our productivity and maintain our production, even with low sustaining capital spending levels going forward. As a result, our sustaining capital levels should be below the low end of our traditional range of $1.20 to $1.75 per ton for the next several years. And as to our level of project or growth capital, we will have market conditions dictate future project development timing and ultimate spending levels.
 Finally, we continue to have what I believe to be the best reserve portfolio and project pipeline in the business. And our production base is aimed at the best growth market served from the US and Australia. Within the seaborne markets, Australia is looking increasingly competitive again, given its improving cost structure, proximity to the best end markets, and recent favorable currency movements. Peabody has worked through challenging market cycles before and we find that such conditions allow us to emerge even stronger during the upcycles.

John Allan,  Exel plc - Chief Executive: Right, I'd like to take you through a fairly brief strategic update. And I'll do this pretty quickly because some of this is material you've seen before for background. There isn't a whole heap of news as we're continuing to pursue essentially the same strategic direction. So, in that context the overall strategic direction of the Company is unchanged. We're endeavoring to surround our customers successfully with a whole bunch of capabilities that lead them to conclude that we're the right people to entrust their business to and that is working pretty successfully.
 But what we did say in November was that within that there would be some very key management imperatives and things that we were going to be particularly focused on over the years ahead. But we'd essentially concluded the phase of building our global scale and global footprint. Tibbett & Britten was a final piece in the jigsaw in doing that. And that for the next, at least, 3 years we would be very strongly focused on delivering value to our stakeholders, to our customers so that we can win more business for our shareholders and indeed hopefully if we succeed with the first 2 categories to our people.
 And the key imperatives to do that were to  the completion of integration, successfully and productively. Demonstrating that we could show very strong financial performance and then showing the underlying organic growth capability of the business. And I'd like to comment briefly on each of those during the course of the next few minutes.
 But starting with integration as an issue, we've already touched on Tibbett & Britten but let me take it a little bit further. We have actually achieved quite a lot. We talked before about the overhead synergies, the cost savings we've made that's fine. But we have now completely integrated our organizational structures worldwide and there no longer is a Tibbett & Britten business  separate Tibbett & Britten business units. The integration is totally complete in 70% of the business.
 The biggest places in the U.K. and the U.S. and Canada there is now 1 business. For example, in the U.K. we closed the Tibbett & Britten U.K. head office in Daventry before the end of the year. We closed the Tibbett & Britten accounting center in January. We moved Tibbett & Britten contracts on to our accounting platform, management teams are integrated. Really there is  Tibbett & Britten is no more and a similar picture in the U.S. and Canada.
 Over the course of this year we have more integration work to do in mainland Europe. Tibbett's had some quite substantial businesses in France, in Spain and elsewhere and putting those together with the historic Exel businesses was a little bit more complex but we have very, very clear plans which are going to deliver real benefit through the course of this year and will be fully realized in 2006, principally in mainland Europe.
 And that's  I'm very satisfied with the rate of progress, the amount of focus that that's getting. We are making good progress with the principle under performing margins, businesses, operations within Tibbett & Britten. We have made significant management changes in Mexico. Frankly, the management team there now is the historic Exel management team is 1 of our strongest management team led by a gentleman called Jose [Nava].
 In South Africa we've had to take out most of the senior Tibbett & Britten management and we've drafted in a strong management team from the U.K. and we're close to appointing a new business leader within South Africa itself, somebody with a very good track record. And I think we're pleased with the progress. By bringing the larger Tibbett & Britten business together with the historic Exel business we're releasing about £2m of annualized synergy savings. And we've brought the head office much closer to the business.
 In Mexico we have integrated the back room operations, moved Tibbett's on to our systems. We've still got an issue which is they had invested in quite a lot of new space in Mexico, mostly good quality space. That's a bit of 2 edged sword. It means that we have space to fill but on the other hand the incremental impact of filling that space over the course of the months and years ahead will be very, very beneficial. And so is our major sales drive to grow the business in Mexico to make use of that new space.
 And we're certainly very confident that we're now well placed to make improvements in 2005 and particularly in full year in 2006. And I think these operations hopefully will have disappeared off our watch list before the end of this year. And we're continuing to look for further synergy opportunities. We haven't totally drained the swamp in terms of synergy potential. So, we continue to look for more.
 Can I turn just for a moment though to look at the customer side of Tibbett & Britten? That's all to do with efficiency and integration and costs and so on. What about the customers? Well, I think it's been a very, very pleasing result so far. We were very focused on delivering strong operational performance during the winter peak period. A lot of Tibbett & Britten customers were major retailers, the delivery of peak performance in the run up to Christmas absolutely crucial to them. I've been around to see quite a lot of their U.K. customers. And I think universally they're very pleased with the fact that service standards have been at least maintained and in some cases improved.
 And I think the evidence of that is that we have now either renewed contracts or gained additional business, you know renewed. By renewed I mean extended contracts. With two-thirds of Tibbett & Britten's hot 15 customers since the acquisition. And those wins include 7-Eleven in the U.S., Proctor & Gamble a number of sites around the globe, Seiyu Wal Mark which I'm going to talk some more about, particularly significant strategic win for us in Japan.
 And losses remain minimal. We talked to you last autumn about the contracts that we had exited by mutual agreement in the U.S. There have been none further. We have lost 1 contract in mainland Europe. And frankly I'm not aware that we have lost any business at all in the U.K. which is the largest single market. And we are very, very confident that the previous guidance we gave you of about perhaps £5 to £7m of contribution loss through lost contracts still remains appropriate.
 Now, let me talk now about other aspects of integration. Tibbett & Britten's clearly been a major preoccupation for the last few months, now starting to be behind us. But we've also had a lot of work to do in Japan. During the course of this year we bought a very substantial business about £200m of revenue from Fujitsu. That company has exceeded. It's now been renamed Exel Logistics. It's exceeded our financial expectations in it's first 7 months of operation. It's given us a very strong presence in the technology sector in Japan but not just in the technology sector. And frankly, there is further potential with Fujitsu elsewhere in Asia Pacific. They've actually become our large  single largest customer within the region.
 And it's given us a platform, a base upon which we can build. And we've won some business from technology companies unsurprisingly 1 very large 1, which is already in operations and then our first major retail contract in Japan, more of that later. So, very pleased with the progress that we're making in Japan.
 Turning for a moment to perform, I hope our results I think begin to speak for themselves in terms of the emphasis and focus that we're putting upon performance. Over the next few years we'll brief you on a series of initiatives in this particular box. And the only 1 I want to comment specifically on this morning is GCM, our Global Capacity Management program. That's an Airfreight procurement initiative and just a few words on that.
 It's still early days. We only began to implement this at the back end of last year after quite a lot of planning. But it's focused on the fact that we buy in about $1b worth of Airfreight spend which significantly reduced the number of preferred carriers down from about 26 to 16. We think we're going to see some benefits not just in terms of cost but high levels of service from those airlines, more stable pricing, improved consolidation efficiencies, better availability in peak periods and so on. And pleasingly that program is meeting its early targets. We track it week by week and month by month and thus far it's on track.
 Now let me turn to the third aspect, our third really key management imperative for the years ahead and that's to grow. And within that the primary focus is going to be on sustained organic growth. We're not turning off the gas on acquisitions but we're certainly turning the tap down very considerably and I'll say a word about that in a moment. Such acquisitions as we make are going to be bolt on, highly focused.
 So, the real focus is, the real challenge is can we generate sustained organic growth. And we believe we can. And we have some very clear strategies to deliver that growth. We're working very hard on deeper penetration of our existing customer base. It's a great customer base. In most cases there is a huge amount of additional potential if we are competent enough and smart enough and capable enough to realize it.
 We're focused hard on fast growth in developing markets. We've talked to you about that before. I'll say a word or 2 in a moment. And we're turning up I think significantly the resource we're devoting to the development of new solutions and value added services, which we think is 1 of the keys to not only ensuring that we've got healthy revenue growth going forward but that we actually do something to enhance our margin potential as well. And to support all of that, we continue to focus on growing our global talent pool through both management development of the talented folks that we have got right across the globe and also by recruitment at all levels.
 And all that we believe will enable us to deliver sustained revenue growth. And in the 13% organic growth number for revenue that we delivered in the second half of 2004 that will take some doing to match that on a consistent basis but that's the sort of aspiration that we have, something that is certainly around double-digit level.
 Now last year we actually, I think, saw pleasing progress despite you might have argued the potential distractions of dealing Tibbett & Britten. We saw our net contract wins in Contract Logistics up 28% where we are maintaining margins on gains in all regions. We're absolutely relentless and ensuring that we don't take on business that is not satisfactory and profitable, certainly not intentionally anyway.
 And the trend in outsourcing continues to be particularly strong, particularly in the Americas where over 60% of our gains were from first time outsourcers and that's good business to make. And we've made a good start in 2005. And we've included in this slide, I won't go through it, an indication of what is the source of those wins. I've talked about 60% in the Americas coming from first time outsourcers, across the globe it's rather lower than that it's about 43%. About a third of the business was won from competitors and about a quarter comes about because people set up new operations. They restructure and that creates a new contract opportunity.
 Turning to Freight Management I think John's mentioned earlier the strong performance in terms of volume. The left hand side of the slide shows our performance for the year against our estimate of the market. Those are banded sort of estimates because I think it'll be a while before firm market estimates are available. But we were clearly ahead at 18% of a market that grew somewhere between 9 and 13%, even if it's the high end of that estimate we were significantly ahead of it. And pleasingly we were ahead of the market in all 3 regions as well.
 Now the Airfreight market continues to be predicted to grow at about 6.3% over the next 20 years. And you know what that means, if that is delivered and it's not out of line with historic rates of growth that the market will more than treble over that period. So, there is very substantial market growth available here.
 And the same is true in Seafreight where we managed to grow our revenues by 19% in 2004. Again, we believe ahead of a market growth of about 13%. And this is growing if anything faster than Airfreight. International Seaborne Container trade is estimated to grow at 9% in 2005. So, we are out performing the market again after a brief lapse from that and believe that we are capable of doing so on a going forward basis as well.
 I said we'd be spending less time on acquisitions. And I'd like to really repeat the message and slightly expand on the message we delivered at the Investor Relations day. We're very clear the areas that we are potentially prepared to consider are these. There are a few key developing markets where in order to either create market entry or critical mass it may be sensible to make modest size acquisitions.
 We are very interested in this area of value added services and I'm sure we'll have more to say about that in the years ahead. And we're still interested in Seafreight although we're tilling the Seafreight field quite intensively and not finding much that is worth looking at at the moment.
 Since the Investor Relations day we've made 1 significant acquisition and 3 small ones Power Packaging in the U.S. I've got a slide on that at the moment. A small Portuguese healthcare business called SODILOG. This is just adding to our network of healthcare businesses around the globe and particularly around Europe. And 2 small specialist waste businesses which enhance the capabilities of core Environmental.
 And we believe that our acquisition spend between now and the end of 2006 will not exceed £100m. To give you an indication of the level of acquisition spend we anticipate going forward about £50m per annum.
 Now, 1 [plant] in our growth strategy is value added services and Power Packaging fits very, very firmly into that. We acquired the business really right at the end of last year, December 31 or January 1 this year. I can't remember which technically. It's a very, very sound business with a very strong customer base. You can see some of the customers on the right. They include some of the world's largest food companies Kraft, Unilever and General Mills and Campbells and there are a number of others not on this list. It's essentially producing new products for branded manufacturers. It's not involved in commodity sectors. It's got 7 very good [ESGA] approved facilities in the U.S. and Canada. And we've only got a month's results under our belt but for what it's worth that first month was very satisfactory.
 And we think that this right at the front end immediately after core manufacturing between that and our campus warehouses, our secondary packaging capability we had already, is going to permit us to bring some interesting bundled offerings to some of our major branded food customers in the U.S. And at the moment this is a U.S. and Canada business only. No immediate plans to extend it beyond that unless and until we've really learnt the market and are satisfied that it is extendable into other geographies.
 Now, we continue to work very hard on our customer base. We've shown you the ways that we are working round the world with Unilever and Proctor & Gamble and others in the past. Here's a new example, 1 we haven't quoted before really just to have something fresh to say. Johnson & Johnson another major customer of ours, and interestingly we are working with them in 6 continents now North America, South America, U.K. and Europe, in South Africa. A very strong business in Australia and New Zealand where we managed to transfer the relationship that we had at senior levels of J&J to a new acquisition we made back in 2000. And now increasingly we're making inroads in Asia as well.
 And that slow, patient addition to the business contract by contract we are working with the consumer products part of J&J. We're working with the [ethical] pharmaceutical people. We're working with medical devices, medical equipment. Frankly, we are only scratching the surface of this customer. There is potential to double, treble, quadruple the level of business we have here if we are diligent enough I think in applying ourselves to really understanding the potential that exists within this customer and what we need to do to get more access, that potential.
 Now the third strand of our growth strategy is really working very hard. This footprint that we've got and we showed you this slide at the Investor Day in November that showed that we'd now bought coverage virtually everywhere that matters both in terms of GBP and also population. And I think population because in some ways that a proxy for [the] future economic growth for those sort of current economic substance and future, perhaps economic potential.
 And we continue to work very hard at developing our business in China. It's going very well in India. It's going particularly well in Brazil, great progress there. But I thought just because we hadn't used it again before and to bring something fresh to the party that I'd just spend a moment on Indonesia. Now this is a country we only entered in the early part of 2003, principally on the back of a couple of our freight forwarding customers, customers wanting us to be directly represented in Indonesia and also the opportunity to pick up and manage a new contract with Unilever.
 Since then we have begun to build a very solid business. Not only with a lot of multi-national customers, consumer products people like Gillett and in this case J&J, pharmaceutical companies like Glaxo Smith Klein, some automotive customers, some technology customers like Dell and Hitachi and others and Eriksson. But also interestingly our first significant retail contract in Indonesia was a company that frankly I hadn't heard of before we pitched into pitch to them called Matahari.
 They're the largest retailer in Indonesia. They're very anxious to have access to best practice in terms of supply chain, very mindful of the fact perhaps that their market is going to be attractive to international competitors in future. And they want to be in good shape to stand up to that competition and they really came to Exel and said "look we'd like you to show us just how good a retail supply chain can be". So, I think a very interesting relationship which we've started there and I think very significant business potential in Indonesia. And pleasingly, this doesn't I think take away from the terrible tragedy at the turn of the year, no impact on our business within Indonesia.
 And I talked a moment earlier about our first retail win in Japan and I'd like to just dwell on this for a moment because I think we've actually managed I think to generate very quickly there living proof of the way we go about things. And that really reflects 3 things. First of all starting to mine the Tibbett & Britten customer base and 1 of Tibbett & Britten's best relationships and they had some very good customer relationships was with the international division of Wal Mart with whom they were working in Canada in a very large way and also in Germany. And we've obviously worked very hard to reassure that customer that the arrival of Exel was good news rather than bad.
 Secondly the fact that we had now got this Japanese Logistics platform as a result of the Fujitsu acquisition and thirdly, if you like, I think Exel's approach to global account management and the consistent processes that we bring to bear on that.
 Anyway putting all of those 3 things together and putting together a team from Europe, from Canada and from Japan, we were successful in winning a major piece of business which we announced on Monday of this week with Seiyu which is an associate company of Wal Mart in Japan. This won't actually commence until 2006 but it really puts us on the map in terms of Japanese retail. And we are delighted. It's substantial. It's relatively long term and I think more important, it's breaking new ground for us within that market.
 And I talked earlier about the need to keep refreshing our talent pool in order to be able to support this level of growth. And I've got a slide just  I could spend time talking about all the recruitment and development we're doing at the various levels of the Company, but I thought I'd just spend a moment on what's happening closer to the top of the house. And quite a lot actually, in January we announced 3 new appointments to our Executive Board Clifford Herbertson, Siegfried Putzer and Paul Venables. And as of this week we have a new starter John Pattullo, who's joined us from Proctor & Gamble as the CEO of our EMEA business, our largest division and also he will also be joining our PLC Board.
 I think John is with us this morning. Please don't ask him any hard questions. He's on his fourth day with Exel and cannot be held accountable for either any failures or successes that we've had thus so far. So, please don't give him a hard time. But we're delighted to have him joining our team and I think bringing to us, I think, some real insight from the customer side as to how major customers view the developments of their global supply chains.
 And within our global Freight Management business 2 new recent appointments both now up and running, a new man to head our global Seafreight business who joined us from UPS within the last couple of weeks. And Al Benki and Steve Hoisington who's joined us to actually put more drive into the issue of improving both operational excellence but also operational cost effectiveness who's come from Johnson's Controls more recently but prior to that with IBM, who is a real guru in this particular space. So, yes we continue to look at pulling in external talent but at the same time to develop our own talent as fast as we can.
 And to finish really the outlook and summary, we are still headed in the same direction. We've got some very, very clear priorities for the next few years about delivering value through inspiration, performance and growth. We're comfortable that we're operating in markets that are going to continue to grow and we're really very confident about our short and medium term prospects. And the quote at the end is from the statement, so I won't detain you with it. I think it speaks for itself.
 And now we'd be happy to turn to any questions that you'd like to put to John or I. I think perhaps while you're thinking about the first questions may be let me guess 1 of the questions that we might get. You know scratching our heads yesterday and thinking what are the audience likely to ask us about? We  1 thing we thought was that perhaps we'd get a question about market rumors and bid speculation and so on. I think perhaps we were wrong to expect that, but I don't know.
 And we thought it might helpful to address that up front before we got into other questions. And let me just say a few things. First of all, we've got a very clear policy on not commenting on market rumors. If every company currently that was the subject of market rumors commented every time there was a rumor, frankly they would have time to do very little else. But we're also very mindful of our legal and regulatory obligations. And we've taken great care with the help of our advisors to ensure that we've been compliant with those obligations at all times. Now what those obligations say is that if something happened which required us to make a statement clearly it would be incumbent upon us to make 1.

 During the third quarter, crude  U.S. crude oil prices remained in mid- to upper-40s per barrel moving above $50 per barrel towards the end of the quarter. Our U.S. segment recorded revenues of $6.1 million, which is an increase of over 100% year-over-year and 7% sequentially, due to higher occupancy in our Permian and Bakken camps and improvement in our wellsite services business.
 With oil prices slightly above $50 a barrel currently, business conditions in U.S., light tight oil plays continues to be resilient, enjoying a completion activity in the Bakken, Rockies and Texas has much improved over last year. However, the pace of U.S. onshore rig count growth began to flatten in the third quarter, and some of the large independent E&Ps appeared to be considering a heightened emphasis on capital discipline rather than strictly production growth, which is a trend we'll need to continue to monitor during our 2018 budgeting process.
 In the interim, we remain focused on operational quality, increasing our wellsite services market share and EBITDA improvement.
 Moving to Australia. In our Australian segment, met coal prices continue to be constructive with the macroeconomic question being where will met coal prices stabilize? The spot met coal price remains relatively strong at approximately $180 per tonne. However, many forecasts are calling for met coal prices to retreat to approximately $130 to $140 per tonne. In the meantime, Australian met coal producers are generating significant cash flow at either of those price levels.
 With approximately 80% of our Australian rooms located in the Bowen basin, servicing met coal mines, we are optimistic that this could lead to increased customer activity levels. Anecdotally, some major customers in the region have begun to publically discuss the attractive returns associated with opportunities to unlock latent capacity within their respective met coal portfolios and the desire to potentially pursue expansionary projects.
 To summarize, from a macroeconomic perspective, oil prices above $50 per barrel is conducive to continued production and positive cash flow from our oil sands customers as well as fairly good drilling and completion activity in the U.S. oil shale plays.
 Met coal prices of about $180 per tonne generate significant cash flow for Australian met coal customers. Generally, what is missing from both the U.S. and Australian markets is conviction on the long-term prices for oil and met coal.
 In Canada, the prospects for greenfield and expansionary programs are generally less vibrant. However, with the oil above $50 per barrel, our customers are generating positive free cash flow from existing oil sands projects.
 While we are encouraged by the macroeconomic trends in our core end markets and the recent modest occupancy and utilization improvements in Canada and the U.S., we remain committed to our strategy of positioning the business to succeed in any commodity price environment. We continue to focus on working safely, delivering unmatched service, generating free cash flow, delevering the balance sheet and driving strong operational performance across all segments while pursuing strategic growth opportunities.

Dan Dinges,  Cabot Oil & Gas Corp - Chairman, President, and  CEO: Thank you Maureen, and I appreciate all joining us for this third quarter conference call. With me to answer any questions is Scott Schroeder, all know him, CFO; Jeff Hutton, our VP Marketing; Steve Lindeman, our VP Engineering Technology; Matt Reid, VP Regional Manager; and Todd Liebl, our VP of Land and Business Development. Let me just say the standard boilerplate forward-looking statements, including in our press release last night do apply to my comments today. On the call this morning we plan to cover the third quarter operating and financial results. We will give you an update on our '12 and '13 guidance. We will also update our hedging program for '12 and '13, followed by an update of our operations in the Marcellus, Eagle Ford, Marmaton, and now we're going to add a brief comment in the Pearsall.
 Before I do go into the details on those topics, I would like to highlight some of the items that were brought up in our press release last night. Cabot's production is up 42% over comparable year-to-date periods. Third quarter production was up 6% over the second quarter, even with the delays that we've discussed in permitting and gathering lines in the Marcellus earlier this month. As far as a little bit granular information, we brought on Line 2, a two-well pad 1.5 miles west of our Zick compressor area. That pad site with two wells had peak rate of 43.8 million per day from only 25 stages, which I think further demonstrates the productivity of our Marcellus wells and the benefit of our reduced spacing between stages.
 We also recently drilled and completed the first Pearsall short lateral well under our joint venture with Osaka. The well was drilled in Frio County and tested at a 24-hour rate over 1400 barrels equivalent per day. I think most importantly, and from a macro standpoint, Cabot will deliver industry leading production growth in '13 with a cash flow positive program using a $3.50 gas price. I think certainly all those stack up to good information. Last night, our financial results, the Company reported clean earnings of approximately $43.1 million or $0.21 per share for third quarter of '12, up from $35.3 million or $0.17 per share for the third quarter of '12  excuse me, of '11. The increase was driven by higher equivalent production and higher realized crude oil prices that more than offset weaker natural gas prices. Cash flow from operations and discretionary cash flow for the third quarter was $164 million and $175.7 million respectively, both up from last year's comparison.
 Moving to a comment on production, Cabot continues to provide industry leading production growth, driven by our premier Marcellus assets in Susquehanna County. Equivalent production for the nine-month period ended September 30, 2012 was approximately 189 Bcfe, which represents an increase of 42% compared to the nine-month period ended September 30, 2011. Taking into account last year's fourth quarter sale of our Rocky Mountains property, our pro forma year-to-date growth in production is 51%. This nine-month production level already exceeds our full-year 2011 reported production.
 Now to get a little forward-looking as far as our guidance is concerned for '12, we have updated our equivalent production growth range to 38% to 44% and our liquids production range to 60% to 70% to better reflect our outlook for the remainder of the year. We had hoped for and scheduled earlier timings for our Marcellus gathering permits, i.e., being able to turn wells in the line; however, as previously mentioned, the permits were just recently received by Williams. This resulted in not achieving the high end of our guidance. With that said, we are comfortable with the guidance range that we have just put out. Full-year per unit cost range were also tightened based on year-to-date results and our expectations for the fourth quarter. We reaffirmed our net capital spending for '12 at $775 million and $825 million.
 Okay, for '13 we have updated our equivalent production growth range to 35%, which is up from the 30% we had previously posted to 50%. So 35% to 50%, and we've established our liquid productions growth range at 45% to 55%. The midpoint of our guidance ranges, when you look at 2012 and 2013 implies three consecutive years of 40%-plus equivalent production growth, which is an impressive number on an ever-increasing base, while at the same time maintaining our capital discipline, not encumbering our balance sheet or diluting our shareholders. We have also provided initial guidance on costs for 2013, which reinforces our industry leading cost structure and the continued trend for decreasing per unit cost. We've further refined our estimates for capital spending in 2013 to between $950 million and $1.025 billion, with approximately 70% of that capital being allocated to our high rate of return projects in the Marcellus. Our 2012 production, excluding the five basis-only hedges, the Company has 37 contracts in our hedging books, 27 are gas swaps at $5.22, 5 are gas collars with a floor of $3.60 and a ceiling of $4.17, and 4 are oil swaps at $99.30, with an additional oil swap at $105.05. Last quarter we reported that the 2012 slowdown in the permit approval process did delay the construction of various gathering pipelines that ultimately affected the dates we turned our wells in line. In fact, we have no less than 12 different pipelines that are currently in the construction phase. This is great news on the pipeline construction side of the infrastructure.
 On the other half of the infrastructure picture, deals with the timing of compressor stations and freeflow interconnects into the interstate pipelines. These projects have made significant progress, and while we are not going to see any of these individual projects have an in-service date earlier that we expect, we do still expect to be close to our original goal of approximately one point Bcf per day of takeaway prior to year-end 2012. But just to be clear, and as we have previously discussed, when you put your models together, as the infrastructure requirements grow requirements grow and the facilities are placed into service throughout our acreage position, we will in some cases have excess capacity in some areas, but still slightly constrained in other areas, and that phenomenon is simply the result of where we need to have our drilling rigs throughout the year. One other point regarding infrastructure, we have already provided Williams with the necessary information for our 2014 program. We anticipate Williams will submit the completed application for permits in January 2013 for our 2014 program.
 Now let's move to the south. This region has five rigs operating as we speak, two are in are in the Marmaton and three rigs are drilling in the Pearsall, with one of these rigs moving back to the Eagle Ford program fairly soon. This rig level is expected to continue throughout 2013, as current plans call for about 50 net wells to be drilled. The region accounts for roughly 30% of our overall capital program, and of that amount 75% is dedicated to drilling.

As mentioned, one additional Pearsall well is completing and three wells are drilling. A total of six Pearsall wells are planned for the 2012 program. We hope our early drilling and completed wells will fall in the $9 million to $9.5 million range. Cabot's net well cost will be 9.75% during the Osaka carry period, and we will have a 65% working interest in the wells on first production. We have accumulated over 70,000 acres net in the play, and as I mentioned, we do not normally discuss exploration efforts at this early stages, however with the level of interest and the number of questions we have been receiving I felt it was necessary to provide an update.
 In the Eagle Ford, we announced our release of another successful well with 4500 foot lateral entry with 15 stages. To date we have 38 Eagle Ford wells in our Buckhorn area. As with other plays, we have seen well costs come down as efficiencies are gained, and we are now in these $6.5 million to $7 million completed well cost range. Also in the third quarter, the integration of field to full pipeline access versus trucking our oil, that occurred just a couple of months ago. We are now able to produce the oil and transport it by that pipeline to Corpus Christi where we receive LLS pricing.  Now let's move to North Texas, the Panhandle of Oklahoma and the Marmaton. Cabot recently completed a well with a 15 stage frac stimulation. The well produced at a initial 24-hour rate of 664 barrels of oil a day, and an average of 593 barrels over the last 20 days. We also drilled our first extended lateral well with a lateral length of approximately 9500 feet. The well was stimulated with 30 stages, and is presently in the early stages of flowback. The second extended lateral well has been drilled and will start completion at the end of October. Completed well costs continue to average around $2.9 million to $3.3 million, with early drilled extended laterals coming in between approximately $4 million to $4.5 million. To date we have accumulated about 70,000 net acres in that play.
 So in summary, our drill bit success continues to drive our significant production and reserve growth expectations. What I am most pleased about is the continued innovation our team has come up with, with new ideas that certainly is going to translate into incremental value. My expectation that we will post excellent numbers at year-end '12, and it is also as a forward-look my expectation that Cabot that will in 2013 certainly have industry leading production growth. We will have a significant reserve addition at a very low cost of finding. We will also have an improved balance sheet with a positive cash flow program using only a $3.50 gas price. I think we will see a milestone reached in '13 where we will have a Bcf per day of net production at some point during the year, and we will achieve these results with only 10 operated rigs for most of the year. I think a couple of these points may set us apart from some of our space.
 Anyhow, Maureen, with that brief summary, I will be more than happy to answer any questions.

During the quarter, Chesapeake produced a record 122,000 barrels of oil per day, and we increased our oil mix percentage to a record 25% of total production. The oil volume increase is driven by the successful integration of our Brazos Valley asset, steady growth from the Powder River Basin and improved base production performance from South Texas and the Mid-Continent.
 Accordingly, we have raised the midpoint of our full year 2019 oil production guidance by approximately 250,000 barrels. Higher oil volumes and our focus on cash cost leadership yielded the highest second quarter margin per BOE in 5 years.
 We have lowered our full year guidance for production expense as well as gathering, processing and transportation expense. I'm very excited with the rapid progress we have made in our new Brazos Valley asset. After only 5 months from closing, we have a clearly defined plan to fully achieve the forecasted annual [synergy] savings of $250 million to $280 million per year. We'll continue to build upon the cash cost improvements and capital efficiencies identified.
 Notably, we see further opportunity to the projected $600,000 capital reduction realized on a per well basis as we've recognized up to $2 million in savings on certain wells. As a result of our capital efficiency, we have lowered the breakeven oil price for our Brazos Valley well to $39 per barrel, an approximate 26% improvement.

Nick will share additional detail on our liquidity, liability management and financial improvements for the quarter.
 As noted in our earnings release, in 2020, we expect to allocate more capital to oil growth areas with less capital going towards our gas assets. Driven by stronger adjusted oil production, an increase in our production mix towards oil and lower total cash operating expenses, we reported a 26% increase in adjusted EBITDAX margin per BOE compared to last year.
