David Voyticky,  Miller Energy Resources, Inc. - President, Acting CFO: Morning, and thank you for joining us to hear a little bit about Miller. That is a picture of our Osprey Platform in the Cook Inlet. It is one of the assets that we picked up in 2009 in the Pacific Energy bankruptcy process.
 Our Company has been around for 45 years. In the last four years we have gone through a period of dynamic growth, most important of which was the acquisition that we made in 2009, and I am going to focus on that today.
 Our story is very simple. There is quite a lot of detail, but it is very easy to do diligence; and once you go through the details I think it is very easy to understand.
 Deloy Miller started the Company 45 years ago. In 2008 his son-in-law Scott Boruff joined him, made a number of acquisitions, and led the Company through a period of dynamic growth. The stock was a Bulletin Board Company when Scott joined in 2008, and the stock has risen from $0.05 a share in 2008 to over $5 today, so it has been a nice period of appreciation for shareholders.
 As you can see on the bottom, the last year has been a period where we have seen our production ramp up, and we will go through the reasons for that shortly and what we think is going to happen in the future. You may notice on the left-hand side of this page that management has a big ownership position in the Company. The decisions that we have made over the last three years have been long-term focused, and we are just starting to see some of the fruits of our labor and we expect to see that over the next year as well.
 In summary, we have about 8.5 million barrels of reserves, proven reserves. We are oil-focused or oil-weighted, and we operate 100% of our production. As mentioned, we have a big lease position up in the Cook Inlet, and I will walk you through some of the things that are interesting about the Cook Inlet today.
 This page gives a good summary of our two basins. As I mentioned, Tennessee is a much smaller part of our value proposition, but we have interesting players in both basins. And the Cook Inlet I think is one of the most interesting places to do business in the oil and gas industry in the US today.
 In 2009, as I mentioned, we acquired our Alaskan assets. Quite frankly, we picked up what we believe is a multibillion-dollar play for $2 million.
 As a Bulletin Board public company, we had a number of things that we had to do to put our house in order so that people would feel comfortable investing and so we could attract capital. We added three independent directors, of which I was one. We hired KPMG as our auditor. And over the last three years we have tracked some institutional financing partners in Guggenheim and currently we are with Apollo.
 Over the past three years, we have really spent our time positioning the Company so we could efficiently deploy capital and develop this asset base. I think we are at an inflection point today which makes us a very interesting time to look at investing in Miller.
 This page is a pretty good summary of the transaction that occurred in 2009. To give it some perspective, we give you the transaction that occurred in 2007 on the same asset base.
 So in 2007, Pacific Energy purchased the assets that we now own up in the Cook Inlet for $500 million. They financed it with about $400 million of debt from Goldman Sachs and Silver Point.
 And the assets, if you look at this darker blue box on the left-hand side, also included some assets that had a lot of P&A liabilities with them. The estimate on those P&A liabilities was in the $0.5-billion-plus range, and the properties that they were associated with were 50 years old and were negative cash flowing at the time.
 Through the bankruptcy process we were able to cherry pick the good assets and leave behind the bad. So in a sense we did a good bank/bad bank with an oil company, and we ended up with all the good assets, as I said, for $2 million.
 So people have a hard time understanding how you could pick up $1-billion-plus of assets for $2 million. But if you go back to 2009 and you think about the time frame, the world was falling apart; oil was going down towards $30 a barrel; and Goldman Sachs was looking for Buffett to help bail them out of their issues. In fact, Goldman Sachs didn't even show up to credit bid on the assets. So by hanging around the bank for it, and figuring out how to get rid of these assets that were not financeable, we found ourselves in a position to pick up these assets for a very low price.
 To give you a sense of the size of our infrastructure and what $2 million bought you in 2009, you can see some of our facilities. The West McArthur River Unit, the Kustatan Production Facility  those facilities can process up to 65,000 barrels a day. There is about 21 megawatts of power, about 40 miles of pipeline. The Osprey Platform was designed to produce over 25,000 barrels a day.
 So we own those properties outright. Our most recent appraisal had those at over $200 million today. So I think replacement value would be about twice that, but clearly we have a lot of infrastructure.
 I think that is important for us, because as we produce additional oil from our properties we don't have to spend any money on midstream infrastructure. We are essentially vertically integrated.
 For $2 million not only do you get those assets but we got a very large reserve base. The key part of our story is really understanding this reserve base, because it has changed over time.
 Forest Oil originally developed these assets. When they drilled the first two wells into the Redoubt Shoals structure they actually got 50 million barrels of PUD credit from the first two wells.
 As you can see today, we only have about 6.8 million of proven reserves, and still less than 50 million of total reserve credit. That is essentially the story that we would like you to focus on as you think about Miller Energy.
 If you focused on the right-hand side, our proved reserves, most of our PUDs are from the wells that Forest drilled in 2000, 2001, and these are all story wells. After they drilled the initial wells they had a number of issues with their completions. And our thesis has been that they completed the wells incorrectly, very simple, and that by changing the completion we could actually restore the original PUDs that were in this asset base.
 Just to give you a summary of where we are in terms of our Alaskan assets and why we think about things the way we do, as I mentioned, these assets were in a state of disrepair through the bankruptcy process. We thought the previous operators had made a number of mistakes with the assets.
 So our plan over the past three years has really been to take the low-hanging fruit, spend the least amount of money, and restore as much production as we can. And today, we are at about 2,800 barrels a day.
 We have had a great deal of success with our development program; we will go into that in a minute. But we have been successful in nearly all of our wells, and we think that we will be economically successful on everything that we have done to date eventually.
 Our management team is led by David Hall, and David has been with these properties for over 20 years. Through the bankruptcy process we were able to pick up the best of the previous operators, so we have a team in the Cook Inlet that we feel is second to none, and so far they have made us proud.
 I will talk about this in more detail later, but the tax credits up in Cook Inlet make this a very interesting place to do business. For every dollar that we spend, we get back $0.40 from the state of Alaska. So we have been able to look at financing structures that a company that had our production base wouldn't be able to look at, because we know on the money we spend we're going to be getting back money from the state of Alaska, which is a very advantageous.
 We have been paid back over $8 million to date. We will expect to get back another $15 million to $20 million before the end of the year.
 You have seen the infrastructure. That is good for us because we don't have to spend any more money. We are vertically integrated, so we are very much in control of our own operations.
 We think that we have about a $5 a barrel incremental cost for every additional barrel of oil production that we bring online. That is what we have seen. It may actually be better than that.
 And we have got a large land position, which gives us a large runway. Most of what we're going to talk about is just the 5,000 acres of the Redoubt Shoals structure, but we have a very large land position. And as we develop the Redoubt Shoals and have more wellbores versus casings we will take advantage of some of the other opportunities that are in front of us.
 Just to give you a sense of our success on reworks to date, the bottom line is that we took assets that before they were abandoned they were producing 200 barrels a day. And just by going back and reworking previously drilled wells we have restored production to what today is 2,800 barrels. But most of those wells have been producing for some period of time, so there has been some decline curves.
 But it's been a very efficient deployment of capital, and I think today we are in a position where we can take on some bigger risk.
 Briefly we can talk about Alaska, but essentially since we have been in the Cook Inlet it has changed dramatically. Apache, Hilcorp have come in; they have committed hundreds of millions of dollars. They have done so because of the tax credits, but they've also done so because the belief is that Cook Inlet is a largely undeveloped basin.
 That started to be developed in the 1950s, but as the North Slope was discovered the majors lost interest. So what Apache end Hilcorp believe today is that there is at least as much oil and gas to be discovered and produced as has been produced in the last four years.
 The Cook Inlet has a unique gas price, essentially a closed loop system. So all the gas that is produced within the Inlet is what is used for 80% of Alaskans. Today, with the gas prices between $6 and $7 over the last year, spiked as high as $22 during periods of high demand during the winter, unique for the United States is the fact that there is an LNG exporting facility that has been in use for over 30 years. So once the demand for the internal Cook Inlet is satisfied, there is plenty of opportunities to put additional supply to work.
 This gives an overview of where we are. Our 5,000 acres in the Redoubt Shoals is in red; we also have some fields in the Western parts of the river structure that we will talk about.
 But you can see that there are these big trends where there has been a large amount of oil found. This Redoubt area is significant in size, and we think that it is large as the ones that are above it.
 As I mentioned before, Forest Oil when they drilled these wells had some very good initial results before they completed them. Ryder Scott thought there was about 370 million barrels of oil in place.
 Typical recovery rates in the Cook Inlet are in the high 20%s to low 40%s. You can do the math, but that really implies that we have a very large field if we can prove out the thesis that the field was completed incorrectly.
 Of the wells that have been drilled in the Redoubt Shoals structure, the average initial production has been over 1,000 barrels a day. For us, the decline curve has been less than 10%, which is markedly different than what Forest experienced.
 Our reserve engineers currently estimate that we will see someplace around 1 million barrels recovered from each of these wellbores. That would be low for the Cook Inlet. We expect that to go up as we have additional production history.
 We are spending about $10 million net on developing each wellbore, and so we are getting some very, very good IRRs on our projects.
 This is the page I would like to focus on. If you look at the Central fault block, that is where the first well was drilled by Forest, and that is the areas they got about 10 million barrels of PUD credit. And below it is the Southern fault block; they got about 40 million barrels of PUD credit for that.
 So, the RU-2 well we're going to go into in detail because it is a well that we just reworked and we have got some good initial data. But there's positive DST tests all the way up to the Northern stepout and as far down as the bottom left-hand part of this page, so we have a lot of runway.
 But all of our reserves right now are being carried in those two fault blocks. And as I said, they were written down from 50 million barrels of PUDs to the 6 million barrels of PUDs that we have today. You will see from our recent data that there is good reason to expect that we will be able to recover a lot of those reserves that were lost over time.
 This page highlights essentially the main reason behind the poor performance of these wells under Forest. Simply put, on the left-hand side, all the oil wells in the Cook Inlet are under some sort of artificial lift, gas lift or ESP. The ESP is depicted in red here, and this is about 10,000 feet vertical depth.
 Underneath it there is an LLC, a liquid level control valve. And essentially in the Cook Inlet the state of Alaska requires for all offshore wells for there to be some sort of subsurface well [spinner]. The LLC is that device, and typically this would be placed a couple hundred feet below the wellhead.
 For whatever reason, the engineers that designed these completions decided to put it all the way down at the bottom of the hole and right under the ESP. The way our engineers have explained this to me is like trying to such through a straw that has a pit at the bottom of it.
 It didn't work very well. They're trying to force or such up to 5,000 barrels of fluids through a 6-foot-long valve that has an ID they would have trouble fitting a pin through. So it just was a poor completion technique.
 When we first took over the properties, we spent a lot of time trying to understand why it was done. Obviously, the old Forest employees thought this was incorrect and pointed this out to us.
 The first well that we reworked was our RU-7 well. We simply just went in, pulled the completion, took out the LLC valve, and we saw a big change in the flow rates, bottom-hole flowing pressure. A well that was thought to have about 40,000 barrels left in it and was flowing at about 30 barrels of oil a day, IP-ed at 250 barrels and two years later is still producing 200 barrels a day for us.
 The bottom-hole flowing pressure went from 1,000 psi up to 2,300 psi. And what was important for us is that the characteristics changed to exactly what was expected in the Ryder Scott report that was done in 2002.
 So it really proved out our thesis, and over time it has performed exactly as we would have expected it to perform. Had a very large increase in recoverable reserves, and we have recovered over 120,000 barrels from this wellbore. That is about three times more than was expected to be recovered from it; and now we carry reserve credits of about 250,000 additional barrels.
 And this was one of the smaller wells on the flank of the structure, but it gave us the data and the confidence to go forward with our plans. This gives a summary, obviously, of the change in production and the impact on the PV-10.
 Most recently, we did a rework of a well in the Southern fault block, so now we have data from both the Central and Southern fault blocks. This is a well that was producing for Forest about 100 barrels a day of oil for the last six months before it collapsed. That completion actually led to most of these wellbores collapsing.
 So we had to sidetrack out of the good casing and abandon the old wellbore. We went to a bottom-hole location that was about 200 feet away from the original wellbore, and the well IP-ed at about 1,281 barrels a day.
 Since that time, and it has been about 50 days, the well hasn't declined at all. In fact, it has averaged about 1,320 barrels a day.
 But again the same sort of change in the performance of the wellbore. We saw bottom-hole flowing pressures go from 800 psi up to 2,400. They stayed there and were rock steady.
 And, obviously, this is going to be a big change in the PV-10 value we have on our reserve report. When we give guidance, we always give guidance with respect to whatever the reserve engineers have in their report.
 So for this well they have 600 barrels of expected production; we are at 1,300. The oil-water cut changed from 90% water to 90% oil. And we think as we get additional data from these wells we're going to go a long way towards getting a new reserve report that is going to be reflective of what we think the reserve size is for Redoubt Shoals.
 Obviously, the paybacks on this sort of well for us are very good. We think it's about 90 days. As mentioned our cash cost was $13 million, of which we will get a little over $5 million back from the state of Alaska.
 This well, I think we are netting someplace close to $3 million a month profit off this well. So for us, we are getting Alaskan North Slope minus $4; Alaskan North Slope closely mirrors Brent. We have 83.5% net revenue interest on the Redoubt Shoals structure; (inaudible) as I said, $5 of incremental lifting costs; and we've got about $5 of transportation costs. So we are netting close to $80 a barrel.
 We have a number of fields that are similar to the Redoubt Shoals field. The West McArthur River Unit has three different plays.
 This is a field that was discovered in the 1960s but not developed because it was assumed to be too small when oil was in the single digits. Stewart Petroleum came back in 1991 when oil was in the high teens and drilled some wells into the Southern part of the structure.
 The average initial production was well over 1,500 barrels a day for the seven wells. The EUR has been 2 million barrels per well, which is what we see as typical and that is what we ultimately think we will get out of the Redoubt Shoals structure. We have a couple of additional PUD opportunities, and we are currently drilling a well into the Sword structure which we expect to complete sometime in September.
 This gives a sense based on the West McArthur River fields and the Redoubt Shoals, so just those two structures, what we think we are going to do with our production over the next year. We have already completed some of the things on this chart, but essentially this is our development plan over the next year.
 It is not in chronological order, but it is by field. The West McArthur River 5 and 6 have been done. We are drilling the Sword right now and we will drill the West McArthur River 8 and 9 over the winter.
 We have restored production to five of the six producing wellbores on the Osprey Platform. We have come in well above these numbers, which are reflective of the reserve report, as I mentioned. And then we will expect to drill two new wellbores before the end of our fiscal year in April.
 So we think that this is a realistic picture, a conservative picture, of where we're going to be within the next year.
 As I mentioned, with our infrastructure, most of our revenue falls to the bottom line. This gives a sense of what we think our run rate EBITDA will be as we bring these fields online.
 We have a 4,000 BOP-per-day target by the end of this calendar year. We think we will  that is a conservative target. So we think that our Company is going to transform as we complete our next couple wells and then produce financials based off those results.
 There is really  Tennessee is essentially equal to one wellbore, so we're not going to spend that much time on it. We think there is a lot of value there. That is something that we are taking, again, a long-term approach; but really the story is Alaska.
 This chart is a little bit busy, but essentially each one of those light and dark blue lines are one of our reworks. We think that over time that we are going to be seeing someplace between $100 million and $120 million of PV-10 to wellbore.
 So those are as depicted in the current reserve report, but the value proposition is simple. As we rework these wells and get additional PUD credit, we are going to take this Company from something that has 8 million barrels of PUD credits to something that is significantly higher, and we think we are going to do so in the next year.
 As we have gone along we have been very protective of our equity. We haven't sold equity in three years. When we started this plan three years ago we had two wellbores, and we went out and got debt.
 People thought it was questionable, but as owners we felt very comfortable with the structure. A, because when you think about it, the $55 million that we borrowed over the last year and now $75 million, if you just spend that in the state of Alaska and you get 40% back, you're going to get $30 million back in tax credits; and that is very close to the interest that we will pay over that period of time. So even though our debt looks expensive, it was very cheap for us and cheap for our equity holders.
 Being the bankers that we are, we have tried to reduce our cost over the last year. Over the last two weeks Apollo has extended another $20 million of credit to us. Instead of at 18% they extended it to us at 9%, so we have been happy with the progress that we have made and we think with the changes in our production profile we're going to have some improvements in capital structure over the next 12 months as well.
 The recent developments, I mentioned Apollo. We were very fortunate to add Marceau Schlumberger to the Board a couple weeks ago. We think we're at the point now where we can start to look at making acquisitions and doing some things that are strategic up in the Cook Inlet; that's very important to us.
 We are very happy with the well results. And we are about to bring our RU-1 well online right now, so within the next two weeks we will have an announcement on how that project is going.
 Just to summarize, we think it is a very simple story. Again, if we just took the forward [path] from drilling two wellbores and 50 million barrels of PUDs, it is going to take us a little while for the reserve engineers to get back to that level, because they keep looking at the old production data and saying  well, you have to show us some history before we can give you that sort of credit again. So that is essentially our strategy.
 I would be happy to answer any questions in the breakout session. Thank you.

 At a high level, our number showed a marked improvement sequentially from Q1, which is largely a result of strong revenue  recurring revenue and adjusted EBITDA from IRD and VIZIYA.
 On the M&A front, we made some important progress in the quarter, which we'll get to in a moment. But first, I'll spend a few minutes on each of the businesses, highlighting some of the respective developments in the quarter. WiLAN's results in Q2 again reflect the variability in the overall transformation going on in the patent license industry. WiLAN is a unique asset capable of generating significant cash flows as it did in 2017, and its results need to be viewed over a longer period rather than quarter-to-quarter. The announcement we made on August 1 regarding our trial results with Apple is a case in point.
 In a trial verdict rendered that same day in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, a jury awarded WiLAN $145.1 million in damages against Apple for infringement of 2 of WiLAN's U.S. patents related to cell phone technology. We're obviously very pleased with the jury's decision and believe that it reflects well on our team, our portfolio and our process and enhances our already strong reputation in the industry. We have a rich portfolio of intellectual property and a seasoned team with a proven multiyear track record of identifying high-quality intellectual property and maximizing its value.
 Apple was business as usual for us. We have a strong pipeline of license opportunities with many active licensing programs in place today. Our preference is always to avoid litigation where reasonably possible and to obtain a fair license. However, when litigation unfortunately becomes necessary, we have the confidence to see the process through to the end. Our level of litigation activity remains constant with suits outstanding in various technology areas against global companies such as Sharp, VIZIO, OmniVision, LG, Bell, Sony and Kingston, to name just a few.
 We also will continue to pursue and acquire patent portfolios where we believe appropriate returns can be met. So far in 2018, we have acquired 3 patent portfolios via our partner model. Acquiring patents gives us an inventory for future license opportunities. And doing so under the partner model means we pay little to nothing upfront for the patents and then share the license proceeds with the seller. This keeps  this helps us keep the cost down and expands the revenue opportunities for the business.
 In June, we announced that Keaton Parekh will join WiLAN as its President and CEO and that, as previously announced, Jim Skippen was retiring from his position as Executive Chair of Quarterhill and interim CEO of WiLAN while continuing as an outside Director and Chair of the Quarterhill board. Keaton is an accomplished patent attorney and an experienced business leader with significant experience related to running a patent licensing enterprise. He obviously, has big shoes to fill at WiLAN. But with 20 years of experience in all aspects of IT  IP, including licensing, litigation, sale and purchase of patent assets and patent prosecution, Keaton has the skills, global perspective and proven track record to drive WiLAN forward through its next phase of success.
 IRD had a strong Q2, which is generally a seasonally stronger quarter for the company. As we said on our last call, a few agreements had slipped from Q1 and we picked up some of those in Q2. Among our new contracts in the quarter was a $5 million agreement with the California Department of Transportation. This included an upfront component with the remainder spread out over the 3-year term of the agreement.
 Overall, results for IRD in Q2 reflected the type of performance we believe the business can deliver more regularly, and importantly, from which it can grow. IRD's Q2 revenue was $12.7 million and adjusted EBITDA margin was 12%, which were both very significant improvements sequentially from Q1. We think the outlook for IRD is very promising. We have a loyal sticky customer base and several new and exciting products in the market that are complementary to their existing solutions and provide the potential for new recurring revenue streams. We expect these products to become meaningful over time. And in the short term, we expect them to help strengthen our value proposition when pitching for new business. Also, we believe the improved margin profile for some of these new products is attractive.
 Shortly after the end of Q2, IRD announced the retirement of Terry Bergan as President and CEO and the appointment of Randy Hanson to that role. Prior to this, Randy was COO and Executive VP, a role he held beginning in 2000. Both Terry and Randy have been instrumental in helping IRD become a world leader in the ITS industry. Randy is a natural successor to Terry as he has deep institutional knowledge of the business and close relationships with many of the key customers.
 Earlier this year, on our Q1 call, I spoke of my commitment to work with our portfolio companies to help them optimize their operational and financial performance. Based on my initial views of IRD and in collaboration with Randy and his team, subsequent to quarter end, IRD made the decision to consolidate or eliminate certain roles where it made sense to do so and remove some excess costs from the business. While such a process can involve difficult decisions along the way, we think that because of it, IRD will become a more  have a more competitive cost structure and focused strategy, which we believe will help put it in a better position to capitalize on its growth opportunity.
 VIZIYA also had a strong quarter with good top line performance and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 34%. We like what we've seen so far with VIZIYA. They're bringing in new license customers, courting larger and more intricate business opportunities, expanding the scope of their partner relationship with the likes of SAP and Oracle and driving good financial results. They fall into the category of verticalized software companies that we think are well suited for our M&A strategy, and I've been impressed with the team's ambition, entrepreneurial spirit and customer focus. As with IRD, we think there's the potential for financial performance to improve in the coming quarters for the business to scale profitably, and I'm committed to working with the team there to drive those results.
 On the M&A front, building our pipeline remains a top priority, and we're seeing real progress in this area. Expanding the scope of our targets to include verticalized software companies has led to a promising expansion at the top of our target pipeline funnel.
 As most of this work goes on behind the scenes, I'd like to shed a light here on some of the metrics we use to gauge activity. Despite being somewhat of a sellers' market right now, in Q2 alone, we submitted multiple nonbinding expressions of interest and held discussions with several companies in various disparate market verticals, such as health care, ITS, fintech and analytics. In terms of specific deal flow metrics, in Q2, we signed more than a dozen NDAs and reviewed an equivalent number of sale process documents and held discussions with more than 70 sell-side financial advisers, typically an excellent source of transaction opportunities. This level of activity and the scope of market opportunity in our sweet spot in a relatively short period of time is very encouraging and validates the strengths of our strategy and ability to expand our deal ecosystem.
 We know investors are eager for the next transaction. But while deal flow is robust and the pipeline is growing, we will remain patient negotiators. We're not going to do a deal for a deal's sake. We're going to do the right deal, which means remaining disciplined with our criteria: return on revenue, stable cash flows and margin, sticky customer relationships, et cetera. But when we see the right opportunity, we won't hesitate to aggressively pursue it and execute to deploy our capital.
 To summarize, a key priority for us now is to invest capital and to build a critical mass of businesses in our portfolio, but it is critical that we stick to our playbook in terms of doing deals and that we remain financially disciplined when pursuing them. There are few we have walked away from recently. And as hard as that can be to do, it was the right thing to stay disciplined and stick to our criteria. The wait can be difficult, but ours is the type of strategy that builds momentum over time so the periods between transactions will narrow longer term.
 A second top priority is to ensure that the companies we own today are operating as effectively as possible and that they're getting the support needed to generate the growth, profitability and reliable cash flow streams that we believe they can deliver. At the same time, we won't hesitate to be proactive with any businesses if we feel action is required to improve profitability and align costs more effectively to invest sustainably in growth. We believe that executing well on those 2 fronts will ultimately drive performance in our financials and value in our stock price.
 With that, I'll pass it over to Shaun for a closer look at the numbers.

Mike Creel,  Enterprise Products Partners L.P. - CEO: Thanks, Randy. We reported solid results this quarter, with four of our five business segments posting improved results compared to the second quarter of last year. Record NGL and crude oil transportation volumes and contributions from new assets put into service more than offset the impact of lower NGL commodity prices in our natural gas processing business, leading to an 11% increase in gross operating margin for the quarter.
 These increases were primarily driven by growth in NGL and crude oil production in the Eagle Ford Shale, higher crude oil volumes flowing on Seaway, and increased propane loadings at our export facility.
 Net income attributable to limited partners was $553 million. And earnings per unit on a fully diluted basis were $0.60 for the second quarter of 2013. This compares with net income of $566 million and earnings per unit of $0.64 for the second quarter of 2012. Included in net income this quarter was approximately $46 million, or $0.05 per unit, of non-cash charges related to asset impairments; non-cash expense for changes to the Texas margin tax; and a loss related to the sale of assets.
 Net income for the second quarter of last year included non-cash gains of $45 million or $0.05 per unit related to the sale of assets and insurance recoveries.
 Distributable cash flow was $925 million this quarter compared with $876 million in the second quarter of 2012. Included in distributable cash flow were proceeds from asset sales and insurance recoveries of $69 million this quarter, and $159 million in the second quarter of last year. After adjusting for these nonrecurring items, distributable cash flow increased 19% over the second quarter of 2012. Distributable cash flow generated by our predominantly fee-based businesses allowed us to increase the quarterly cash distribution to $0.68 per unit with respect to the second quarter of 2013. This is our 36th consecutive quarterly increase in our cash distribution per unit, and is 7.1% higher than the cash distribution paid with respect to the second quarter of 2012.
 Distributable cash flow provided 1.5 times coverage of the cash distribution for the second quarter of 2013. And after adjusting for the proceeds from sales, it would've provided 1.4 times coverage. We retained $318 million of distributable cash flow this quarter, and $621 million through the first six months of the year. We also raised $214 million through our at-the-market, or ATM, program; and $135 million from our distribution reinvestment plan, or DRIP, and our employee unit purchase plan in the first half of the year.
 When added to the $487 million of proceeds we received from our equity offer in February, we have raised or retained approximately $1.5 billion of cash this year that is available to reinvest in growth capital projects, reduce our debt, and decrease our reliance on the capital markets.
 Absent an acquisition, we expect our ATM and distribution reinvestment plan will be sufficient for our remaining equity needs for 2013, and we do not otherwise expect to be in the public equity markets.
 The NGL Pipelines & Services segment reported gross operating margin of $545 million for the quarter, slightly down from the $566 million for the second quarter of 2012. Our natural gas processing and related NGL marketing business had a $75 million decrease in gross operating margin compared to the second quarter of last year. Like last quarter, we had lower processing margins across all of our processing facilities and reduced ethane extraction. Partially offsetting the impact of lower natural gas processing margins was an increase in gross operating margin from fee-based processing and NGL marketing.
 Higher sales volumes, which include propane sold for export, more than offset lower margins in our marketing business. Our fee-based natural gas processing volumes increased to 4.6 billion cubic feet per day this quarter, from 4.2 Bcf per day in the second quarter of last year. Fee-based natural gas processing volumes rose 40%, and equity NGL production from our South Texas processing plants increased 460% to 40,000 barrels per day as a result of production growth in the Eagle Ford Shale.
 The three natural gas processing trains at our Yoakam facility continues to perform above expectations. The increase in fee-based processing and equity NGL production from the South Texas plants more than offset a decline in fee-based processing and equity NGL production from our Rocky Mountain plants, due to lower production and reduced recoveries of ethane.
 Gross operating margin for our NGL pipelines and storage business increased 19% to $188 million this quarter, from $158 million for the second quarter of last year. Our South Texas NGL pipeline system contributed $21 million to this increase, primarily due to a 125,000 barrels a day increase in transportation volumes on increased Eagle Ford Shale production. Our LPG export facility and related Channel Pipeline reported a $12 million increase in gross operating margin on a 202,000 barrel per day increase in propane volumes.
 We increased the refrigeration capacity of our export facility in March of 2013, and are now loading an average of 7.5 million barrels a month of propane, compared to 3.5 million barrels a month before the expansion. NGL pipeline transportation volumes were a record 2.7 million barrels per day this quarter.
 Our NGL fractionation business reported a gross operating margin of $93 million this quarter, compared to $69 million in the second quarter of 2012. This 35% increase was primarily due to higher average fractionation fees and increased volumes from our Mont Belvieu fractionators. Our sixth NGL fractionator at Mont Belvieu began service in October of 2012. And fracs 7 and 8 are scheduled to begin operations in the fourth quarter of this year.
 Gross operating margin from the Onshore Natural Gas Pipelines & Services segment was $198 million this quarter, $22 million higher than the second quarter of last year, primarily due to higher firm capacity revenues in volumes from our Texas intrastate pipeline system, which benefited from increased production from the Eagle Ford Shale.
 Our Onshore Crude Oil Pipelines & Services segment reported strong results again this quarter, with gross operating margin of $197 million compared with $96 million for the second quarter of 2012. Total onshore crude oil pipeline volumes were a record 1.1 million barrels per day this quarter, up 58% from 725,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2012.
 Our South Texas crude oil pipeline system, which includes the new 24-inch pipeline from Lyssy to Sealy that began service last June; and the Seaway pipeline, which was reversed in June of 2012 and fully powered up during the first quarter of this year, were responsible for 83% of the increase in gross operating margin.
 Enterprise and Plains All American announced the formation of a 50-50 crude oil pipeline joint venture in the Eagle Ford Shale in the third quarter of 2012. A portion of this system is in service now, and we realized equity income from this joint venture in the second quarter of this year. The remaining part of the system is scheduled to be placed in service during the third quarter.
 Our Petrochemical & Refined Products and Services segment reported gross operating margin of $163 million this quarter, compared to $157 million in the second quarter of 2012.
 Refined product pipelines and services business reported a $31 million increase in gross operating margin, primarily due to higher transportation fees on our TE Products pipeline. Included in these fees is a $24 million that is recognized in connection with the settlement of a rate case. We also had higher intrastate petrochemical and refined products transportation volumes. Total pipeline transportation volumes for the business were 555,000 barrels a day in the second quarter, compared to 482,000 barrels a day for the second quarter of last year.
 Partially offsetting this increase were decreases in gross operating margin from our propylene fractionation, octane enhancement, and high purity isobutylene business. The propylene fractionation business was impacted by lower sales margins, and the octane enhancement facility had an unplanned outage for a catalyst change-out and maintenance. The facility was down 11 production days during the second quarter and 10 production days in July. We estimate lost gross operating margin was approximately $9 million in the second quarter, and will be about $11 million for July.
 In addition to the strong operating performance this quarter, we also completed construction and began operations of approximately $700 million of growth capital projects. Included in these projects is the expansion of our propylene splitter at Mont Belvieu; the completion of our NGL pipelines from Yoakam to Alvin, Texas; and an extension of our West Texas crude oil pipeline system. In the first six months of this year, we've placed $1.1 billion of capital projects in service. And we have another $1.5 billion of projects that we expect to be completed in the second half of this year.
 These projects include the Texas Express pipeline and gathering system, and the seventh and eighth fractionators at Mont Belvieu, a new pipeline connecting Jones Creek to our ECHO crude oil terminal, and the joint venture crude oil pipeline with Plains that I mentioned earlier.
 We are pleased with the solid results generated by our businesses this quarter, especially given the weak NGL prices that affected our processing and marketing margins. We do not expect NGL prices, especially ethane, to improve significantly near-term, given the continued increase in natural gas production from shale plays. This growth in natural gas production and NGL supplies, however, will create additional investment opportunities for our partnership, as Jim will discuss in a few moments.
 While new supplies have outpaced demand for some parts of the NGL barrel, the demand side in the US is responding with large projects like new world-scale ethylene crackers and new PDH facilities. In the meantime, increased international demand for domestic LPGs is helping balance the market through expanded LPG exports. Although this transition period has proven to be challenging for some midstream operators, we feel good about our ability to deliver and continue to grow, given our predominantly fee-based diversified portfolio of assets, a solid balance sheet, strong liquidity, and significant growth opportunities.
 I'm confident that our team of dedicated employees will continue to execute our growth plans and find new opportunities. And we continue to be excited about the prospects available to Enterprise, and we look forward to working for our investors to create even more value.
 And with that, I will turn the call over to Jim.

 Last year at this time, oil prices were $90; natural gas had fallen below $3; ethane had lost $0.35, propane $0.50. And our processing margins were $0.60 a gallon, down from close to $1. And we were just over $1 billion in gross operating margin.
 Today you've got ethane trading at gas value, virtually; propane at about $0.95; and processing margins are in the neighborhood of $0.35 a gallon. We come in at something just north of $1.1 billion in gross operating margin. Earnings continue to show the strengths of diversification.
 And when I say diversification, I mean the new assets we're bringing on, but also mean how we have changed our contracting strategy on existing assets. The strengths of that diversification can weather that feared processing margin storm so many of you worry about. And as Mike mentioned, over the next couple of quarters we're going to be bringing a large number of new assets into service across all of our business lines.
 If you can call $3.50 to $4.00 stable, natural gas has stabilized from a downward spiral. US oil prices have been pretty stable, in and around $100. But NGL prices have really suffered, as demand has not been able to keep up with the rapidly growing supplies from the shale plays.
 Led by ethane falling apart, ethane is now firmly in the excess category; and trading, as I've said, at its natural gas values. Processing margins are around that $0.35, and Enterprise's processing income is on the receiving end of that slump. However, petrochemicals finally get it. They understand the size of the shale resource and they know that they have to participate in order to be competitive.
 And, as Mike said, the US is witnessing a large petrochemical expansion along the Gulf Coast, most of it focused on low-cost ethane. I started to say that they had the largest petrochemical expansion in history, but I haven't had a chance to compare that to the second half of the 1980s.
 At Enterprise, we've said before, we are connected to every major ethylene plant in the US. We understand their needs. And that's why we're building a dedicated US Gulf Coast ethane header to meet their growing needs. Other parts of the barrel have also suffered, and I think sometimes in sympathy to ethane, but generally because of their ability to compete with other hydrocarbons, including their ability to be exported in some form or fashion. These new NGLs are making their way into the domestic and global markets, and we're participating in that.
 We've seen propane spreads between the Gulf Coast and northwest Europe almost double over the last two years. We also recently completed agreements, besides waterborne exports, we completed agreements that will enable us to deliver substantial amounts of natural gasoline from Mont Belvieu to customers in the Chicago area; these volumes ultimately bound for the diluent-hungry markets in Western Canada.
 The flip side of this wave of NGLs is the investment opportunities it has created for Enterprise. Mike mentioned a lot of the pipelines that we are bringing on. That's about 800,000 barrels a day of new capacity between MAPL, Texas Express, Front Range, ATEX, and Aegis, that are all underwritten by fixed-fee contracts.
 We currently have an open season underway to gauge shipper interest in modifying ATEX to also ship propane. Mike mentioned fracs 7 and 8, and to put it in this context, in just three years we will have added over 400,000 barrels a day of fractionation capacity at Mont Belvieu.  We recently announced plans to build refined products export facilities in and around what we call our Southern Complex on the Gulf Coast. The US refining industry is running at high utilization rates, upgrading and expanding, and has become significant exporter of refined products. With this project, we will build capacity to export refined products by upgrading our refined products pipeline that connects to 12 Gulf Coast refineries, and connecting it with export facilities at both Beaumont and the Houston Ship Channel.

Our Eagle Ford buildout for natural gas, NGL, and crude is just about complete with most of the assets currently in service. In NGLs, we are nearing the completion of the major buildout we started three years ago, with most of our large transportation and fractionation initiatives coming on over the next few months.
 Oil continues to be a growing part of our business. And our natural gas assets, situated throughout the Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast, are seeing growth in both supply and demand, and are perfectly situated to serve some very large demand markets that will be constructed over the next several years. In NGLs, we've always had a strong franchise. And we say that we serve both the supply and demand side of the equation. We're going to also concentrate on both the supply and demand side of the equation for other parts of our businesses.
 For petrochemicals, this demand side focus has been confirmed by the Aegis pipeline and our PDH plant. In refined products, our Southern Complex export project is another validation of our determination to be on the demand side of the equation for refined products. And for crude, our buildout of the ECHO terminal and its downstream pipelines to support the very large Gulf Coast refining industry is an example of focus on the demand side of the equation.
 As the industry continues its transition from a state of chronic shortage of hydrocarbons that required waterborne imports of natural gas, LPG, crude oil, and refined products; to the significant growth of inland, domestically produced hydrocarbons, we feel like we're pretty well situated to capitalize on that.
 And with that, I'll turn it to Randy.

Randy Fowler,  Enterprise Products Partners L.P. - EVP, CFO: Thank you, Jim. A bit of housekeeping before we get started. Some general business media customarily overemphasize either changes in our revenues or changes in our operating expenses in isolation. This is not necessarily a good use of time or reporting when evaluating a midstream energy company or a utility, for that matter. These income statement items are influenced in large part by changes in commodity prices from one quarter to the next. In general, higher commodity prices result in an increase in our revenues attributable to the sale of NGLs, natural gas, crude oil, petrochemicals, and refined products.
 At the same time, however, higher commodity prices will also increase the associated cost of sales as purchase costs rise. Therefore, an increase or decrease in revenues due to an increase or decrease in commodity prices may not generate a corollary increase or decrease in gross operating margin or in distributable cash flow, because cost of goods sold would also increase or decrease with commodity prices. This is why we believe gross operating margin is a better performance-based financial measure than isolating on either revenues or cost of goods sold, and why our earnings press release and this conference call focus on gross operating margin.
 So, pardon me for preaching to the choir, to those investors and security analysts who follow us closely.
 Now, interest expense increased $200 million in the quarter of 2013 from $187 million recorded in the second quarter of 2012. Our average debt balance for the second quarter of 2013 increased $2.4 billion from same quarter last year. Our weighted average cost of debt decreased to 5.4% at June 30 compared to 5.8% a year ago.
 The provision for income taxes increased to $20 million this quarter from $9 million for the second quarter of 2012, primarily due to recording a deferred tax expense and a related liability with respect to certain changes to the Texas margin tax that were enacted in June 2013.
 Our capital spending was over $1 billion this quarter, including approximately $990 million spent on growth capital. We expect to invest an additional $2.4 billion in growth capital expenditures through the remainder of 2013. Total growth capital expenditures for 2013 are expected to be approximately $4.2 billion.
 Sustaining capital expenditures were $75 million this quarter compared to $90 million for the second quarter of 2012.  Adjusted EBITDA for the 12 months ended June 30 was $4.5 billion. Our consolidated leverage ratio of debt principal to adjusted EBITDA was 3.6 times for the 12 months ended June 30, 2013. And this adjusts debt for the 50% equity treatment of the hybrid securities.

This is just base tree awards but it is something that gives us great confidence that moving forward the tree market is going to continue to grow and ultimately the subsea market will continue to grow.

As we indicate over the next five years, customers that we have very strong relationships with make up over 50% of this market. As you can see obviously Petrobras drives this market but it is very dispersed. When you look at some of the major players in deepwater, BP, Chevron, Shell, Total, companies that we've had long relationships with, some formalized, some not formalized, but all customers that have a great amount of respect for what we can do for them in subsea and customers we continue to expect will drive a tremendous amount of business for us in the coming years.
 The subsea processing is the piece of the business that I think brings the most excitement not just to the industry but to our Company as well and this is something that we have broken down into three primary areas  boosting, separation, and to a lesser degree, gas compression.
 Looking at these, pretty much all subsea processing has an element of boosting because ultimately if you are  even if you are doing a separation project, you are dealing with removing pressure from the wellbore and ultimately boosting will be needed for all projects, whether there is a separation element or a gas compression element.
 Separation on the other hand, we're looking  and I will discuss it a little more  separation is ultimately trying to deal with problems, whether it be high water cuts, not enough  or excuse me  high water cuts, issues with gas and the well causing hydrates or economics that allow for a separation at the seafloor to be more economical than adding a platform.
 And then finally, gas compression. These projects are fewer in nature but typically tend to be very expensive. I know the Asgard project was about a $0.5 billion project. We would not expect to see more than one of these maybe every two or three years, but it is the third piece of the subsea processing as we see it.

 For brownfield recovery, we look at Marlim or Tordis. Marlim is the one we delivered to Petrobras here about three or four weeks ago and ultimately they have already put the system on the seabed and expect it to be operational by the end of the year. But in these cases there were very high water cuts, water cuts that were making the platforms and ultimately the production up at the sea level not as economical as it should be. By us adding our separation units, in these cases water-oil separation units, we are able to separate the water at the seafloor and ultimately produce a greater volume of oil up to the platform, thus making the production from these wells tremendously more economical than what they were when the water cut was at least from what we can tell in excess of 50%.
 Then finally cost reduction, and Congro Corvina, a project that we won back in May of this year, ultimately Petrobras was able to remove a platform using the separation system that we install or that we will be installing for the Congro and Corvina fields. In this case, each field had 10 wells that were producing that they were needing to separate gas from the liquids. And the separation units we installed will allow them to ultimately separate the gas at the seabed and produce the oil and reduce the amount of gas that  or actually remove the platform that was previously necessary.

What makes us excited about the Marlin project is it will  this pilot will ultimately be working on one well, but we see that there's approximately 70 wells in this field that have very similar characteristics. And we would hope that we would be a large participant in this further expansion.

What we're doing in this case is we're working on aging wells and performing intervention services that ultimately increase production from what it currently is. The reason people use the well intervention services is they are less expensive than using a rig. In many cases we estimate that it's about a 50% to 70% cost reduction from using a conventional rig to perform these types of services.

 As far as on the M&A front, we have not been active as far as in the large types of M&A that make the headlines. We have created or we have expanded our frac tree business, frac trailers as far as being able to tie flowlines together are businesses we are looking at and we will continue to pursue the shale markets going forward.

As our subsea revenue goes up, we realize we should be able to leverage our fixed cost much better but you look at our Q1 revenue, our first-quarter revenue of a little less than $700 million and our anticipated fourth-quarter revenue of somewhere close to $1 billion in subsea and we realize that execution where it's something that is a challenge is something that we will be able to successfully perform at a higher level. And as we do that, we should see some margin improvement based on a greater ability to execute.

James Fazzino,  Incitec Pivot Ltd - MD and CEO: Well, thank you Charlie, and thanks to all of those joining us in Sydney today, and all on the call. Today Frank and I will assume that you've read the profit report and the disclosures that we've made in the accounts. What we'll endeavor to do is to keep our comments at a high level to unpick the result and give you some insights into it. As is always the case we are very happy to take questions at the end.
 Let's start with zero harm on slide 4. Zero harm is the more important metric in the business. It is the most important aspect of execution because it is a function of our right to operate which is why it's always number one on my list of priorities.
 What we've done this year is reviewed zero harm in the context that a balance score card and the strategy that we put in place in 2012 and on the slide on the right-hand side you can see our progress in terms of the two metrics which is both the recordable case rate and the injury severity rate. Really what we're really interested in is the injury severity because zero harm's about stopping fatalities, significant incidents, and on a PSM side, it's stopping significant incidents on our sites.
 What's pleasing for me about the slide is it shows a 45% improvement in the total recordable incident rate or TRIFR to just under 0.76. That's well under our long-term objective or milestone that we set back in 2012 which was 1. In some respects, more importantly an 80% decline in injury severity.
 Moving to process safety, we've seen also a step change in process safety incidents. For example, we saw a 52% reduction in incidents this year. The outstanding performance over the last few years is the construction of our Louisiana ammonia plant, where over 5 million hours were worked without a lost time injury. That's a benchmark performance for any construction project anywhere in the world.
 Overall, we've seen a substantial improvement in safety. I think this is a great lead indicator of how we're executing in the business because to get safety right, you have to get everything right. However, in saying this we'll never be satisfied and it will always continue to be my number one priority.
 Turning to the financials on slide 5, 2016 reported NPAT was AUD128 million, and that was AUD271 million down on 2015. The reported NPAT includes individual material items of AUD167 million after tax. They related to the Gibson Island Plant impairment which we told the market about in the first half results. That number hasn't changed.
 In addition, we've booked restructuring costs under the BEx organization focused improvement plan. We've booked roughly around about AUD90 million worth of costs for that plan on a before tax basis. It delivers AUD100 million of cashflow benefit so the payback is less than a year. Frank, will talk you through both items in more detail in his presentation.
 Looking at the big picture, 2016 was really a result of a story of what happened outside IPL where the external impacts were really tough. Really tough markets, in particular fertilizer commodity prices compared to what happened inside IPL. That was all about what we call controlling the controllables which I think was very good performance, and in some cases, outstanding performance.
 Let me touch on both of those aspects of the performance. In terms of the external impacts outside IPL, we saw significant cyclical and structural influences. Those in total impacted EBIT by around about AUD231 million. They reflected on one hand the decline in the global resources industry, and far more significantly the declining international fertilizer prices which were somewhere towards their cyclical lows, particularly from the second half.
 In terms of the internal impacts, we recognized the external environment ahead of time. We took action quickly to do as what I've described as controlling the controllables. Accordingly, we're able to partially offset the external negatives by AUD71 million, and that was delivered through BEx, productivity improvements over what we call both continuous improvement, and also focused improvement.
 Because of that ability to respond to the external environment, when I look at the numbers, I'm actually very pleased at the way our people have responded to the challenges in 2016.
 In terms of how I saw the businesses, and highlights in the businesses, firstly in the Australian fertilizer business we saw margins recover to their historical levels. I think that was a particularly great result. It's far harder in the business to maintain margins in an environment of falling fertilizer prices because, obviously, we're a bit manufacturer and we are always long. To rebuild the margins to what they should be in terms of the historical level, I thought that was very notable. I give the Incitec Pivot Fertilizers team a huge tick for being able to do that.
 The Asia Pacific explosives business when we looked at earnings, they were broadly flat if you add back the impact of Fabchem losses, and Frank will cover those losses later on.
 In terms of the Australian business flat, it was a great result in what is an over supplied market. Really, it's built around Moranbah. Later on when we look at the operating metrics, Moranbah produced record production. Of course, that is reflected in the earnings in the business. The downstream business has done a great job at supplying our customers in as what I've said is a really challenging market in terms of the Australian explosives market.
 That was also the case in our Americas explosives business, where once again if you look at the US business, so take away the international initiating systems sales, once again that was broadly flat. Given the structural change in US coal I thought that was also a very good result.
 Turning to slide 6, provides a little more detail around the impact of fertilizer prices. On the result, and if you look at fertilizer prices from 2015 to 2016, and the impact of the reduction in those prices, it was around about a negative AUD220 million impact on the result.
 Prices were either at or somewhere near their cyclical lows with urea and DAP at 10 and 12 year lows respectively. However, when I look at more recent trading, in particular urea, there are signs of some green shoots starting to show through. They're green shoots that have occurred in around about the last month. However, we will need to wait and see how sustainable that is.
 In terms of the cycle, we are a business with an implicit cycle in it. I've worked in fertilizers for 20 years, and I know from deep experience that looking from the outside you can't extrapolate off the bottom of the cycle, and at the same time you shouldn't extrapolate off the top of the cycle. The answer is somewhere in the middle.
 That's exactly the approach that we take inside the business. We look through the cycle and always focus on the things we can control. That's exactly what we did this year. By doing this we take appropriate action, and that action ensures we can make appropriate returns at the bottom of the cycle and exceptional returns at the top. When I move on to the BEx OFI that's exactly what that's designed to do.
 Flipping to page 7, let me talk in more detail about what I mean about controlling the controllables. Really from my perspective we had, as I said earlier, very good and in some cases exceptional execution across the business. What was pleasing was that that was on a balance scorecard through the business from safety, to productivity improvement under BEx, through to the way we executed growth with Louisiana being a highlight, and then finally the way we looked after our balance sheet.
 Given that I've already touched on safety, I won't re-cover that. I'll talk about Louisiana separately. I'll focus on the elements of BEx manufacturing performance, and also the balance sheet in my comments on this slide.
 In terms of BEx, continuous improvement driven by BEx was again a key contributor. As I said during the year we became aware of the cyclical and structural changes. Given we've got a business system that drives continuous improvement, our action was to accelerate BEx. You can see the result in the numbers.
 BEx generated in terms of continuous improvement, net productivity benefits of AUD55 million. That brings cumulative productivity benefits under the BEx program to about AUD162 million since we started it in 2013.
 Now the important thing is that the numbers that we report under BEx are net of inflation increases. So when our business, like a lot of businesses, to stand still you've got to drive productivity improvements of AUD40 million per year. BEx covers those cost escalations and then we're able to add value onto the bottom line.
 When you look at the slides that Frank will talk about later, you will see that there are no negative bars for cost escalations. They're covered by BEx. That's exactly what continuous improvement is all about.
 The key take away really is that through BEx we actually have built a business system that drives year-on-year productivity improvements, and it's across multiple facets of the business. The important thing is because it's grounded in a business system, those productivity improvements are sustainable rather than being one offs in terms of cost cutting.
 Let me talk a little bit about manufacturing which was for me at the stand out in the results. Once again, the improvement in our manufacturing performance is driven by BEx and reflects the business system. After all our BEx system is based on the Toyota production system. So it's all about lean manufacturing, and lean principles in manufacturing.
 For me, three of our largest plants were the stand outs. That being Phosphate Hill, and Moranbah, and in the US, Cheyenne. Although, I could make the same comment on a number of our plants globally. That includes our initiating systems business which is sometimes forgotten, but IS also had a fantastic year.
 In terms of Phosphate Hill, the team at Phosphate Hill delivered the second year of more than a million tonnes of production. I think that's an outstanding result given that we lost around about 39,000 tonnes of DAP production due to the train derailment over Christmas this year.
 Importantly in 2016, we put in place long term gas supply agreements from the Northern Territory which will reduce gas costs by AUD55 million from 2019, compared to what they were in 2016, with an interim saving of AUD20 million from calendar 2017. That AUD20 million is included in the OFI savings that we talk about.
 Now, what was really pleasing about that is whilst a lot of people are talking about the rising gas prices, once again we're ahead of the game and we've done something about it. The Northern Territory pipeline was something that people said would never happen. Well, the really good news for Incitec Pivot is that it's being laid today.
 I think it's a great example of our value of challenging the status quo and bringing new gas to Eastern Australia is changing the status quo in that market. So particularly pleased about that. What that means is we can start pushing the Phosphate Hill plant back down into the second quartile which is our long-term goal.
 At Moranbah, the team delivered record production. That's a fantastic outcome given that we're in the fourth year of a four year turn around program. In the profit report you'll see production from Moranbah improves every year. That's what we mean by continuous improvement. I think that's just a great year.
 In some respects, we call Moranbah our school of hard knocks because it has been a difficult plant to commission. In fact, a lot of people in the industry said it would never work. It was really pleasing to be able to send a few emails out around half year to say the plant that you said would never work has produced over a million tonnes of product. I thought that was a great result.
 As is the case with Cheyenne. Cheyenne had a fantastic year. It is still our largest plant in North America in terms of its complexity. It's even more complex than Louisiana because it's a complex of plants, not just a single ammonia plant. Once again, in the final year of a four year turn around period, we saw the ammonia plant produce at record rates. That's a real tribute to the team at Cheyenne.
 Moving to the BEx OFI, or the Organization Focused Improvement Plan. As you recall we announced that plan at half year this year. It has a goal of driving AUD100 million step change in cashflow through productivity. AUD80 million of that to be reflected in the P&L, and AUD20 million reduction in sustenance spending.
 The really good news is we've already delivered AUD16 million worth of benefits from the OFI in the last few months of the 2016 year. Really, what the program is all about is aligning our cost base to market realities, and ensuring as I said earlier, that we can make satisfactory returns at the bottom of the cycle, and exceptional returns at the top.
 I think the OFI is a great example of our ability to take action early, and to use BEx to drive a step change in our business. If you consider that we've totally restructured the business in four months, and have a very clear plan through 627 initiatives to deliver that AUD100 million, you can see the power of BEx. Actually, Elizabeth Hunter who leads the OFIs sitting here in Sydney. So great job Elizabeth. So far so good.
 As I said the cost of implementing that program is about AUD90 million. It has less than a year's payback.
 Then finally, moving to the balance sheet, the really big picture message on the balance sheet is we're in great shape given that we've just been through a period of spending AUD1 billion at Moranbah, and almost AUD1 billion at Louisiana.
 On top of that in an environment where we've seen significant structural and cyclical changes in our markets to number 1) maintain our investment grade balance sheet, and secondly end up with leverage that's less than the target that we set at the time that we kicked off on Louisiana. That's a real tribute to Frank and his leadership.
 If you look at leverage, it's around 2.1 times. I can recall standing in front of you when we kicked on Louisiana saying that we didn't want it to go any more than 2.5 times. So we're well under that target. As I say the degree of difficulty is higher because in that time, we've had that cyclical downturn in fertilizer prices.
 Let's move along to growth and slide 8. By far 2016's highlight is the successful completion of our world scale ammonia plant in Louisiana. By any external measure, by any Australian measure, by any global measure, project execution has been outstanding.
 When we benchmark the project against major construction projects throughout the world, and we did this by using a global management consultancy. What they found is Louisiana is in the top 2% of projects completed globally.
 That's on a range of dimensions. Firstly, benchmark safety. As I said over 5 million hours worked without an LTI. Benchmark cost. It is under budget and it is a fair way under budget. We're predicting the final cost to be under $850 million, and that's what we approved at sanction. How that stacks up against global averages, on average major construction projects over the last five years have blown out by 80%. So ours is under budget, whereas your benchmark is significantly over budget.
 Benchmark schedule. The plants on time, and that compares to a global average for major projects at 20 months late.
 Benchmark capability. It's quite rare to have a project this early in operation where we know that there's a demonstrated ability of the plant to operate at name plate volume and also name plate efficiency. The last 24 hours for example, we produced 2,470 short tons of ammonia. Name plate is 2,500. So, so far so good in terms of early operation.
 Benchmark risk management. With lump sum turnkey construction contract keeping us in good stead. Also, the plant sold out from day one. And it?s sold out between 10 and 20 years, in terms of long term contracts.
 And then finally, benchmark investment returns. We reran the numbers on Louisiana around a couple of weeks ago, and the returns that we're forecasting are still 50% above our cost to capital.
 So a really really good project. And Jamie Rintel, who was part of the investment case, Morris Hofman who built the plant. Alan Grace. And also, Chris and the team who are running the plan, just a fantastic execution through that project.
 We'll see the benefits over the next two, three years as the plant ramps up to full capacity.
 Moving to strategy on slide 9, whilst our strategy has evolved over time, it has been anchored around a number of key strategic themes. These really align to how we think we create value in IPL.
 The first one of these is nitrogen based chemical manufacturing. So if you look at everything that we've done, it's had a nitrogen link. Running big nitrogen plants, building them, and running them, is our core competency. And I think that's distinctive.
 And secondly, what we've also done is ensured that whatever projects we do leverage are market dislocation.
 Really, this slide tries to show our transformation back to when we were a fertilizer co-op. That's not that long ago. It's 2003 to where we are today.
 And what we see on the slide, if you notice, that we've made a couple of very big moves every two to three years, and importantly after making those moves, we've always gone into a period of consolidation. That's exactly where we are today.
 Importantly, every big move that we've made in the Company's history is built upon the previous moves. So we have ensured we've only stepped out one step from the core.
 So with the completion of the Louisiana plant as I said we've transformed ourselves from a East Coast fertilizer Co-op to a global diversified industrial chemicals company which is how we think about ourselves today.
 That actually means we've got far more balance in our portfolio. For me I think that diversification and balance will be something which will bear out over the next few years for investors.
 On page 10 I've tried to give some insight the way we think about the balance in the portfolio post Louisiana. The first element of those is from a geographic or economic exposure point of view.
 If you look at the geographic and economic exposures in the portfolio around about half of the business is exposed or driven by China and more broadly the development of Asia.
 For me I think that's a really good thing because despite what the dooms-dayers  China will still grow at 2%, 3%  sorry 2 or 3 times global average GDP.
 So that's what our Australian explosives business or Asia Pacific explosives business is exposed to. Of course, that's exactly the thematic that drives food demand and fertilizer prices.
 On the other side of the world we've got the benefit of the energy disconnect in the US. That'll be an enduring benefit over time. I notice that US gas prices today are at $2.20. That just shows the strength of that market.
 Of course that's what Louisiana is underpinned by. I think that gap between the US energy advantage  as I say will increase over time and that'll benefit our business particularly as oil starts to come back, which it will over the medium term.
 From an end market dimension we've got a much more balanced portfolio. So roughly 50% of our business is explosives, 30% industrials and 20% fertilizer. Of course those percentages will move around depending on where we are in the cycle.
 Both of those factors mean that in the business we've got a lot more strategic flexibility. That bodes very well for the future for the business.
 However before we embark on the next wave of growth we firmly understand we need to earn the right to grow. And that actually means our primary focus now is in driving value out of the assets that we already have in the portfolio.
 So then finally, how does all of that play out in terms of our operating model? Slide 11 shows that. And it really does show the way that we run the business. We have global manufacturing which is our global business  our upstream business  which has nitrogen competency at the core. And we service our customers through downstream businesses that are very customer focused, very customer-centric.
 There through to segments of explosives, industrial chemicals and fertilizers. And you will note this is the way we'll report going forward. And I would also like to give Charlie shout out here. I mean this is exactly what we mean by challenging improving the status quo.
 That extra clarity in terms of the segments in our business hopefully will allow you to understand the numbers in more detail.
 So I'll just hand over to Frank and he'll go through the numbers in a little more detail.
