David R. Warren,  A. O. Smith Corporation - Senior VP, President & GM of North American Water Heating: Good afternoon, everybody. Thank you, Kevin, for the introduction. Before I get into the North America Water Heating presentation, I wanted to talk a little bit about my past and the experiences that I've had with A. O. Smith.
 I started out with A. O. Smith about 30 years ago in 1989, believe it or not, as an inside sales coordinator and worked my way up through the sales organization on the wholesale side of our business. Back then, A. O. Smith was maybe about $300 million in the water heater space, and stepped into a regional sales manager position. We acquired State Industries. I had some experience in the retail side of the business, managing our hardware co-op business. And then had a great opportunity to move to Europe and get some P&L experience, managing our European operation. From there in about 2007, I had the pleasure of traveling to India and exploring the opportunities in India for A. O. Smith. 2008, we started importing products into India. 2010, we started manufacturing products in Bangalore, India, as the water heater space. And then in 2015, we got into water treatment.
 So I spent maybe about 18 years in the international side of the business with A. O. Smith. And last year, I was privileged to move up into the position to run our North America water heater business. So 30 years of experience, both internationally and in the U.S.
 My presentation is first going to cover the North America water heater business, and then I'll jump into India and give you a little bit of an overview of what we have going on in the Indian market today.
 Going to start off by just kind of setting the stage here as far as what we do within the North America water heater group. We produce, manufacture, and sell products in both the residential gas and electric market. As Kevin had mentioned, our strength is on the commercial side of our business. And then we have a number of other product categories, somewhat niche categories that we participate in to ensure that we have the broad product offering that our distribution base is looking for. We sell through various channels, the wholesale channel and the retail channel, in the U.S. And in Canada, there's another component which is the rental component. So in Canada, it's about 20% residential  excuse me, rental and about 30%, 35%, on the retail and then 40%, 45% on the wholesale side of business in Canada, so a little bit different market.
 We do some export out of North America around the world. The markets that my group is responsible for is Mexico, Central and South America. And when we take a look at that and the breakdown, from a revenue standpoint, the U.S. represents about 89% of our business. We've got Canada representing about 10% of our business and then export, 1% of our business.
 Taking a look at the economy and how we see things going forward. We have seen some growth in starts and completions in 2018. I think we've got it pegged at about 50,000 improvement over 2017. We are definitely taking a look at the rising interest rates, the import tariffs and some of the logistic costs that we are seeing and trying to understand the impact on the housing market going forward. At this point, we're optimistic that we'll see growth moving forward into 2019, maybe a little bit slower rate on new construction.
 As Kevin mentioned that the world is changing, and we are somewhat in transition. And we have a number of things that we keep our eye on. Kevin mentioned the omnichannel. The existing channels that we've had, the very traditional channels of retail and wholesale, the lines are blurring. We have the millennial influence, and we'll get into that a little bit. But there's no question that technology is giving us some opportunities we didn't have 10 years ago, and so we're keeping an eye on that to understand how we can take advantage of it going forward as an organization.
 When we get to policy and regulation, we anticipate that there'll be more federal regulation moving forward, but probably more state regulation as the federal government has backed off a little bit. We're starting to see some of the states actually step up and look at changing the regulations in their markets. So we're keeping our eye on that.
 Utilities, very interesting. A lot of utilities are taking a look at the water heater as a source of storage for energy to lessen the peak demand that they have in the marketplace. And a lot of rebate dollars from the utilities going to high-efficient products and heat pump products. And so we follow that very, very closely. When I travel around the country, and I just got back from an association  American Supply Association conference last week in Phoenix, and as we sit down and talk to our customers, one of the biggest challenge is the talent scarcity that we see out there. With the unemployment at 3.7%, it does get challenging in making sure that you've got the right people within your organization. So we see that throughout the supply chain today, and we also see that in the new construction market.
 And we have some initiatives internally to make sure that we have a very attractive work environment. Ajita mentioned that we have had various employee development programs. And through lean, we're getting more and more of our people engaged and aligned with our strategy going forward.
 Our competitors. We really kind of break out tank-type. And then we look at tankless, and then we look at the others. We have 2 very strong competitors in the residential tank-type business. They've been around for a long time, that being Bradford and Rheem. Rheem is playing in the retail side, as are we. Bradford is wholesale only. And then we have a number of tankless players out there today, coming from Japan and also South Korea. And Rheem plays in both the tank-type and the tankless. And then we have some others that, again, are playing in niche categories, primarily in the commercial business. So we really feel that we've got a very strong position. We've got a strong portfolio of products both in the residential and the commercial space. And as Kevin mentioned, we are market leaders, and we'll get into that a little bit further into the presentation.
 So we talk about the channels, and again, these are the traditional channels. And the way we look at it, you've got your wholesale channel and you have your retail channel. And within each one of these boxes, I have the major players that are being highlighted here within the wholesale and the retail channel. And as Kevin mentioned, we're very blessed in that we've got the significant players working with A. O. Smith today, the Fergusons, the Wins, large regional players. And on the retail slide  side, we've got Ace, Do it Best and Lowe's. And so we're in a great position, moving forward, in the market to continue to grow.
 When we take a look at the wholesale versus retail split, it's 55% wholesale and 45% on the retail side of the business. This fluctuates a little bit, but not much. If there's a strong new construction year, the majority of that business is going through the wholesale channel. So we'll see the mix shift just a little bit.
 We have about 9.4 million water heaters that are sold in North America on an annual basis, about 9.2 million is the residential, and about 250,000 or so are commercial units. So through the presentation, what I'd like to do is dive a little bit deeper into the commercial and then we'll follow-up with the retail.
 But before I do that, let me just go back. The blurring of the channels, what's  what I forgot to mention is what we're seeing are progressive wholesalers and the progressive retailers are really going across the boundary that has traditionally been there. So we find a lot of our wholesalers or leading wholesalers are looking at paths to go B2C. And then you've got your retail side going B2B, okay? And so we have to make sure that we pay attention to that. We understand it. We put ourselves in a position that we can manage that transition as we go forward with the right tools.
 Looking specifically at the commercial market, as Kevin mentioned, we are by far the market leaders in the commercial space and have been for quite some time. It's about 246,000 units. We've got a strong value proposition that has allowed us to enjoy this market share, and we intend to maintain and grow this share going forward.
 This is a split of the industry. And the light blue-shaded area of the graph are commercial electric units, and the gray-shaded area is the commercial gas units. And we have seen a transition over the last few years. We've seen the commercial electric grow by about 70,000 units. And that growth, primarily, was driven by a residential standard regulation, NAECA III, that took place in 2015. The regulation prevented us as a water heater manufacturer to sell residential products larger than 55 gallons. And so what we found out there is, we found a lot of smaller commercial establishments that had in the past been putting in large-volume residential products, shift to now our light-duty commercial product. And we also found some home owners that were out there that had large-volume residential electrics that had to go in with a light-service commercial.
 So the market grew by about 66,000 units since the regulation was put in place. And so that's why you see the shift in mix. Now I'll tell you from a revenue side, it's just  it's almost flipped, okay. On the revenue side, it's about 65% commercial gas and about 35% commercial electric. And I will tell you that the commercial gas is a little more profitable than the electric side.
 So we talk about our market leadership position, and we talk about how we continue that leadership position and grow. We have a great network of distributors in the market along with sales associates that over the years have put together some very strong programs. We do deal direct with some of the restaurant chains and have a turnkey. In those situations, we're actually buying it from our local distributors and then arranging for that installation. As you can imagine, if a restaurant goes down, doesn't have hot water, they're out of business and they need it quickly. So over the years, we put ourselves in a position to meet that need.
 Restaurants aren't the only commercial businesses that need hot water quickly. And so you'll see that the strength of our programs and services is to make sure that we have local inventory when the commercial customers are actually looking for the products. So we have 24/7 programs that are out there that we build with our distributors. They inventory a considerable number of commercial units, and they have it available, and they deliver it direct out to the job site when need calls. We also have UL-certified conversion kits. Again, that allows the distributors to reduce their inventory a little bit. And with the conversion kits, they're able to reconfigure the commercial electric units to meet the requirements of the customer.
 The other real strength though of A. O. Smith, quite honestly, is our ability to work with the engineers that are specifying commercial product on projects. And so when we look at the Dodge data that's out there today, you'll find a little over 60% of all the projects that are being spec-ed that require a water heater to have had A. O. Smith product being specified. And so when you put this all together with our national accounts and you look at the programs that we have to support inventory and the specifications that out there, there's a strong value proposition for the distributors out there to align themselves with A. O. Smith on commercial.
 The other thing that Kevin had mentioned was product, and we have a very robust new product development pipeline. We plan on bringing out new innovative products in 2019 and beyond. And just an example of some of the things that we're able to do, it's not always a brand new product, sometimes it's simply modifying and upgrading the existing product. So we talk about the connectivity on our Cyclone. The Cyclone is by far the leader within the commercial condensing space. We've had it on the market since 1997. Since that time, we've had 6 major upgrades to the product. We've actually extended the product line. We've improved the efficiencies. We've improved the serviceability of the product and the installation  ease of installation of the product during that particular period of time.
 And now in 2018, every Cyclone that's going to the market has the capability of being connected. And so this will help us drive specs in the marketplace. But more importantly, it puts us in a position, as Kevin had mentioned before, to collect data and really understand how our products are performing in the marketplace and look at ways in working with customers that we can add additional value on top of the value that we do today with preventive maintenance possibly or predictive failure. So it's really exciting opportunity as we see the data coming in and having a better understanding of the functionality of our products in the marketplace. Again, the Cyclone is leader in the industry. It's 96% thermal efficiency, provides for a very short payback period and justifies the increase in cost on the front end and represents a significant percentage of our commercial water heater revenues. This is all supported with training and our 24/7 programs with national accounts and customer service.
 So now let's jump a little bit into the residential market, if we can. As you saw on the commercial market share slide, A. O. Smith, once again, is the market leader within the residential space. And we play on both sides, the wholesale and the retail side, as does Rheem. But again, with the innovative products that we've been able to deliver to the market, the broad range of products that we're able to deliver to the market, I think quite honestly, having the very strong position we do in the commercial side, helps bring the residential product forward and allows us to post the share that we are today, just under 40%.
 When we look specifically at the residential water heater market, we kind of break it down by replacement and new construction. So the slide that we have up here in front of us is taking a look at that over a period of time from 1970 to 2016,'17. And what you'll see is that there's a significant amount of business that happens on the replacement side, okay. In that replacement, some of that is emergency replacement, some of that is proactive replacement. And then the dark green-shaded area is the new construction piece, okay.
 We've received some questions, and we've also kind of wondered ourselves, what would be the impact of the recession on our industry and on the business moving forward? The recession from about 2006 through 2008, you can see that the replacement business was, again, very, very stable. And so we've done some modeling in trying to understand better the potential impact that the recession would have on the industry going forward. So we've looked at the U.S. housing stock and the growth of the housing stock and I've got  the next slide will get into that, but we also looked at the warranty replacement cycle that we see.
 So in the light blue bars, what you're seeing is some KeyStat data that we've pulled together, showing the percent of units are replaced at any given time. So less than 5 years, 7% of the units were replaced. 5 to 9 years, 19% replaced. The green bars indicate the data, the same survey approach from 2017, okay. So what you see here is you see that when water heaters are installed, they generally  there's replacement that happens in year 1 out through 20-plus years. And you'll also note that about 46% of those replacements happened post the 14th year of installation. So it's a very elongated bell curve. And with this, we don't feel that there'll be any tremendous impact with short-term recession on the new construction side of our business. It'll really be muted as we go forward.
 So that was one piece that we took a look at. The other piece that we took a look at was, again, the housing stock in the U.S. The gray-shaded area here is the housing stock in the U.S. pulled through the Census Bureau. And what you'll see here is about 120 million homes in the U.S. Now every one of those homes will have a water heater, and some of those homes have more than 1 water heater. So it's really fairly significant that the blue, again, is the replacement water heater industry and the green that you see there are the water heaters that we feel are going into new construction.
 So with the size of the housing stock, the market is very, very stable. Again, it's about 14x the size of the industry. Now there are some factors that come into play when we take a look at the replacement business. I had mentioned that there's emergency replacement and there's also proactive. And so we have a strong feeling on the proactive side, it's when you sell your house that's 14 to 15 years old and somebody new is coming and would rather have a new water heater than something that's 14 years old. It has to do with the product life cycle, but it also has to do with consumer confidence and disposable income. So those are all factors that are out there, and a little bit of a swing on some of those factors can have a very positive impact on the replacement market in any particular given year.
 So when we take a look at the elongated bell curve that we find on warranty replacements or replacements of product, and when we take a look at the very significant large size of the housing stock and the replacement business, we don't anticipate there'll be any major impact at all going forward due to the recession that took place in the 2006-to-2008 timeframe. So it is a very, very sizable market. How do we plan to grow moving forward? And Kevin had mentioned technology. We really feel that we need to do as much as we can to support our distributors and our downstream channel partners by using and leveraging our existing capabilities and expanding our digital capabilities and tools going forward.
 So part of that is having a technology and the tools. The other part of that is to make sure that we align with the right groups in the marketplace that are actually replacing the water heaters. So today, we deal with 6 professional plumbing contractor organizations. We also have a service network and our contractor loyalty program with over 30,000 contractors that are buying A. O. Smith product on a regular basis. So it's technology, but also having the right alignment. And we feel we're in really good position with our wholesale distribution and working to expand our contractor network throughout the marketplace.
 As I mentioned, on the replacement side, the utilities are out there today incentivizing the replacement of products. There's 17 states right now that are offering incentives, 217 different programs out there, touching over 30 million people. And so the incentives range from $300 up to $1,000 in some markets, if the consumer will pull out their existing electric water heater and replace it with a heat pump residential product. So we're really tuned into the utility and the utility activity to help us for our growth moving forward.
 And so you see a heat pump that's located there on the slide. You'll also see that we've got some new products that we're launching. We've launched with Lowe's in October, when we were launching at the wholesale, is tankless electric. This is a product segment that we weren't in before. The industry is about 370,000, 380,000 units, about 70,000 of that is residential. The rest are more point of use and commercial. So we're excited about bringing out those new products and nurturing the residential electric heat pump product, working with the utilities and contractors.
 There's been a lot of talk about tankless. When I fly around the world and fly around the U.S. and I let them know that I'm working with A. O. Smith, it's, so what about tankless? What are your thoughts about tankless? Tankless offers some unique value proposition on the market. It's been out there for a while now. It's about 8% of the total residential market today, but it is growing at a little bit faster rate than the tank-type side. So we definitely have our eye on that particular market, the segment of the market. We have a buy-sell relationship with a company in Japan, and we're continuing to work with them to work on innovation, on the bringing out new solutions on the tankless gas product offering and also on the tankless electric that we're just bringing to market.
 So the market is somewhat of a niche. It is growing, and we feel that we're in a very, very strong position with the infrastructure that we have today with the distribution base, with the contractors that currently buy from us and then with the technology that we have in place to really create downstream demand. So our expectations would be going forward that we'll improve our position in the tankless space, and there'll be some focus in that particular area.
 The other thing that we talk about, we talk about the new construction market, we talk about technology. And I'm sure you've seen similar slides to this and the discussion around the millennials, the discussion that many of their major purchases have been delayed, as they pay off their student loans and work down their debt. But we see tremendous opportunity for the millennials moving forward. And you see the size of the millennials at 79 million. The Gen X is 65 million. And then you look at the transition from 2018 to 2026. The important thing here is when we take a look at this, the digital adopters will kind of move along with it. The digital natives, those are the generations that are actually pushing the technology further.
 And there's no question that they'll still have an impact on the way we do our business going forward, as the millennials are seeking the seamless purchase with a seamless transaction going forward.
 Our retailers and our wholesalers are also reacting to this particular trend. In the past, our wholesalers or retail customers would simply utilize technology, throw it out there and see what sticks. And now the consumer is saying, well, it's nice that you have a Facebook page, it's nice that you've got a way in which I can order from a mobile device, but is it all connected? And so the omnichannel is about making those connections happen, okay. And so we have our wholesale customers and our retail customers trying to transition from that multichannel approach to the omnichannel approach.
 Why is that important? Well, it's important that we're in a position to be able to support that. Really going forward, we've heard from our large customers, it's all going to be about managing the content. And so just recently, this year, we put in a PIM system, a product information management system, that allows us to manage the data and the content that we have, one source of truth. If we make a change, we push it out to our websites, push it out to our spec sheets, push it out to Facebook, push it out to our retail customers and wholesale customers. It's not only having accurate data at one particular time, it's being able to maintain that going forward. And so that foundation with the PIM system is quite important.
 There's other things that we're doing to expand our digital capabilities. We got some snapshots here. On the top, you see our product-selector tool that's out on our website. It allows the consumer to go in and select the water heater that's right for them. It's not static. We do take information, for example, the cold water  incoming cold water temperature, different in Minnesota than it was in Florida. And so the water heater is kind of different as far as the energy output of that particular unit.
 We also take a look at the energy rates, and we look at the incentives that would be in that particular market. So there's a tool that consumers can walk through. It's a product selection tool. I mean, it's amazing when you get done with that, the different options that they have in front of them. It so often isn't just a 40-gallon gas or 40-gallon electric, it's energy efficient products, it's residential heat pumps. And when those options are made available, the mix has a tendency to improve.
 So there's reasons why we're making a little bit easier, and we're seeing some success in that area. The other thing that I mentioned was aligning with the right contractor groups out there and actually providing leads to the contractors. So we do have a lean  lead generation tool that's on our website. We work it with our contractor loyalty programs. And the site and the network is so strong, we now have the EPA using our database and our contacts to promote energy efficient water heaters on their particular site, and you see an image of that there.
 The other thing that we're doing is customizing the tools for our contractors. We have a very, very broad product offering, and a contractor in a certain market may not have that product locally available. So the tools then also allows them to customize to only show to the consumer the products that are available in their particular market.
 I want to finish up a little bit. Kevin had mentioned lean. And within the North America Water Heater group, we have a initiative that we launched this past year to really take a look at lean concepts, lean tools, lean thinking, so that we can lean up our organization. And we've been very successful with the launch of the program within the North America Water Heater group. We plan on expanding that moving forward. A. O. Smith has always been known for continuous improvement and lean initiatives within the factory, and we continue to do that. But as Kevin mentioned, we are now taking a look at our processes from start to finish. So order to cash, all the way through plan to manufacture, all the way through to lean up those processes. It really involves everybody every day within our organization and also involves our management team when we need to look at changing and revising our policies.
 The product information, we have talked about. The other tool that we are looking at in our factory that is relatively new is SCADA, for supervisory control and data acquisition. This gives us some real-time information on the processes within the factory to understand whether or not we're moving the product along as we should. And if there's opportunity for improvement, we've got a tremendous amount of data to point us in the right direction to improve those efficiencies.
 So going forward, the 4% growth for the North America Water Heater group. We're very optimistic that we're going to be able to meet the goal going forward, as we have in the past. We will get some assistance with the price increase that we had in 2018, that'll rollover into 2019. That '18 price increase was implemented around June. What we see with the commercial growth, BRG is forecasting 4.4% growth in the commercial space, both gas and electric. We do see transition from standard efficiency product to condensing water heaters. And we also see a sizable housing stock. And we do expect that the starts and completions will continue to grow on into the future, and really capturing the business with leveraging technology to improve our downstream demand for our products.
 So a lot of talking there. I appreciate you listening. And I'd open it up at this point in time to anybody that has any questions about the North America Water Heater business. We got one back there.

Bob Giardina,  Town Sports International Holdings, Inc. - President & CEO: Thank you, Dan, and good afternoon.
 Our second quarter had a couple of important milestones, so I'm going to jump right into the numbers. First, comparable club growth was a positive 1.5%, our first positive comp in almost 3 years and better than our expectation for no growth in the quarter.
 The upside to comp was driven by membership, which increased by 7,000 net new members from the end of the first quarter, as well as personal training revenue, which grew by 7.2%, our highest personal training growth in more than 2 years. This led to better than planned revenue, which contributed to an improvement in our EBITDA of more than 26% over last year. We have now added 24,000 members to our base in the first half of 2011 and we now expect to end the year with roughly 4% to 5% more members than we started the year with. And these additional members and the momentum in personal training will continue to boost our revenue in the back half of the year, which Dan will address in his guidance section.
 We're very proud of our second-quarter results and the initiatives that are now driving our renewed growth. One initiative that we have discussed and that continues to produce new members is our student-and-teacher restricted membership program. We added an additional 12,000 members to this program since the end of the first quarter and 20,000 since the end of the second quarter last year. These members boost utilization during nonpeak hours, which adds incremental revenue and earnings.
 Another initiative that helped boost our top and bottom line was a focus on small group training and for-fee exercise classes. This was an area where we needed to improve and the energy we had dedicated to it is paying off. Other ancillary revenue was up 22% in the quarter to $7.5 million.
 And we are not out of ideas yet. We recently introduced a new personal training program that allows members 1 monthly personal training session on a use-it-or-lose-it basis for $49 a month when they commit to 6 months. After 6 months the programs turns to month to month. In the second quarter alone we signed up 1,500 members to this program and are very encouraged by our ability to raise the percentage of members utilizing personal training services.
 What I really like about our growth in the second quarter is that it was multi-faceted. It came from new members, improvements in our attrition rate, nice growth in personal training, and an increase in our joining fee of more than 40%, to $64. Membership revenue was still down on a year-over-year basis because of lower average dues and a lower joining fee revenue realized. But we see membership revenue turning slightly positive in the second half of the year versus the prior year, which will be another nice milestone for us.
 And finally, we had good expense leverage in all areas of the business, which Dan will discuss in more detail.
 One aspect of the business that has not been a part of our results for a while now is new clubs. As I discussed in the past, we have two clubs opening in the fourth quarter of this year, projects that have been in the works since 2008. They are larger, about 30,000 square feet, multi-rec suburban clubs that will cost roughly $4 million each to build. We are excited about their potential. One will be in Garnerville, New York and the other in Bayonne, New Jersey.
 And now we are again analyzing our markets and we believe after not signing a lease for a new site since 2008 that there are some pent up great opportunities out there. With that said, any decision we make about club growth will include only modest growth and will not disrupt our plans to continue to expand our free cash flow.
 Looking out to 2012, there are currently no leases signed and at most we would open 2 to 3 clubs in the latter part of the year as our lead time on a new club is generally 12 to 18 months. Also, any new leases would be for smaller clubs to fill in the network that we have already established in our markets. They would likely be 15,000 to 20,000 square feet in size, cost less than $3 million to build, and be in our urban markets, so smaller and less expensive on average than the last 13 clubs we opened in 2008 and 2009.
 Our principal goals remain to continue to improve earnings and increase free cash flow from our existing club base. If we were to build 3 clubs in 2012, we expect total CapEx would be similar to the $29 million to $32 million we are planning for 2011.
 Based on current plans, we see continued improvements from our existing club base delivering another 4% to 5% of revenue growth in 2012, with EBITDA growth almost doubling that growth rate, net of any drag from clubs in their first year of operation. While it may take 2 or possibly 3 years, our goal is to be get back to a sustainable EBITDA margin of 20% or higher.
 In summary, all areas of our business are moving in the right direction and we do not rely on economic rebound for this to take shape. To my delight, the improvements made to the business are ahead of where I thought we would be 12 months ago. So if you can't tell, we're excited about our current business momentum, our outlook for the rest of the year and next year, and our ability to deliver on the goals we have previously stated and also to potentially find new opportunities that will drive longer-term EBITDA and free cash flow growth.
 With that, I'll go ahead and turn it over to Dan.

Dan Gallagher,  Town Sports International Holdings, Inc. - CFO: Thanks, Bob.
 I'll run through the details of our second-quarter results and then discuss our outlook for the third quarter. In the second quarter our consolidated revenue was $118.3 million, up slightly from $117.4 million in the second quarter of 2010.
 Our net member count increased by 7,000 members to 517,000 members in Q2 2011. This compares to a net increase of 1,000 members in the second quarter of 2010. The number of restricted student and teacher memberships increased by 12,000 members since the end of Q1 2011 to approximately 31,000 members at the end of the second quarter.
 Our joining fees collected continued to show improvement, averaging $64 per member this second quarter versus $45 in the same period a year ago.
 Monthly attrition for the second quarter averaged 3.2% compared to 3.3% in the second quarter last year. This represents a sixth consecutive quarter of year-on-year improvements in attrition. For the second half of 2011 we are expecting monthly attrition to continue to improve and be on average 10 to 20 basis points lower than the second half of 2010. Assuming consumer sentiment and the economic climate are similar to what they are today, we expect 2012 attrition rates will level off at 2011 rates.
 Total ancillary club revenue increased 11.4% to $24.2 million from $21.8 million a year ago. Within ancillary revenue, personal training revenue increased 7.2% to $16.7 million. This represents our fifth consecutive quarterly year-on-year improvement in personal training revenue and we expect this trend to continue for the remainder of 2011.
 Revenue at clubs open over 12 months increased by 1.5% for the quarter. The components of comparable club revenue were as follows. Memberships increased 2.5%; ancillary club revenue and fees and other revenue increased 1.5%; and price declined 2.5%. Given our net member gain of 7,000 members for the full year 2010, the 24,000 additional members netted in the first half of 2011, coupled with our favorable ancillary revenue trends and continued improvements on the amounts of joining fees collected, we are expecting comparable club revenue to continue to improve in each of the next two quarters of 2011, with Q3 approximating 3% and Q4 approximating 4%.
 Turning to expenses, we continue to benefit from the cost savings initiatives that we put in place over the past 2 years. Total operating expenses decreased 6.3% to $107.8 million in the second quarter of 2011 when compared to the second quarter of 2010. Total operating expenses decreased 3.9% when removing $2.9 million of impairment of fixed asset charges from the 2010 total.
 Total payroll and related expenses were $45.1 million, down 7.2% from a year ago, representing 38.1% of revenue. Club operating costs totaled $43.4 million, down 1% from the same period last year.
 General and administrative expenses totaled $6.1 million, a decrease of 3.1%. In the second quarter we again benefited from decreases in liability insurance expenses. In each of the remaining quarters of 2011 we expect our quarterly G&A costs to be closer to our first quarter total of $7.4 million, with Q4 being approximately $300,000 higher, given our planned continuing education event.
 Depreciation and amortization expense decreased 1.7% to $13.2 million. We expect total depreciation and amortization to approximate the second quarter amount in each of the remaining quarters of 2011.
 Operating income for the second quarter was $10.5 million compared to $2.5 million of operating income realized in the second quarter of 2010. Excluding the effects of $2.9 million of impairment charges recorded in 2010, operating income in the second quarter of 2011 improved $5.2 million.
 We incurred $4.9 million of loss on extinguishment of debt charges this quarter related to our refinancing. These charges include a $2.5 million call premium paid to our 11% senior discount note holders and the write-off of deferred financing costs. I will touch on our refinancing shortly.
 We experienced a $1.4 million increase in our interest expense during the quarter when compared to the same period last year. This is in large part due to $1.3 million of incremental interest recorded in connection with the 30-day mandatory call period required with the refinancing of our 11% senior discount notes.
 Net loss for the second quarter was $410,000, or $0.02 per share.
 Our $4.9 million of early extinguishment of debt charges and the aforementioned $1.3 million of incremental interest charges recorded in the second quarter together totaled $6.2 million, or approximately $3.6 million net of taxes, or $0.16 per share. We also recorded $549,000, or $0.02 per share, of discrete tax charges in the quarter.
 Net income, excluding these charges collectively, approximates $3.8 million or $0.16 per diluted share. This compares to a loss per share of $0.04 per share in the second quarter of 2010, or $0.05 per share when excluding fixed asset impairment charges and severance charges net of taxes.
 EBITDA, adjusted for early extinguishment of debt charges, totaled $24.3 million in Q2 2011 versus $19.3 million in Q2 2010 when adjusting 2010 EBITDA upward for the $2.9 million asset impairment charges recorded in the second quarter of 2010. This represents a $5 million, or 26.3%, increase.
 While we expect to see revenue improve modestly over the remaining 6 months of fiscal 2011, our two new club openings planned for the fourth quarter will have a negative contribution during their presales periods and their initial club opening periods. And we do not expect to achieve the year-on-year savings at the G&A line that we did in the first half of 2011. Therefore, our rate of improvement in EBITDA is not expected to continue at the second quarter pace. EBITDA in Q3 is expected to increase 18.5%. Q4 EBITDA, when adjusting 2010 EBITDA downward for the $2.7 million of expired personal training sessions recorded in the fourth quarter of 2010, is expected to improve 12% to 15%.
 Cash flow from operating activities for the first 6 months of 2011 totaled $35.1 million, an increase of $5.6 million when compared to the first half of 2010.
 Capital expenditures totaled $11.7 million in the first half of 2011, compared to $6.3 million in the first half of last year. Given our modest club growth plans, we continue to expect total capital expenditures for the full year of 2011 to total between $29 million and $32 million. This includes approximately $8 million for the 2 clubs we will open in the fourth quarter of 2011. We expect our 2012 capital expenditures to be similar, or less than, this 2011 level, given we are currently targeting to open at most 3 smaller clubs next year.
 As mentioned earlier, we were happy to report that on May 11, 2011 we completed a refinancing of our debt. On that same day we filed a Form 8-K that provides more detail around this refinancing. Our debt now consists of a $300 million term loan facility that matures in May of 2018 and a $50 million revolving credit facility that matures in May of 2016. These facilities provide us with sufficient liquidity for years to come.
 The credit agreement contains leverage and coverage covenants, as well as a covenant that restricts capital expenditures when leverage exceeds certain specified thresholds. There are additional customary covenants and, again, all the details are contained in the just-mentioned Form 8-K that we filed in May. We are quite comfortable with our ability to stay within the respective covenants.
 We ended the second quarter with $299.3 million of principal outstanding on our new term loans and cash on hand totaled $34.5 million, putting our net debt at $264.8 million. We expect to reduce our net debt by $15 million to $20 million in the second half of 2011 and another $40 million to $50 million in 2012, moving our net debt close to $200 million by the end of 2012.
 Turning to our outlook, based on the current business environment, recent performance, and current trends in the marketplace, and subject to the risks and uncertainties inherent in forward-looking statements, our outlook includes the following. Revenue for Q3 2011 is expected to be between $116 million and $117 million versus $113.1 million in the third quarter of 2010, an increase of approximately 3%. We expect revenue in Q4 2011 to increase 4% when compared to Q4 2010, when adjusting Q4 2010 revenue downward for the $2.7 million of expired personal training sessions recognized in the fourth quarter of 2010.
 In Q3 2011 we expect payroll and related expenses to approximate 38% of revenue and club operating expenses to approximate 38.4% of revenue. Club operating expenses as a percent of revenue in Q3 2011 are expected to increase from Q2 2011 in part due to seasonal increases in utilities and marketing costs. General and administrative expenses are expected to approximate $7.4 million. Depreciation and amortization expense are expected to be similar to Q2 2011 amounts in total dollars.
 We expect net income in Q3 2011 to be between $1.2 million and $1.7 million, or $0.05 to $0.07 per diluted share, assuming a 26% effective tax rate and 23.3 million weighted average fully diluted shares outstanding.
 We expect EBITDA to improve $3.3 million, or 18.5%, to $21 million in the third quarter.
 That concludes our prepared remarks. We would now like to turn the call over to any questions anyone may have.

 The cost savings and the creation and management of rental homes in a manufactured home community are considerable when compared to apartments or single family homes for rent.
 In the Marcellus and Utica shale regions of Pennsylvania and Ohio, the recent drop in oil prices have reduced shale drilling for the moment. Manufacturing is beginning to come back in these areas with Ford Motor Company moving production of certain product lines from Mexico to Ohio.  In Nashville, Tennessee, the economy built around technology, and manufacturing, and business services is strong and job growth is outpacing population growth. Favorable demographic trends, an improving economy, and strength in the job market have driven the increase in demand. Household formations have ramped up during 2015. While both owner and rental sectors benefit from the growth in households, the declining home ownership rate indicates that the rental sector is benefiting more from this trend.

Roe Patterson,  Basic Energy Services, Inc - COO: Thanks, Ken, and thanks to everyone joining us on today's call. As we discussed in our first-quarter call, our customers began to increase their activity in the latter part of the first quarter. The net increase gradually continued in most markets throughout the second quarter. Some heavy, but seasonal, rain and snow storms did affect activity in our northern Rocky Mountain market and the Mid-Continent region. Generally, activity improved as a result of increased daylight hours. While we were pleased with the ramp in activity, the much-anticipated rig count increase in oil-driven markets that many companies have forecasted has really yet to materialize in any kind of significance. We anticipate a flattish count for the remainder of the third quarter, as many of our customers have suggested their spending will be flat or even slightly down from current levels for the remainder of the year.
 Now let's review each of our reporting segments. Completion and Remedial Services, our largest segment, experienced a 12% increase in revenue quarter over quarter. Strong demand for our pumping, and reel and fishing tools, services made this segment our best-performing segment in the quarter. Despite higher discounts in our Permian stimulation services and overall coil tubing markets, margins in this segment rose from 33% to 35%, driven by higher utilization and our efforts to reduce costs. Looking forward, pricing will remain very competitive in this segment, as excess capacity remains an issue. However, we have essentially full calendars in the third quarter, which may portend price stability, if not some pricing power, between now and the end of the year. That remains to be seen, as current activity levels and rig count would suggest revenue and margin for this segment will remain flat in the near term.
 Our Well Servicing segment showed a 6% sequential increase in revenue, as utilization rose to 74% on improved daylight hours. We have shown two sequential quarterly increases of 2% in our average rig rate. Pricing overall remained flat, but a steady flow of 24-hour work in our land and barge fleet, and a full calendar of more comprehensive plugging and abandonment activity, drove the increase in these average rig rates. Margins in this segment rose 200 basis points to 28%, due in part to lower unemployment taxes and higher utilization. Near term, we expect revenue and margins to be flat until the industry utilization stabilizes above the 75% range.
 Our Fluid Services segment saw an increase in revenue of about 2% in the second quarter. The increase was mainly due to investments we have made in expanding our water solution services, where we've received full-quarter contribution from the Atlas Equipment and Petro Water acquisitions. Segment margin declined slightly by 70 basis points to 30.7%. This segment remains highly competitive, as competitors continue to migrate to busy oil markets. We have seen significant discounting of frac tanks and other ancillary services within this segment, which holds that margin in the low-30% range. We expect attrition among some of the small players in this segment in the near term. That, along with some possible increase in drilling activity or stronger gas-oriented business, could consume capacity overhang in this segment over the next six months, and allow margins to move up.
 Our Drilling segment revenue was flat with that of the first quarter at $14 million. Rates in this segment were also flat with the first quarter, as we experienced revenue of $16,500 per drilling day. Utilization was down slightly from the prior quarter of 79% to 77% in the second quarter. This decrease was due to some of our customers transitioning their drilling dollars to deeper horizontal drilling programs in the Permian Basin.
 In addition, a few of the oil-driven vertical drilling programs have been reduced due to regulations restricting the flaring of associated natural gas. We stacked one of our 3,000-horsepower Super Singles in response to this decrease in demand for mid-depth vertical drilling rigs; however, our shallower mechanical rigs and our larger-horsepower electric rigs have maintained stable rates and utilization. Margins in this segment fell from 35% to 30% on lower utilization, and some major repair and maintenance on our work fleet.
 Now I'll turn the call over to Alan for more of a view of the financial results for the quarter.

Kiran Rao,  Great Canadian Gaming Corporation - CFO: Thank you, Angela, and good afternoon, everyone.
 Great Canadian's revenues for the first quarter of 2013 were CAD100.5 million. This CAD2.3 million or 2% decrease from the first quarter of 2012 can be attributed primarily to a challenging economy, which continues to impact many of our properties. This impact was only partially offset by strong contributions from both River Rock Casino Resort and the newly opened Chances Chilliwack.
 Boulevard's revenues decreased by CAD1.9 million or 13% during the first quarter of 2013 when compared to the prior year. Boulevard's gaming volumes witnessed significant decline, with table drop and slot coin-in decreasing by 10% and 12% respectively. We believe these results can be attributable to multiple reasons, including a challenging economy, increased levels of competition, on-site construction related to the property's upcoming refresh and repositioning, and most notably, disruption a heightened level of construction on an adjacent highway.
 This construction forced intermittent weekday and multiple weekend/evening closures of primary access routes to the facility. These closures greatly impacted Boulevard's guest volume. The adjacent highway construction is expected to continue through the end of 2013.
 Revenues at our BC Racinos decreased 11% in the first quarter 2013 when compared to the prior year period. This was primarily due to a CAD0.5 million or 19% decrease in racetrack revenues, which reflects the prolonged industry-wide trend of declining horse race wagering.
 Revenues from our Georgian Downs and Flamboro Downs racinos also decreased by approximately 9% and 7% respectively in the first quarter of 2013 when compared to the prior year's first quarter. These declines were primarily due to reduced gaming revenues at the properties. Racing revenues at Flamboro Downs were also impacted by 3 fewer live race days during the first quarter of 2013, a significant decrease from the 65 live race days conducted during the first quarter of 2012.
 River Rock's revenues increased by CAD0.4 million or 1% during the first quarter of 2013, as both gaming revenues and hospitality and other revenues displayed improvements from the first quarter of last year. River Rock's table drop and slot coin-in increased by 4% and 11% respectively during the first quarter.
 However, the benefit of this growth in gaming volumes was mitigated by 0.6 percentage point decline in table pool percentage and 0.4 percentage point decline in slot [in] percentage. Hospitality and other revenues increased 4% during the quarter, primarily to growth in food and beverage sales.
 Chances Chilliwack, Great Canadian's new community gaming center, continued the strong performance it has displayed since its opening November 1, 2012. This property is part of our other BC casinos group, which generated first quarter revenues of CAD4.6 million, a 44% increase when compared to the first quarter of 2012.
 We are encouraged by Chances Chilliwack's result and look forward to the similar permanent community gaming center that we are developing in Maple Ridge. That project is progressing well and should reach completion during the fourth quarter of 2013. We anticipate that Maple Ridge facility will feature approximately 150 slot machines, an increase from the current temporary compliment of 100 slot machines, as well as both improved food and beverage offerings and parking.
 Great Canadian's consolidated EBITDA for the first quarter of 2013 was CAD38.3 million, a decrease of CAD0.7 million or 2% when compared to the first quarter of 2012. EBITDA as a percentage of revenues was 38.1%, a level that is relatively consistent with the prior year's first quarter. This stable performance was primarily due to the revenue increases at River Rock Casino Resort and other BC casinos, which offset the decreases elsewhere.
 Debt earnings of CAD31.3 million were CAD63.2 million higher than those recognized in the first quarter of 2012. This increase was primarily due to the CAD57.4 million long lived asset impairments reported in the first quarter of 2012. These impairments arose from the Ontario Lottery & Gaming Corporation's early termination of the property's site reserve agreements, which ended March 31, 2013.
 During the first quarter of 2013 the Company recognized a CAD28.5 million reversal of this previous long-lived asset impairment. This reversal is based on the combination of letters of intent reached with the OLG and the Ontario government for the continuation of the slot operations and horse racing operations at Georgian Downs and Flamboro Downs beyond March 31, 2013, and the subsequent receipt of CAD31.5 million settlement payment from OLG in connection with the Georgian Downs facility and for which the Company provided the OLG a release of claims.
 After adjusting for the above mentioned items as well as CAD1 million of non-recurring severance cost accrued in first quarter of 2013 that related primarily to our anticipated reduction of Ontario horse racing operations, Great Canadian Gaming's net earnings were CAD11.1 million during the first quarter, an 8% reduction from the CAD12 million adjusted net earnings reported during the first quarter of 2012.
 Great Canadian continues to maintain its stable and flexible financial position. During the first quarter 2013 the Company purchased and subsequently canceled approximately 750,000 common shares under our normal course issuer bid at average price per share of CAD9.29 for total cost of CAD6.9 million. At March 31, 2013, the Company had CAD120.9 million of cash and cash equivalents, in addition to CAD320.1 million of remaining credit available on its revolving credit facility, subject to compliance with its related financial covenants and after deducted the CAD29.9 million of borrowing capacity needed to secure outstanding letters of credit.
 Subsequent to March 31, 2013, the Company purchased and canceled an additional 1.77 million common shares at an average price per share of CAD9.34 for a total cost of CAD16.5 million.
 I will now pass the call to Rod, who will provide commentary on both our operations long-term strategies. Rod?

Rod Baker,  Great Canadian Gaming Corporation - CEO, President: Thanks, Kiran, and welcome,everyone.
 Great Canadian's financial results for the first quarter of 2013 reflect the consistent results at River Rock and encouraging growth from our newly opened Chances Chilliwack. However, these results also reflect continuing challenges present at the majority of our other properties.
 Foremost among these properties is our Boulevard Casino in Coquitlam. As Kiran mentioned, Boulevard has been impacted by multiple factors; a weakened local economy, increasing levels of competition, on-site construction, and perhaps the most significantly, an increased level of nearby construction associated with the adjacent highway upgrade project. Only one of these factors is within our control; the on-site construction at the facility.
 Our repositioning of Boulevard began during the third quarter of 2012 and accelerated during February 2013 when the construction hoarding went up at the facility. This hoarding reduced the number of available slot machines at the facility from 990 to 842. As of May 1 this number has been further reduced to 817 machines. While we have carefully planned the property's repositioning, we believe that combined with the increased level of ongoing proximate highway construction, some of our guests have decided to take a break from their regular visits during the first quarter of 2013.
 In response, while we continue to provide our most loyal guests with exceptional service and work diligently and creatively to make sure that Boulevard offers them a memorable entertainment experience, we are also implementing a variety marketing, promotional and guest service initiatives. These initiatives are designed to encourage our current and lapsed guests to continue to visit the facility during this period of transition.
 The casino floor and associated food and beverage phase of Boulevard's redevelopment is anticipated to conclude by the fourth quarter of this year in order to align with completion of the adjacent highway construction. We believe this repositioning will allow Boulevard to take full advantage of the improved facility access that will be available once the surrounding construction concludes. As of March 31, 2013, the Company has spent CAD3.9 million of an estimated CAD13 million on this phase of Boulevard's redevelopment.
 Great Canadian's BC Racinos continue to witness considerable decreases in their revenues. The 19% or $500,000 decrease in racetrack revenues or the prior year's first quarter reflects a prolong industry-wide trend of declining horse race wagering. The BC Racinos revenues in the first quarter of 2013 were also impacted by 7% reduction in slot coin-in.
 We believe this decline can be attributed to both local economic challenges and increased competition. This competition includes our own newly opened community gaming center in Chilliwack, a recent property refresh at the community gaming center in Abbotsford, and the introduction of 150 slot machines at the nearby Surrey-Newton gaming center in November 2012.
 The decline in the BC Racinos slot revenues was partially offset by a 9% improvement in the table drop and 2.4 percentage point increase in the table hold percentage. As a result net gaming revenues were consistent in the first quarter of 2013 when compared to the prior year period.
 In March of 2012 the government of Ontario announced the cancellation of the slots at racetracks program at all Ontario racetracks and directed the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation to find more strategic locations for their province's slot facilities. As part of that plan and as permitted under the related agreements, the OLG provided notice to all slot and racetrack facilities in Ontario, including our Georgian Downs and Flamboro Downs locations, that their site holder agreements would terminate on March 31, 2013. Subsequent to March 31, 2013, Georgian Downs Limited received from OLG a one-time settlement payment of CAD31.5 million in connection with the Georgian Downs facility, and the Company and Georgian Downs Limited provided OLG with release of claims.
 On March 9, 2013, the Company and OLG signed non-binding letters of intent outlining terms by which OLG will lease the slot machine areas to Georgian Downs and Flamboro Downs for a five year term commencing April 1, 2013. Since that date both the Company and the OLG have been operating as though the key provisions of these leases came into effect, including the OLG making lease payments for the two properties in April and May. In the coming weeks the Company expects to sign definitive agreements with the OLG related to these letter of intent, and until they're signed and appropriately approved, there remains some risk that such agreements may not be reached.
 In October of 2012 the horse racing industry panel of the government of Ontario released a report that included a number of recommendations to help transition the horse racing industry to a self-sufficient business model. These recommendations included reducing race dates by roughly half, pooling all mutual wagering revenues and directing those funds to purses, as well as funding from government provided to track operators on a cost reimbursement basis. On March 26, 2013, the Company and the government of Ontario signed non-binding letters of intent outlining terms under which the Company will operate a reduced level of horse racing at Georgian Downs and Flamboro Downs for up to two years, commencing April 1, 2013.
 In the coming weeks the Company expects to sign definitive agreements with the government. Under the terms of these letters of intent Georgian Downs is expected to operate an estimated 25 race days over a three month period per year,as compared to 103 race days over a 10 month period that were raced in 2012. Similarly, the Company expects Flamboro Downs to operate 100 race days over a six month period per year, as compared to the 188 race days over an 11 month period raced in 2012.
 These represent significant reductions in the scope of our racing operation at each track and required the Companies to take  to make adjustments to their staffing levels at the end of March 2013. These adjustments resulted in approximately CAD800,000 of non-recurring severance expenses recorded this quarter. Based on the terms of the letters of intent, the Company expects Georgian Downs and Flamboro Downs' EBIDTA will decline compared to the levels realized prior to March 31, 2013.
 While the Company has established a practice of refraining of providing forward-looking financial guidance due to the number of factors that could cause actual results to vary materially from those expressed or implied, we estimate that our Ontario properties' combined EBITDA for the 12 months ending March 31, 2014, will range from CAD10 million to CAD11 million, which compares with combined EBITDA of CAD17.3 million recognized in the 12 month period ended March 31, 2013. We caution our listeners that this is a preliminary estimate only and is based on a number of assumptions that include but not limited to the assumption of that definitive agreements associated with the letters of intent are signed, that thereare no material changes to the terms of these agreements, and that necessary reductions in our horse racing costs will be achieved.
 Consequently, actual results may vary from those estimated, and we will assume no obligation to update these estimates should information or assumptions change as we move forward. Furthermore, if definitive agreements for these letters of intent are not signed, the Company may need to record additional impairments against the remaining CAD91 million carrying value of long-lived assets at these properties.
 We continue to investigate ways in which we can play a part in the various new directions gaming is taking in Ontario. As part of their plan to modernize gaming in Ontario, OLG issued a request in May 2012 for information to obtain input from potential industry participants regarding the expansion of private sector gaming in province. Considering this feedback, OLG has stated that it will group many of the province's 29 gaming zones into gaming bundles to ensure that the gaming market is effectively managed. Each gaming bundle is expected to represent a separate bidding opportunity.
 In November 2012 OLG initiated a process for prequalify services providers for eligibility to participate in the request for proposal process for the following three gaming bundles;the Ottawa area, which includes one zone; the East gaming bundle, which includes three zones; and the North gaming bundle, which includes five zones. The request for prequalification for these gaming bundles closed in March 2013.
 We anticipate the request for the prequalification process for additional gaming bundles will commence by the summer of 2013. We believe that the modernization of gaming in Ontario represents considerable growth opportunity for the Company, and we will actively explore any new opportunities that may arise as the province's plan takes further shape, while we will not commenting on our priorities or interests with respect to any particular gaming bundles due to both competitive reasons and confidentiality requirements.
 As Kiran mentioned, Great Canadian concluded the first quarter of 2013 in a strong financial position as evidenced by our cash balance, the undrawn capacity on our revolving credit facility, and our continued strong cash flow generation. This flexibility will remain invaluable as we develop our new community gaming center in Maple Ridge, reposition our Boulevard Casino, and continue to pursue new opportunities for increasing shareholder value should they arise in Ontario or other markets. Thank you.

 At the end of March, Husky’s long-term debt and bank operating notes, including [inaudible] within one year and net of cash of $336m, total $1.8b compared to $2.3b at the end of March 2002. Net debt to cash flow was 0.7:1 at March 31, 2003, compared to 1.4:1 at March 31, 2002.
 Now, I would like to give you an overview of the operational highlights for the first three months of 2003. Upstream  production in the first quarter of 2003 averaged 312,000 barrels of oil per day, 8 percent higher than the 289,000 barrels of oil per day achieved in the first quarter of 2002. Total crude oil and [NGLs] increased 10 percent to 214,000 barrels of oil per day, compared with 194,000 barrels of oil per day realized in the first quarter of 2002.
 The Terra Nova and Wenchang offshore projects and the light/heavy oil program, and [inaudible] celtic Thermostar have contributed to the increase in oil production.  The increase in natural gas production was due to tight yields in the foothills region and a full quarter of production from the second development, which averaged 31m cubic feet per day in the first quarter of 2003.
 Commencing January 1, 2003, Husky has reclassified its light, medium and heavy oil production in line with American Petroleum Institute, API definitions. The classifications in our previous production guideline have been restated to reflect this change in methodology. I am pleased to be here to report on our progress during the fourth quarter and CryoLife's overall successful 2016. Although we came in just below our twice upwardly revised revenue guidance at $180.4 million for the full year. We did deliver adjusted earnings above our guidance.
 Furthermore, we believe our Q4 top-line performance does not reflect the demand issue or loss of momentum for our core products, and we will detail why we believe this in later comments. We suggest you view our progress on an annual basis as quarterly progressions can vary from time-to-time.
 We also reported a significant improvement in our gross margins for the quarter and for the year, which was primarily driven by our continued productivity improvements in our Tissue Processing segment. Those who have followed us over the past year know that 2016 was a transformational year for CryoLife as we laid out a series of new strategies and objectives and made substantial progress on each.
 As a result, we believe we had a very successful 2016 and are well positioned to drive continued growth into the future. One of the biggest organizational changes we made was to expand our cardiac surgery sales force. That move has led to increasing momentum in the market leveraging cross-selling opportunities and expanded awareness for On-X valves and their unique clinical benefits to patients.
 In addition, we believe our products are the preferred heart valve replacement technologies for patients under the age of 60, which represents about one-third of the market. Given our progress in the quarter and strong positioning, we are confident in our ability to continue to capitalize on the opportunity in the cardiac surgery market we serve.
 You may also recall our decision to focus the product portfolio the pipeline and business development criteria. The goal was to strengthen our presence in target markets to which is typically enjoyed by much larger companies.
 That goal was effectively executed and now we offer our customers in most cases multiple clinically differentiated solutions for their patients. The key takeaway is that things are on track. Our top-line in Q4 was slightly impacted by issues that we believe are short-term in nature.
 Looking ahead, as we continue to advance our strategic objectives, we expect to generate solid returns. This morning, I will provide a progress update on our 2016 key initiatives and outline our objectives for 2017. Ashley will provide a detailed review of our fourth quarter financial results and our initial 2017 financial guidance and then we will take your questions.
 Let's begin with an update on our 2016 objectives. Our first key initiative in 2016 was achieving our full year revenue and EPS guidance. Revenue for the fourth quarter of 2016 was $45 million representing a 13% or 2% decrease from non-GAAP basis. This was primarily due to three main issues.
 One, a shortfall in the cardiac tissue segment; two, a shortfall due to fewer orders than expected from our distributor for BioGlue in Japan; and three a shortfall in On-X revenues in our non-strategic OEM business and a regulatory issue from our On-X AAP in Europe.
 As far as we can tell, we do not believe demand has changed for any of our core products, but I'd like to give you a little more color on these three areas contributing to the shortfall on the top-line.
 First, on the tissue processing revenues and specifically cardiac tissues, we are below our expectations for the quarter due to two factors; first, a limited supply of small valves which are used for pediatric cardiac reconstruction; and second, a lack of execution in utilizing our recently published SynerGraft data to convert market share in the adult congenital market.
 We estimate that these issues cost us almost $1 million in the quarter in Q4. Importantly, as I said, demand for these tissues remains strong as we have over $4 million in back orders in pediatric tissue alone.
 We are optimistic that we will be able to increase both supply and sales of these important tissues, due to the recently published clinical data that demonstrates our proprietary SynerGraft processed pulmonary valve provides superior clinical outcomes when compared to non-SynerGraft processed cardiac tissues.
 Specifically, a multi-center study show that at ten years, patients with our proprietary SynerGraft valves had a 17 re-operation rate, whereas patients with a non-SynerGraft valves had a 40% re-operation rate. We have a strategy in place to leverage this compelling data to increase utilization of our SynerGraft valves over valves of our competitors, by demonstrating to physicians and hospitals that our valves are better for their patients.
 We believe this strategy will also be effective when the procurement groups to make us their preferred partner for the supply of these tissues and especially pediatric tissues.
 Second, our BioGlue revenues were affected by our Japanese distributors' inventory management which resulted in BioGlue sales to them were approximately $500,000 lower than anticipated. Our distributor made us aware of their desire during 2016 to reduce their inventory levels which they accomplished.
 Now that they've achieved their 2016 inventory goals, they've informed us they plan to grow their business by 20% in 2017 over 2016.
 Finally, we had a revenue shortfall of about $200,000 in the On-X AAP revenues in Europe due to issues with our CE Mark and another $300,000 related to an unexpected softness in our non-strategic OEM business, which is a business that where we apply our proprietary carbon coating technology to non-valve devices of other companies.
 As for the AAP regulatory issue, we've already submitted our paperwork and expect to be back on the market in the second quarter. As with the non-strategic OEM business, we expect this to be a continued headwind. We've already taken both of these issues into account for our guidance for 2017.
 Importantly, excluding the non-strategic OEM business, North America On-X business increased 22% year-over-year in the fourth quarter. We believe this points to the underlying strength of the On-X valve platform and the success of our North American direct sales efforts.
 As a reminder, our non-GAAP revenues include On-X revenues for the period in 2016 prior to closing of the acquisition and On-X revenues for the comparable periods in 2015. It also excludes revenues for the divested HeRO graft and ProCol product lines for 2016 and 2015.
 Regarding our earnings for 2016, I am pleased to report that we finished ahead of our revised guidance, which came in 50% higher than our expectations entering the year. This was primarily driven by our continued improvement in gross margin which reached 69% in the fourth quarter.
 Our second initiative for 2016 was realizing the potential for our On-X acquisition with a goal of delivering double-digit compounded annual growth over the next five years. We are confident that our goal is well within our reach. Having worked with the product for three full quarters now, we believe we have a winner in our bag.
 We continue to work through the administrative requirements to get On-X into more hospitals, which unfortunately can be a lengthy process given all the constituencies involved. It is much more complex than just getting a surgeon on board with a product, but we know how to navigate the process and continue to add new customers and that will further allow us to achieve our growth objectives.
 Physicians are very receptive to using On-X valve once we are able to explain the clinical benefits to them. We spent a lot of time in 2016 working our way through the consignment process and that work is ongoing. Those efforts don't always show up in the revenue-line right away but we are optimistic these efforts will be rewarded in the future.
 And as I just stated, we are extremely pleased with the performance in the US. When you exclude the OEM business which is non-strategic, we had a 22% year-over-year growth rate. We also anticipate the results of the On-X pivotal study to be published in a major journal sometime this year.
 Recall, that this study led to the On-X valve receiving the indication of 1.5 to 2.0 INR label in the US in April 2015. The balance of 2015 we spent negotiating acquisition and in 2016 we focused on integrating operations of On-X into CryoLife.
 A paper detailing the results of this pivotal study was recently submitted to a major journal and if accepted and published, we believe to provide significant tailwind for the On-X platform to generate incremental interest in this important technology. Our enthusiasm for the On-X opportunity is never been greater and we remain very bullish on the On-X platform.
 Our third key initiative for 2016 was driving efficiency in our tissue processing business. Our fourth quarter results demonstrate that we continue to make good progress in this area. In the fourth quarter, our tissue processing revenues were up 1% year-over-year and for the full year, our tissue processing revenues increased 6%.
 Importantly, our tissue processing gross margins improved to 56% during the quarter, which is an 800 basis point quarterly year-over-year improvement. Ashley will have more commentary on tissue processing revenues and gross margins during his remarks.
 Our fourth key initiative for 2016 was continuing to grow BioGlue in the US and international markets and although BioGlue revenues in the fourth quarter were down 3% to $15.9 million, compared to the fourth quarter of 2015, BioGlue revenues increased 7% for the full year.  Looking forward, we continue to see opportunities for BioGlue. First, we expect to see some growth from the expanded indication in Japan as I mentioned earlier or procedure volumes were up 20%. Longer-term, we see upside from our BioGlue clinical trial in China which I will detail later in my comments.
 And lastly, we expect to benefit from BioGlue end-user pricing as we continue to execute our strategy to go direct in certain OUS markets.
 Our fifth key initiative for 2016 was investing in clinical programs focused on gaining regulatory approvals that will significantly expand our future market opportunities. I am pleased to report that we resumed enrollment in the PerClot trial during the fourth quarter. We currently have IRB approval at nine sites including full site activation at five centers where patients are currently being enrolled in the trial. We expect the pace of both IRB approval and enrollment to improve as we move forward.
 As a reminder, in Q3 of 2016, the FDA approved their revised study protocol that we believe will drive faster enrollment and based on our estimates for enrollment timelines and follow-ups, we believe we remain on track for FDA approval in the first half of 2019. In China, we also remain on track to begin patient enrollment of our BioGlue clinical trial in the second quarter of 2017 with approval sometime in the second half of 2019.
 Our last key initiative for 2016 was continued business development activity. To recap, in 2016, we successfully repositioned the company to focus on cardiac surgery with the On-X acquisition and subsequent divestiture of HeRo and ProCol. And then the completion of the integration and transaction and transition of activities related to those deals.
 In addition, we continue to make progress in transitioning manufacturing of the PhotoFix product line to CryoLife and remain on track to complete this transition by mid-year 2017 providing another tailwind for gross margins. In terms of additional business development, we continue to evaluate opportunities to add or acquire rights to complementary cardiac surgery products to our portfolio.
 Before I turn the call over to Ashley for a more detailed review of our financial results and our 2017 guidance, I would like to provide an update on one more new item we've been working on. This is a new tissue offering and potential new revenue opportunity for CryoLife, which we refer to as NEOPATCH. NEOPATCH is an allograph derived from human amniotic tissue that can be used among other things as a covering in advanced wound care to treat diabetic foot ulcers and venous leg ulcers.
 We are very excited about this new opportunity. For those who are not familiar with the advanced wound care market and specifically, the amniotic tissue use in this area, the current market is approximately $300 million and is growing at over 11% on a compounded annual basis over the last five years.
 This is a technology that we've been working on for a few years and although the wound care market is not synergistic with our existing call points, NEOPATCH is certainly synergistic within one of our core competencies which is tissue processing.
 We have recently completed enrollment in a 50 patient first-in-man single-arm clinical trial to evaluate NEOPATCH outcomes in a real world population of diabetic foot ulcers. Follow-up data collection is ongoing, but we are very excited about this opportunity and the early clinical results that we are seeing in this series.
 The 12 week follow-up on this initial series will be completed in mid-May of 2017, and as a result, we have recently started to secure a marketing partner for NEOPATCH. There are no guarantees we will be successful in securing a partner, but we are very optimistic about the prospects given the compelling clinical results we have achieved of NEOPATCH in this large market opportunity in diabetic foot ulcers and venous leg ulcers.
 This opportunity demonstrates given our size and our internally developed products where smaller acquisitions can have a meaningful impact on our business.
 I will now turn the call over to Ashley for his financial review.
