Vicki Maree Brady,  Telstra Corporation Limited - CFO and Group Executive of Strategy & Finance: Thanks, Brendon. Good morning, and thank you for joining us. This morning, I'm very pleased to take you through our financial strategy for T25. We will then open for questions.
 Our financial strategy has 5 building blocks to deliver growth and value for shareholders. These blocks build on the strong foundations provided by our T22 strategy. First, we will build financial momentum across our portfolio to deliver growth; second, we will deliver $500 million of net fixed cost reductions from FY '23 and to FY '25 while investing for growth; third, we will focus on cash conversion and generation; fourth, we will be active in portfolio management to unlock value and manage our balance sheet; and finally, we will create shareholder value through our capital management framework.
 Before providing you with more detail on each of the building blocks, I will comment on our financial growth ambitions to FY '25, which Andy spoke about earlier. Our underlying EBITDA and ROIC ambitions build on our current T22 commitments. As announced at our FY '21 full year results, our guidance for FY '22 underlying EBITDA is $7 billion to $7.3 billion. This represents mid- to high single-digit growth. Our ambition is to achieve $7.5 billion to $8 billion of underlying EBITDA by FY '23, and mid-single-digit CAGR from FY '21 to FY '25. As illustrated today, we have confidence that the momentum we've built towards growth will continue to FY '25.
 For underlying ROIC, our ambition is around 8% by FY '23 and to grow beyond this to FY '25. For underlying EPS, our ambition is a high teens CAGR from FY '21 to FY '25. This level of underlying EPS growth from $0.097 in FY '21 provides earnings clarity as we maximize our fully franked dividend and seek to grow it over time. For excess cash flow, our ambition is to invest for growth and return excess cash to shareholders, in line with our capital management framework.
 Turning to the first block of our financial strategy, building momentum across our portfolio to deliver growth on Slide 48. This reflects the turning point we have reached, thanks to our T22 strategy. We are entering a different phase and expect top line revenue growth to be a driver of EBITDA growth.
 Our ambition is to do the following: first, to drive value growth through our 5G mobility leadership. Our FY '21 results included around $300 million of second half mobile EBITDA growth on the prior corresponding period. We are confident that mobile EBITDA growth will continue, underpinned by our ambition for a mid-single-digit mobile services revenue CAGR and ongoing productivity. We also have the final EBITDA benefits flowing through from migrating customers of subsidy and lease plans in FY '22.
 Second, to profitably grow our fixed product portfolio across C&SB, enterprise and wholesale. This includes nbn resale, data and connectivity, and MAS.
 Third, to deliver further net cost reductions while investing for growth. Our T22 strategy has achieved simpler and better outcomes for our customers. And we have delivered $2.3 billion cumulative cost reduction since FY '16.
 Fourth, to profitably grow new markets to scale across Telstra Health and Energy. And finally, to grow returns from our infrastructure business.
 Let me now turn to how we will drive mobile value growth on Slide 49. Our ambition is to deliver a mid-single-digit CAGR for mobile services revenue through our T25 strategy. Let me now speak to the drivers that support this ambition shown on this slide.
 First, our technology solutions and our network leadership, including Australia's largest 5G network, are critical to our strategy. Maintaining and extending our 5G leadership will underpin our market position and our price premium.
 Second, with the foundation built by T22, we are customer-first with simplified plans and no lock-in contracts. The migration of all customers to these simplified mobile plans will provide us significant operational benefits and flexibility beyond T22. We are also positioned to grow our hardware margin through unbundling, removing subsidy and the in-sourcing of our retail stores.
 Third, we believe value growth from 5G experience-based propositions can drive further ARPU growth. Our lead indicator of postpaid handheld ARPU, transacting minimum monthly commitment, or TMMC, has grown by more than $5 since FY '19. This increase as well as pricing changes across the base are flowing through to ARPU and EBITDA. We believe 5G experience-based propositions can drive further ARPU growth beyond FY '22.
 Fourth, new C&SB and enterprise 5G products and an expanded device ecosystem will also provide new opportunities. As you heard from Michael today, there is an increasing array of connected devices beyond handsets and tablets to wearables, AR, VR and appliances. There are also emerging enterprise 5G products that David discussed from enhanced Ethernet wireless to one of Australia's largest banks reimagining the branch of the future, and 5G and Edge in sports stadiums. These new products will all create optimized experiences for our customers, and drive value and growth in our core mobile business.
 And finally, we also expect to continue value accretive growth through our multi-brand strategy. We will continue to use this highly successful strategy to increase reach. This includes Belong, JB Hi Fi, Boost and our wholesale model where we have consistently achieved strong SIO and revenue growth.
 In addition to mobile growth, there are other areas of growth across our portfolio, which I will explain in more detail on Slide 50. Our full year FY '21 results highlighted an inflection point in our fixed products. In fixed, C&SB, the nbn-driven decline is now substantially complete. We expect growing and profitable home and business Internet services, and are targeting a mid-teens nbn resale margin by FY '23. Across small business apps and services, our target is to double revenue between FY '21 and FY '25.
 While we continue to explore, test and develop alternative technology options, we expect to limit legacy copper losses to less than $100 million per annum. We are further through the nbn driven decline in C&SB than in Enterprise.
 In Enterprise Fixed, our ambition is to return to growth in data and connectivity by FY '24 and a mid-single-digit NAS revenue CAGR to FY '25 with mid-teens EBITDA margin. Across Enterprise, we are targeting FY '22 revenue and EBITDA growth in aggregate.
 In Fixed Wholesale, our ambition is to maintain annual EBITDA of around $350 million until FY '23, before the portfolio returns to growth. Within Fixed Wholesale, we expect data and connectivity to contribute to growth post the nbn driven legacy decline. Our focus is to grow through investment and product differentiation, including wireless resilience, active and dark fiber hybrid solutions and API-based services.
 Turning to Infrastructure, we will continue to drive the performance and recognition of our world-class infrastructure assets. In FY '22, we expect to revise our disclosure to further elevate Amplitel and InfraCo Fixed, giving more focus and clarity on their performance. As you heard from Brendon today, for Amplitel, we are targeting low to mid-single-digit EBITDA after leases CAGR, 250 new towers and 700 additional tenancies by FY '25.
 For InfraCo Fixed, we are targeting low single-digit EBITDA after leases CAGR, $600 million of new infrastructure investment and 6,000 kilometers of additional fiber deployed. This infrastructure investment will be within our business-as-usual CapEx.
 Turning to new markets. Telstra Health is well positioned, and we are excited by the acquisitions of MedicalDirector and PowerHealth. Our ambition is to grow Telstra Health to become a $500 million revenue business by FY '25. We are also focused on diversifying growth across other verticals including in energy, where our ambition is to be a top 5 retailer by FY '25.
 Turning to the second block of our financial strategy, to deliver net cost reductions while investing for growth on Slide 51. We have achieved $2.3 billion of annual cost reductions since FY '16, and are confident that we will deliver our $2.7 billion T22 target by the end of this financial year. We are targeting cost reductions in FY '22 of $430 million. This includes benefits from digitization, reductions in IT and network costs, ongoing vendor optimization and labor efficiencies.
 From FY '23 to FY '25, and we are targeting another $500 million of net fixed cost out while also investing for growth. We believe this ambition will ensure we maintain and improve our leading operating cost metrics for a full-service telco. We are already top quartile across many metrics. However, we believe shareholder value is better supported by not targeting top quartile across all metrics given our premium position in the market.
 We have 5 focus areas to achieve cost reductions during T25. We will significantly reduce our IT operating costs. The investment we have made transforming our IT digital stack during T22, enables us to now focus on removing legacy systems and consolidating platforms. We will transform the Telstra Enterprise customer value chain cost base across order, delivery and activation processes. We will deliver operational efficiency across C&SB billing, fixed assurance and fixed activation customer episodes. We will realize further labor productivity through agile@scale across back-of-house and support areas. And we will expand productivity discipline across total costs, including sales costs, fixed costs and CapEx.
 Turning to the third block of our financial strategy, a focus on cash conversion and generation on Slide 52. Pleasingly, in FY '21, we delivered free cash flow of $3.8 billion, an increase of approximately $400 million compared to the prior year due to working capital improvements. Cash generation continues to be a priority in our financial strategy, with a focus on converting EBITDA into cash. CapEx discipline and efficiency will benefit cash. Our expectations for business-as-usual CapEx are unchanged at around $3 billion per annum, excluding spectrum. Volatility in hardware revenue in FY '21 impacted our CapEx-to-sales ratio. This highlights a shortcoming in this metric.
 Consequently, we have updated our capital management framework to reflect CapEx in absolute dollars rather than as a ratio. This change is consistent with how we manage CapEx internally. Spectrum payments are more irregular than BAU CapEx. We expect to pay for the recently acquired millimeter wave spectrum over 4 further equal annual installments. Full payment for any licenses awarded in the upcoming 850- and 900-megahertz spectrum auction is expected in late FY '24.
 I will return in a moment to further investments for growth above BAU CapEx. In addition to CapEx discipline, there are several areas of additional focus that will benefit cash. Enduring working capital improvements will benefit cash. We will continue to manage mobile handset receivables and focus on initiatives to deliver ongoing improvements in working capital across inventory management, receivables and payables. Reducing leases will benefit cash as flagged at our full year results. Given our shift to hybrid working, we continue to assess our property requirements and may exit some leases early. This may have short-term negative impact on D&A but should result in financial benefits over time.
 Reducing finance costs will also benefit cash, finance costs paid have been reducing due to both reductions in net debt and lower average borrowing costs. We expect this trend to continue as high-cost debt matures.
 In addition to our focus on converting EBITDA into cash, we expect cash flow to remain ahead of accounting earnings, largely due to structurally lower CapEx than D&A. In FY '21, CapEx was $1.4 billion lower than our D&A of $4.5 billion. After adjusting D&A for $532 million of lease depreciation and $239 million of spectrum amortization, CapEx was around $700 million lower. We expect that business-as-usual CapEx will continue to be around $600 million lower than adjusted D&A due to historically higher CapEx and mix of asset lives.
 Cash flow remaining ahead of earnings provides flexibility for further investment and capital management that I will discuss shortly.
 Turning to our fourth block of our financial strategy, active portfolio management to unlock value on Slide 53. We have a strong record of generating additional cash, unlocking value and managing our balance sheet. We illustrated this through T22 with our successful monetization of $2 billion of assets. We have also now completed the sale of a 49% noncontrolling stake in our towers business. The transaction valued Amplitel at $5.9 billion, representing an FY '21 pro forma EV to EBITDA after leases multiple of 28x. Net cash proceeds were $2.8 billion.
 On Telstra InfraCo more broadly, we are delivering on the promises we made in our T22 strategy, to provide greater transparency of our infrastructure assets, improve the efficiency of how we manage those assets and provide optionality in an evolving industry. This optionality includes ensuring InfraCo Fixed is ready to explore future monetization or other opportunities.
 Across our portfolio, we also retain the discipline to grow or exit investments depending on their ability to exceed ROIC targets. We will take an active approach to portfolio management to unlock value.
 Now that I've taken you through how we will drive underlying EBITDA growth, cash generation and unlocking value, I will turn to the fifth block of our financial strategy and our capital management framework on Slide 54.
 We will continue to apply fiscal discipline and use this framework to manage capital and deliver shareholder value. The objectives of the capital management framework are to maximize returns for shareholders, maintain financial strength and retain financial flexibility. These objectives are unchanged.
 The framework includes 4 principles, and we have made changes to 3 of them effective from today. The first principle is a commitment to balance sheet settings consistent with an A-band credit rating. This commitment is unchanged as it continues to be important to shareholders and debt holders. The A-band credit rating demonstrates the strength of our business and provides continued access to global low-cost capital.
 The second principle is to maximize our fully franked dividend and seek to grow over time. This principle reflects continued feedback from shareholders of the importance of our fully franked dividend. It also reflects our intention to return as much cash flow to shareholders via fully franked dividends, which can be sustainably supported by earnings and franking, while also balancing the objectives and principles of the capital management framework.
 We are confident in maintaining a minimum $0.16 per share fully from dividend, subject to no unexpected material events and the requirements of our capital management framework. However, our franking balance is low. We reported FY '21 EPS of $0.156 and underlying EPS of $0.097.
 We need to grow underlying earnings in line with our financial ambitions, and grow our franking balance in order to grow fully franked dividends. This replaces our previous principle to pay fully franked ordinary dividend of 70% to 90% of underlying earnings.
 We have replaced this principle because we expect our cash flow to remain ahead of accounting earnings, and we are focused on growing underlying earnings into our total dividend. The split of ordinary dividend funded by underlying earnings and special dividend funded by net one-off nbn receipts, becomes less relevant in the future. We remain committed to returning in the order of 75% of net one-off NBN receipts. However, we expect FY '22 to be the last year of special dividend funded by the nbn receipts.
 The third principle is ongoing business-as-usual CapEx of around $3 billion per annum, excluding spectrum, as I have already discussed.
 Turning to the last principle of our capital management framework, to invest for growth and return excess cash to shareholders on Slide 55. This replaces our principle to maintain flexibility for portfolio management and strategic investment. The new principle is more specific and illustrates our intention to use the flexibility provided by our cash flow being greater than earnings to invest the growth and deliver additional returns to shareholders. We expect to generate excess cash flow after capital is deployed in accordance with the first 3 principles of our capital management framework.
 With excess cash, our focus then shifts to investing for growth and returning excess cash to shareholders. When we invest for growth, we will continue to be disciplined and apply our previously communicated criteria for organic and M&A opportunities.
 Our criteria for organic opportunities are an NPV that is positive, using WACC and appropriate risk analysis. Organic opportunities could include a long-term or nation-building infrastructure investment or a major customer project. We are currently exploring opportunities in these areas.
 Our criteria for M&A opportunities are to be EPS accretive in year 2, to have a return on investment above our weighted average cost of capital by year 3 and any acquisition needs to be more value accretive than a share buyback of a similar size. We preserve discretion to take advantage of longer-term strategic opportunities where we expect them to deliver financial returns that exceed the cost of capital and long-term value creation for shareholders.

Going forward on M&A, we expect our in-sourcing of retail channels will cost in the low hundreds of millions. We also continue to assess other M&A opportunities.

We are now a simpler, leaner and a more digital company compared to where we started T22. We are also a market leader with unparalleled scale, brand and network. We are values-based and focused on doing business responsibly. We have world-class infrastructure assets, and we will deliver further value from them.
 We are excited by the future, with FY '21 marking an important inflection point for our financial performance. We will deliver growth through our T25 strategy by staying disciplined and focused; by continuing to build financial momentum across our portfolio to deliver growth; by delivering $500 million net fixed cost reduction from FY '23 to FY '25 while investing for growth; by having a strong balance sheet and focusing on cash conversion and generation; by being active in portfolio management to unlock value; and by creating shareholder value to our growth strategy and updated capital management framework.

 Due to the productivity initiatives and on the back of the expansion program launched at Ocampo pro  despite the unfavorable gold to silver equivalency ratio Company-wide increased by 15% over the prior year to 251,000 ounces.  Now attributable to the higher gold equivalent production results and the realized benefits from our numerous cost reduction initiatives, cash cost per ounce decreased year-over year by 22% to $525 per ounce. The Company has always maintained that we are well-leveraged to the Mexican peso and you saw that in our full-year results.  Those familiar with the Company will note that at the end of Q3 2008, the Company had recorded $6.1 million in non-cash mark-to-market inventory evaluation adjustments predominantly on our heap leach inventory. The reason for these adjustments that we booked during the first nine months of 2008; it all coincided with the third quarter of this year when the economic volatility that we saw worldwide really started to resonate and that had an adverse impact on gold prices and especially so on silver prices. This led to a situation where the inventory values that we had recorded in our balance sheet was valued in excess of the values that we could realize at that point in time, based on the prevailing spot metal prices. As we saw at year end, gold prices recovered significantly. And silver prices also recovered as the Mexican peso devalued. We quickly found ourselves in a position where our inventory value had reclaimed a lot of that lost value.
 In this fourth quarter as a result of the strengthened commodity prices, the Company actually recorded a reversal of a portion of the net valuation adjustments that were originally posted in Q3. Mike Haefner,  Atmos Energy Corporation - President & COO: Thanks very much and thanks for the applause without needing to be prompted, appreciate that. Good morning and thank you for joining us and thanks for your continued interest in our Company.
 I'll talk about our safety policy, our safety strategy or safety programs and give you a better feel for where some of our investments are going in safety and reliability, a little bit of a drill-down. But first starting with our vision, our vision is to be the safest provider of natural gas services in the country and it's not only our highest priority but it's a core value that we constantly work to ingrain in our culture and everyday practices, the commitment we make to our employees, customers, communities and regulators as well as shareholders.
 The capital investments we make are prudent and necessary to maintain the integrity and reliability of our system, to meet the expectations of our customers, and the increasingly stringent state and federal safety requirements. These investments along with running every detail of our business exceptionally well drive our earnings growth and also enable us to achieve our ultimate goal of being incident-free every day.
 If we look at the landscape, we are experiencing very favorable trade wins in our industry today. The period of time  a rare period of time when the interest of all of our stakeholders are nearly perfectly aligned. There continues to be a sharp national focus on pipeline safety. In the wake of several significant pipeline incidents, the Secretary of Transportation issued a call to action in 2011 as a proactive measure to engage all pipeline safety regulatory agencies as well as the operators to accelerate the repair, rehabilitation, and replacement of the highest risk pipeline infrastructure. Similarly, state commissions and legislators have increased their focus on safety regulation and infrastructure modernization. They've been very supportive of increasing investment and fortifying and upgrading our system to improve safety and reliability.
 New and emerging pipeline safety rules will continue to provide a partial roadmap for significant future investments in safety reliability for both Atmos Energy and the entire industry for years to come. Regulators in our marketplace have encouraged capital investments to improve safety and reliability by adopting rate mechanisms that have eliminated or reduced lag and also provide the opportunity to earn a reasonable rate of return. But you note that the capital markets remain healthy and our strong balance sheet, successful track record, stable, predictable earnings growth and long-term value proposition make us an attractive investment.
 Both nationally and in our service territories, we continue to experience a very stable, low price commodity environment. NYMEX December contract price is trading at $2.39, highest prices winner is $2.60. You have to look out for the year 2024 before you find a contract price over $4. The 2015 Energy Information Administration or EIA, Annual Energy Outlook predicts a continued increase in dry production  US dry production, resulting in daily production greater than 90 Bcf by 2029 with consumption trailing demand by 10 Bcf per day even after accounting for increased consumption by power generation and also LNG exports.
 To further keep our customers' gas bills low, our gas supply team partners with our regulators, employs a combination of storage, hedging and market purchase strategies to ensure reliable supply at an affordable price. We know State and Federal regulations will continue to increase, compliance is going to become increasingly challenging and that will require us to continue to make a significant capital investment in our system.
 Our strategy has been very simple and it starts with leadership and focus. Earlier this year, Marvin Sweetin was appointed to the new role of Senior Vice President of Safety and Enterprise Services. He sits on our management committee. To my knowledge, he's the only senior executive in that similar role in our industry. And Marvin brings tremendous experience, education needed to oversee our operational framework for our safety and reliability investment programs.
 The foundation of our safe system is a robust compliance and integrity management program focused on monitoring the condition of our transmission and distribution assets, as well as assessing risks associated with those assets. We employ risk based models using output from our integrity management programs to identify and then forecast our infrastructure replacement investments.
 Furthermore, as we evaluate and make improvements to our system or constantly employing modern materials and innovative technologies. All of this works because we would proactively and in partnership with public officials and regulators to align around the need and our plans for significant investments in our infrastructure and to manage the implementation of those plans with minimal disruption to our customers and the communities. And finally, we spend millions of dollars every year on selecting, training, developing our highly skilled workforce. Our success begins and ends not only with our people, but also with our culture.
 Looking at slide 14 on our capital spending mix, safety and reliability investments account for greater than 80% of our capital spending. The majority of that goes towards infrastructure renewal and particularly pipeline replacement and system expansion to increase reliability. The broad range of investments include fortifying, repairing and replacing both transmission and distribution pipe, replacing our steel service lines, enhancing storage and compression capabilities and installing equipment such as pigging facilities that enable our integrity management program. All those pieces together give us the framework that we need to keep our safe system even safer.
 Drilling down a little bit into our pipe replacement, specifically in 2015, our team replaced 470 miles of distribution pipe and 105 miles of transmission pipe. Approximately two-thirds of the distribution miles replaced were materials that PHMSA, the pipeline safety arm of the Department of Transportation has deemed as highest risk, that includes vintage plastic such as PVC, as well as cast iron and bare steel. Approximately one-third of the distribution pipe replacement in 2015 was coated steel and polyethylene plastic or PE. These are more modern materials, however, both have been in use for many decades, a period of time over which the industry has seen many significant advances in both those materials as well as the method used for construction, maintenance and inspection.
 Our comprehensive pipe replacement programs focus on the highest risk segments of our system, regardless of the material type. Besides considering age and material pipe, we factor in construction practices used at the time, soil conditions, maintenance records, leak history, evidence of brittleness or corrosion and proximity to populated areas as we determine the pipeline's risk profile. In 2016, we intend to replace between 500 miles and 600 miles of distribution pipeline, and 75 miles to 125 miles of transmission pipeline.
 Slide 16 shows the increase in pipe replacement since 2012 and our expectation to replace in the range of 500 miles to 600 miles of distribution pipe and 75 miles to 125 miles of transmission pipe each year through 2020. We have approximately 69,000 miles of distribution pipelines, 6,500 miles of transmission pipeline, approximately 60% of distribution pipe and 90% of transmission pipe is in Texas. 5,500 of the 6,500 miles of transmission pipe are in Atmos Pipeline-Texas that Dick will talk about in just a little bit. On an annual basis, we are currently replacing between 0.75% and 1% of our entire system or total asset mile. So, as you can see, that leaves us a very long, and almost indefinite time horizon in terms of, if we're looking at capital investment.
 Turning specifically to older generation pipe, materials like vintage plastics, cast iron are subject to brittleness, cracking and possible separation due to environmental conditions like soil movement and it's much more true of that pipe than materials being used today. Steel pipe was a significant improvement over those earlier materials due to its strength, durability, its ability to be welded, the connection points and it's been used in gas transmission and distribution for 100 years. Steel pipe, however, can be subject to corrosion, if it's not protected by suitable coatings or as to prevent contact with soil or water and by the application of small amounts of electrical direct current referred to as cathodic protection.
 So this is why uncoated or bare steel is deemed by the industry and regulators as posing a potentially higher risk. We've replaced 800 miles of these materials since 2012. We have a current inventory of approximately 6,700 miles, which includes about 590 miles of cast iron. We've eliminated cast iron and all our states except Texas and within Texas, all but five cities. Our team is working closely with those cities on replacement timelines, we expect to be cast iron free by 2023. We anticipate replacing 300 miles to 350 miles per year of these pipe types combined or 1,700 miles between now and the year 2020. If you look at this pipe combined starting with this year, we would expect that this pipe would be replaced over a 20-year time period.
 As we're replacing distribution mains with polyethylene plastic, we also replace the steel service lines that run from the mains to customers' homes and businesses. This plastic pipe they were installing is not subject to corrosion and cost less to install and maintain, it's flexible and the connections are made by fusing the pipe and fillings with heat that reduces the possibility of pull-out separation due to the disturbance of the pipe or movement of the soil. Given that service lines are in close proximity to homes and businesses, these improvements are very important and prudent at a replacement rate of approximately 40,000 service lines per year, we have a 20-year investment in this area as well.
 There has been a awful lot of attention in the industry focused on pre-1970 transmission pipe, because all pipe of this vintage was constructed and placement in service prior to the existence of regulations that governed construction, maintenance and records management practices. The national debate centers on how this pipe should be regulated with the universal consensus that it must be operated safely.
 We operate today approximately 3,500 miles of pre-1970 transmission pipe. We are obviously operating it safely. We closely monitor it in our integrity management systems and in our compliance programs. We've estimated that replacing all of this vintage pipe would take over 30 years. This has got one simple example of the complex and challenging nature of safety and compliance in our industry with materials, construction methods, inspection technology and safety standards continuing to evolve, it just illustrates why investing in our infrastructure is the most appropriate strategy today and into the foreseeable future.
 Looking at slide 20, foundation of our safety focus is a robust pipeline integrity management program. Federal regulations for transmission pipeline safety place specific focus on segments of pipe that operate on high-density population areas, also referred to as high consequence areas. One of the most significant advances in inspection technology is in-line inspection of the condition of our pipeline. These so called smart pigs go through the transmission pipe and electronically assess the condition of the pipe. These in-line inspection devices can detect irregularities that may indicate flaws such as pits, gouges, cracks, well defects, corrosion or other wall loss. New and developing sensor technologies will provide even better detection capability in the future. So the technology here is evolving fairly quickly.
 This pipeline integrity data is critical input to the prioritization of our capital investment by indicating where and when our transmission pipe needs to be replaced or repaired. Since much of our transmission pipe was constructed prior to smart pigging technology, we have to make a significant capital investment to modify our facilities in order to accommodate this approach to inspection. Over the past four years, we invested approximately $175 million to make our pipelines capable of in-line inspection and to repair and replace segments identified by those assessments to be in need of repair. We project that by the year 2020, approximately 70% of our transmission pipe in high consequence areas will be capable of in-line inspection with an ultimate goal of making  eventually making all lines piggable.
 Another key use of capital allows deploying in new technologies that will improve the safety, reliability, and efficiency of our operations. One technology we're evaluating now relates to leak detection. And we leak survey approximately 20,000 to 25,000 miles of pipe a year. Traditional leak survey technology has limited detection distances. The new leak detection technology claims to be a thousand times more sensitive with potential detection distances of hundreds of feet. It would allow us to leak survey both our distribution mains and our services at the same time at driving speed. Once we integrate this with our asset management, our mapping and reporting system, the technology has the ability to show us the survey area as you see in a map format as well as indication of possible leaks, the yellow cones you see there and that will greatly improve our leak surveying and our assessment of the condition of our pipe. As with our any other new technology, we really do a careful evaluation to ensure that we have a strategy to deploy it that integrates with everything else that we do.
 A great deal of rigor is used to track the condition and the performance of our system and frankly, most of those metrics are only meaningful to our engineers and our operations personnel. One set of metrics that we can all understand highlights the positive impact of our safety-related investment, our leak count. Now, let me say right up front, that any hazardous leak or leaks that could potentially harm people or structures are fixed immediately. But using a plumbing analogy, a hazardous leak would be like a broken water pipe. A Grade 2, or what our industry calls a Grade 2 or a Grade 3 leak would be like a dripping water pipe. So we monitor those very, very closely. We track the leak counts by grade, age, and route cause. So we've seen that active leak counts, leak aging, leaks attributable to corrosion specifically have been reduced significantly since 2012 as we increased our investment in our infrastructure.
 Lastly, as I mentioned at the start, our success begins and ends with our people and our culture. We've invested $14 million in creating one of the leading training centers in the industry, named after our founder Charles K. Vaughan, a center which opened at 2010, just north of Dallas, hosted 18,000 visitors this last year and was the site of more than 37,000 hours of compliance, technical and safety training. Unique part of the center is outdoor gas city, stimulates the many community with houses, apartments, commercial buildings, city streets, distribution lines, other underground utility infrastructure. The center is also the site in the upper right of a state-of-the-art flow lab containing most of the advanced metering valves, regulators and monitoring equipment that you find in the industry today.
 Employees are able to apply the knowledge they learned in the classroom by practicing on the job skills in real life situation. Classes are designed to accelerate employees' learning. It used to take approximately a year before a service tech would be allowed to operate independently. We have accelerated that to under two months. When new employees get into their role, they come to the Charles K. Vaughan center and go immediately into a five-week class where on day one they're actually out there already working with the equipment they are going to see in the field.
 New programs are being introduced every year so that we can stay ahead of the constantly evolving practices and regulation to make sure that we have a healthy pipeline of well-trained, qualified gas professionals.
 So just to recap, we've got a clear focus and strategy to become the safest utility in the country. Our journey to safety has required and will continue to require significant investment in our infrastructure and our people as well as partnership with our regulators, communities and customers. State and federal regulations will continue to become increasingly stringent and compliance will become more challenging. With approximately 20 years of investment required to replace vintage materials in our distribution system and more than 30 years to replace vintage transmission pipe and overall system replacement rate of 0.75% to 1%, investing in our infrastructure will be required obviously for many decades to come.
 So thank you very much. I'd like to introduce Dick Erskine. Dick is the President of, what we call, APT or Atmos Pipeline-Texas or our intrastate pipeline in North Texas. Dick has been President of that division since 2004, the year that we acquired APT from TXU. He has got over 31 years experience within this Company in a variety of roles. He's very well respected in the industry and he is the best darn, intrastate pipeline operator in the country. So, Dick?

Dick Erskine,  Atmos Energy Corporation - President, Atmos Pipeline - Texas: I got younger with that introduction, especially 42 years. So I will attempt to stay alive for the next 15 minutes and share what little I can after Kim and Mike have given you some of the high-level particulars of the pipeline business.
 Let's just get rid of my picture and I get to wander around and point and show you pictures of what the business is. So hopefully I have a little bit more fun doing this. But the one thing that Kim said about our business and he made a point of this. He said, this isn't a midstream business which can be kind of confusing because what is a midstream business and so, I will differentiate it just a little bit for you.
 A midstream business by our definition is that pipeline company or that producer servicing company that goes out and seeks new supplies, provides producer services, lays well lines to connect wells, treats processes gas, contracts with producers to provide those type of producer services. Our business model is on the other end of the spectrum. We're a regulated intrastate pipeline whose primary mission is to provide transportation and stored services to end use customers, the largest of which is our Mid-Tex Division, about 1.5 million customers. We also serve some other local distribution company customers like CoServ that operates in the northern Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, and then we've just now entered into an agreement with ONE Gas in the Austin area to provide transportation and storage service for part of their load in that area.
 So if you look at our map, and you just think in terms of our primary purpose in serving local distribution companies, they are our only firm customer. And because our largest customer is an affiliate, that puts us into the mode of having our great services and fees, cost regulated by the Texas Railroad Commission, but that is our primary mission. Over 450 cities and towns are scattered across that pipeline system that spans the State of Texas.
 As you look at this configuration, I am going to point out the stars that are located in and around the Dallas area. Those are our storage facilities. You don't just put storage facilities wherever. They have to be put in a place where it's either a depleted reservoir or in the case of this facility in Southeast Texas, it's a salt dome facility, and we leached out two salt domes in order to provide natural gas storage service for our customers. But as you look at this overall map and you look at our pipeline system, the thing that I would point out that puts us in a favorable position for success, aside from being in Texas and aside from having what I would call reasonable and logical rate regulation location, pipelines have usually always have to have one thing going for them. They have to be connected to supply, that's one thing that can make them successful, or they can be connected to markets, or they can be interconnected between other pipelines to provide a useful service, any one of those three things can make a pipelines success. In our case, we have all three. Our pipeline system spans a very, very robust market area, the Dallas Fort Worth area and spanning out to Austin and other areas, it's been growing at a rate of 30 million to 50 million a day in terms of peak demand for deliveries off of our pipeline system.
 We have electric generation facilities that are being built to keep up with that load growth on the electric side; we compete to serve some of those facilities. Our industrial market is at least stable if not also growing on our pipeline system, so we have a robust market place.
 On the other end of the pipe we have a very, very robust producing opportunity. You can see by the shaded areas on the slide, we've pointed out the producing basins that we're in, the Barnett Shale, everybody has heard a lot about over the last several years. The Permian Basin, the Haynesville, Eagle Ford all of those are pipeline system accesses. With the current market conditions, you probably heard, well, wait a minute; drilling is slowing down, what's happening? How does that affect your business?
 If you look at the Barnett Shale, over the last five years it reached the peak of close to 6 Bcf a day and now it's drifted downward to about for 4.5 Bcf a day, but fairly well stabilized in that level. For us, we've been accessing and taking delivery into our system five years ago about 700 million a day.
 Today, we are taking in about 900 million, so it may be shrinking or leveling off, but our accessing of gas, bringing it to our markets or transporting it to other markets has actually increased a little bit. Some of that's due to contracts that were initially entered into by the producers in the Barnett Shale, those contracts have reached the end of their primary term, so some of that gas is coming to us, where they once were contracted with other pipeline. So, we're finding ways to be successful in the Barnett, even though the production has leveled off.
 The Permian is a different story. Five years ago it was at about 3.5 Bcf per day. Now, it's approaching 5 Bcf per day, it's an oil play, it's a gas play, it's a liquids play and apparently their cost of finding and producing gas out there is lower, so it continues to grow. The amount of gas that we're accessing in that play is also growing. We've added facilities on the west side of our system to enhance our capacities so that allows us to be successful.
 The third element that we have were tied to three different market hubs, Katy, Waha, and Carthage. That puts us interconnected in what I would just call the National Pipeline Grid. We can take gas and move it across our system and very often we found ourselves in a position where prices between those points, those liquids pricing points have separated and that gives us an opportunity to transport gas and make a margin simply by charging a transportation fee. Right now the basis spreads between those hubs are pretty narrow and so that opportunity is lower, but we continue to find opportunities in transporting gas for producers who were looking to flow their gas and get to those liquid hubs when the gas in our systems exceeds or on-system market demand.
 On slide 27, this just gives an overview of our business from a regulatory standpoint. I mentioned that we are regulated but the Texas Railroad Commission. They established a cost of service rate for our services and that cost of service rate is made applicable to our tariff paying customers. 100% of our costs all rolled into our tariff rates and recovered from our tariff customers.
 All of our competitive business, all the business we do for producers and marketers, electric generators those that are competitive, all that incremental business is also looked at by the Railroad Commission, but they take it as a revenue credit, dollar-for-dollar, a 100% of what we charge and make in that arena when it's reviewed in a rate proceeding is then applied to our cost of service netted against it before the cost will then spread out to our tariff paying customers.
 And what that does in our last case, as they take those cost and spread them out, it includes the cost associated with 11.8% return on equity and overall return of 9.36%. And very importantly, the rate design associated with the manner in which we charge rates is called straight fixed-variable, which is just an overly complex way of saying our fixed cost, which represent the vast majority of the pipelines' cost are embedded in our customer charges. In other words, they don't vary by volumes, they are charged flat across the year on a customer charge basis and so we don't have a lot of volatility based upon whether the weather is extremely warm or cold on a given year.
 Another mechanism we have in places in-between full rate cases with the Railroad Commission is an annual look at our invested capital. The Gas Reliability Infrastructure Program was put into law in the early 2000s, it allows us on an annual basis to look at our net plant investment and make an adjustment to our rates based upon that change in net investment. So, on an annual basis we're updating.
 One of the requirements associated with that law is that we have to have a full rate case every five years and with each one of those annual filings, we make a filing called an earnings monitoring report, they want to make sure that within the time period of five years those incremental adjustments are not putting us in a position of greatly over earning and so we track along, make investments, do the things we need to improve our system, operate our system safely, upgraded and fortify the system for growth and make annual adjustments.
 We'll file our next case no later than January of 2017, no earlier than about December of 2016, but we're trying to figure out what to do with the Christmas holidays and whether we want to be answering discovery questions and things like that while we are opening present. So, we're trying to figure out exactly when we'll make that filling.
 On slide 28, this just gives you a recap of what our GRIP filings have done for us over time. The blue bars represent the change in net plant investment. The gold bars represent the incremental annual revenue associated with each of those filings. We'll make another filing for calendar year 2015 in February of this coming year, we anticipate based upon what weather does to us and what projects we're able to close by the end of the year. Net plant investment will change somewhere in $175 million to $200 million range and that should result in $31 million to $35 million of incremental revenue.
 If we  to save your moment of just totaling all that up and seeing what that looks like from our last case going forward for 2015, that's somewhere in the vicinity of $170 million of annual revenue increases on about $1 billion worth of net plant investment change. So the mechanism has been very important to us as we seek to continue to improve our system and serve our customers.
 On slide 29, this just gives you a look of the future. We plan to continue investing in Atmos Pipeline-Texas, the marketplace, it's growth opportunity, the status of our pipes. All of those things provide us with an opportunity to continue to invest and continue to grow with our customer base and we would look to spend between $250 million and $350 million a year on Atmos Pipeline-Texas and that would be generally broken out by these categories, which you can see, there is a lot of range-ability. Pipeline integrity and compliance $50 million to $100 million; maintenance and replacement, the same thing; fortification and growth; other projects and opportunities, if we see an opportunity to connect new supply to the system and we want to fortify our mainline system with compression that allows that supply to have a place to go where our on-system markets are taking it.
 We'll flex between those categories to free up dollars and take advantage of that opportunity, and we typically try to do those things, because the gas system is a living, breathing organism. Gas supplies never stay the same, they're shifting, they're moving up and down, supplies and reserves come on, they deplete, they move on, they connect to other pipes, so we're constantly seeking to replenish the gas supplies attached to our pipeline system all the time. Everything is geared towards system safety and enhancing capacities and everything we do in this regard is GRIP eligible because it is use and useful and dedicated to serving our regulator on-system customers.
 On slide 30, I get back to maps and this is my safe zone, this is where I'm most comfortable. All I have done here is try to give you a visual of what we'll be doing and investing over the next five years. The color coding just simply means which fiscal year these investments are likely to take place. And it shows you in general, the most of where the colors are is most of where the market is. If you're looking at the red line, that's actually under construction right now and all of the multi-colored lines on the north side of the Metroplex, all of that is geared toward serving that additional 30 million to 50 million a day of peak day demand growth that we're seeing. It doesn't take many years that type of repeated incremental growth or you run out of capacity. And so we're staying ahead of it. We are modeling it, we are trying to find the best way to serve it either from flowing suppliers or from storages. And so some of the projects I will be talking about in just a minute will show you how we are meeting that demand.
 But as you can see, centered around the Dallas Fort Worth area, we've got some projects that are kind of north of the Austin area, Bryan College Station area, all where we've seen growth. This represents, because  I mean these are just high-level things representing $700 million to $750 million worth of total expenditures. We would look over the next five years if you take $250 million to $350 million over five years, that totals up something closer to $1.5 billion. And so in addition to just these projects, there is a host of cats and dogs that are small pipeline replacements, exposures, pigging, launching and receiving facilities with pipeline integrity testing, those things are all part and parcel to what we will be spending in capital over the next five years.
 Now, I get to have fun, slide 31. This represents a project that's currently underway. We somehow or another long before, I came on the scene, we started naming our pipelines according to letters of the alphabet. There are no rhyme and reason, I can't even tell you why geographically they matter, but they are what they are. This is our Line F. It runs from Dallas up the I-35 East Corridor to Dayton, Texas where we have our Lake Dallas storage facility. In this particular instance, what you're looking at is boring under Lake Louisville. The Highway Department is actually replacing their bridge and widening I-35 that put us in a position of replacing our facility, that also put in motion part of our five-year plan to replace the rest of the pipeline. You are looking from north to south here and what you can see is pipeline that's strung out and that's where it's actually going underground and going under the lake itself. This is a multi-year project. At the end of it is 33 miles of 16-inch pipe and we look to spend up to $60 million on that replacement. But because it is in the northern corridor and connects our storage facility to our market area, it will be a critical element of our ability to serve our customers in the future.
 This picture, if you here last year, you've seen it before and I've put this up again because this project is still underway and it's growing. But this gives you an idea of what it's like to lay pipeline in a congested metropolitan area. This is moving up through [Carlton the colony] and to Frisco. Frisco is where Jerry Jones has popped his practice facility and there is all kinds of growth up there. And if you ever move to Dallas in the future, stay away from it, because it almost rivals your traffic here when you are trying to commute from that area. But in this instance, we are replacing now up to 59 miles of 20-inch pipe. It was 16-inch pipe before this, but 20-inch pipe all through this corridor. And this has to do not only with growth but the integrity of the pipeline itself. This pipe was installed in the late 1950s and some parts of it due to stresses and integrity testing, we determined it was an appropriate time to take it out of service and so we've undertaken the project.
 The next picture you're looking on slide 33 is part and parcel to the largest capital project that Atmos Pipeline-Texas, TXU Gas or Lone Star Pipeline before that has undertaken in my career. This is our Tri Cities storage facility. And what we are endeavoring to do is improve this storage facility, improve its capability to work with the Bethel storage facility and lay a new pipeline to the east side of Dallas. So you put all of those three things together and you get one big complex project that by June of this coming year should all be in service. This particular phase of it, again you're looking at our Tri Cities storage facility, it's our largest, about 20 Bcf of working gas. The general plant is in the middle, the buildings you see are either office buildings or the compressor yard, all the surface equipment and pipe, the withdrawal train, dehydration and things of that nature. These are two active horizontal rigs that are running. And we are accessing our reservoir and there are three other wells to do. By the end of this calendar year, we'll have at least two of those wells in service, the other three should be in service shortly after the first of the year, if we don't get them done by the end of this year. The total project cost with surface equipment and wells for just this base is up to $86 million.
 This is our Bethel storage facility. Compressor buildings, surface equipment, we have two wells. Again, this is a salt dome facility where we leached out two caverns in a salt dome. But what is unique about this, I'll just call your attention to these two pipelines. The Bethel and Tri Cities storage facilities are approximately 19 miles apart. Those two pipelines will connect those two storage facilities together for the first time. It's hard to tell from this particular distance from these pipes. This is a 12-inch pipe, this is a 24-inch pipe. This 12-inch pipe will operate at pressures up to 3,400 pounds and what that pipe will allow us to do is use the compression at either of the facilities 19 miles apart to double up. And so right now, each facility has approximately 120 million to 130 million a day of injection capability to go into its dedicated storage facility. Now we'll have the ability to double up, one way or the other and inject between 250 million to 300 million into one facility. That's important for Bethel. This is our salt dome facility. It is our highest deliverability storage facility, but it's a smaller cavern size, so it depletes rapidly. Currently on this facility, we have a 6 to 1 ratio. One day of withdrawal it's 600 million to 700 million a day, takes close to six days to replace. In the middle of winter where you have cold fronts one after another, you can find yourself getting in a bind pretty quickly.
 With the addition of that high pressure pipeline and the ability to either direct gas from Tri Cities out of storage to storage and/or use compression of Tri Cities in conjunction with Bethel storage compression, it will move more to a 2 to 1 to a 3 to 1 ratio, a much more high turn, high cycle storage that will help us meet our customers' needs.
 The 24-inch pipeline is simply another connective line that allows for a second outlet for our Bethel gas. Currently, we only have a single pipeline outlet for that facility, and it is critical to meet peak day needs. Having a second outlets just makes sense. And so, that allows us to just use it in a simple analogy belt and suspenders. We make sure we can serve our customers by having a secondary outlet. This is simply the construction of the 30-inch pipe, the new 30-inch pipe that will go from Tri Cities, all the way to the east side of the Dallas Metroplex. You can tell by the picture on the right, this is on slide 35. May was a nasty month in Texas and in fact if it keeps going at its current pace this year will be our wettest year on record, and we're trying to complete our largest most complex construction project in the midst of that. So we can bring out our water waders and try to figure out how to get it done, but right now, we're on schedule, on budget, on time. So everything is looking good. The pipes between the two storage facilities are being tied in and tested even as we are talking here today and they'll be in service. And this line, at least the first 30 miles of it, will be in service by December, all made part of this current year's GRIP filing.
 Lastly, I'll show you again our compression at Waha, and Waha is not a place that any of us want to visit. I've been 42 years into my career and I am very proud to say I have never been there. I know what compressors look like, I know what meters look, I know what pipes look like, I don't need to go to the engineers to see him. So here is a picture, I will save you the trip.
 But I show you this because we talked about this third compressor being added last year. It was just barely being put into service, but it adds another 4,700 horsepower and allowed us to connect in over 250 million a day of new production that was coming from the Permian Basin. Our Mid-Tex affiliate, the LDC is accessing that supply and right now about 25% of their annualized load is supplied by that new production source that is tied into our system.
 I show this to you again because Waha is not done. There is so much still going on out there. There are two new pipelines that are proposed to go from the Waha hub to Mexico to serve power plant load there, there is still growing production in that area and we plan to be tied to new pipelines, we plan to be tied to new production and we will continue to seek that supply for our customers, but also seek incremental business to continue to build that revenue credit offset that benefits our customers and so more to come out of Waha and next time you talk to me, I still won't have been there. So that's it.
 That's it from me, if you're looking down you're probably not going to notice that speakers have switch, because to the next guy looks a whole lot like me. So, Conrad Gruber is our Vice President of Strategic Planning and he will talk specifically about how we take these investments and recover them through rates.

Conrad Gruber,  Atmos Energy Corporation - VP, Strategic Planning: Thank you, Dick. I appreciate that. And yes, we have changed people, but the looks haven't changed much. It is our proposed and I'm in-between our operational needs that Mike discussed and Dick discussed and our financial strength that Greg will cover after me, because our rate regulatory plan is how we convert their operational demand into financial results, and let me figure out.
 And so quickly, I'll go through what our rate strategy is, how much we're running through our rate programs annually and how those meet the demands for safety and reliability among both our distribution systems and our pipeline systems. And of course the work we do with regulators and the support that's needed from them to make those results possible.
 Our rate strategy never really varies much, it's tried, tested, trusted methodology. Basically, we increase our revenues through rate-making. So the primary goal in rate-making is do have the regulatory lag that allows us to make the needed investments in our system without having lag that cuts off our financial ability to  or our ability to finance those investments and also attract capital through equity.
 The lag and I'll detail them here in a minute, we address lag primarily through annual mechanisms, we also have some forward-looking test periods among the jurisdictions that we do business in and we also use some expense deferrals that are meaningful to us in a couple of jurisdictions. In addition, we have mechanisms that also I'll talk about that improve our margin stability, and then finally, we're continuously working to reduce the risk of recovery in all of our jurisdictions.
 What's driving the need further the amount of rate-making that we've done, it's our rate-making and I'll show you a chart of it here in just a moment. Our rate-making has increased quite a bit over the last eight or ten years. And the need for that has been driven by our operational needs.
 Our systems, as Mike talked about after the call to actions in the 2011 time frame, the recognition and the need to address aging infrastructure and the amount of pipe that's going to have to be replaced, both in our systems and in systems across the country. It's driving a lot of what we're having to invest in and it's driving a lot of what we're doing in rate and regulatory relief work on. Additionally, we have system growth and then we're also  I'll have a couple of slides at the end that talk about rate affordability, all this is we're able to do it and we're able to work with our regulators and it's quite affordable for our customers.
 This chart details our capital spending from 2010 through projected 2020. As you can see, we have over that span of time, we're going to invest between $10 billion and $12 billion in capital, our growth rate for capital spending continues to be quite risk as the demand for being able to invest and replace our pipe on a reasonable timeframe. As Mike said, we replace between 0.75% and 1% of our pipe a year, this rough math gives you about 100 years on that, even I can do that one.
 And as you can see, that requires us to continue increasing our investment on safety and reliability annually. The amount of rate relief that's come from that over the same time frame, starting with 2010 and running through 2015 and our 2016 budget and then our projections through 2020, there is some variation on an annualized basis, this chart is annualized on two or three different ways to look at rate relief. You can look at it as what comes through the door in any given year; you can look at it as, what kind of annualized rate increases you put in place in any given year. This chart does it on the latter.
 And as you can see, there's a little bit of lumpiness with it and that has to do with the timing of when cases resolve themselves. Whether they are  some years you get a little bit more in a year, because you get early or late implementation on rate cases. We also have had quite a bit of adjustment in the last three years or four years. And as you can see, there's sort of nice rate results and rate relief with that. This underpins our ability to continue to grow the Corporation within 6% to 8% EPS growth.
 Regulatory filings; we do about 20 filings a year. In 2016, we anticipate doing about 18 filings to 20 filings, 18 filings to 21 filings. Most of those  and again I'll detail these in just a moment with mechanisms. We have eight formula rate mechanisms, as they are typically called our annual rate filings, we'd adjust rates in various portions of our jurisdictions. We have seven infrastructure mechanisms that work along with those. And then we still have a couple of jurisdictions where we do general rate cases or traditional rate-making and then we've got some cats and dogs that we do with tariff filings and tax and expense deferrals also.
 This next chart, shows our regulatory recovery mechanisms, I've broken them out two ways here. This chart and you heard both Kim and Mike talk a little bit about this chart, Tim in particular. This chart talks about the amount of lags that we have in general with our capital spending and again over 90% of our capital is less than six months of lag, which is very important to us. We'd be unable to spend at multiple of depreciation that we're currently clicking along at without that kind of support from our regulators. About half of this is unlagged and it's split between deferral mechanisms and mechanisms that are forward-looking.
 The other mechanisms are, they're short in the traditional rate-making process and work on annual basis; they reduced the cost of rate-making, so our customers get a better deal from it. So they work quite nicely and as you can see, $450 million to $500 million of our annual capital comes in through rate-making that occurs within six months of the end of the test period or less. Then we have a small amount of rate-making that is traditional rate-making, there is a little bit longer lag, Kansas and Virginia, small mechanism in Texas and then also Kentucky and Colorado are longer lag jurisdictions, where we filed traditional rate cases.
 And also there is some overlap in those jurisdictions where we do have Infrastructure mechanisms that are working also in those jurisdictions, where 30% to 40% up to 60% of our capital is being covered by infrastructure mechanisms, even though we have traditional rate-making. So we've had a lot of success in getting regulatory support to be able to move investment into shorter lag situations in those jurisdictions, even though we don't necessarily have annual mechanisms.
 The mechanisms that we do have and we call them by all kinds of acronyms and 8209 is the rule number. They are very meaningful to us, they mean nothing to you all, but what is important is that  and I've broken them in two ways here.
 The first is infrastructure mechanisms and how they work. Albert Chao,  Westlake Chemical Corporation - President & CEO: Thank you, Dave. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. And thank you for joining us on our earnings call to discuss our first-quarter results.
 In this morning's press release, we reported quarterly net income of $146 million, or $1.10 per diluted share on sales of $1.1 billion for the first quarter of 2015. Our first-quarter earnings reflect the sharply lower crude oil price environment in which Brent crude oil prices declined 55% from their peak of approximately $112 per barrel in June of 2014 to lows of approximately $50 a barrel in January of this year.
 Most global petrochemical producers utilize naphtha feedstock, which is produced from oil and priced off Brent crude. Naphtha-based producers are seeing lower manufacturing costs, as their feedstock costs have declined in response to these lower crude oil prices. And as a result, global sales prices for the end products, including polyethylene and PVC, have lowered also.
 North American producers who mainly utilize natural gas derived feedstocks which are globally cost competitive, have had to lower selling prices for these end-products in response to lower global sales prices.
 Reflecting industry conditions, beginning in the fourth quarter and continuing into the first quarter of 2015, sales prices for our products have declined from the levels seen in 2014 as crude oil prices declined and integrated olefin margins moderated, partially offset by the decrease in ethane feedstock costs.
 In spite of dropping oil prices, our business continued to perform well, as profitability and cash generation were both strong, benefiting from the improvement of our global Vinyls business and our capacity integration.
 Our Olefins segment benefited from record ethylene production, improving global demand for end-products and solid integrated margins. The results from our Vinyls segment reflect the benefit of our recent investments to extend our ethylene and chlor-alkali capacity, and our feedstock conversion from propane to ethane feedstock as well as from the contributions from our Vinnolit, and North American specialty products acquisitions.
 I would now like to turn our call over to Steve to provide more detail on the financial and operating results for the first quarter of 2015.

Tom Nimbley,  PBF Energy Inc - CEO and Director: Good morning, everybody, and thank you for joining us on today's call. The first quarter was challenging for the refining sector as a whole, and for PBF in particular, as we experienced significant unplanned downtime on our East Coast operations. The East Coast experienced approximately 2 weeks of unplanned downtime at the Delaware City refinery as a result of a storm-related loss of power in late January. And given the prevailing market conditions, we elected to accelerate the timing of the Delaware City coker and hydrocracker turnarounds, which were previously scheduled to begin in late March.
 As a result, Delaware City was without coking and full upgrading capacity for more than two months of the first quarter. We ran the lowest volume of heavy crudes on the East Coast since before 2012, which was a headwind to our overall capture rate as we consumed lighter and more expensive feedstocks.
 The downtime and coker and hydrocracker turnarounds impaired our ability to convert our typically advantaged slate of heavy and medium crudes into salable clean products at Delaware City; and also resulted in a higher yield of low-value products, as can be seen by the roughly 8% swing between clean products and low-value product yield on the East Coast versus the prior quarter. We estimate the margin loss of the planned and unplanned downtime at about $75 million for the quarter.
 Before moving to the other regions, I'd like to comment on Delaware City's operations. As I said, they had a tough first quarter with the storm-related downtime and advance in the turnaround. The team adapted to the accelerated timeline and completed the turnaround near the end of the first quarter. Unfortunately, coming out of the turnaround, a crack developed in the piping weld at the hydrocracker. The unit underwent a normal shutdown; repairs have, in fact, been completed as of last night; and the hydrocracker is expected to be restreamed this weekend.
 Given the prevailing market conditions, the Toledo and Chalmette refineries operated well under the circumstances. The Toledo refinery saw a 30% decline in its market crack, and the Syncrude-WTI differential widened significantly versus the fourth quarter. As we mentioned on our year-end earnings call, with gasoline margins approaching zero, we optimized our production in response to the market conditions. Currently, mid-continent cracks have recovered from their first-quarter lows.
 Chalmette continued to operate well despite facing similar market pressures as our other refining regions. Chalmette has delivered positive results for the two quarters of our ownership, and we continue to explore opportunities to further enhance its profitability, including opportunities around Chalmette's logistical assets. We are also seeing the benefits of our more selective crude purchasing efforts for the refinery, and our commercial team has been successful in establishing new, high-end netback outlets for Chalmette's production.
 In November of last year, we began the process of evaluating the optimal configuration of the refinery, given the potential of the currently idled units, consisting of a hydrocracker, naphtha hydrotreater, a reformer, and a light ends recovery plant. We have undertaken projects to evaluate the restart of several idled units, which would convert unfinished naphtha that is currently being sold out of Chalmette to high-octane reformate and ultralow-sulfur gasoline blending naphtha. We expect that this project could enter service late in 2017.
 We have also begun the initial scoping work for a new crude tank which should reduce our demurrage and provide opportunities for additional waterborne finished product sales. We are continuing to explore a variety of options for the idle hydrocracker and will provide further updates as we proceed.
 Before commenting briefly on the market, I would like to provide an update on the pending Torrance acquisition. Our expectations for closing the transaction remains consistent with our initial announcement, which was closed during the second quarter. As we have mentioned previously, the acquisition will only close once ExxonMobil has proven the refinery to be fully operational.
 Going into the second quarter, we believe the outlook for clean products remains mixed. Year-over-year clean products demand is up approximately 2%, and average vehicle miles traveled statistics are up over 3% since 2014. We expect that demand will remain strong for gasoline in 2016. Distillate, however, is a bit more of a concern, and the current inventory overhang may take longer to resolve itself. However, certainly with the agricultural demand increasing over the last several weeks, things are improving.
 Despite that, PBF is currently taking steps to increase gasoline yield and manage distillate yield by optimizing unit operations to meet market demands.
 With that, I will turn the call over to Erik.

But basically, for our four refinery system, ex-Torrance, you should assume that we have swing production capability of about 50,000 barrels a day between the four refineries. So all I'm saying there is there's overlap in the molecules, if you will, between distillate and gasoline. And dependent upon the economic incentives, we could go as  if we had a very weak distillate market and a strong gasoline market, we could swing 50,000 barrels a day of production from distillate into gasoline.  Now, how is that 50,000 barrels a day, what does it come about  is really just two simple parts of it. And this is a little bit simplistic but it's pretty much on the money. One is simple fractionation. You just change the cut points in the various towers that carve up all the stuff that we run. And basically, for example on the crude tower, you can take  you can change the temperature profile and drop naphtha into distillate, or naphtha into jet fuel. You can do the same thing on the cat cracker fractionation towers. So, about half of that 50,000 barrels a day just comes from changing the temperature profiles and moving barrels, and drawing them off in a distillate cut versus a gasoline cut.
 The second half is what you started to allude to, is you can do the same thing and drop distillate molecules into the gas oil streams. And, therefore, then that becomes a feedstock to your conversion units, particularly your cat cracker. If the cat cracker is already running full, or you think you're running at the optimum rate, you would increase the available feed to the cat cracker. You'd make the same amount of gasoline effectively; but you'd reduce distillate make, and you'd have to back out feedstock, because the cat plant, for example, in this example, runs out of room. So you'd either back out PGO, gas oil purchases, or crude. So that's the way it comes out.
