Lois Cormack,  Sienna Senior Living Inc - President & CEO: Thank you, Melanie. Good morning and thank you for joining us on our call this morning.
 With me on the call is Nitin Jain, our Chief Financial Officer. I will begin by reviewing some of the key highlights of the quarter. I'm going to speak about Sienna's recent announcements, and Nitin will then discuss the financial results of the quarter in more detail.
 Now during the quarter, we continued to execute on our key objectives. To provide quality care and service to seniors, building on local brand recognition, maintaining a strong financial position, enhancing the value of the Company's assets and promoting the growth of our portfolio, and improving support services.
 During our remarks, we will touch on some of the key achievements on these four priorities. I will also refer you to page 3 and 4 of our MD&A, which outlines how we are executing in these key areas.
 Now 2016 is off to a great start, with strong operational and financial performance, including a 6% increase in same property NOI. 11.6% increase in diluted OFFO per share, and a 10.5% increase in diluted AFFO per share. Our retirement residences finished the quarter with our overall occupancy of 91.5%, which was up 4.7% over the first quarter of last year.
 Same-property net operating income was up 14%. We believe that this strong year-over-year increase is attributable to our rebranding efforts, our continued focus on improving the resident experience, as well as strengthening our operating platform.
 Now in long-term care, which is slide 7, our same-property NOI increased by 3% from the prior year. And subsequent to the quarter, on April 4, 2016, Associate Minister of Health and Long-Term Care, Dipika Damerla, visited our long-term care community in Stouffville and announced the Ministry's approval of our application to redevelop 31 beds from C class.
 When completed, this will be a significant improvement to our residents. In addition, we continued to make good progress on our future redevelopment plans for our class C homes, which are all subject to further feasibility and regulatory approval.
 I will now touch on some of Sienna's recent announcements. Now during the first quarter, we announced the sale of Preferred Health Care Services to Spectrum Health Care. The transaction subsequently closed on April 28 for cash proceeds of CAD16.5 million before working capital adjustments. This disposition is consistent with Sienna's strategy to focus on growing our core business of high-quality, retirement living, and long-term care residences in Canada.
 And in mid April, we were very excited to announce that Sienna has entered into an agreement for a CAD255 million acquisition of a high-quality senior's living portfolio in BC. This transaction contemplates the purchase from Baltic Properties, Baybridge Senior Living and Amica Mature Lifestyles of a senior's living portfolio in BC consisting of eight high-quality assets which will add 984 beds to Sienna.
 The transaction also contemplates a 50% ownership interest in a BC management company, as well as the option to acquire ownership interest in two newly built senior's living residences at a discount to fair market value. We do expect that this acquisition to be immediately accretive to OFFO per share and AFFO per share on a leverage neutral basis. As well, as a result of this acquisition, we expect to welcome over 1,300 dedicated and experienced employees to the Sienna team.
 Now turning to slide 11, we're really excited about the opportunity to increase our presence in British Columbia, including the greater Vancouver area. The properties to be acquired include two retirement residences, the Mayfair, 85 suites in Port Coquitlam, and Regal Manor, 138 suites in Burnaby.
 There are six Baltic properties with 761 beds, which are all best-in-class senior living residences providing long-term care, independent living and assisted living, as well as some specialized programs. 20% or 154 of these beds are private pay. Each of the properties are very well located throughout British Columbia, and have excellent reputations in their respective communities.
 Now on slide 12, this acquisition will increase Sienna's retirement suites by 29% and funded beds by 11%, further solidifying our position as a leading senior's living provider in key markets in Canada.
 Now turning on to slide 13, Sienna will also acquire a 50% ownership interest in Pacific Seniors Management. This partnership will provide Sienna with the opportunity to leverage a strong operating platform, a development partner and relationships with local stakeholders, including the BC Regional Health Authorities.
 Over a two-year period, we will be working with our Partners to fully transition the management of the Baltic homes to Sienna. We believe that our relationship with our Partners will also lead to further growth opportunities.
 The third component of the deal is Sienna's option to acquire ownership interest in two newly built state-of-the-art long-term care residences. Nicola Lodge in Port Coquitlam, and Glenmore Lodge in Cologne. Together, these properties consist of 374 beds, approximately 10% of which are private pay.
 In summary, this transaction represents a great opportunity to expand our presence and our operating platform in BC. It is in line with our strategy to diversify the mix of senior living in our portfolio. We do expect to complete this acquisition in the third quarter of 2016.
 Sienna is on a path to growth, and we believe that this transaction is an excellent example of our focus and our patients in the pursuit of accretive acquisitions that improve the quality of our portfolio and drive long-term value creation for our shareholders.
 I will now turn the call over to Nitin for our financial summary of our first-quarter.

Nitin Jain,  Sienna Senior Living Inc - CFO: Thank you, Lois, and good morning, everyone. Before I begin, I would like to note that you'll find a more fullsome discussion of our results in our MD&A and financial statements for the period which are posted on SEDAR and can also be found on our website Siennaliving.ca.
 I will start on slide 16. In the first quarter of 2016, Sienna Senior Living generated net operating income of CAD21.4 million, which is up CAD1.4 million or 7.2% versus the same period last year. Our retirement division had another strong quarter, with same-property NOI growth of 14% and CAD0.5 million of NOI from Traditions of Durham acquisition which closed on December 31, 2015.
 Our same property long-term care NOI growth with 3.4%. The retirement growth was driven by strong occupancy gains as our as at occupancy increased by 4.7% to 91.5% versus Q1 2015.
 The long-term care NOI was driven by increased in deferred rates, disciplined cost management, timing of expenses year over year, and lower utility expenses due to the warmer temperature. We are very pleased with our overall operating performance, and particularly pleased with achieving over 90% occupancy in our retirement division over the winter season.
 Moving to slide 17, in the first quarter of 2016, diluted operating funds from operations per share was up CAD0.03 or 11.6%. And diluted adjusted funds from operations per share was also up CAD0.03 or 10.5% over the first quarter of 2015. The increase was primarily driven by strong year-over-year operations performance in both the retirement and long-term care divisions and the Traditions at Durham acquisition.
 Our maintenance capital expenditure for Q1 2016 was CAD400,000. And as previously advised, for total year 2016 we expect to spend similar amounts as in 2015 adjusted for inflation. Our Q1 2016 administrative expenses were CAD4.4 million, which are consistent with the spend in Q1 2015.
 Now moving to the next slide and our focus on reducing leverage. At the end of Q1 2016, our debt-to-gross book value was 55.2%, which is 120 basis points below our first quarter 2015 metrics. The decline was driven by voluntary repayments towards the Company's revolving credit facilities, monthly payments to the series B debenture principal reserve fund and to mortgage liabilities. Our interest coverage ratio increased by 30 basis points from 3.1% at the end of Q1 2015 to 3.4% at the end of Q1 2016.
 Subsequent to the quarter, we completed the sale of Preferred Health Care Services on April 28, 2016, for total sale proceeds of CAD16.5 million, with an estimated tax payable of CAD700,000 on the sale. We have used the proceeds to pay down our credit facilities by CAD14 million, approximately the same amount of that we drew to pay down for the Traditions at Durham acquisition in December 2015.
 Moving to slide 20, the pending CAD255 million acquisition in the BC market is a great growth opportunity for Sienna. To partially finance the acquisition, we launched CAD120 million bought deal public offering of subscription receipts on April 18, 2016, with an over allotment option of 15% which was fully exercised for total proceeds of CAD138 million prior to the underwriters fee. Total received issued were CAD8.8 million.
 We will also be assuming approximately CAD137 million in existing mortgages, at a weighted average interest rate of 3.9% and a weighted average term to majority of 5.5 years. In addition, we'll be issuing 10 million of shares to the principle of Baltic Investment Company at the same price as the offering price for the subscription receipts.
 Going forward and the impact of subscription receipts, as discussed, the receipts were issued as of May 6, 2016. While these receipts have been outstanding, the holder of these receipts would be entitled to receive payment equivalent to dividends paid on common shares.
 Between now and the closing the acquisition of the BC portfolio, which is expected in the third quarter of 2016. These dividend equivalent payments and the receipts will have a dilutive impact on our funds from operations, operating funds from operations and adjusted funds from operations on per share metrics.
 We intend to identify at the impact of these receipts and their dividend equivalent payment by adding new metrics of diluted OFFO per share with subscription receipts, and diluted AFFO per share with subscription receipts in the disclosure going forward for the applicable time period. The first dividend equivalent payment would be made to the receipt holders on June 15, 2016.
 With that, I would like to turn it back to Lois.

So 148 systems made up that EUR2.2 billion.

  So the market overview, so semiconductor unit growth is back to historical trends. And we're having a structural capacity catch-up. So, we can see later on that we reduced a significant amount of capacity in the DRAM and NAND space, and even in the foundry space. There's a sense of urgency to get their processes and wafer starts converted to the next node because the only real comeback for falling prices is falling costs or reduced costs.

  So at least in this timeframe, there is, again, I want to emphasize, a sense of urgency on the guys that have their stuff on order and they want it delivered as fast as possible, especially in the second tier. And the first tier guy is going to continue to push harder and harder, and more of his capacity is going to go to 4X so he can try to gain market share.
  So, over  I would suggest, then, now through the end of the year, we're okay. And by the way, ASML doesn't expect DRAM to expend as much next year as they did this year, anyway. So we expect a significant falloff in DRAM spend as it moves over into NAND, and as it moves over into logic and into microprocessors.
  So again, just wanted to address a couple of the key data points that may cause you to be concerned about what our business might look like in the near term.
  I don't think I need to mention that we're well ahead of the competition in terms of the supply of the leading-edge tools that are being consumed in quantity today to reduce costs and increase the functionality per square centimeter of silicon in the logic areas. So we've shipped well over 160 at this point in time. We have the best specifications of anybody in the business. We have more than 20 of our latest and greatest NXT tools installed and we are continuing to grow our backlog in that area.
  So every major customer in every application in the world today has or will have shortly an NXT, one or more of those, that they're using in production eventually.
  And then, on the bottom right-hand side is our next challenge. Technical challenge is EUV. So there is, by now, a broad-based acceptance of EUV as the solution for the future in terms of imaging. It will  even though at EUR65 million apiece in 2012 will provide the most cost efficiency as the industry continues to meet their shrink targets. I think our technical people and our customers are confident that we'll get there in time. But consider or expect some bumps along the road here.
  So, if you hear about things happening, you can certainly ask us about it and how we feel about it, but expect some of that stuff as we go.

  So the competition could be considered to be three years behind, and as importantly or maybe more importantly, $2 billion in spend behind us.   They have a plan. And they have to execute on that plan in order to have any hopes of achieving their goals, and they have enough money, I would suggest, to execute on that plan, so any short-term demand issues are not going to stand in the way of them executing that plan. That puts pressure on the big guy, that owns most of the 40 nm and below business today in that space, and we know that another big guy in Korea is intent on growing his total semiconductor business by growing his foundry business against his continued pursuit of more market share in NAND and DRAM.
  So, that's going to require a significant amount of spend, we think, in the next year or two or more, and then the MPU sector, which we're going to participate in fortunately, is going to be much more lithography-intense than they were at the last node. So they're not going to, again, change, adjust yet their ramp plans of their brand-new 22 nm product at this point in time based on, I would guess, again I don't want to speak for them, but I guess they wouldn't, based on some short-term PC demand decrease.
  So, the execution of our customers are against a strategy, a strategy of market-share gain, a strategy of new market  new product introduction, et cetera, et cetera, and more importantly in the memory space, this strategy of cost reduction.
  Again, in the short term, supply/demand may find its way out of balance, but if it's just short term, then we wouldn't expect any real discussion about that with our customers because, again, nine-month lead times were solidly booked out, and we are undersupplying today, and they are beating on our door. I don't want to be too dramatic about it, but I do want you to understand that we are undersupplying today.
  And long term, certainly for the reasons  many of the reasons I just mentioned, the competitive position, et cetera, the fact that Moore's Law will continue for the next five years at least, probably longer  we're prepared for longer than that, but who knows? But we are set to grow long term to the levels that we have been suggesting in the past, those are our EUR5 billion target. We see that there's an opportunity over the next five years to go somewhat above that or, might I say, well above that in the future, and that whole opportunity is certainly still intact.
  So, I don't know how long that took, but in any case, hopefully we have a few minutes for questions and answers.

Craig DeYoung,  ASML Holdings NV - IR: To make it very simple, slippage of EUV isn't the worst thing that could happen to ASML from a topline, revenue growth, tool demand standpoint. Because obviously, as you recognize, double patterning is just that. You need two tools to do one layer, roughly.
  So if it is extended, the EUV implementation time, for some technical reason, I don't think it will be  if we do what we're intent on doing, it won't be for an economic reason that it will be delayed.
  So, this is  Moore's Law is an economic law, it's not a law of physics. It says the doubling of transistor density at the same cost, which is  ends up being 30% to 50% reduction on a cost-per-function basis. That's what drives the industry.
  If [EUDV] will do it more cost effectively in the different sectors, it will be implemented. Again, if the technology is mature enough to do it on a day-by-day basis.
  But if it doesn't happen, if it is delayed a year, indeed the pain is put on our customers. Because double patterning, let's say NAND, for example, double-patterning process, nitrate spacer double patterning, which is employed today, can be extended to the teams. We know that. Our customers know that.
  But it's hugely expensive, so you need a bunch of  deposition. More litho tools, so it's usually expensive. Just talked to one of the NAND manufacturers about the anticipated cost as you get to 22, and then to the teens. So, it puts a great deal of pressure on our customers if EUV is delayed, and so that's why we are intent on getting it to the marketplace as quickly as we can.

Henrik Norremark,  Vestas Wind Systems A/S - CFO: Good morning, everyone. And a very warm welcome to this video presentation, which is a continuation of the Stock Exchange announcement that Vestas has released this morning concerning the change in accounting principles which Vestas are to apply going forward.
 My name is Henrik Norremark. I am the Chief Financial Officer of the Vestas Group and, together with Chief Executive Officer, Ditlev Engel, I am making up the senior management of the Vestas Group.
 Today, I would like to cover with this presentation a number of items. And the goal is that when you have listened to this entire presentation, that you will have a thorough understanding of the change in the accounting principles; the understanding of Vestas' business and activities, as well as how they are recognized, both before on the Vestas financial statements as well as how they will be recognized going forward.
 Specifically, we are going to cover these items in seven sections. Section one, which we'll get to in a moment, is the IFRIC 15 and the continuation of that, the International Accounting Standards, and the exposure draft for change of those; what IFRIC 15 is and what the exposure draft is and why this is applicable to Vestas.
 Second, we are going to cover which type of sales agreements, or contracts if you will, that Vestas is operating with; how we have recognized those in the past and how we will recognize those going forward in our financial statements.
 To understand that, we will go through a couple of examples which I have made up to illustrate both the activity that Vestas carries out and how these are actually recognized in the financial statement.
 Having done that, we will go to  take a start in the financial statement which Vestas has published as of September 30, 2010, which happens to be the latest financial statement we have published; how are these changed principles going to effect these statements; how did they look like; and how have they now been re-stated and will look like going forward.
 Having looked at that, we will look at the more overall and understanding of the change in picture on particularly P&L, our profit and loss, and balance sheet that the change of accounting principles actually how they effect Vestas and that view.
 And finally, the 2010 guidance; how are these translated into the new accounting principles.
 And finally, a little guidance on how do we look at 2011.
 Before we start on all this, if you have not already done it, I would recommend that you actually go to our website and download this presentation in full, printed out, so that you have a much better chance to actually follow and see the figures when I'm going through the presentations here as it may be a little bit difficult to read the particular figures as I'm going through the individual slides.
 Before we are starting on the presentation itself, I would like  for those who may be further interested in this, and for those who may not want to watch this whole presentation here right now, that this week I will actually hold the same presentation in New York tomorrow, November 23; be in London the following day, November 24; Paris and Frankfurt, November 25; as well as Stockholm and Copenhagen on November 26. You are most welcome to show up. You will be able to see this one live, as well as for the questions and answer session.
 Before we go into what these change of accounting principles actually mean for reading the investors financial statements of Vestas Group, I would like to underline a few things which is absolutely essential that we keep in mind.
 First and foremost, Vestas does not run its business based on how our accounting principles are laid out and which accounting principles by law we are to follow. Vestas operates its business based on what serves Vestas' business best, meaning that our contracts are based on a balanced agreement between the customers and Vestas. This means that when we are talking about the change of accounting principles, there are absolutely no change in the way that Vestas does business. And certainly, since this is a matter about revenue recognition, then Vestas' cash flow is also unchanged after we have changed the accounting principles here.
 Furthermore, when we are talking about IFRIC 15, IFRIC means the International Financial Reporting Interpretation Committee. This is a committee who has issued an interpretation of how to read certain paragraphs in the international accounting principles.
 This is a matter of reporting, as I was saying before. This is not a matter of re-evaluation of all Vestas' assets. All valuations are the same. We are using the same evaluation, no matter if we are talking about the fixed assets or if we are talking about current assets, debts, etc., etc., etc. This is all about revenue recognition and about the timing of the revenue recognition.
 What is IFRIC 15? IFRIC 15 was first published in 2008. It is a publication that mainly was addressed to how to further interpret the two main principles under which in the international accounting principles that Vestas is recognizing its revenue. There are two main paragraphs; the main paragraph IAS 18, and then the IAS 11. Number 11 is a paragraph that talks about contracts which usually are over a longer period of time; now generally known as work in progress or construction contracts.
 IFRIC 15 has mainly been addressed to talking about real estate. However, it is also stated in IFRIC 15 that it may apply to other business but real estate. However, the interpretation is mainly talking about real estate.
 Vestas was, when we published our 2009 report, listing in the report that we will have to look at this interpretation, IFRIC 15, again, the International Accounting Standard 11 versus 18, and evaluate what, and if any, effects this would have on Vestas' financial statements.
 In June 2010, the exposure draft concerning future revenue recognition was published. This exposure draft is talking about how to in future interpret the recognition of revenue and will eventually become an International Accounting Standard, after which we have to recognize the revenue.
 It is the intention, with this exposure draft, that that will replace the two main paragraphs, IAS 11 and IAS 18, and thereby also the IFRIC 15, and thereby be the standard after which that you have to recognize the revenue. So the entire matter that we are about here today, and the change of accounting principles is a matter about revenue recognition according to these documents.
 And what does it mean to Vestas? Well, the essence of it is that we have to change, for a certain part of the contracts or the activities that Vestas has, the way and the time that we are recognizing the revenue on the profit and loss statement.
 Currently, we are for a part of the Vestas' contracts recognizing revenue as per the International Accounting Standard 11, meaning over time as the work is progressing versus the International Accounting Standard 18 where it is at the time that the customer has accepted to take over the turbines and the wind parks that we have constructed. I will in a few moments return to this specifically.
 The other essential part of the changes are concerning our service contracts, again, at which time is it that we have recognize the revenue on these and how are we to treat the revenue and the cost at which time. For both of these, I will later during my presentation go through extensive examples to illustrate how this has been recognized previously and how this is to be done going forward.
 Having been through the first section here, where we have now covered what IFRIC 15 actually is about and how it effects Vestas, then I would like to go and talk about the types of contracts that Vestas actually operates with and how they are recognized in the financial statement, both before and after the new accounting principles will have been implemented.
 Going into Vestas' contracts, Vestas is at any point of time negotiating individual contracts with each and every customer. It is key in the understanding of the customer and the customer's need that the contracts are tailored made to the customer's business. This means that we will have basically individual contracts for each and every customer that will take into consideration and reflect the risks, the opportunities of both the sites on which the turbines are to be put up, and certainly also any other circumstances that may be applicable for; if there are certain risks in terms of wind; if there are certain risks in terms of installation, whatever it may be; if it is on water, on mountain, that are tailored made into these contracts.
 When we take the pile of contracts that Vestas has entered into, we for the understanding here have divided those into three main categories. We have what we have named supply-only. This means that Vestas is manufacturing and selling wind turbines, towers, blades to customers, which are either picking them up at the factory themselves or, in rare cases, we are shipping them to a harbor or a destination where the customer basically takes over the risk of these and have bought them and are putting  installing these turbines for their own cost and risk.

 A quick look to 2011, and this is the same slide as you have seen in connection with our third quarter presentation for 2010. We still expect to manufacture and ship 6,000 megawatts.  There will  before we are going to the questions and answers, which will be held as a session this afternoon, Central European Time, 3 o'clock, let me reiterate what this means and does not mean for Vestas. Bear in mind that none of Vestas' business has changed. Nothing of what Vestas see of forward-looking activity, [treble 15], etc., nothing has changed.
 The only thing that has changed is the time at which we actually record our revenue over the profit and loss statement.  And with that, thank you very much for listening to this very, at least in my mind, elaborate walk-through of not only Vestas' main activities but certainly also how it's reported in the financial statement.
 And I will look forward to listen to you both at the Q&A session, which we will have at 3 o'clock this afternoon, as well as, for those of you who I may see, during this week on my tour both to America and to Europe. Thank you very much and have a good day. Bye.

Phil Wright,  Lundin Mining Corporation - President, Director and CEO: Thank you very much operator. Welcome everyone. Thanks for joining us. I'm conscious that our results have only been out for a short while and so therefore, people might not have had as much time as normal to analyze, anyway, I'll try and make it as clear as I can and a chance to ask questions at the end.
 I have with me on the call today Joao Carrelo, our Chief Operating Officer; Marie Inkster, our CFO; and Paul Conibear, who is our Senior VP of Corporate Development. They'll help me with questions at the end once I finish.
 What I'll do now is turn to the Q2 performance. I think as most of you are aware, metal prices Q2 this year somewhere between 30 and 70% stronger than they were a year ago and we've seen the euro Q2 this year to Q2 last year down some 7% on average, so both of those have been good news for us. Our production recovered well from the issues in Q1. Our net income is well up. Net income this quarter contains a number of nonrecurring and in part offsetting items and I've got a slide to show our adjustments for this.
 As far as zinc is concerned, our results include equity earnings from Tenke of 8.3 million; not as high as last quarter and that's largely owing to lower sales, it's a timing difference the production was higher than sales and we should catch that up as the year progresses. We have also for the first time recognized from an accounting perspective the minority interest in the earnings. The Tenke earnings, as I'm sure many of you are aware, are basically a non-cash equity accounted item and I think it's interesting to note that the excess overrun facility has been reduced by 26.8 million in the quarter, down to 188 million.
 Looking at progress on projects; we continue to make really good progress on our internal projects. The Neves?Corvo shaft has been successfully expanded and that's key to some of our future plans for Neves and the Lombador prefeasibility study is now complete and the Zinkgruvan copper project was successfully started up during the quarter.
 Here's a slide on the normalized earnings so we do have a table in the news release for the first time that does this. You can see there's a number of nonrecurring and partially offsetting items in the quarter and this table basically sets those out. I think most of the adjustments there are pretty self-explanatory and as you can see, our results on a normalized basis are well ahead of last year and last quarter.
 I'll just point out, I think compared to last year there's something like a $75 million pretax difference in pricing adjustments between Q2 this year and Q2 last year and this is really masking just how big an improvement there has actually been in the results one year on.
 Looking at the adjusted results, one of the things that I think has probably disappointed us is that we did not manage to capture any of the nickel price spike during the quarter. Our earnings for Aguablanca don't reflect the high nickel prices that we saw in the market during the March, April, May period. We have inherited an off take contract when we bought Rio Narcea and that contract gave to the off take a tremendous amount of flexibility regarding quotational periods.
 None of Aguablanca's concentrate sales this year have been settled and the effect of that we reflected in the first quarter positive price adjustment unrealized of 12.4 million and that's been reversed in this Q2 and consequently had quite a dampening effect on earnings this quarter. I think the deficiencies in this contract are really felt during periods of high volatility such as we just experienced. That contract is now expired and I'm very pleased to say that the new contract that we have put in place addresses all of those issues. We get higher realizations for ourselves from Aguablanca, we also invoice more frequently and there is now a fixed quotational period which means that we would come very close to LME averages rather than the large seesawing that we've seen in our results today.
 So I think taking the big difference in price adjustments between the quarters into account, the recovery from Q2, I'm quite satisfied with the results that we have got this quarter.
 Looking now to financial position. I think the financial position is pretty good now. We had good cash flow in the quarter and the cash flow really is better than what appears here. Again, just reflecting on the fact that we've had 26.8 million (inaudible) from Tenke that's gone to repay the excess overrun facility and is not reflected here. So cash is building and continues to do so.
 Production; this chart compares Q2 this year to Q2 last year. As far as copper is concerned you can see that what's really been driving copper. As far as the effect on copper you can see we've had a lot of head grade which is primarily accounting for the difference between last year and this year. That's really the effect of two issues; lowering of head grade because of the fact we've got a higher copper price this year and also we are mining some out of reserve material in order to rebuild the stockpiles for industrial action in the first three or four months of this year.
 Our estimate looking at the industrial action is probably reduced our expected production by somewhere around 10,000 tonnes of copper in the first half of the year; 7,000 in the first quarter and somewhere around 3,000 in the second quarter and obviously this copper is not lost; it's basically a deferral as it's going to be mined in the future. I think what I'm encouraged about is that the efforts to recover are well underway. Production in June was above budget levels and again this month we are running above budget. So I think that issue is now well behind us and we continue to try and recover as much as we can this year.
 As far as looking at lead/zinc is concerned, year-on-year we're down, totally accounted for by the closure of Galmoy, in fact, if we look at the results for Zinkgruvan by our head on a quarter to quarter basis, the work they've done to restore their volumes coming out of the first quarter I think has been very good and so a year-on-year basis excluding Galmoy, we are well up on zinc and lead production.
 As far as nickel is concerned we had further flooding of the pit in April and to date we're not far below our plan for Aguablanca. We've seen some loss of throughput and that's been made up by some better grades on the nickel.
 Looking at cash cost performance this chart shows the cash comparison from this year to last year or this quarter to the same quarter last year. It's included on page 12 of our MD&A for anyone who doesn't have the presentation up on screen. What this slide shows is changes in the unit cost included in the cost of sales. This is not our cost of production during the quarter; this is our cost of sales during the quarter and the increase that you're seeing from this year to last year really relates to two issues. One is that we had high cost brought forward from the first quarter in terms of our inventories because of the production challenges in the first quarter. And secondly, you've seen some elevated costs as we're implementing recovery plans to recover the production that we were down.
 This next slide gives you some idea of our present metal exposures. In Q2 of this year, 68% of our revenue came from copper and just bare in mind that that is not including any element of Tenke in there, so Tenke is additional on top of that. So at the moment copper is pretty dominant determinant in terms of our revenue line. Zinc is obviously comparatively smaller at this stage but we do have tremendous leverage when the zinc prices do rebound, as they're inevitably going to. I guess my own view on zinc prices is still pretty much unchanged; there's no way that the industry can replace capacity at these prices and we may well see a surplus. I think some estimates are that that surplus may last for a couple of years, but certainly after that we move into a deficit situation and I think Lundin is very well placed when that occurs.
 This slide just looks at metal prices, as you can see, quite mixed but all up and quite volatile during the period. I think you see on this slide these are average LME; nickel at $10.15 and all of our sales during the quarter are valued at $8.94 because none of them are separate so you can see the effect that this contract has had in this period of volatility. I think just looking in terms of our operating costs, mixed performance here. The Euro is actually on average 7% weaker against the US dollar. That's good news for us. Of less effect to us, the SEK is actually up by 5% because of rounding these numbers on the slide don't show it, but the SEK was actually stronger by 5% which obviously increases slightly our costs at Zinkgruvan when measured in US dollars.
 So looking at results, there's not really a lot that is worth commenting specifically on this slide. One thing you will notice is that there's a large increase in tax expense. It was $2 million in Q2 of last year and $31 million in the present quarter. Of that 13.5 million, 13.6 million relates to a charge for un-current taxes or for future taxes and therefore doesn't really relate to the period and some of the other changes accounted for by the fact that we have used up some of our loss carry forwards and other allowances and in addition, last year's expense was really artificially lowered by some 6.2 million as a result of some nonrecurring recoveries that were included in last year. The tax issue is covered I think pretty comprehensively on page 11 of the MD&A.
 This waterfall chart compares earnings for this quarter to the corresponding quarter last year. You can see our sales volume was down; that's really related to the lower copper production at Neves and Aguablanca. Just a point, I think our inventories at the close of this quarter within the realm of what we consider normal, so sales were reasonably normal for the quarter.
 Metal prices you can see according to this waterfall, 16 million effective of the price changes. That is masking the $75 million difference in pricing adjustments, so the effective prices on their own between this year and last year has been way larger than what we're showing there because of the fact that there is a difference in pricing adjustments of some 75 million and without that we would have seen a pretty substantial change from last year because of the stronger metal prices.
 As far as our costs are concerned, you can see there the costs are up quarter-over-quarter. Approximately 6 million of that relates to Aguablanca. I think most of you recall that last year Aguablanca was operating on a very limited non-sustainable operating plan because of the difficulties with the low nickel prices and we were treated oxidized all on surface, so this year we're back to full scale mining operations and as we made clear at the time that we resumed production at Aguablanca, we anticipated two years of very high strip ratio. So fundamentally there is nothing happening at Aguablanca that is different to what we anticipated as far as costs are concerned. The rest of the change is really the effect of high cost brought forward from Q1 in inventories that have now been expensed as part of cost of sales and also some additional money that we're spending in order to be able to recover from some of the challenges in the first quarter.
 Looking at Tenke; I'm pleased to say that we are now managing to give some more fulsome statistics in relation to Tenke and this production sales and unit cost information is being shown here now for the first time. You can see copper production was in line with nameplate capacity and that was really despite some issues that occurred during April. I think without the issues in April we would have seen production that was quite a bit higher than what we have here. The issues that occurred in April, there was nothing unusual at this stage of startup and having had them occur, I don't think that there is anyone who could have dealt with them better than what Freeport did.
 And suffice to say now that I think Freeport is now performing consistently above design capacity and Freeport has announced some procurement of additional mining equipment. They have advised that they're expecting production to increase from nameplate capacity this year of 115,000 tonnes to over 130,000 tonnes in 2011 and they are continuing to address some of the startup and quality issues that remain I the cobalt circuits and have concrete plans for implementing some corrective actions over the next few quarters.
 Cash costs down to $0.79; this is after byproduct credits. I guess from Lundin's point of view as we reported in the MD&A, we expect cash costs will benefit in the future. Freeport are talking about higher throughput on the copper side. I think once some of the issues get resolved as a result of the efforts in the cobalt circuit and just on cost reduction efforts that are underway, so we remain optimistic as far as that's concerned.
 Looking at the effect of Tenke on us during the quarter. I've mentioned the change; 8.3 million this quarter compared to 17.2 last; large sales volume, ton difference and you can see from the production numbers and sales numbers that we've sold some 3,5000 tonnes of copper less than we produced and that will obviously get picked up in the normal course of events. We've also seen 3.2 million effect as a result of recognizing minority interests for the first time and that's recognized during the current quarter because we've now absorbed the accumulated pre-operating period losses. The excess overrun facility is dealt with here. As far as expansion studies are concerned, as reported by Freeport, the expansion study work is going to continue into the third quarter 2010.
 Turning now to Lombador. The prefeasibility study has concluded that Lombador can be economically developed and this is now subject to further study. Just some of the general parameters of Lombador; we are expecting that it will lift zinc production at Neves from a nominal 50,000 tonnes to somewhere around 140,000 tonnes per annum and the capital cost of doing that is in the order of 140 million euro. We're expecting a startup date during 2013 and at this stage we are expecting cash costs to be in third quartile based on a normal costing basis. So it is a very low capital cost. I think our benchmarking puts this at about or equal to the lowest capital cost expansion that you can envision for a zinc plant.
 We have commenced the ramp. We've reported this previously. We are due to reach the 300 level, which is some 900 meters below surface in Q1 of 2012. That's a very significant milestone for us. By the end of this year I think we will have pushed the envelope as far as we can in terms of continuing to explore Lombador from surface, so this first phase of development on Lombador gets us down not only into production and with attractive economics, but it also gets us down to the 300 level approximately where we have plans to put in an exploration drive. And I think really it's only once we get that exploration drive in that we will be able to fully define what we have like Lombador South which is all we're dealing with here and Lombador East and also out into the Lombador mid-zone where we have been getting encouraging results.
 So turning to outlook; we're holding our guidance with the exception of Aguablanca. I'll just point out for analysts as well just note that we are, for comparability purposes, we're maintaining our cost estimates on a go-forward basis still of 1.40 Euro to the US dollar. If we change our estimates every quarter then it becomes pretty hard to track. So the one that we've reduced, Aguablanca, where we stand today we're probably going to be on budget for Aguablanca come the end of August.
 The issue we're dealing with there is really the pit has taken a tremendous pounding from the very high rainfall that we had in the first four months of this year and also into December of last year. And some of you might recall, but our pit bottom was inaccessible to us own to flooding for around half of the time. We started the pit cleanup in April; during that cleanup we have identified the number of unstable areas which had some potential to disrupt the main ramp system. We discovered a couple earlier in the year, December and January and those (inaudible) remediated.
 One of these areas which we only discovered pretty late in May has compelled us to really think quite seriously about bringing forward our next pushback. We had only planned to do pushback number three in 2011. So it appears now that we will probably bring that forward to last August or September, so we're going to be in a situation where we're on budget at the end of August and probably produce nothing for September. That decision is not finally made, but it's pretty likely and as a consequence we've taken that into account in terms of looking at our outlook. Put it in perspective, we've got a five-year mine life at Aguablanca. This pushback was going to be done next year within our five-year envelope anyway, so effectively whilst we will see a reduction in metal output this year, it's really just a deferral and this is not lost production to us.
 I think as we mentioned in the MD&A, we've also had notification of some possible [volume] industrial action commences at the end of this month and I think really just as a precaution taking these two items into account we've reduced our guidance at Aguablanca and unlike particularly for analysts that this is a guidance that we're giving plus or minus 5%. My question here is we're dealing with really geomechanical issues that are not entirely possible to nail down and also the threat of industrial action, so we're being a little cautious on this.
 Again, maybe just to put some perspective on this; I think our large operations are running well. We are maintaining our guidance in respect to those. We obviously are still aiming to try and pick up as much as we can between now and the end of the year and I think the revenue effect of the change in Aguablanca - the revenue effect alone is going to be less than 10 million and is a deferral, so really no huge change as far as outlook is concerned.
 We're still considering an early restart of zinc at Neves but having said that, I think looking at where zinc prices are at the moment, it's not something we're finding hugely compelling although we think we can make cash at these numbers. I think we're probably just as likely to possibly use that capacity for additional copper production using low grade copper.
 We've reduced CapEx that is entirely related to a reduction at Tenke. We guided for the year at Tenke between 40 and 100; we are now guiding 40 and as a consequence we expect our CapEx this year to come down under 200. We have had something of an increase in exploration and there's a number of reasons for that. We are doing a bit more near mine at Neves. We have defined a couple of quite interesting copper/gold prospects in the Spanish side of the Pyrite Belt in Ossa Morena region and we are presently testing those. We're also encouraged by the continuing results we're getting at the property in Ireland and there's a little bit more as far as Ireland is concerned.
 Just a note; at the end of July our cap and collars on copper have expired and at this stage we have no derivatives and we presently have no plans for any. Outlook as far as the market's concerned - who knows? I think our view is that volatility is still likely to remain high during the rest of the year and our feeling is that there will be an improving outlook thereafter. So I guess in summary for the quarter, we've had a pretty solid recovery during the quarter, major operations are running well and our cash continues to grow and we are still pretty active in terms of continuing to look for new opportunities. So with that, thank you very much. Happy to open it up to questions. Over to you operator.

Bill Thomas,  EOG Resources Inc - Chairman & CEO: Thanks, Tim. Good morning everyone. There are a couple of items I will cover with you on the call today. First, I will discuss the outstanding progress we have made transitioning the Company to be successful in a lower oil price environment. And I will explain why EOG is uniquely positioned to accomplish this. Second, I will describe the framework we are using to determine our activity level for the remainder of the year.
 Our goal this year is to remain laser focused on improving returns. At the beginning of the year, we noted that our after-tax rate of return at $65 oil were better than at $95 oil three years ago. We are pleased to report that we have further improved these well economics, even as oil prices have declined. Through improved well productivity and lower cost, our key oil plays now earn a 30% after-tax rate of return, with a flat $50 oil price.
 We have multiple decades of drilling inventory in these high-return, world-class assets. EOG is rapidly adjusting to lower oil prices. We believe that our ability to quickly adapt to this new environment illustrates our competitive advantages.
 There are five drivers which make EOG uniquely positioned to improve returns year after year. The first is large, high-quality assets. We have captured the sweet spots in the best horizontal crude oil assets in the US: the Eagle Ford, Bakken, and Delaware Basin. The quality of our assets is why EOG drills the most productive oil wells in the US. The scale of our positions drives tremendous efficiencies, and the diversity of our assets allows us to transfer technology gains and cost savings from basin to basin.
 The second driver is innovation and technology. New ideas and technical  technically drive continuous productivity improvements. For example, we developed in-house, integrated completion technology that consistently drives field recoveries higher and maximizes NPV. During the first five years of drilling the Eagle Ford, we increased its reserve potential 250%. This quarter, we increased our Bakken net potential reserves to 1 billion barrels of oil equivalent, a 150% increase. EOG has over 10 years of horizontal shale experience to build on, and we expect to continue advancing our knowledge through innovation and technology.
 The third is low cost. We believe EOG's well and operating costs were already the lowest in the industry, and 2015 is proving to be our best year ever for realizing additional cost reductions. EOG's scale and high-quality assets, and proprietary technology, will continue to drive future efficiency gains and cost reductions.
 The fourth driver is organic growth. This is the lowest-cost, highest-return approach to adding drilling potential. Being first movers in exploration allows us to capture large amounts of high-quality rock at much lower cost than through acquisition-and-exploit strategy. Organic exploration is an important competitive advantage for EOG, and we see significant opportunities ahead of us.
 Last, but not least, is EOG's organization and culture. This is the catalyst for the first four drivers, and underpins our competitive advantage. A decentralized structure encourages asset-level, bottom-up decision making, which leads to better execution. Our core culture is return driven. Employee performance is incentivized by greater return, which is the key driver to our peer-leading return on capital employed. Return-based decision making and incentives drive EOG's success.
 The second item I will cover today is our plan for the remainder of 2015. We are maintaining total Company oil production guidance, while reducing 2015 CapEx guidance by approximately $200 million. In addition, our projected year-end uncompleted well inventory has increased from 285 to 320. The bottom line is, productivity improvements and reduced costs are allowing us to produce more oil with less capital.
 Many of you are asking: When will EOG grow oil again? We have said all along that we do not want to grow production until we see the oil market is firmly rebalancing. We will be watching the supply-demand fundamentals in the second half of this year closely as we determine our plan for 2016. Currently, we intend to spend within cash flow. The capital efficiency gains we have made this year, along with our large high-quality inventory of uncompleted wells, positions us for an excellent 2016.
 My number one message is this  we are resetting the economics of our business. EOG is quickly adapting to be successful in a low oil-price environment. We expect EOG to remain the lowest cost US shale producer, and competitive in the world oil market.
 I will now turn it over to David Trice to discuss the update on our Bakken resource estimates, as well as other activities in the Rockies.

David Trice,  EOG Resources Inc - EVP of Exploration & Production: Thanks, Bill. We're pleased with the performance from our spacing tests using our integrated completion process in the Bakken. We now estimate that our Bakken and Three Forks total net resource potential is just over 1 billion barrels of oil equivalent. That is almost 2.5 times our original estimate of 420 million barrels of oil equivalent. Remaining drilling inventory increased from 580 to over 1,500 net drilling locations. This represents 760 million barrels of oil equivalent of remaining net potential reserves and decades of drilling in this premier North Dakota asset.
 In addition to the updated resource estimate, we split the Bakken into two categories that we have titled core acreage and non-core acreage. The core produces returns that are competitive with both the Eagle Ford and the Delaware Basin, and includes our acreage in the Bakken core and Antelope Extension. Non-core represents acreage in the Bakken Lite, State Line, and Elm Coulee areas. Although our main focus will be in the core area, we believe that, with modern, high-density completions, and current well cost, the non-core acreage will be very economic, even with low oil prices.
 We defined 120,000 net acres and 590 net drilling locations in the core, which represents remaining net resource potential of 360 million barrels of oil equivalent. This inventory alone offers over 10 years of drilling. Non-core acreage represents remaining net resource potential of 400 million barrels equivalent. In this acreage, we defined 110,000 net acres and 950 net drilling locations which provide decades of inventory.
 Our wells in the Bakken continue to exceed expectations. A great example of the progress we're making is the Riverview 102-32H well. This is the first Bakken well in the Antelope Extension we have drilled using a high-density completion. The well came online with a maximum rate of 3,395 barrels of oil per day and 6 million cubic feet of rich natural gas. With an average rate of 2,760 barrels of oil per day for July, this short, 4,300-foot lateral will be the highest rate oil well ever recorded for the Bakken or Three Forks. We are excited to continue applying high-density completions throughout the entire play as we move forward.
 In addition to improved returns to advance completions, we have made tremendous progress on Bakken completed well cost, which are now $7.1 million for an 8,400-foot treated lateral. This is a almost 20% decrease in well costs from 2014. Most of the well cost savings are due to efficiency gains rather than vendor cost reductions, and, therefore, should be sustainable over time. Drilling times are now averaging 8.2 days, spud to TD for an 8,400-foot lateral, with our best being a record 5.6 days. We are also realizing significant completion efficiencies. Currently, we are averaging more than 10 completion stages per day, up from 4 to 5 stages per day in 2014. In addition, plug drill-out times have been cut in half since 2014.
 Finally, cost savings are not just limited to CapEx. We added infrastructure this year in the Bakken core and, as a result, we have seen dramatic LOE reductions. Second-quarter LOE is down more than 25% from the first quarter. The increase to our Bakken reserve potential and drilling inventory illustrates the value of the EOG's exploration and technology leadership. We enter plays as the first mover and capture the best assets. Then we grow them through the drill bit and improve recoveries over time with drilling and completion technology developed in-house. This is how EOG continues to grow organically.
 Here is Billy Helms to update you on the Delaware Basin and the Eagle Ford.

 The completed well cost for the second Bone Spring Sand are currently averaging $6 million per well, representing a 22% reduction from last year's average. A major portion of the cost savings can be attributed to sustainable efficiency improvements in both drilling and completion operations, rather than solely vendor cost reductions. Improved well performance, coupled with lower well cost, make this play very attractive in this low-commodity price environment. We will continue evaluating well performance to determine the proper spacing and ultimate recovery.
 During the last quarter, we also completed several strong Wolfcamp wells in the overpressured oil window of the play. Two recent completions in Lea County, New Mexico, the Dragon 36 State #701H and the Hearns 27 State Com #703H had initial production rates per well of 2,650 barrels of oil per day, along with 285 barrels per day of NGLs and 1.9 million cubic feet per day of natural gas.  Similar advancements have been achieved in the Leonard play. A typical well now costs $5.5 million, and we're testing spacing patterns of 300 feet and 500 feet between wells. One recent completion in Lea County, New Mexico, the Gem 36 State Com #1H had an initial production rate of 2,200 barrels of oil per day, 460 barrels per day of NGLs and 2.6 million cubic feet per day of natural gas.
 Our downspacing efforts demonstrate that we can drill wells closer together without sacrificing production. These new completion designs are allowing us to improve the overall economics and ultimate recovery. Due to these strong results, we anticipate the Delaware Basin will play a significant role in EOG's long-term growth. Also, the productivity of the wells continues to show steady improvement through our emphasis on targeting and high-density completions. Some of the recent wells are highlighted in our press release. The combination of cost reductions and better well performance through the application of technology is ensuring that this world-class asset will continue to deliver strong growth for years to come.
 I will now turn it over to Tim Driggers to discuss financials and capital structure.

Randall Stuewe,  Darling International Inc - Chairman and CEO: Thanks Brad. Good morning everyone. Thanks for joining us. It is my pleasure to welcome you to Darling's International's earnings call to discuss our second quarter results.
 As noted in our press release yesterday, momentum carried forward from the first quarter and all segments of our business are performing well. Escalating finished product prices for fats, proteins and bakery [by-]products led to a strong top line and bottom line. Resulting in a net income of [$52.2 million] or $0.44 per share. I would like to light a few key areas that impacted our 2011 second quarter.
 Rendering volumes were essentially flat for the quarter as compared to both first quarter 2011 and prior year. Surprisingly, poultry tonnage remained strong while mild spring weather in the Midwest reduced the amount of mortalities available for processing. Restaurant grease volumes increased seasonally but we are now beginning to see the impact of significant theft.
 Animal fats and grease prices rose 60% versus first quarter. The improving biofuel demand, increasing exports to Europe and a solid feed demand contributed. Protein prices, although moderately stronger than first quarter, declined as the second quarter came to a close. Typical seasonality kicked in for pet food demand and hot summer temperatures started to influence animal feed consumption. Both ruminant and poultry protein prices increased by 20% to 25% versus our first quarter.
 The bakery segment made a strong contribution to second quarter results. Increasing corn prices and consistent tonnage led to the increase. From an energy perspective, prices remain fairly consistent compared to last year's second quarter, and we continue to benefit from historically low natural gas prices and favorable forward ownership.
 We achieved the significant milestone towards implementing our renewable fuel strategy in this quarter. Doreen A. Toben,  Verizon - EVP and CEO: Thanks Tom and good morning everyone. Let me start by saying that as we close out 2004 and move into 2005 our business fundamentals are stronger now than they have been in years. Our fourth quarter completes the year in which we produced our strongest overall revenue growth in three years. 
 We generated incremental revenues of $5.2 billion as Verizon Wireless which continues its outstanding performance demonstrating once again that it is far and away the industry leader. Our wireline business also turned in a very solid performance with steadily improving revenues and stable operating margins. Importantly, we continue to see strong cash generation throughout the entire business. So let's start with the financial highlights. 
 Revenue growth of 6.2% for the quarter and 5.7% for the full year. Consolidated revenues grew $3.8 billion in 2004 and totaled more than $71 billion. Consolidated revenues were also up for the third consecutive quarter. Growth was primarily driven by Verizon Wireless which now represents about 40% of our quarterly revenue stream. 
 We had another quarter of solid margins demonstrating our ability to drive growth in new areas while increasing productivity and reducing costs. 
 Cash from operations remains strong at $6.3 billion in the quarter. We ended the year with $39.3 billion of total debt, a reduction of more than $6.0 billion or 13.5% in 2004. We also ended the year with $2.3 billion of cash on hand. 
 Adjusted EPS was sixty-four cents for the fourth quarter bringing us to $2.51 for the full year 2004. This is a significant increase over fourth quarter 2003. These solid financial results were made possible by continued excellent operational performance inductive of our strong business fundamentals. 
 Verizon Wireless capped off an outstanding year with a very strong fourth quarter. 
 Net ads were $1.7 million for the quarter and $6.3 million for the year. Service (inaudible) of 5032 grew 3.0% over fourth quarter of last year. More than 16.6 million customers use our data services. A 62% increase over last year and our commitment to network quality and customer satisfaction helps us reduce total churn to a new record low of 1.43% in the fourth quarter. 
 In the wireline business customers continue to respond to the excellent value proposition of our bundled services as package penetration grew to 56%. We added another 306 DSL subscribers in the quarter for a total of $1.24 million for the year. An average consumer revenue per customer in wireline grew to just short of $50.00 per month, a 4.0% increase. 
 More details on each of these areas in a few minutes, but first let me take you through our earnings reconciliation for the fourth quarter. 
 Reported earnings were $1.08 per share reflecting several one-time gains that we have excluded from adjusted earnings. During the quarter we recorded net after-tax gains of just over $1.0 billion or thirty-six cents per share on the sale of our Canadian directories and our interest in Telis. The sale of our Canadian directories also resulted in a taxable capital gain which allowed us to utilize some previously unrecognized capital losses. The resulting tax benefit was $234 million or eight cents per share. Excluding these effects, adjusted EPS was sixty-four cents for the quarter. 
 Again, we are obviously very pleased with another quarter of strong quality earnings. I want to bring one additional item to you attention regarding a recent accounting ruling dealing with the inclusion of contingently convertible debt and diluted earnings per share calculations. There is a footnote on our income statements detailing this information. Essentially here is the change. 
 Our zero coupon debt which is convertible into Verizon common stock is now included in both current and prior periods diluted EPS calculations and will be going forward. The retroactive effect on 2003 is worth about two cents per share meaning that the $2.62 adjusted EPS from that year is now $2.60 for comparability. In 2004 the effect of this change diluted EPS by about one cent, so without this change EPS would have been $2.52. 
 Now let's move on to a real story of 2004 which is the growth and change of our revenue base around wireless, broadband, long distance and the enterprise markets. As you can see on the chart 55% of our revenues now come from these initiatives up from 49% a year ago. 
 Over the course of last year these growth areas generated incremental revenues of $6.2 billion representing growth of almost 20%. Looking at annual revenue trends you can see that we have grown revenues by nearly $5.0 billion in 2002 highlighted by 5.7% growth this year. You can also see the increasing contribution of our high-growth wireless segments of these results and the fact that this growth has greatly exceeded the decline in the wireline business.

This business continues to be a significant source of cash generating CFFO of about $1.1 billion during 2004. During 2004 we did an excellent job of controlling cash expenses. The reduction in wireline expenses were driven by full year wage savings from our force downsizing initiatives last year offset in part by higher cost of sales due to the growth in DSL and long distance markets. 
 In wireless our scale distribution and productivity program resulted once again in lower growth and cash expenses than revenues. Our adjusted operating income margins excluding (inaudible) remain strong. On a consolidated basis full year margins grew 90 basis points from 20% driven by nearly a 300 basis point increase in wireless to 21.1% and stability in wireline at 17.1%. 
 Verizon Wireless generated another very strong quarter relative to both EBITDA and operating income. However, I want to draw your attention to one item in particular. Fourth quarter margins include the effects of a sizable accrual of compensation expense related to the Verizon Wireless long-term employee incentive plan. This is a plan that virtually all Verizon Wireless employees participate in. The increase in the amount recognized as compensation expense in the fourth quarter reflects both the extraordinary operating performance of the business as well as its significant appreciation in value in 2004.

It could happen, and one of the biggest drivers that would cause that to happen more quickly is a global recession, which I'm very hopeful that that won't happen.  Clearly, in the short term from a retailer's perspective, if they raise price and already have product and inventory, they can make a little extra margin. From our perspective, that's not our goal. Our goal right now is to make sure we're pricing on a run rate basis that we believe we need to be successful and be able to continue to invest in our business, not trying to game this to make a little extra margin in a particular quarter. Neil Koehler,  Pacific Ethanol, Inc. - President, CEO: Thanks, Joe. I want just to take a minute to update you on the views of the ethanol marketplace. Corn prices have declined significantly in the last number of weeks, ethanol prices have declined as well with all commodity prices, but there has been some margin improvement in ethanol production economics.. Tight margins and credit markets have both slowed the completion of new production capacity and the run rates of some existing capacity. Virtually no new construction has been initiated this year. Very favorable ethanol blending economics continue to increase the demand for ethanol. With a 50% increase in domestic production year-over-year, supply is pushing demand, which along with high corn prices has contributed to margin compression.
  As we move through 2008 into 2009, new plant openings are slowing in the industry, while ethanol demand will continue to accelerate. We still believe that production margins improve significantly, as this will be necessary to encourage a new round of production expansion needed to meet future demand. In spite of the negative propaganda campaign by the grocery manufacturer's association, the policies support for ethanol remains solid. We are encouraged by the EPA denial of the Texas waiver request from the renewable fuel standard. EPA administrator Johnson summed it up succinctly in his press conference last week by stating that "the RFS remains an important tool in our ongoing efforts to reduce America's greenhouse gas emissions and lessen our dependence on foreign oil in aggressive yet practical ways." We agree, and stand ready to do our part as company to deliver increasing supplies of cost competitive, low carbon ethanol fuel to the transportation fuel market. And Erica, at this time, please open up the lines for questions.

Gary Grove,  Bonanza Creek Energy Inc. - Executive VP, Engineering Planning: Thanks, Mike. This morning I'm going to address production, operating and capital cost trends, and our expected drilling program for the remainder of 2012, taking into consideration our increased capital budget.
 Our production for the year, as of June 30th, averaged 8,022 BOE per day, our second quarter production averaged 8,944 BOE per day, and June production averaged 9,137 BOE per day, a 131% increase over June of last year.
 Production for the second quarter was negatively impacted by unscheduled gas processing facility maintenance at our Dorcheat-Macedonia field in Arkansas. During the second quarter this facility was operating for some time at constrained efficiencies, and was fully shut down for 10 days.
 In the Wattenberg Field, you've heard that  you have heard a number of our neighbors comment on high line pressures throughout the system causing production interruptions. These pressures, which were not a material issue for us in the first quarter, did impact our production in the second quarter.
 A more significant impact we felt on our lease operating expense. We have experienced these high line pressures to be a localized gathering issue, not a regional takeaway problem. We believe that installing compression in the appropriate areas and further transitioning from vertical wells to horizontal wells, will allow us to mitigate the impact of this issue.
 The combined production impact of the gas plant downtime and the high line pressures was approximately 200 BOE per day for the quarter. Our increase midpoint production guidance for the year to approximately 3.5 million BOE takes into account the impact of these issues and the production uplift from the incremental capital program.
 Activity levels across the Wattenberg will likely remain elevated, as the midstream operators are actively keeping up with processing capacity needs. DCP, for example, just announced that it will double the size of the DJ Basin gathering and processing system by 2014. On the oil side, or DJ Basin differential remains at a flat $8 deducted WTI, which is an all-in fee incorporating transportation cost.
 In the second quarter, per unit lease operating expense continued to decline to $9.45 per BOE, down from $12.03 per BOE in the first quarter. This is a significant improvement, but is still above our original estimates. The biggest contributor of our higher LOE expense has been the increased cost of our operating horizontal wells in the initial months of production which have required, in most cases, 24-hour supervision and equipment rentals as permanent infrastructure is installed.
 Our annual guidance was based on limited historical data for the horizontal wells, and the initial operating cost were the most difficult to predict. As the horizontal wells produce in the later months, their monthly cost to operate comes more closely in line with our original estimates.
 In addition, our lease operating expense was negatively impacted by the high line pressures, which knocked some vertical wells offline and required insulation of compression to push gas into the gathering system, in addition to the cost of reestablishing production.
 Going forward, we are revising our full-year lease operating expense guidance to be in the range of $8.50 to $9.50 per BOE, an increase of $1.30 per barrel. The last topic I'd like to discuss is our drilling plan and capital budget for the remainder of the year inclusive of a significant increase in capital.
 Our development capital budget now stands at $298 million with the addition of 5 horizontal Niobrara B bench wells, and different inventory catalyst in the Wattenberg and Arkansas. In addition, we continue to transition our Niobrara Development Program away from vertical wells to a horizontal development program. In the second half of this year, we plan to reallocate capital away from 20 vertical wells and instead drill  and instead, drill 4 more horizontal Niobrara wells.
