Keith Rattie,  Questar Corp. - Chairman, President &  CEO: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for joining us. 
 The bottom line is we're off to a pretty good start in 2006. Note that we've bumped both earnings and production guidance for 2006. We now estimate that this year's earnings could range from about $4.50 to $4.80 per diluted share. That's a $0.20 increase from our previous guidance. We put a table in our release to reconcile the current and previous guidance. Note that we haven't changed our price or basis assumptions for the guidance we gave in February. That $0.20 increase reflects better execution and generally a quick start in 2006. 
 Also note for reference that the current Rockies basis is about $1.80 per million Btu and current Midcontinent basis is about $1.45 per million Btu in the west and about $1.30 per million Btu in the east. Both of those are less than what we've assumed in our guidance. 
 Note that we've now hedged about 68% of forecast 2006 gas and oil-equivalent production at significantly higher realized prices than in 2005. So as a result, we've taken commodity price risk pretty much out of the equation for Questar in '06. 
 Also note that we've now hedged 60 Bcf of gas in 2007 at an average net-to-the-well price more than $1.00 above the average hedge price for 2006 production. And note that we've also added some hedges in 2008 at higher prices. 
 Let me turn to highlights from operations. Questar E&P reported production of 32.3 billion cubic feet equivalent in the first quarter. That's up 23% from the first quarter a year ago. Excluding a one-time increase of 0.7 Bcf equivalent from the settlement of an imbalance, we grew first-quarter production 20%. And that's on the heels of 15% year-on-year increase in Q4 and 16% year-on-year increase in Q3 2005. 
 We now estimate full-year 2006 production could range from 124 to 126 Bcf equivalent. That's compared to previous guidance of 122 to 124 Bcf equivalent. This assumes 45 to 48 wells at Pinedale, which is unchanged from our previous guidance. Also note that first-quarter gas and oil-equivalent production was up significantly in every Questar E&P operating unit from the year-ago quarter. Pinedale production was up 29%, Rockies legacy production was up 24%  7% if you exclude the imbalance settlement  and new Vermillion Basin volumes offset normal declines from mature properties. I'll talk about Vermillion here in a bit. 
 One of the biggest highlights, Midcontinent production was up 26% driven by our Elm Grove tight-gas play in northwestern Louisiana and the successful high working interest exploratory well in the Arkoma basin. 
 We had seven rigs operating at Pinedale this past winter. That's compared to just two rigs during the winter of 2004 and 2005. Note that due to winter-access restrictions we did not complete any new wells at Pinedale in the first quarter of this year. So we'll come out of the winter with 33 new wells to complete in the second and third quarter of this year. 
 We are going to add two more rigs for a total of nine this summer. Now, I will remind you that our production typically declines during the first and second quarters due to winter-access restrictions at Pinedale and elsewhere in the Rockies. But with a big inventory of new wells coming out of Pinedale midsummer, Questar E&P production should turn up again in the third quarter and then again in the fourth quarter. 
 Our Pinedale team continues to drive drilling efficiency higher, and if that continues, there's some upside in our estimate of 45 to 48 new wells this year. 
 Recall that in 2004 we averaged about 65 days to drill, log, and case a typical Pinedale well. In 2005, we reduced that to 47 days. This winter we've averaged less than 42 days per well, and if you strip out a couple of problem wells, our average is under 40 days. Our Pinedale team is delivering these results on directional wells that average 14,300 feet measured depth. We are not aware of any other operator at Pinedale that's getting these results. 
 Let me briefly update you on our Pinedale deep test. Recall last September we produced gas from the Hilliard Shale at peak extrapolator rates of 10.7 million cubic feet a day equivalent for about 32 hours and then the well plugged off and flow abruptly stopped. For safety reasons we shut down for winter but we're now moving back on location to re-enter and clean out the well. We hope to circulate out the obstruction and re-establish production from the Hilliard. 
 Now, depending on what we find, we'll either continue testing the Hilliard or we'll move uphole and test our primary target, the Rock Springs. Note that from logs, we've identified multiple completion intervals in the Rock Springs at depths from about 16,000 feet to about 18,000 feet. 
 Turning briefly to Gas Management, our gathering and processing company had another good quarter on the heels of a 70% jump in net income in 2005. And Gas Management has another big construction program this summer. We are building a 20-inch pipeline from our Blacks Fork plant to Kern River pipeline near Opal, Wyoming. We're expanding the Blacks Fork processing plant and building additional gathering facilities to handle growing Pinedale production volumes. 
 Now, let me give you an update on our emerging new play in the Vermillion Basin. The bottom line here is that well performance thus far has been repeatable, well costs are coming down, and our confidence in this play is growing. Recall that the targets are the overpressured Baxter Shale and the deeper Frontier and Dakota tight-sands formations. The Baxter really is the key. There's an enormous amount of gas-in-place across an interval of about 3,500 feet at depths of about 9,500 to about 13,000 feet. But as you folks know, with Shale gas, it's all about rate and recovery, not gas-in-place. And overpressure is one of the keys to rate and recovery. We believe that the Baxter is overpressured over most of our now 146,000 net acres in the basin. 
 Recall that we kicked this play off over a year ago by re-entering two old wells, Canyon Creek 34 and Hiawatha Deep #2. We frac’d the Baxter, Frontier, and Dakota formations and today production has flattened in these wells at about 500,000 cubic feet per day from each well. The early performance of these wells suggest per well reserves of 2 to 4 billion cubic feet equivalent, but I would note that neither were optimally stimulated due to casings, cement, and other mechanical problems. 
 Our first modern well on the the play, Alkali Gulch #1, went to sales in June last year and has produced almost a half Bcf of gas in just over 10 months. Production decline in this well has flattened at about 880,000 cubic feet per day equivalent, which, if you extrapolate that, could mean reserves on the order of 3 to 4 billion cubic feet equivalent. 
 Production declined in our second and third new wells, Canyon Creek 41 and Hiawatha Deep #5, have also flattened at about 700,000 cubic feet per day and 600,000 cubic feet per day, respectively. 
 In the first quarter of 2006 we turned our fourth and fifth new wells to sale, Canyon Creek 47 and Canyon Creek 61, and we've now recently completed our sixth new well, Trail 31. 
 Let me give you some numbers on these. Canyon Creek 47 has averaged about 600,000 cubic feet equivalent per day for the first 77 days. Canyon Creek 61 has averaged about 1.7 million cubic feet per day equivalent in the first two weeks of production and is now making about 1.3 million cubic feet equivalent per day. 
 Earlier this week we turned the 6th well, Trail 31, to sales. This well is currently making about 4 million cubic feet equivalent per day. Also note the location. Trail 31 well is 3.7 miles northeast of the nearest established Baxter production at Canyon Creek 61. 
 Further, we're drilling ahead on our seventh and eighth new wells, Canyon Creek 74 and Whiskey Canyon. 
 And for those who are following this in detail, we're going to post a map on our Web site later today to help you locate all of these wells along with additional locations for some of our other 2006 drilling programs. 
 Again, what this means is that well performance thus far appears repeatable. And that's a good sign. Our technical team is focused on optimizing completion design to maximize frac extension and rate while driving down well costs. 
 Now, to give you some context, some economics, if these wells recover an average of about 3 billion cubic feet equivalent, we're going to need to get our average well costs down to about $3.5 million to earn a 15% IRR at a $5.00 NYMEX gas price. If ultimate recoveries average 4 Bcf equivalent per well, we'll earn about a 15% IRR with an average well cost of about $4.5 million. Obviously, we're going to benefit from economies of scale once we get to program drilling like we're doing at Pinedale. And I'd caution you that we're in the early days of this program. We still need additional production data from the wells we've already drilled to get comfortable with reserves. And we're going to need more wells to sample our large acreage block to determine the areal extent of the play. Finally, note that we've started the process for a new EIS for the project and don't expect that to be a limitation. 
 Questar owners are going to want to stay tuned. We plan to drill about 12 wells in the Vermillion Basin this year. 
 Let me turn to the Uinta Basin. First quarter production, as you note, was above plan, up 9% from the year-ago quarter. We began the year with about 80 Questar-operated and about 55 non-Questar operated locations yet to drill on 40-acre density in our core Wasatch upper Mesa Verde tight gas play. And this is at depths from about 8,000 to about 10,000 feet. 
 We now have about 65 Questar operated and about 50 non-operated 40-acre development locations left in our inventory. Our average working interest in these remaining locations is lower than the average of the wells we've drilled thus far, so we're going to need success in other plays in the Basin to keep production headed up. Now, towards that end, we've stepped up the pace of our evaluation of a potential deep play, where the targets are unconventional reservoirs in the lower Mesa Verde, Blackhawk, Mancos, and Dakota formations. 
 Based on what we've learned in the Vermillion Basin and at Pinedale, we've now drilled and tested our first Mancos shale and Dakota formation well down to about 16,000 feet. Now, I will remind you, the Mancos is a thick, overpressured shale section. It's the age equivalent of the Baxter Shale in the Vermillion Basin and the Hilliard Shale at Pinedale. The Mancos and Dakota are present and overpressured across most of our Uinta basin acreage. Our first Mancos test, the Glen Bench 16D-28 well, averaged 1.4 million cubic feet per day for the first 41 days and is now making 1.2 million cubic feet a day, again, from the Mancos and Dakota formations. 
 Interestingly, this well performance is similar to what we have seen thus far in the Vermillion Basin. And we still have the shallower Mancos B and Blackhawk behind pipe to test at a later date. 
 The economics of a deep play in the Uinta Basin benefit from multiple targets and might be further improved by completing the shallower Wasatch formation tight sands on 20- acre density. The Wasatch alone, as we've said in the past, is probably not a candidate for widespread increased density from 40 to 20 acres, but some incremental reserves and some rate acceleration might lower the reserve threshold and improve the economics of the deep play. 
 As always, the caveat is that one well does not a play make. It's going to take a lot of wells to validate a play like this, but we like what we've seen with our first Mancos to Dakota test and in fact, we're almost at total depth in our second Mancos/Dakota well and we plan to drill several more wells this year. 
 Turning to the southern Uinta Basin. We've now drilled four wells on our Gar Mesa Flat Rock play. Our first well, the 100% Flat Rock 9P-36 is currently producing 2.2 million cubic feet a day equivalent and has already produced over 1 Bcf of gas. We recently completed our second 100% working interest Flat Rock well, the Flat Rock 1P-36. This is a direct offset to the first well. It's currently making about 2.8 million cubic feet equivalent per day after about 20 days on line. 
 Our third well, the Wolf Flats 1P-1 well  and this is the first under the JV with the northern Ute Indian tribe  has averaged about a million cubic feet equivalent per day in the first 115 days on production and is currently making about 800,000 cubic feet equivalent per day. We have a 50% working interest in this well. 
 We've also drilled, cased, and started testing a fourth well in the area. This is a 75% working-interest wildcat. Note that it's located seven miles south of the Flat Rock area. 
 Just a reminder, under the terms of our deal with the Ute tribe, Questar has leases covering about 12,500 acres of tribal minerals and the tribe has the right to participate in the first well in each section with up to 50% working interest. 
 Let me turn to the Midcontinent. First quarter production was up 26% from a year ago. Our experienced teams are doing an outstanding job, replacing decline and growing production in mature areas. Our tight-gas play in the Elm Grove field is driving the Midcontinent growth. We started this year with an inventory of over 100 operated well locations yet to drill at Elm Grove, with an average working interest of about 86%. 
 Note this; Our current inventory could be about 50% larger. As we continue to develop our Elm Grove leasehold, our comfort in increased-density drilling has increased. As a result, we now estimate that we have about 148 operated locations and another 105 non-operated locations yet to drill at Elm Grove. 
 Turning to Wexpro. Under the 1981 Wexpro agreement, you know Wexpro recovers its costs and earns an unlevered after-tax return of approximately 19 to 20% on its investment base. In the first quarter of this year, Wexpro invested $12.2 million, which increased the investment base to $214.5 million on March 31st, 2006. And that's $28.8 million or about 16% higher compared to the first quarter, or the end of the first quarter, '05. 
 During the first quarter, Wexpro produced almost 11 billion cubic feet equivalent on behalf of Questar Gas at a cost of service far below current market prices. The good news for both investors and for our utility customers, Wexpro has identified about $700 million of new investment opportunities that should drive continued growth in the investment base and therefore growth in net income while helping to keep Questar Gas rates among the lowest in the country. 
 Let's turn briefly to our regulated businesses. I hope you took note that Questar Pipeline earned a record $11.4 million in the first quarter. That's up 37% from a year ago. There were four factors. Number one, higher revenues from new firm-transportation contracts in both the southern-system expansion project and on Overthrust Pipeline. Two, operating improvements, including increased park-and-loan revenues and lower fuel-gas consumption and NGL-handling costs. Three, higher gas-liquids prices. Under the settlement agreement with shippers last year, we share incremental liquids recovered at the Clay Basin Kastler plant. And finally, ongoing cost reduction is flowing straight through to the bottom line. 
 Questar Pipeline also has a busy summer ahead. In the first quarter we finalized a 20-year contract to build and lease to the Rockies Express Pipeline sponsors the westernmost segment of Rockies Express Pipeline, that goes from the Opal Hub to the Wamsutter Hub in southwestern Wyoming, and we will utilize capacity on our existing 36-inch Overthrust Pipeline. This summer we're going to extend Overthrust west to Opal and then next year we'll extend Overthrust east to Wamsutter. 
 Also in the first quarter, Questar Pipeline finalized a 12-year contract with Wyoming Interstate, WIC, for firm transportation of 125,000 decatherms per day from Opal to Kanda for delivery into WIC. To do this, we're going to install 5,800 horsepower of new compression to move the incremental volume through the Overthrust expansion. 
 Questar Pipeline also expects to finalize long-term contracts for another $58 million expansion of its southern system from the Uinta Basin. That's a core Questar producing region in eastern Utah, which interconnects with Questar Gas, our utility, at Price, Utah, and Kern River Pipeline at Goshen in central Utah. 
 In short, our pipeline company's task is to identify and eliminate bottlenecks in our core Rockies producing basins and I think the first-quarter results show that they're executing well. 
 Turning briefly to our utility. Questar Gas net income was essentially flat in the first quarter compared to a year ago after adjusting for the settlement of the gas-processing dispute. For the trailing 12-month period, our utility earned a 10.9% ROE. That's below its 11.2% allowed return. 
 First-quarter results benefited from strong customer growth in Utah. At the end of the quarter we were serving over 834,000 homes and businesses. That's up 4.2% from a year ago. 
 But on the downside, high prices hurt utilities like Questar Gas. Of course, that's contrary to what the public believes. Average temperature adjusted usage per customer declined about 2% in the first quarter compared to a year ago. As you would expect, our customers responded to high prices by cutting consumption. Utilities like Questar Gas make money on the volume of gas we deliver to customers, not on the sales price of natural gas. 
 Of course, some customers had difficulty paying their bills. So bad-debt expense was also up in the first quarter. That's another predictable consequence of high prices. 
 In summary, Questar's off to a good start in '06. We'll come out of the winter drilling season at Pinedale with about 33 wells to complete this summer. We're gaining confidence in our Vermillion Basin play. Well performance thus far appears to be repeatable and costs are coming down. 
 In the Uinta Basin we are intrigued by our initial test of the Mancos Shale on our core acreage. The first well looks pretty similar to our Vermillion wells and unlike the Vermillion, in the Uinta Basin deep play, we have uphole reserves that may boost economics. 
 Our seasoned Midcontinent team once again surprised, on the upside, replacing decline and posting 26% production growth. Our midstream business posted double-digit growth on top of 70% growth in '05. Questar Pipeline had by far its best quarter ever. High prices hurt our utility, but despite declining usage, we're still earning near our allowed return. 
 I want to thank you for joining us today. Thanks for your interest in Questar, and now we'll be glad to take your questions.

 We, historically, have shunned basis hedging in favor of using simple fixed-price swaps, which give us a known price for a fixed volume of equity gas at the relevant pipeline sales point. But given the fundamentals right now, we are warming up to the idea of doing a little bit of basis hedging. Unlike the swaps that we use, these would not be cash- flow hedges under FAS 133. And our reluctance to use basis hedging has been in part because we don't want to introduce a little bit of uncertainty in the quarterly earnings, as you mark to market the basis hedges.

Alvaro Garcia-Tunon,  Wabtec Corporation - SVP and CFO, Secretary: Thanks very much Greg and good afternoon, everybody. As Greg mentioned about conductive brief review of our financial results for the quarter and then turn it over for Q and A. Sales decreased slightly from last year. Last year's total sales were approximately $180 million. This year they were about $175. Freight group sales increased during the period to increased by about 20% due to increased sales of OEM freight car components and commuter locomotives. However transit group sales decreased by 37%. For the most part, this is expected because the decrease was primarily due to the completion of this R142 order for New York City, but the transit market has been a little bit softer than we anticipated at the beginning of the year. Overall, these two tend to offset each other and because of mixed freight tends to be more profitable than transit. 
 We think we will meet projections for the year. Gross margin, the results are favorable. It increased to 27.2% versus 25.2% last year and 26.7% in the first quarter of '02. This improvement was due to operating efficiencies and continued application of lean techniques and favorable product mix, which I mentioned earlier. SG&A expense increased by about $2 million from last year. This was due in large part to insurance costs both casualty insurance cost, you know insurance cost etc as well as medical cost, which everybody has been experiencing. SG&A will fluctuate somewhat from quarter-to-quarter, but in large part, this is the due reason for the increases. Interest expense was substantially lower. This is due to the reduction in debt and the continued favorable climate for interest rates. Other expenses, I think Bill mentioned at the outset, we booked foreign exchange loss of approximately $2.3 million during the quarter or 3 cents per share, which was mainly due to the weaker U.S. dollar relative to the Canadian dollar. About half of this expense was paper expense. It was due to an accounting convention, which we had to adopt, but it did not really have a substantial economic effect and about half of it was a true economic effect, cash effect just from higher expenses in Canada due to the exchange rates. 
 Income tax expense we are accruing slightly higher than last quarter, 36.5 versus 35% due to higher effective state tax rates. We typically try to give you a simple bridge, simple causal of one quarter to the prior quarter and to the prior quarter we were 2 cents higher than last year. We had a negative effect due to lower volume of about 2 cents, negative effect due to the higher SG&A insurance of 3 cents and about 3 cents lower due to foreign exchange. However, because of mix and higher gross profit margin, that had a 5-cent positive effect and then a 5-cent positive effect due to reduced interest expenses. Again, showing the benefits of reduced leverage. One thing you noticed when you compare numbers to last year, is that the EBITDA numbers are slightly different. During the intervening period, we adopted with Regulation G, which was issued by the SEC, which provides guidelines on the use of GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures. We now report EBITDA again this is how we do it now with net income and we only add back interest, taxes and D&A. That is what Reg G says -the only item Reg G says is that you are allowed to add back in calculating EBITDA according to their methodology. The traditional way in the past we started with income from operations rather than net income and then we added back line items below that which tended to be non-recurring, such as restructuring expenses or non cash. But again, the numbers we disclose now are Reg G compliant. 
 In terms of working capital, our working capital increased slightly during the quarter by about $2 million. Receivables increased by about $2 million. Inventories increased slightly and it is offset to a certain extent by an increase of payables and other accruals. The effect was $2 million. 
 Debt net of cash was $173 million, which translates to 44% of total capital at June 30 compared to $179 million at end of the prior quarter March 31 and compared to $203 million a year ago. We continue to make progress in generating cash and maintaining our more conservative credit profile. We generated $6 million of cash in the current quarter. 
 In terms of non-cash items, depreciation was stable in line with the prior quarters at about $5.1 million. Amortization of about a million during the quarter. Capex, we continue at a very reasonable level mainly through the continued implementation of lean principles which really were resolved in low capital expenditures and we had only about $2.6 million during the quarter. For the year we anticipate the run rate may be a little higher than that, but we think we will certainly under spend the depreciation level. And we are still aiming for free cash of $40 million or $1 per share for '03. 
 In terms of backlog, the total backlog for the company was very stable at about $300 million versus $311 million a year ago. As we shift a little bit more to freight mix and transit and less of dependence on transit, the backlog will be less and less significant. In freight, the backlog was very stable about $155 million this quarter and $153 million a year ago. Transit was lower a year ago, about $159 million, this year about $147. This was expected to the completion of the R142 contract for New York. 
 One special note of interest, we sound a little tired because we have been on the road the last few days. We began a road show last week to offer a $100 million in senior notes due in 10 years. The proceeds would be used to repay bank debt and general corporate purposes. This is the start of the refinancing project that we have been discussing on prior phone calls. This would allow us to lock in favorable long-term rates and give us more flexibility for growth opportunities in the future. In the future, we probably will refinance our revolving credit, as well. 
 Go ahead, Bill, if you would like to summarize before the Q and A that would be great.

So a decade or so ago we could put 1,000 or so different biomarkers on a chip, today we're pushing up toward 7 million independent markers on a chip, so that is a pretty dramatic process.
  There's also a lot of flexibility in leveraging the platforms, so our costs are really driven by passing a wafer through the manufacturing facility. We can chop these wafers into different formats depending on the amount of information that a customer needs. So at the far left of your screen you see the 49 format which is the standard format for most of our research products.
  At the far right is actually the format we're using for a lot of diagnostic products. So if you look at the Roche P450 product, we actually get 400 independent chips from a wafer with a Dx product as opposed to 49 in the research setting. So obviously that provides a lot of flexibility and an ability to meet specific applications that a customer requires based on information needs.
  Moving into the commercial markets, there are several that are really the bulk of our efforts today. So gene expression is what we're best known for; that is really looking at what genes are turned on or off in response to any kind of stimuli. A classic experiment using these products would be to take a healthy sample of tissue versus a cancerous one and look at what genes are turned on or off and obviously use that to try to identify targets for drug development. And certainly when you look at the libraries of targets that pharmaceutical companies are working on today, the vast majority of those have been generated using our technology.
  The next major area for us is in genotyping; this is really looking at human genetic variation. This has been an area of very high growth for the Company. We actually moved into this market in 2003 and have seen very significant growth over the last few years. This really is the foundation for what people talk about as personalized medicine and we're certainly seeing a lot more in the way of interest, not just from pharma companies but also from the payers and regulatory bodies as well. There are a lot more in the way of these targeted  particularly in the field of oncology, a lot more in the way of targeted therapies. And really the key is to try to develop tests and technologies to identify who's going to benefit from those.
  Molecular diagnostics is an area we've moved into in the last few years that uses both gene expression and genotyping technologies depending on the tests. And lastly in the field of emerging markets, so this would include things like plant and animal genomics, biological pathogen surveillance and things of that nature.
  So starting off with gene expression, we are certainly the gold standard in that marketplace. There are more than 10,000 peer reviewed scientific publication. Certainly we have the leading marketshare there as well. Recently the FDA conducted a platform comparison for gene expression technologies; they looked at five commercially available platforms and Affymetrix was found to be the best performing platform of anyone available. So certainly that was a great endorsement, one we're very excited to have.
  We've got far away the largest installed base as far as  and the broadest productline in the marketplace. And that includes things like not just looking at human expression products and mouse and rat which tend to be the bulk of the marketplace, but also hundreds of different model organisms that customers like to study.
  We're focused on expanding the market. This is really, again, getting back to innovating with new technology. So we are the only company now that provides technologies for looking at both splice variation and looking at the non-coating regions on a whole genome scale. So probably many of you will recall with the completion of the human genome project there was kind of a profound disappointment that humans had only 20,000 genes, which is very similar to some insects and plants.
  What people didn't appreciate is that humans have a unique ability to splice those into various gene products. So this idea of splice variation, to able to generate hundreds of thousands of proteins with only 20,000 genes is unique to human beings and that's a technology that Affymetrix is the only company providing that.
  Automation is certainly an important area for us now. We've seen, particularly in the field of clinical studies and genotyping studies, that sample volumes have gone up very dramatically. So the ability to provide customers with automated solutions is certainly increasingly important and that's a high focus for us. We've introduced some new chemistries and reagents to try to expand the markets; some of these include technologies for looking at formalin-fixed paraffin embedded samples, so FFPE.
  If you think about the millions of biopsy samples that are stored out there, these tend to have degraded DNA and traditional technologies and chemistries have not really been amenable to working with those. So we have partnered with other companies to develop new assay technologies to study those samples.
  We've also introduced what we call gene level arrays where it's a smaller format of chip, lower-cost, and this is really to try to convert those who are still making their own arrays, particularly in the academic setting. There are academic centers that like to spot down their own arrays still, so we've introduced a new line of products to try to convert those customers over to commercially available technologies.
  Lastly in the field of gene expression we think that the clinical setting is going to be an important growth driver for us. In the first quarter this year we had our CLIA Laboratory brought online so we now have the ability to run expression and genotyping products in a clean environment, homebrewed type testing and provide that information on to diagnostic partners.
  And certainly clinical trial use is another area we're focused on. So in our CLIA Lab we're able to run large sample volumes for pharmaceutical clinical trials. These studies tend to be fairly lumpy and a lot of the pharmaceutical companies have been looking to outsource that given that there are kind of ebbs and flows in the work load they found it more efficient in many cases to outsource that and certainly that's an area we're trying to capitalize on.
  Changing gears to the genotyping market or DNA analysis. This is a market that we created and really introduced the first whole genome products back in 2003. This past June we launched the fifth iteration of this technology for us, the SNP 6.0, which is now far and away the most comprehensive product on the market for doing such studies. You can see the chart on the right gives you an overview of the content of commercially available products from Affymetrix and our primary competitor in the marketplace. In gray you have SNPs; in the blue are copy number variations. And this is another I think good example of how this complexity has gone up pretty dramatically.
  If you went back 18 months or so ago, people were focused exclusively on SNPs. There's been a study published in the last 12 months or so now that has found that variations in copy number can have as much of an impact on personal genetics as SNP can as well. And copy numbers are really looking at when you get obviously copy of a genome from your mother and from your father in certain circumstances you can get two copies from one parent, two copies from another or have a copy deleted and these can have actual  pretty profound clinical implications.
  So this is a growing area of focus and you can see that from the level of content out there we've got the better part of 1 million markers to study copy number variation and that compares to about 20,000 or so on the highest content competitive product.
  As far as performance and accuracy, the 6.0 has been very well received by customers. The column at the far left is samples that were run at Affymetrix, the two to the right were run by collaborators and customers of ours and you can see very consistent results and call rates in excess of 99%. So this is certainly best in class performance regardless of the metric you want to look at.
  We're also seeing a fundamental change in how these studies are done. So historically customers would run a fairly large number of samples at the whole genome level and then would very quickly try to pick the SNPs they thought were most important and they would run a much larger number of samples using a smaller number of markers. And what we have found is that many customers have now found in studies that you missed things that are statistically significant when you do it that way.
  So we've seen a fairly fundamental shift now where many customers are shifting to looking at the whole genome through not only the first phase of their studies, but also through the replication phase. And this is very important because if you went back even a year or two ago the economics of these whole genome products would not have allowed that. But with the launch of the 6.0 the economics are compelling enough that we're now seeing customers use this through both the Phase I and Phase II of these studies.
  And in effect there's been recent recommendations by both the National Cancer Institute and the NHGRI that these studies should be conducted at the whole genome level to get the best statistical power, streamline the workflow and make sure that there aren't markers that are missed and certainly this is an area that we'll be a beneficiary of.
  Diagnostics is also area that has been a part of our business model for the last three or four years now. It's a slightly different business model; we call this Powered by Affymetrix. It's one in which our partners, our commercial partners develop the biological content, we actually manufacture the product for them but our partners are the commercial channel, our partners complete the regulatory filings and things that are done on the commercial side of the business.
  So this is the first or array-based in vitro diagnostic platform that has received FDA approval. We've now got 11 partners to date; there are more than 20 tests in development, the vast majority of those for studying cancer. They span a wide variety of cancers and really everything from screening and diagnosis to classifying, prognosis and even monitoring of patients.
  So this is an area that if you look at third party market surveys, most of those pegged this market at about $2.5 billion to $3 billion right now annually and growing at 25 to 30%. So this is an area certainly we're excited about from the standpoint of future growth opportunities.
  There's been a lot of buzz in the press recently about consumer genetic applications. This is an area that we have moved into and already formed some partnerships and certainly as healthcare costs continue to spiral and that what is now more than 15% of our GDP annually is predicted to go to more than 20% in the next four or five years, so something absolutely needs to be done to make sure we're being more efficient with the use of our healthcare dollars.
  So this kind of one size fits all approach, which has been the historical model, really doesn't work anymore, particularly when you get into therapies that can cost $50,000 to $100,000, you want to make sure you're not giving those to patients that don't get any benefit from it. So we think this is going to really be the cornerstone of personalized medicine going forward.
  Some of the advantages of doing array-based consumer genetics is it's very comprehensive and scalable. Again, the point we're working at today is millions of biomarkers. If you went back two or three years ago these markers were about $1.00 a piece to assay. Customers can now get thousands of markers per dollar using our technology. So it's been a pretty dramatic shift in what you're able to do with the economics today.
  So we are partnering to serve this market. Our first partner is a company called Navigenics. You may have seen some coverage in the press. They received certainly a great deal of attention with the launch of their service and we certainly expect to have additional partners going forward.
  From the standpoint of top priorities this year, certainly expanding and strengthening the management team has been a key priority. Many of you will know we've got a lot of new members of the senior team and certainly have seen a better focus in results as we've proceeded this year as far as exceeding revenue and profit goals. We've delivered a large number of new products into the marketplace and we certainly have strength in our overall global manufacturing capabilities.
  We recently completed a convertible note offering, $275 million, initial conversion price of $30.12 which represented a 39% premium over the closing price of November 13th, and we intend to use the proceeds of this for our working capital and other general corporate purposes and certainly that will include M&A activity as well. We have seen a tremendous amount of consolidation in our space over the last year or two and we do expect to see that continue.
  Looking at year-over-year financial metrics, so this is Q3 '07, Q3 '06, you can see total revenue was up 12%, operating expenses were down 18% and a significant improvement in both net income and EPS as well. You see in the lower left-hand corner that our balance sheet is significantly stronger. We had about $256 million prior to completing our convertible note offering. We now have about $525 million on the balance sheet which puts us in a very good position to be opportunistic with respect to inorganic growth opportunities.
  Year-to-date metrics, again good consistent performance here as far as revenue, revenue up, operating expenses being down and significant improvements in EPS and net income. As far as the mix of the business, North America represents about half the business today, Europe is about a third, Japan about 12% and the balance is the rest of the world.
  And as I said earlier, if you look to the right of this chart, this really is a consumables driven business model, very much a razor/razor blade type model. About two-thirds of our revenue comes from these single use chemistries and reagents, about 15% from instrumentation and about 19% from product related which includes things like software, service contracts and genetic services that we provide.
  So in summary, we've made great progress this year in really driving growth in the business and momentum. We've tightened up our R&D focus and our focus on some high impact programs to open up new commercial opportunities. And we've been creating excellent operating leverage to generate improved profit and cash flow. So with that I'd like to open up the floor for questions.

 As we've mentioned previously, we have significant exposure in Chicago, which is our largest group market, and 2019 has been a very weak year. Our group room revenues in the market are down 15% for the first half, and overall RevPAR in the market for luxury and upper upscale hotels is down 3.6% through the second quarter, and the central business district is down 5.5% for the same period.  Looking across the U.S., overall group production for the quarter was weaker than we had expected primarily coming from association and SMERF business having lower participation rates.
 Turning to corporate group demand. We've actually seen corporate group business continue to hold up quite well, and cancellations have been minimal. While our total group production in the second quarter is down in the high single digits, our corporate group production is up approximately 2%. We expect group business in the second half, most of which is on the books at this point, to be approximately flat versus last year and then strengthen into 2020.
 While group rooms revenue was down for the quarter, we've seen impressive demand on the transient side of the business where our hotel teams have done a remarkable job driving significant transient business to fill gaps created by softer group business. This was especially true in our group based convention hotels in markets like Chicago, Orlando and San Antonio. Transient room revenue was up about 4% in the U.S. and over 5.5% in constant currency across the broader Americas region because of certain particularly strong markets outside of the U.S. Both business and leisure transient demand improved, and we gained significant market share in transient business and our full-service hotels in the U.S. during the quarter.

 Our industry-leading net rooms growth continues to drive levels of fee growth well in excess of RevPAR growth even as we face some headwinds and tough comparisons to last year on incentive fees in certain international markets. Our mix of earnings from our managed and franchised business is at 54% of adjusted EBITDA before corporate and other, up from 51% in the second quarter of 2018.

Total U.S. RevPAR declined 0.3% driven by select-service hotels. Net rooms growth for the segment was approximately 11%, including the Two Roads hotels. Excluding Two Roads, net rooms growth for the segment was approximately 4%. Base, incentive and franchise fee growth of approximately 10% drove adjusted EBITDA growth of about 6% for the quarter on a constant currency basis. Full-service group rooms revenue in the U.S. decreased approximately 3% driven by a decrease in group room nights partially offset by a rate increase of approximately 1%.

 While group business was down for the quarter, U.S. full-service transient demand filled the gap, as Mark mentioned earlier, with solid room revenue growth driven entirely by an increase in room nights driving record occupancy levels.
 Moving on to our Asia Pacific segment, which accounted for approximately 15% of our management and franchising adjusted EBITDA in Q2. I'd to begin by introducing the management team members with us on the call starting with Pat Malloy, Company's Chairman of the Board, Robert Turnham, our President and Chief Operating Officer, David Looney, Executive Vice President and Chief Executive Officer and Mark Ferchau, our Executive Vice President, Engineering and Operations. As is our practice, we'd like to make everyone aware that comments we may make and answers we may give during this teleconference may be considered forward-looking statements which involve risks and uncertainties and we have detailed those risks for you in our SEC filings.
  2009 was both a transitional and transformational year for Goodrich Petroleum. A year ago on this earnings call, I said we were in the process of a significant transition that would see us dramatically reduce the number of vertical Cotton Valley wells and increase the number of horizontal wells with particular emphasis on the Haynesville Shale play. Not only did we make the transition, we accelerated it during the second half of 2009 and currently expect 100% of our 2010 drilling budget will be associated with horizontal wells with approximately $200 million or 78% earmarked for the Haynesville Shale.
  At the end of 2009, we conducted a careful and deliberate evaluation of our horizontal drilling results. The new SEC rules governing improved reporting. In particular, the five year rule relating to proved undeveloped reserves as well as year-end 2009 SEC natural gas pricing and determined the proved undeveloped reserves associated with future vertical well drilling. Primarily in the Cotton Valley, no longer fit with our amended business strategy.
  Consequently, a strategic decision was made to remove all undeveloped reserves associated with vertical well drilling from our proved undeveloped reserves, our impairment test calculation and our project inventory. While we believe some, or perhaps all, of these reserves will ultimately come back into our estimates through continued horizontal development and delineation drilling in particular for the Cotton Valley Taylor Sand in East Texas. We firmly believe this is the proper approach going forward for our Company, our shareholders and perspective investors. As our reserves will now be significantly higher quality and more closely aligned with our current business strategy and capital plans.
  As we reported in our press release, excuse me, press release last week regarding our year-end proved reserves, the removal of all vertical proved undeveloped reserves from the year-end reserve report resulted in negative revisions of approximately 260 BCFE. However, we successfully achieved in 2009 with our horizontal drilling program more than offset the negative revisions and resulted in new reserve additions of 314 BCFE. All of which were associated with the Haynesville Shale and Cotton Valley Taylor Sand. These strong reserve additions allowed us to grow SEC proved reserves by 4.5% to 420 BCFE despite the new SEC mandated natural gas price of $3.87 for MMBTU. Using the old SEC year-end pricing method or $5.79 per MMBTU our proved reserves would have grown by 14% to approximately 460 BCFE.
  At our current rate of development, the proved undeveloped capital requirement as booked at year-end 2009 equates to approximately 35% of our annual capital expenditure budget. Thus, leaving sufficient capital to be allocated to the development of our nonproven reserves and new business ventures over the next five years. We believe the reserve growth and, in particular, the reserve additions are an excellent indicator of the enhanced and improved quality of our reserves and the tremendous proved reserve growth potential yet to come from our inventory and future development plans.
  However, the change in business strategy and the associated removal of all future vertical well reserves did result in a one time non-cash impairment charge in the fourth quarter of approximately $185 million. By this impairment charge have a significant negative impact on the fourth quarter and year-end financial results on a go forward basis, it will result in materially lower DD&A rate per MCFE and will significantly improve our reported financial results in the coming quarters. Haynesville Shale has proven to be a fantastic natural gas play and a huge catalyst for Goodrich Petroleum.
  In 2008, we initiated our Haynesville Shale program by drilling 12 strategically located vertical wells across our acreage and subsequently drilled 38 gross horizontal wells through the end of 2009. In January of last year, gross Haynesville Shale production from horizontal wells in which we owned working interest was effectively zero. Yet during the fourth quarter of 2009, gross production average from the Haynesville averaged 118 million cubic feet a day and our net Haynesville production averaged 36 million cubic feet per day or in excess of 40% of our total net production volumes. Just one example of the prolific nature of the Haynesville Shale is our initial operating Haynesville Shale horizontal well in the Bethany-Longstreet field that plants 26H, which came online on October 21st of last year and has already produced in excess of one BCF of natural gas and equivalents.
  As we look forward, we have increased both the absolute amount of our capital expenditures planned for 2010 and the percentage allocated to the Haynesville Shale. We are confident this accelerated and focused plan will lead to expanded growth and production and for reserves in 2010. Addition to the Haynesville Shale, our efforts to prove up and define the economics of drilling horizontally for the Cotton Valley Taylor Sand in East Texas during 2009 were very successful.
  At year-end, we were able to add approximately 118 BCFE of proved reserves associated with horizontal Cotton Valley Taylor Sand activity at an average gross estimated EUR in excess of five BCF per well. As the geographic area on which we have currently drilled and booked reserves for the Taylor Sand horizontally in East Texas only represents about 25% of our existing East Texas acreage. And which we currently believe will be perspective for the Cotton Valley Taylor Sand, we will continue to pursue a strategy of stepping out and proving up additional acreage. We believe this plan will lead to continued Cotton Valley Taylor Sand reserve growth and additional opportunities in 2010.
  2009 was another year of strong double-digit production volume growth. With production increasing 23% over 2008. Strong production volume growth coupled with our excellent 2009 hedge position and a material improvement in cash operating expenses led to a record $140 million of discretionary cash flow. While a portion of our 2010 budget will be spent further delineating and developing the Cotton Valley Taylor Sand and testing a couple of exciting new areas for the Haynesville Shale in East Texas. Including our 22,000 net acre position in the eastern portion of the Angelina River Trend. A majority of our capital will be spent further developing the Haynesville Shale in our core area and we will have already enjoyed very good success.

With approximately $125 million in cash and short term investments and a current borrowing base under our senior credit facility of $175 million. Which is currently undrawn. We enter 2010 with approximately $300 million of liquidity. In fact, we believe we can fully fund our planned $255 million capital expenditure program with a combination of cash flow from operations and cash on hand and enter 2011 with no material amounts outstanding under our senior credit facility. With that I'd like to turn it over to Rob Turnham.

  In the fourth quarter, we saw a continuation of strong production volume growth, declining per unit operating costs and independent validation of the quality of our Haynesville Shale and Cotton Valley Taylor Sand reserves and inventoried through year-end reserve analysis with very attractive EUR's. Production grew by 4.5% sequentially to an average of 86.1 million per day. Which came in above guidance and 24% year over year which was at the high end of guidance. As Gil said earlier, Haynesville Shale volumes averaged 118 million cubic feet per day. Gross or 36 million per day net for the quarter or 42% of the total. Which was a 40% increase from the previous quarter.
  The midpoint of first quarter 2010, guidance of 89.5 million per day would yield similar sequential growth while we maintain full year-over-year volume growth guidance of 15% to 25%. We grew volumes in the quarter in spite of reduced capital expenditures of 44 million. Down from an average of 65 million in the first three quarters of 2009. We conducted drilling operations on 14 gross five net wells during the quarter all of which were Haynesworth hail wells. We added nine gross 4.5 net wells production during the quarter.
  For the year, CapEx was $237 million with $215 million of that allocated to drilling on completion and the remainder split over leasehold acquisition, infrastructure and other miscellaneous items. Gil said earlier year-end reserves increased by 4.5% to 421 BCFE. Even with the elimination of 259.6 BCFE of reserves due to price and the removal of all vertical proved and developed reserves. Reserves were 99% natural gas, 39% developed, 47% attributed to reserve additions in the Haynesville Shale and an average EUR of approximately 6.5 BCF. In addition to the Haynesville Shale reserve additions, we had significant adds from Cotton Valley Taylor horizontal reserves of an excess of five BCF per well even though we only booked 25% of the prospective acreage.
  In total, we had proved reserve additions of 315  314 BCFE from $215 million of drilling and completion CapEx. Yielding a $0.68 per MCF finding cost. Proved developed reserve additions were 67 BCE before price revisions for a developed finding cost of $3.21. We also limited our PUD bookings such that our capital allocations and tort undeveloped reserves over the next five years is 35% of our current year budget. As Gil said, the quality of our reserves on the books now is the best we have ever had. An example of that is to look on the our current proven developed reserves versus the legacy vertical proved undeveloped reserves we took off the books.
  The estimated finding and development costs of the current proved and developed reserves is more than 50% lower than the vertical proved undeveloped reserves we took off of the books. Which will continue to provide very attractive economic and lower our per unit operating cost structure going forward. Focusing somewhat on our core areas at Bethany Long Street at the Caddo and DeSoto parishes of Louisiana, where we own Haynesville rights of 13,500 net acres. We had 17 gross, six net wells producing in the field at year-end. At a fourth quarter average of 27 million per day net or 31% of company production. We had four gross, one net well waiting on completion in the field at year-end. We have completed our third operated well in the field, the Fallon 18H number one, where we own a 59% working interest at 21.2 million cubic feet per day with 6,800 pounds of pressure on a 24 64-inch choke.
  This is our best completion rate to date and we feel that as a result of our continuing efforts to optimize our completion technique. The well had 12 frac stages with the 4,600-foot lateral. In the field, we're currently running three nonoperated rigs and one operated rig. Moving to Greenwood-Waskom Metcalf, in centrally Caddo Parish, where we own approximately 3,500 net acres. We have completed our second operated well in the field, the Wills 14H number one, where we own an 81% work interesting. The well came online at a 24 hour peak rate of 12 million cubic feet per day on a 22 64-inch choke with 5,800 pounds of pressure.
  We are currently completing two additional wells in the field, the Wayne Bryant 3H number one and the Wayne Bryant 4-H 1 number one. With an average working interest of 70% for the two wells. Both wells are set to come online in the second quarter of this year. In East Texas, at Beckville Minden where we are drilling our Billy Harris 2H and McCray 5H wells currently. Which are two Haynesville Shale laterals estimated to come online in the second quarter of this year. Anticipate completing these wells in an increased number of frac stages. Similar to our Billy Harris number 1H that tested at 12.2 million cubic feet per day from a 20 stage frac. That is currently producing consistent with our tight curve and expectations.
  Currently, we have plans to drill two additional Haynesville Shale wells and two to four Cotton Valley Taylor Sand horizontals in the area during 2010. At South Henderson, where we own 87,000 net acres, we are set to commence drilling operations on our first Cotton Valley Sand horizontal well, The Prone 6H, where we will own 100% working interest within 60 days. With a second well our correct 2H to follow. We currently do not have any horizontal flat belly reserves booked for this field but are optimistic based on offset well results. At Angelina River, where we own 22,000 net acres respective for the Haynesville. We currently anticipating setting our first Haynesville well there in the second quarter and with success, plan on drilling a second well in the block later in the year. And with continued success in the area, we would accelerate development of the field in 2011. With that I would like to turn it over to David Looney to walk you through the financials.

David Looney,  Goodrich Petroleum - Executive Vice President and Chief Executive Officer: Thank you, Rob. As a number of the primary financial items have already covered, I'll try to hit the highlights during my discussion and as always, I'll be happy to answer any questions during the q and a period. Reported revenues for the fourth quarter of $32.2 million were based on average prices of $3.92 per MCF for gas and $72.59 per barrel of oil. On gas, our average price was approximately $0.44 below the average any up price during the quarter. Which is within our historical target range of $0.50. As I know many analysts try to fine tune their projections of our price realizations, we should point out that we typically sell about half of our monthly gas at first of the month prices and the other half at daily prices.
  However, those decisions are made by management on a monthly basis and are always subject to change. Additionally, I'll emphasize here that these prices do not include the impact of $21.5 million in realized gains on our commodity derivative portfolio during the quarter. None of our derivatives are designated as hedges for accounting purposes. For the full year we averaged $3.72 per thousand cubic foot equivalent versus $8.91 in the prior year.
  Once again, for the full year we had a realized gain on our hedging portfolio of over $96.5 million. Which again does not show up in our revenue line. Looking at cash flow, our EBITDAX for the fourth quarter was approximately $39.1 million, up by 45% from the fourth quarter of last year. It was driven primarily by a combination of the 22% production increase and significantly reduced operating expenses versus last year's quarter which I'll discuss more in a moment.
  Discretionary cash flow, which is defined as net cash from operations before changes in working capital was $48.9 million for the quarter that actually included approximately $15.3 million in tax benefits. Which were essentially the unwinding of similar tax payments we had made last year after our property sale in the third quarter of 2008. Even without this benefit, discretionary tax flow for the quarter was up significantly over last year's number.
  For the full year, EBITDAX of $141.8 million was only slightly reduced from last year's record level. While DCF actually did set a new record for us at $140 million. Again $15.3 million of which was due the tax refund. Rob mentioned our capital expenditures booked during the fourth quarter totaled $44 million with $33.3 million spent on drilling and completion and $10.7 million on acreage and other. This level of fourth quarter CapEx resulted in our total CapEx for the year coming in at $237.6 million in line with the guidance we've been providing. The full year we spent approximately $215 million on drilling and completion costs with the other $22.5 million going towards a combination of leaseholds, infrastructure and other.
  Focusing on the expense side of the statement, we had one of our best quarters in recent history. With LOE being down 38% from last year's fourth quarter, to a current unit level of $0.86 per MCFE. Additionally, every other category of cash operating expenses was down meaningfully from last year. With the combination of production taxes, transportation expense, expiration expense and G&A being down a combined $0.49 per MCFE or 25% from the prior year level.
  Clearly our expense control efforts are beginning to reap benefits. Much of this improvement is due to the combined effects of our saltwater disposal systems, better compression pricing and finally the increasing importance of our Haynesville Shale production. Which carries a lower LOE per unit cost than our traditional Cotton Valley production. We expect to see LOE costs continuing to trend downward as we maintain our focus on reducing these unit costs and if we have a greater percentage of the production coming from the Haynesville.
  As Gil mentioned, our decision to remove  move from a predominantly vertical based drilling company to an exclusively horizontally focused one led to a non-cash impairment charge of $185 million in this year's fourth quarter. When combined with a smaller $23.5 million charge taken earlier in the year and an inordinately high DD&A rate for the latter part of 2009, this positions us to pose a much lower DD&A rate as we move forward.
  Currently providing guidance at $3.50 to $3.90 per MCFE for the first half of 2010. And as has been our practice the last few years, we will review our DD&A rate when we finish our midyear reserve report which usually occurs before the end of the third quarter. Turning to other expenses, our G&A expense of $7.4 million for the fourth quarter or $0.93 per MCFE versus $6.7 million our $1.03 per MCFE in the fourth quarter of 2008. Virtually all the increase from the prior year period was due to higher non-cash charges which represented approximately 27% of the total G&A costs during the quarter. Interest expense for the quarter at $9 million was up significantly over last year's $5.4 million due to the issuance of our 5% convertible note at the end of September, 2009 and the adoption of the rule which was formerly known as APB14-1.
  I'll remind everyone again that our accounting for interest expense under this rule requires us to book significant amounts of non-cash interest each quarter. In fact, $4.6 million of non-cash interest was booked in the fourth quarter of this year versus $2.1 million in the prior year period. For the full year approximately $12.2 million of 47% of our total interest expense of $26.1 million was non-cash.
  We expect this level of approximately $9 million in total interest expense per quarter to continue for the next several quarters. Our income tax provision was once again impacted by an increase in our valuational balance. Due largely to the size of the impairment, we reverted to a three year cumulative loss position. Which essentially requires us to remove the net deferred tax assets from our books. As such, we booked an incremental $54.3 million in valuation allowance in the fourth quarter. Which both reduced our net deferred tax asset position to zero and reduced our income tax benefit by a similar amount. As such, when you work through the mechanics, our tax provision reflected a total net benefit of approximately $67.3 million or approximately 21% of the pre-tax loss. Going forward, it is highly likely that in the near future any pre-tax loss will be benefited at a 0% tax rate on the income statement and any pre-tax gains will also be taxed at a 0% rate as well.
  Finally, due largely to the non-cash impairment expense and other items I just mentioned, we reported a net loss applicable to common stock of $257 million for the year or $7.17 per share. As we know that many of you follow the accepted practice of many industry analysts and adjust for non-cash items such as the impairment expense and mark-to-market gains or losses on derivatives, we'll provide our calculation of ongoing earnings as a loss of $0.45 per share for the quarter and a loss of $1.27 per share for the full year.
  Turning now to the balance sheet, as Gil mentioned earlier, we exited the year with $125 million in cash and a completely non-cash revolver. Giving us right at $300 million in available liquidity as we started 2010. Given our current production forecasts, pricing levels and hedge position, we're confident that this strong liquidity position will allow us to comfortably execute our drilling plans for the rest of this year without needing to borrow any significant amounts under our bank facility. As such, we should be able to once again deliver solid production volume growth well into the future without needing to sacrifice our balance sheet to get there. With that, I'll now turn it back to Gil for some closing comments.

G. Shivakumar,  The Great Eastern Shipping Company Limited - CFO & Executive Director: Hi, good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the results conference call for Q2 FY '18, '19. I trust you would have been through our results and press release.
 The main item of interest is that has happened in the last quarter, the results have been swung by the movement in exchange rate during the quarter. While in Q1, the rupee depreciated by about INR 3.30, this quarter had seen a INR 4 depreciation in the rupee versus the dollar. The results for the first half therefore include noncash charges of about INR 520 crores relating to exchange rates.
 The depreciation of the rupee is of course beneficial for our NAV since we have more dollar assets than dollar liabilities, and this reflects in our net asset value. However, there's been a drop of about 4% in ship values, mainly in product tankers but also in bike areas. This has resulted in a drop in our standalone net asset value by about INR 8 to INR 352 per share.
 Offshore asset values have remained more or less static, and some deals have been done for good quality, modern assets.
 As a result of valuation that's shown a narrower range for the rigs, and therefore our NAV range has narrowed from 360 to 430 to about 397 to 420.
 Coming to how the markets  the shipping markets have performed. Both crude and product markets have performed very badly in the period from April to September, and that's reflected in our TCYs. This has basically been driven by poor refinery runs, which have been low on the back of lower demand growth for end products, which will resulted, obviously, in lower refining margins.
 U.S. crude exports were the lone positive factor, increasing by about 1 million barrels per day. But this was more than compensated by a drop in [MEG] exports. Overall crude tanker demand was flat on a year-on-year basis, this I'm talking about the first 9 months again versus fleet growth on average of over 4%. This is again first 9 months of this year versus first 9 months of previous year, that's 2018 versus 2017.
 However, this  in this 9-month period, which is between Jan and September, there's been a very marginal fleet growth in crude tankers, if at all, so it's 0 to very marginal. And this is helping to absorb the excess supply overhang. Therefore rates had been very poor during  through the summer.
 However, we are glad to report that in October, rates have picked up very significantly for crude tankers. The spot Suezmax is currently at over $30,000 per day, and on some routes, about $40,000 per day. The VLCCs  of course, we don't have VLCCs. VLCCs are trading about $50,000 per day in the spot market currently. And Aframax is probably in the $25,000 per day range.
 Coming to the product tanker market. Product demand was quite poor and the main increase in demand, so there was an increase in say gas oil demand, but the main increase in demand came really from the consuming areas, which means that there is no transportation of the product really. So consuming regions like China, U.S.A. and India saw an increase in gas, oil and diesel demand, but this did not translate into trade. And as a result, rates have been very poor and they continue to be very poor. There is yet no sign of a turnaround in the market. The fleet growth in this  in these assets has been about 2.5% in this 9-month period.
 U.S. LPG exports have started picking up again, and this may be a contributing factor to the market recovering somewhat in the last few months. We saw Q2 of this calendar year average VLGC spot rates going down to below $10,000 a day. And now they are more in the region of $20,000 per day. Fleet growth so far this year in the 9 months has been 0.
 The dry bulk trade into China has grown by about 13 million to 15 million metric tons during the 9-month period. And again, this is the 9 months over the similar 9 month  same 9-month period in the previous year.
 There is a negative growth in iron ore imports into China, which is in the region of 10 million tonnes. But this is more than offset by increase in coal and bauxite imports, which are about 25-plus million tonnes. The fleet grew by about 2.5% in the 9-month period.
 The order book stands at about 13% for crude tankers and at about 9% to 10% for dry bulk and product tankers.
 The offshore market continues to be challenged. Though it appears that at least the fall in rates has stopped, recent pricing points in the market indicate that there is an improvement of at least 20% to 30% from very low levels. And hopefully the strength in oil prices will, at some point in time, translate to increased demand, and therefore some improvement in the rates. We currently have only 1 asset without a contract, that's an 80-tonne Anchor Handling Tug Supply Vessel. And this is the same as it was in August when we had our last call.
 One of the issues facing the industry in the next 15 months is the new IMO sulfur emission norm, in order to deal with this, we have decided to fix the exhaust gas cleaning system, which is colloquially called a scrubber on 7 of our ships. These are our largest ships with the highest consumption and longest voyage time. And we expect that these  all these installations will be completed in calendar 2019, so we are ready for the new emission norms when they come in on 1st Jan 2020.
 We continue to have a large spot exposure. And as I mentioned over  in the calls over the last few quarters, we have consciously tried not to fix out much of our capacity in the low markets because we have been expecting a turnaround, and the time charter rates were very poor and were not adequately compensating us. Now we can start to see the benefits of it in  a little bit in the gas area market, where the rates have recovered a little bit, though we do have some time charter cover there. But much more in the crude tanker market, where suddenly there's been a spike in the rates, and having a large part of our 12 crude tanker spot is enabling us to take advantage of the increased freight rates.
 So with that, I'll conclude my remarks, and we are happy to discuss these results and we welcome any questions from you.

G. Shivakumar,  The Great Eastern Shipping Company Limited - CFO & Executive Director: Yes, okay. There is no problem, I agree with you. There is no problem commercially. What we have done is that we have dollar assets and dollar income streams. And therefore we match that off with dollar liabilities. Now whether we take dollar loans directly or we take rupee loans and swap them into dollars, we have now created a dollar liability either naturally or synthetically. The accounting treatment specified for this is that any revaluation of the loan, if the loan goes up in value because of changes in exchange rates. So let's say we borrow $100 million, a straight dollar loan. And we borrowed it when the exchange rate was INR 65 to the dollar, and it's now at INR 72.5 to the dollar, that INR 7.5 difference in the loan has to be reflected somewhere. So which works out, on a $100 million loan works out to INR 72.5 crores  sorry, INR 75 crores. And now that INR 75 crores has to be reflected in the P&L as a loss valuation of foreign exchange. This is the accounting. This year we had the option to capitalize it to the cost of the asset. Under the new [NDS], it is not permitted. Now coming to derivatives. We also  so that was  and you just borrow dollars directly. Sometimes we borrow rupees because it's cheaper to do that, and we also get longer tenure loans. We go into the rupee bond market in India and borrow rupees. But we also swap them into dollars because we don't want to keep a mismatch in our currency of our assets and our liabilities. So when that happens, [negative] comes in as a derivative mark-to-market loss. It's essentially the same thing, but it's a mark-to-market on the derivative because what we have done is effectively, we have sold those dollars forward at INR 65, in the same example that I was giving you. So the same INR 7.5 has been recognized on those as well, and it comes in as a derivative loss, mark-to-market on the derivatives. There is no escape from this because all these have to be revalued in rupees when we are reporting. In commercial terms, there is no issue, since we have used these dollar loans to buy dollar assets, and those dollar assets have also got revalued. So we used those $100 million to buy $100 million worth of dollar assets. And those also have gone up in value in rupee terms from INR 65, so INR 650 crores to INR 750 crores because of the same revaluation. Because it's still denominated in dollars. However, in our books, they remain at the original cost. We don't revalue our assets. And therefore you only get one side of the impact. The positive side of the impact you get in the net asset value, because we  that is really showing the assets at the market value in rupee terms. So our P&L part, I think when we have a weakening of the rupee, the P&L will take a hit like this.

The  basically, the benefit from scrubbers is that you  okay, let's go back to what this new regulation is. The new regulation restricts the amount of sulfur emissions from the exhaust gas of the ship to below 0.5%. Now the standard fuel that shipping uses is  goes up to 3.5% sulfur. The  so the new regulation which kicks in from 1st Jan say that it has to be not more than 0.5%. Now you have a couple of choices here. You can use 0.5% fuel, or you can continue to use 3.5% fuel but install a scrubber so that your emissions are less than 0.5%. The issue is that the high sulfur fuel oil is much cheaper than the low sulfur fuel. And currently that spread is being quoted at about $320 per tonne for 2020 and 2021. Now that's a traded market. So the difference in price between Marine gas oil, low sulfur Marine gas oil, and high sulfur fuel oil in 2020 is being quoted around $320 per tonne. Now you just take the consumption of the ship and take the benefit of $320 per tonne, that's the benefit you get from installing the scrubber because you get to use the cheaper fuel. And that's where you get your payback. So but however, the payback comes from the amount of sailing time you have, that's a factor, because you use  you have high consumption only when you sail. When you're standing, you don't have consumption, you have very marginal consumption of fuel. And typically the bigger ships sail for more time. Also the bigger ships have much more fuel consumption. So this is a function of how many tonnes you burn per day while sailing and how many days you sail, which both which lead to your total consumption for the year. This, therefore, works much better in bigger ships which sail for more days. And so we are fitting this onto our biggest ships, basically the large crude tankers, where we are fitting these scrubbers. The larger ships are Suezmax, Aframax-size vessel. So the payback comes from  so let's just put some numbers, right. These are not our numbers, but I'm just putting some numbers as an example. If you can get your scrubber in, and again there are some times when you can't use a scrubber, so if you're in a port, you may not be allowed to use an open loop scrubber. If you're in some territorial waters, you may not be able to use an open loop scrubber, so you will have to discount that somewhat. But let's say you have about $2.5 million of savings on account of the lower fuel cost, and your cost of fitting a scrubber is say, $4 million, then you've got a payback period of less than 2 years. So that's why it makes sense. Now this trade, which is at $320, may be actually $200 or it may be $500. So we don't know that number. But based on today's market expectation or where the forward market is, it seems to be at around $320. So that's where the economic rationale comes in. Okay? Now coming to what can happen to oil price. Now what can happen to oil price is completely dependent on how the refiners have prepared for IMO 2020.
