How about alarming?
 And that's in (INAUDIBLE) with the speedy infrastructure in going with this business mobility framework. It allows us to take these and put them in, in essence into the service layer of our wireless network. So now we can go to customers with a company like an IBM and say, "If you'd like to bring an application to market to mobile environment, we've already taken care of lot of concerns you have. We have it built into our network and give you probably 6 to 12 months speed the market in enabling the application."
 And then fourth component is the master is (ph) - is the master services agreement that designates Sprint as a key vendor to IBM and go into market with IBM to external customers. And enable to IBM to incorporate Sprint's mobile voice and data products and services and our national PCS wireless services in a customized, on-demand solutions for IBM's customers.
 The service agreement will offer both Sprint and IBM the opportunity to extend our offerings and will open the door to new business relationships as nearly two-thirds of outsourcing deals include some components of telecommunication elements.
 Sprint has differentiated itself from other telecom providers by offering a broad wireline or wireless portfolio that is easily integrated into enterprise applications. This approach will allow for it to reach customers reliant system integrators like IBM for the telecommunications decisions. This combination of Sprint's leading-edge networks and services and IBM's integration and I.T. expertise is expected to result in significant new revenue opportunities for both companies. You'll hear Howard Janzen expand on this as the key strategy in working with systems integration within the S.B.S. division.
 The most successful partnerships are linked tightly at the senior executive level. And in order to ensure we execute against these agreements effectively and achieve our mutual objectives, Sprint and IBM have established a governance structure whose primary purpose is to define the processes and procedures that'll be used to manage the contracts and relationships between our two companies.
 Executives in Sprint, including myself and senior executives from IBM have already had a number of meetings and that will continue to focus on the governance of these key agreements in our new partnership.
 Various committees will convene, representing the different areas of the agreement, will go through issues management, change management, escalation and reporting processes to make sure we manage the communication and the delivery of services and that we hit our expectations we jointly committed to.
 Led by an executive steering committee the various committees that comprise this new governance model will help us plan and implement this transition process. In the same old standards that will allow both IBM and Sprint working side by side to coordinate and resolve issues that would likely arise in the first year or two of this partnership.
 In my conclusion, Sprint's transformation to a customer-centered structure - I think you can see is well underway. Even with the possible distraction (ph) to reorganization we executed well in 2003 across all the business and established a framework for future success.
 We are aligned in a manner that will make it easier to do business with Sprint. We have the product portfolio to become the leader in wireless and wireline integration. We have strong strategic partnerships and alliances in place and continue to expand on these to deepen our relationships with our customers. And most importantly, we have a strong focus on our customers ensuring they are considered in every decision we make.
 As Gary mentioned, we have momentum coming into 2004 and our teams are excited by the improvements we have made.
 2004 is setting itself up to be a defining year for Sprint and the leadership team we have here today along with our teams across the country and throughout the world are not going to satisfied with anything but success. And success will be a key driver of more success.
 So now let me introduce Bob Dellinger, our Chief Financial Officer to take us through 2003 and expectations, going forward.
 Bob?

Bob Dellinger,  Sprint Corp. - CFO: Great, thank you Len. And good morning, everyone.
 I've got a couple of things this morning.
 First of all, 2003 success and challenges, our stock-price performance, 2004 financial priorities and our guidance for 2004.
 2003 was a strong year for Sprint and we begin 2004 on a solid foundation. On the success side, we introduce new products such as Ready Link, Video Mail, MobiTV and Complete Sense.
 We improved productivity as measured by revenue per employee. It was up 10 percent, which is exactly what we committed to in December of 2002 at our last investor meeting.
 We designed and launched our transformation effort, which Len just described which we believe will improve the trajectory of our business, create long-term shareholder value, improved customer service and value.
 We increased profitability and improved cash flow and exceeded our original 2003 guidance on most key measures. In fact phone (ph) exceeded the original guidance for adjusted operating income, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EPS and free cash flow.
 The PCS group exceeded the original guidance on adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow and adjusted EPS
 Additionally we made significant progress in reducing costs in areas such as access, compensation cost and bad debts.
 In December 2002, I laid out our financial priorities. One of them was increasing productivity as measured by revenues per employee - I've already talked of that.
 The second was delivering 90,000,000 of savings on the integration of I.T. network and billing. We completed both of those.
 And the third priority was to improve our financial strength and flexibility. And we made great progress on this front as well.
 Net debt is down more than $4,200,000,000. Our liquidity condition remains excellent. And at the end of 2003 we had $2,400,000,000 of cash on hand.
 Finally we made progress strengthening our relationship with PCS affiliates.
 For challenges in 2003, we had wireline data and I.P. revenue growth less than we anticipated.
 We saw continued yield pressure in many product lines.
 And we have opportunities to increase our wireless market share.
 Additionally we had significant write-offs. Many of these write-offs were due to product rationalization, which should yield benefits in future periods.
 Stock price performance. Over the one-year period ending January 31st, 2004, PCS and FON, both outperformed the Dow Jones Total U.S. Telecom Market Index and the S&P 500. And over the five-year period, FON and PCS outperformed the Dow Jones Telecom Index but under performed the S&P 500 index.
 Our financial priorities for 2004, our first, continue to improve Sprint's financial strength and flexibility. That means continuing our progress in de-leveraging the balance sheet by meeting or exceeding our net debt reduction target, maintaining strong cash on hand and liquidity positions.
 Second priority is to generate profitable growth via key partnerships, strategic products and select investments. You'll hear more about those during the course of the day.
 And the third is to reduce operating costs and continue improving productivity.
 In a few pages, I'll share with you some details around the plan that Len outlined to take our costs down by an annual $1,000,000,000 as we exit 2006. We will have a continued focus on improving productivity during 2004. Along with cost reduction and improved productivity, we're focused on improving margins to continue delivery of innovative products in the consumer and business segments.
 We have a well-defined strategy, a clear plan and a strong focus on execution to achieve these financial priorities.
 Like to (ph) stand upon our first priority, which was improving financial strength and flexibility. In 2003 we made excellent progress de-leveraging the balance sheet and improving our liquidity position.
 With our strong free cash flow performance in 2002, which was $1,100,000,000 in excess of our original guidance we have established a new net debt reduction target of $13,000,000,000 which is a $1,000,000,000 improvement from our old target of $14,000,000,000. This represents an $8,000,000,000 reduction in net debt, up from our $7,000,000,00 target, which exits it (ph) previously.
 Year-to-date, our gross debt has been reduced by more than 2,900,000,000 from payment in cash of scheduled maturity as well as some early redemptions.
 Net debt, as I said before was down more than $4,200,000,000 from the end of 2002. At the halfway point, we're at over 50 percent of our $8,000,000,000 reduction goal with the rest of '04 to go.
 When you include the conversion of our equity units in August of this year, we're at nearly 75 percent of that $8,000,000,000 net debt reduction goals.
 The net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio is 1.9 times versus 2.7 times a year ago with a 12/31 target of 1.6 - clearly dramatic improvement in our credit metrics.
 Out liquidity position is strong. We have 2,400,000,000 in cash on hand, which is sufficient to cover all scheduled debt maturities into 2006. Additionally we have 2,200,000,000 in credit facilities, all of which remain fully undrawn.
 The confidence in our ability to deliver our free cash flow and reduce both gross and net debt should be very high based on our 2003 results.
 We'll go back one - I'm sorry - one more forward - thank you.
 Next financial priority is establishing profitable growth. We plan on creating and sustaining profitable growth here in existing and new sources including wireless data, DSL, new products like Complete Sense, our nationwide GDP (ph) offer, key relationships with people such as Virgin Mobile, Qwest and through system integrators like IBM and Cable. And again you'll hear more through the business presentations during the course of the day on these subjects.
 Our third financial priority is to drive productivity and maintain our improved margins. A large part of this priority is to reduce at least 1,000,000,000 in operating cost of our annual operating costs by year-end 2006. We establish this cost reduction commitment through an extensive benchmarking process. Len described a little bit.
 We looked at ourselves versus other telecom companies and other best-in-class (ph) competitors inside and outside of telecom. This study helped us to reset our cost targets, identify specific actions and develop projects and plans around those actions.
 Currently we have 41 initiatives across five broad areas plus enterprise-wide initiatives that are being trapped to achieve this $1,000,000,000 operating expense reduction. And a number of these are already underway.
 Now what is "being trapped" mean? It means we've assigned owners, we've determined timelines as well as tracking and measurement tools. We have senior leader visibility of each and every one of these projects and these savings commitments are built into our cost budgets. Overall we've reduced layers of management, increased span of controls across the company.
 These organizational changes have reduced 12 percent of our officer and director positions by year-end 2003. Year-over-year, we've reduced the number of positions at these levels by 20 percent.
 Additionally in September we announced agreements with IBM and EDS to outsource application development and maintenance work. These are examples of the actions we've already taken to create a very competitive cost structure and streamline our organization.
 Len touched upon the customer care co-sourcing arrangement with IBM. These announced projects alone, when completed are expected to generate 500,000,000 in savings per year or nearly half of our goal of $1,000,000,000. As you can see we're off to a fast start here. And the $1,000,000,000 annual cost reduction target is real and achievable.
 As I mentioned earlier we have detailed plans in place for the 41 major initiatives with over a 100 specific sub-projects. We've talked about the customer care initiative given our co-sourcing arrangement with IBM. Later today, you'll hear from Kathy Walker, who'll talk about the plans and actions in network. You'll hear from Mike Stout on his outsourcing efforts, target state architecture and other progress he's making on cost.
 Other cost reductions examples include - for example, in sales, marketing and service, we've identified opportunities to improve service support, engine (ph) efficiencies to consolidate some order management systems, center consolidations and increase customer self-service capabilities.
 In billing, credit and collection areas we have a plan in place to integrate processes across wireline and wireless operations and to adopt optimal including electronic bill presenting and payment alternatives.
 In addition we plan to consolidate approximately 47 billing platforms down to somewhere between four and six, clearly creating significant cost opportunities for us.
 And in addition to the five major areas, we also have a number of enterprise wide initiatives. I talked about reduction in span of control, layers, reducing our officer and director positions earlier. We've also evaluated and implemented modifications towards Sprint employee benefit plans that will reduce company costs and deliver benefits at parity with our competitors.
 We've also launched a company wide business process redesign effort and as you'll hear from the number of speakers during the day, we are committed to simplifying and improving our processes to drive a better customer experience at lower cost.
 In 2004, we are targeting to continue increasing revenue per employee on top of the 10 percent improvement we realized in 2002 and again in 2003. Over the past three years, revenue per employee has been increased by over 27 percent.
 It's also important to point out that our employee base system reduced by yearly 22 percent from January of 2001 to January 2004.
 Along with improving our revenue per employee, we're also focused on improving our cash expenses, to redefines its cost of services and products, plus SG&A and we compare that to revenues, so we come up with a ratio of the expense to the revenue. Throughout the last several years, this ratio has improved by 800 basis points.
 And just in 2003 alone we reduced our cost of services and products and SG&A by $900,000,000. This far outpays (ph) the change in revenues and includes a healthy reduction in bad debt expense and a variety of other cost reduction activities.
 These productivity improvements are evident across all three divisions and shared corporate functions increasing financial strength and flexibility, profitable growth and driving productivity well positions Sprint for a successful 2004.
 I would like to turn to our financial guidance for 2004.
 In the fourth quarter earnings call yesterday I talked extensively through the drivers of 2003 result. So today we'll focus primarily on 2004.

 For PCS we anticipate PCS service revenue growth in the high single-digit. This is driven by stability in ARPU with continued subscriber growth and gains in wholesale.
 Adjusted operating income guidance. At GMG, we expect adjusted operating income to remain flat.  PCS's Adjusted operating income increases from approximately 900,000,000 in 2003 to 1,200,000,000 to 1,300,000,000 in 2004. It's principally driven by scale and continued strong operating metrics as the business grows.
 I can give you a quick update on pension and OPEB.
 Last year I shared with you our pension requirements would be roughly $1,000,000,000 for the period 2003 through 2005. Although the recent market values provided some additional cushion to the pension fund's sponsors, new record low interest rates continued to be an offset or counterbalance to that.
 As a result of the continuing low interest rates, we felt it was prudent to reduce our pension discount rate at 6.75 to 6.25 as of December 31st 2003.
 In addition we lowered our expected return on plant assets from nine percent to 8.75 percent.
 Based upon these assumptions we estimated pension-funding requirement of $850,000,000 over the next three years including 2004 to maintain a funded level in excess of 90 percent of our liabilities.
 We plan to fund this requirement evenly over the next three years. And in January of 2004 we contributed 300,000,000 that we had budgeted for 2004. This earlier than required contribution will provide nearly a full year of pension expense benefit on that additional contribution.
 We expect to receive future cash tax benefits of roughly $480,000,000 from 2003 to 2006 contributions.  Regarding the 2004 P&L impact, we can expect an incremental pension expense of approximately $80,000,000 with a primary impact in the Local division.
 Switch to adjusted EBITDA guidance.
 For 2004, for the total corporation we expect to grow adjusted EBITDA at a lower to mid-single digit rate. This is based on a single-digit decline for FON and growth and adjusted EBITDA at PCS at 3,800,000,000 to 3,900,000,000.
 At the division level we expect adjusted EBITDA for Local to be down mid-single digit to the higher pension expense, a loss of the recovery on the Local number portability cost and declining revenue. However we expect to continue a strong margin performance as we've seen in that business.
 For GMG, we expect adjusted EBITDA to be flat, down modestly.
 Moving to CAPEX.
 In 2003 total capital expenditures were $3,900,000,000 with a majority of that expenditure at PCS. As with 2003, we will continue to deploy capital in areas that support growth. Investments in the network will be done prudently and with economic returns in mind.
 Kathy Walker will touch on the components of capital spending in her presentation. Mike, Len and Howard will also touch on their focus with regards to areas they're going to spend CAPEX on.

 PCS CAPEX will increase to 2,400,000,000 from 2,200,000,000 in 2003 to support anticipated growth in both their direct segments and strategic relationships.
 Adjusted earnings per share.

 We also expect PCS adjusted for special items loss per share to increase to a range of a loss per share of 18 cents to a 13-cent loss per share. The improvement in 2003 over 2002 is due to growth in adjusted EBITDA and operating income.

 Free cash flow has been strong and has been a key contributor to our ability to de-lever the balance sheet and improve financial flexibility. In 2003 free cash flow improved from under 1,200,000,000 in 2002 to over $2,300,000,000 - a 100 percent improvement.
 I'd like to remind you that our $2,300,000,000 results in 2003 excluded the 2,200,000,000 in proceeds from the sale of our directory business and our net of our $400,000,000 pension contribution and our roughly $450,000,000 in dividend.
 Free cash flow in 2004 will continue to be strong and far outpace our investment needs, dividend and pension requirements.

 We're just going to give you some select metrics here. Overall we expect to improve upon our guidance for free cash flow in 2004. We expect to see strong free cash flow in both FON and PCS. Improvements driven by increased EBITDA in both groups.
 For the FON group we expect to grow adjusted EBITDA by low single-digit percent. This is driven by improved performance of the Local division and improvement in the adjusted EBITDA at GMG.

 On an adjusted EPS basis, we also expect FON adjusted for special items EPS to increase by a high single digit to low double digit growth as it benefits from recent reduced capital spending and improvements in operating performance.

 Sprint has been and will continue to be a leader in high-speed data.

Michael Fuller,  Sprint Corp. - President, Local Communications: Good morning, everyone. It's a pleasure for me to be here to talk about the local division, how we're doing, some of our prospects and what we're focusing on going forward. For those of you that may be less familiar with the local division here, is a snapshot of who we are and where we operate. We're the largest non-RBOC ILEC in the country.
 We cover about five percent of U.S. households. We operate in 18 states. About 7,900,000 access lines and as we announced yesterday, we're a $6,100,000,000 company with adjusted EBITDA, less CAPEX of about $1,700,000,000 in the year just completed.
 We've got a number of competitive strengths that we enjoy in our market including a strong margin performance, as you - some of you well know. We have maintained a 30 percent adjusted operating margin, not only this year - this past year, but for the years prior to that and have consistently out-performed the RBOCs on financial measures and the access line measures. We've got a product portfolio, voice data, wireless, wireline that is second to none.
 We operate in a very diverse set of markets. About a third of our access lines are in top 100 MSAs. Another third of our access lines are in what I would call mid or smaller-sized cities to you, mid-sized markets to us. And the last third of our access lines are in truly rural markets.
 We have a strong culture that has focused on operational excellence for a number of years. We have strong service capabilities at improving customer satisfaction, while we have maintained the margins that I spoke of. We've got good momentum in the business, especially with bundle sales these last several years. And through those, we have achieved total long-distance share of almost 50 percent in our markets and have generated considerable growth this past year in DSL.
 Our edge-out plan that Gary referred to has been a real success story this past year in the five markets since we opened. This is a business that we've now transitioned to Howard Janzen in Sprint Business Solutions. And finally, we began full-scale deployment of our packet network this past year. We converted 130,000 lines roughly to packet technology from circuit. And are on track, as you heard yesterday, to convert 450,000 more lines in the year ahead.
 Let me talk now about some basic business drivers that we face. This is access lines. And what you see here, is that access line losses have actually stabilized in the 2.2 percent, sort of, range. For 2003, we lost 191,000 retail lines. We've picked up 10,000 wholesale lines for a net loss of 181,000.
 Residential second lines make up about half of that loss. But, of course, a lot of that is due to broadband displacement, both customers moving to cable modem service as well as customers moving to our own high-speed DSL service. And of note, we more than doubled our DSL position in the year adding 153,000 DSL lines in the year just past.
 Wholesale competition remains quite modest. What little growth we do see has been on the UNE-P side, where we saw growth of about 20,000 lines to a total now, of 71,000 UNE-P lines. That is less than 1 percent of our access lines.
 Looking at competition more broadly, we have not yet seen any major cable company entry into our markets for telephony service. We do expect Cox to move this year in Las Vegas, perhaps in the second half. And we do anticipate that Time Warner will move into a couple of our North Carolina markets this year. We did see SBC enter just 10 days ago or so in our Las Vegas market with a residential offering.
 We are quite encouraged by the fact we've seen a stabilization of access line losses in the last few quarters. What we see is, principally, a decelerating loss in second lines, business lines, primary lines and residential primary lines have actually stayed about flat. While this is room for - it gives us reason for encouragement, we do recognize, certainly, though that growing competition from cable companies and from the wireless arena will likely offset the benefits of a continued economic recovery on the consumer side of our business.
 Let me turn to switched network traffic or minutes on our network. They have also declined over the last two years in both the case of accesses is while it's long-distance, the principal reason is customers switching their traffic more to wireless networks.
 As a point of reference, if we just look at Sprint data, Sprint PCS saw an increase last year in network usage by their customers from 10 hours to 13 hours per month, some 30 percent and we saw it decline in our minutes of use per using customer of about 8 percent. And that typifies the sort of migration - technology migration that we're looking at.
 As you see on the chart, our access/minute loss rate slowed a bit in the last three quarters of '03. In fact, it picked up a bit on a quarterly basis. Minutes declined 3 percent for the year compared to losses last year that were in the four to five percent, sort of, range. We attribute that uptake to the proliferation, now, of unlimited calling plans, both others as well as our own. Consumer long-distance minutes followed a similar trend. A bit of flattening in the last three quarters of the year. Again, I think that can be attributed in part to our own unlimited long-distance plan that we began rolling out last summer.
 So, again, we've seen a bit of bottoming in terms of traffic losses on the network or declines on the network. And while that's encouraging, we're not yet prepared to call that a long-term trend or a change. Despite those declines in the basic drivers, minutes as well as access lines, we have seen growth in long-distance and vertical features through our bundled service plans; they've truly been a five-year success story.
 We have taken our LD share from the 32 percent range at the end of 1999 to almost 50 percent all in both biz. and res. at the end of this past year. In fact, we're 51 percent market share on the residential side of our business for LD. Looking at the bottom graph, you've seen the tremendous growth we've experienced in calling features, vertical services on our network. Over the last five years, those have grown at a compound rate of 10 percent to about $850,000,000 a year in revenue.
 But, as you can also see by these charts, there has been a slowing as we've reached higher levels of penetration. These are bundled plans - these basic bundle plans are becoming more mature products. What we see though, in DSL, a less mature product, is one that's still in its high-growth phase. We more than doubled our DSL lines in service in the - in each of the past two years. And DSL has now become a very meaningful revenue stream. This past year it was $144,000,000 in revenue. In fact, during the course of '03, DSL product revenues displaced the growth in vertical feature revenue as the principal growth driver on the revenue side of our business.

That's up fairly significantly from the 39 percent range of net ads that we saw in the fourth quarter of last year. And in fact, according to some primary research we've done in our markets, where we have coverage - and the cable company also has coverage for high-speed data, we're splitting the share of decisions with the cable company. We're getting 50/50 where we have the same coverage patterns as do the cable companies.
 Overall, our success in DSL has been driven by better coverage, more effective bundling, better segmentation of our customers and more direct mail that is driven by that segmentation, targeted price promotions and lower turn. Along with these sales successes, bundles, LD, vertical services, DSL, we've done good job in managing expenses. In fact, our cash expense per average access line, before special items and the increases that you know about in pensions and OPEB's expense, those cash expenses have actually declined in each of the last four years.

A number of key efficiency and productivity initiatives that we've undertaken, including a - moving a lot of our customer contacts to the Web. Over the last three years we have seen the total number of customer contacts remain flat in consumer. Yet, we've taken those handled by live agents down from 72 percent of customer contacts to just 54 percent of customer contacts as customers have moved more and more of their contact activity with us to a much improved Web site.
 That has also stimulated revenue growth, as we've seen more revenue come off those Web contacts. On the load side, we've put in a lot of processes to reduce, for example, dispatches based on service order or troubled ticket activity. And last year we took out some 250,000 dispatches per year as a result of that screening activity. An example of productivity improvements is associated with a call distribution technology that we put in, that now, is effectively a single ACD nationwide that distributes customer calls to our call centers around the country, based on skill sets and based on the first available rep.

Now, in that light, I think that we've got a fairly significant opportunity within the local division at Sprint to redefine our market, to get away from that traditional business model, to take a share of wallet approach to the marketplace and find growth.

We have the ability to integrate those products from the standpoint of a single bill, shared minutes, single voice mailboxes, single point of contact for customer service. We have strong customer service matrix and we've got network capabilities both on the wireline and wireless side that our competitors do not have. This graphic illustrates the point I'm trying to make.
 If I now, just look at total consumer spending in our local telephone division markets - I'm moving from national to local, now, that spend is just over $10,000,000,000 a year. We've only got one-third of that spend. 3,400,000,000 today. Now, I'm including in this chart wireless revenues that are actually booked in PCS, but are derived from customers in our local services markets. Just one-third of that. Where our opportunity to grow is, is in that two-thirds of the market that we do not enjoy significant share in. High-speed data, wireless and video.
 On the Internet side, that's a $1,000,000,000 a year market. $460,000,000 of that today is spent on broadband services. And that component is going to grow rapidly. I think we should be able to capture at least one-half of the growth in that market, if not more. The real opportunity, though, is going to be in wireless.
 Today, with our affiliate partners, the Sprint PCS affiliates, we have about 19 percent of revenue share of a $3,000,000,000 market. I think we ought to be able to capture 33 percent share by the end of 2006. That's just a third of the market. That is not dissimilar to the trajectory we actually experienced in long-distance. We took long-distance from 19 percent share to 32 percent share in three years. We took long-distance from 19 percent share to 51 percent share in six years. It seems to me that we should have the capacity to enjoy a similar ramp in wireless as we have seen in long-distance. And, if we're successful in that kind of magnitude in the next three years, we're talking about $400,000,000 to $500,000,000 of additional revenue for the corporation.

That's not going to drive significant revenue for us because it is an agency relationship, but it rounds out our product set, gives us a retention tool and allows us to roll out a complete bundle that is second to none in our markets. Of all of these, I think wireless is the most significant opportunity. In fact, I think of it as the next really big opportunity for the local division.
 Stepping back and thinking about growth in the local division over the long term, here's what I see. Michael Stout,  Sprint Corp. - CIO: Good afternoon. Thank you, Mike. Thank you, Kurt. I'm pleased to be with you this afternoon to speak a little bit about IT at Sprint and to talk about the great successes we've had in 2003 and share with you our plans for the next three years.

 IT operations was separate from development. The consolidation of these groups provided not only the opportunity to take costs out, but to share best practices across the entire enterprise. We've created a business-driven, evergreen IT strategy that provides for the current and future needs of the business.
 We've looked at our applications software portfolio and created a category called a target state architecture - this is a three-year vision that we have of a simpler platform - reduced number of software packages that we have to retain.  We've evaluated the promise, the capabilities and the potential of outsourcing, signed agreements with IBM and EDS. Planned those projects and are now executing on those projects.

 In Turkey, less then one month ago, the Council of Ministers approved the Samsun-Ceyhan Pipeline.  The results we are reporting today are solid and have been supported by the positive external environment, as well as by the strong industrial performance achieved.
 First, a quick overview of the scenario where, as you know, the second quarter of 2006, has been characterized by strong Brent prices, up 35% versus the second quarter of '05, lower European refining margins, down 15% compared to the second quarter of '05, and finally by a stable euro/dollar exchange rate.
 As usual, I would like to remind you that Eni's results are affected by several issues, including the seasonal factor affecting the demand for natural gas and petroleum products used for residential heating, the demand for which is the highest in the first quarter of the year, the coldest months, and lowest in the third quarter, the warmest months. Therefore, Eni's operating profit, and change in net debt in the first six months cannot by extrapolated for the full-year.
 Let me also remind you that as a consequence of the position adopted by the International Accounting Standard Board, Saipem and its subsidiaries have been, once again, included line-by-line in the Eni IFRS consolidated financial statement. For the sake of comparison, we have accordingly restated our 2005 accounts.
 Having said this, let us now comment the results. In the second quarter, the adjusted net profit amounted to €2.5b, with an increase of around 23% if compared to the same period of '05. A positive net financial income for €109m compared to net financial charges of €116m during the second quarter '05 mainly due to the fair value valuation of the financial derivatives instrument, and to the decrease in average in net borrowing.
 These positive effects were partially offset by lower profit from investments, mainly related to the asset write-down in the Engineering and construction business relevant to a GTL project in Nigeria. Higher taxes amounting to around €900m related, to both the pre-tax profit increase and the higher contributions to the E&P result from countries with a higher tax rate.
 Leveraging on the robust industrial performance and on the positive market environment, the second quarter 2006 adjusted operating profit totaled €5.1b, up 32% on a like-for-like basis. Moreover, also the engineering infrastructure contributed with a remarkable performance.
 Let us focus now on the operating profit for each business segment. In the second quarter, the E&P business reported operating profit of €4.1b, with a 47% increase year-on-year. The result includes a negative special item for €152m related to asset impairment. On an adjusted basis, the operating profit amounted to €4.2b, showing a robust increase of more than 45% on a like-for-like basis.
 The strong operating profit is mainly due to higher hydrocarbon valuation prices, denominated in dollars, following the positive oil market scenario. These positive effects were partially offset by higher operating costs in DD&A, as well as higher exploration expenses. Moreover in the quarter, we accounted for lower abandonment costs.
 Turning to the Gas and Power results, the second quarter reported operating profit increased by around 20% to €708m. The second quarter result includes a negative special item for €73m related to asset write-downs, environmental provisions, redundancy incentives, as well as inventory loss. The Gas and Power adjusted operating profit amounted to €791m, up around 24% over the same period of 2005.
 Remaining in the G&P segment, let me elaborate now on the adjusted operating profit by activity area. The result in marketing and distribution activities shows a steady increase, as a consequence of this favorable trend in energy parameters that has affected more positively the sales prices. Then the gas purchase price has changed solely in the sales to more electric users, the higher volume sold in Europe. These positive effects were partially offset by the impact of Authority Resolution number 248, which accounted for €61m.
 The 248 was revised by the 134 Resolution that sets a new regulatory framework from July 1, 2006 to June 2008, and introduces a pricing mechanism, currently linked to the effective gas supply dynamics. In the backup section, you will find a slide that sums up the main differences between the two Resolutions. And a detailed explanation is provided in our second quarter 2006 financial report.
 Let me just highlight that the 134 Resolution, allows us to release part of the €225m provision that has been accounted for in 2005. The destination of the 2006 provision of €275m is still pending, because the new Resolution doesn't afford any indication in this sense.
 Turning to the other gas activities, the operating profit of transportation abroad increased by 23% mainly as a result of higher contribution of the Greenstream project. Eni Power results benefited from the increase of electricity productions sold. This positive element was partially offset by the lower electricity margins, due to the different trend in energy parameters for the determination of gas cost, and the electricity selling price.
 Finally, Snam Rete Gas contribution decreased, as a consequence of the new tariff set by the authority for the sake of regulatory approval.
 Let me now turn to the R&M sector. The second quarter '06 reported operating profit totaled €366m, down 39% versus the same period of '05. The result includes a negative special item for €31m, mainly related to provisions for this, and contingencies relevant to environmental laws, and scientific commissioning and redundancy payments.
 In addition, we also accounted for €207m for inventory gains. On an adjusted basis, the operating profit amounted to €190m, showing a decrease of 43% over the same period of 2005. The result was related to the reduced contribution of the refining activity in Italy due to low refining margins and higher maintenance activity.
 Moreover, we accounted for a lower contribution of marketing activities in Italy as a consequence of declining margins. This was due to the increase of international prices of products, which was not entirely reflected in the selling prices, as well as to the rise in competitive pressure. These negative effects were partially compensated by a higher result in the marketing activities in the rest of Europe thanks to higher retail volumes sold, and to better results from the wholesaler segment.
 Finally, regarding the jet fuel antitrust fine, Eni will appeal to the Administrative Courts. And based on the legal opinion we have received, we are making no provisions at this point.
 As for other businesses, in the second quarter of '06 Petrochemicals posted an adjusted operating profit of €5m. The decrease versus the same period of '05 was mainly due to the falling base chemical margin. This was due to the increase in [inaudible] up costs, which was not transferred to save prices. And the production loss in our Priolo plant, as a consequence of the accident occurred, to the ERG refinery that is totally integrated with our petrochemical plant.  In the second quarter '06, the Oilfield Services and Engineering business accounted for €133m adjusted operating profit, up 146% versus the same period of last year. This achievement was reached thanks to higher results in onshore construction, as well as a higher contribution from offshore drilling, and construction activity.
 In the other activities, that now refer to Syndial only, accounted for an operating loss of €65m mainly due to the decline in unit margin. This was due to the increase in the petrochemical feedstock costs, not entirely reflected in selling prices, as well as higher utilities cost.
 Lastly, corporate activities posted an adjusted operating loss of €84m improvement. The result accounted for in the first quarter of '05, second quarter, yes.
 The first-half of 2006 was marked by a significant operating cash flow, which reached €10.5b, up 22%, if compared to the same period of 2005. On top of this, disposals and ForEx differences contributed for around €100m, bringing the overall sources of cash to €11b. The strong cash flow generated has been better in our core business for €3.1b, and returned to our shareholders via dividends and share buyback.
 During the first half of 2006, the financial structure strengthened. As of the end of June, the net financial debt decreased to €6.4b bringing our debt to equity ratio to 0.16.
 Coming to the end of my session, let me focus on the cash returned to shareholders.  Thank you for listening. And now I hand you over to Stefano for the E&P update.

Mike Bless,  Century Aluminum Company - President, CEO: Thanks a lot, Pete. And thanks to all of you for joining us this afternoon.
 If we could turn to slide four, please, I would like to spend a couple of minutes just giving you an update of what we have been working on over the last couple of months. First, at a high level, obviously, financial market conditions have deteriorated since we spoke with you in October. That goes without saying. And the questions now the market is grappling with are pretty obvious.
 Are we seeing a foreshadowing of weakening economies on the one hand, or on the other hand will the market turmoil, itself, lead to economic deceleration? Last are we seeing some stabilization in these markets? Obviously we can't predict and wouldn't try. But importantly we're confident that the strategy that we've set out for you since this fall is going to continue to make sense in any reasonable range of market conditions.
 Shelly is going to take you through an overview of the industry in a couple of minutes but let me just make a couple of points to set some context for my comments. For those of you who follow the industry know that there's a growing consensus that the global industry, primary industry, that is, will be roughly balanced in 2016, maybe a slight deficit. And this is despite a significant surplus in China, 1.5 million tons or more, potentially much more, which is expected to lead to a continuation of record exports.
 The behavior in China that's produced the situation continues. We'll give you a couple of examples, production as you've seen was up 10% in 2015. That's well above the level of demand growth and that demand growth continues to decline.
 This production growth occurred despite some announced curtailments and talk of some more. I would note that the historical follow-through on these curtailment announcements has been quite low. These announcements have historically been followed by government subsidies that have tended to preserve on economic capacity.
 In addition the announcements of curtailments themselves have come to a virtual stop as markets participants wait to see how much metal the government intends to purchase and stockpile. Those announcements came earlier this year. All this is occurring despite research that says well over a half of Chinese smelters are unprofitable in the current market environment.
 To sum up we're seeing supply growth well in excess of demand growth in China and that, of course, has produced an industry in a severe state of over capacity. The results of this artificially propped-up industry continues to be predictable. We continue to see metals flow out of China, just shy of 5 million tons of total exports in 2015.
 We've come to the conclusion this behavior simply won't stop until and unless it's forced to do so. And thus you saw us over the last couple of months step up our efforts on this vital issue. We believe there's a growing understanding of the problem and a realization that something must be done, and done quickly. For example, you've even seen reports from India that they are contemplating bringing an aluminum trade case against China.
 In the U.S., of course, over the last couple of months the problem has become absolutely acute. By the middle of this year the U.S. primary industry could be down to operating at a capacity of around 0.5 million tons, it's quite extraordinary to think about. This would produce a deficit of over 5 million tons of primary metal in the U.S. So what have we done?
 We have spent a lot of time in discussions with our fellow industry participants. And, importantly, with the administration and members of Congress. We think these talks are going quite well. As you've seen we have been joined by the United Steel workers and we believe we'll soon be joined by some prominent members of downstream industries.
 We think we're gaining good traction and that we could soon see some decisive action. We will not back down on these efforts. The illegal behavior is simply too obvious and it goes without saying that the evidence exists that it's causing material harm to our industry, both in the U.S. and in the rest of the world.
 Okay, let me move on to Mt. Holly.
 In late December you saw that we came to a temporary agreement for power procurement for that plant. As a reminder, we talked about this before, this really is an exceptional plant. For decades it's been a supplier for high-quality billet. It has an excellent reputation amongst its customers. It has a terrific, terrific group of motivated employees and they, for years, have produced industry-leading safety performance and production efficiencies.
 A loss of this plant would be a real tragedy for the state of South Carolina and specifically for Berkeley County and the surrounding regions around the plant, obviously a big loss for our shareholders. As you saw at the end of the year we were unable to achieve our proposal, that we're convinced still makes sense for all parties.
 As a reminder we're simply seeking the right to import power, sufficient for the plant's full production, to import it from outside the system and for that we paid a standard transmission tariff to the local power company to transmit that power to the plant. This is nothing more or less than the structure we reached in Kentucky a couple of years ago and we still rely on today. The structure is based solely on the free market. Instead we have been forced to continue to buy 25% of Mt. Holly's power requirements from the monopoly power provider.
 The remaining 75% we're buying from a dedicated third party source from off-system. The only exception to this is in January, this past January, where we needed to buy 100% of the power requirement from the in-state supplier. This was because the transmission path from the third party supply was already gone for the month of January alone by the time we came to the agreement in mid-December. So that will result in slightly higher power prices for us for Mt. Holly in January.
 As you saw, regrettably we were required to curtail half the plant's production for 2016 and some of our long-term customers were understandably forced to book business with other suppliers. We're convinced we'll regain these customers when we're able to restart that second potline. As I said, Mt. Holly has long been considered a great supplier in the industry.
 During the last couple of months of the year, we became quite encouraged by the support we have been encountering from state legislators and other officials. And for this reason alone we entered into an agreement that still leaves Mt. Holly with a significantly uncompetitive power price.
 Let me just give you a sense. We're aware of several smelters in western Europe that have been entering into multi-year contracts in the range of 40%, 4-0 percent below the price we're having to pay in South Carolina. It's quite extraordinary.
 As you saw we entered into a three year contract but, importantly, we have the right to terminate with two months' notice. And we've procured energy and transmission only through the month of May of this year. This obviously leaves us with a very tight time frame to achieve a path to the free market and we're going to need to have a very good idea within the next, say, month and a half to give us the confidence to procure additional energy and reserve the transmission after May.
 It's difficult at this time to predict how this all sorts itself out. We're convinced the right people are focused on the problem. And we're going to do everything we can, everything within our power, to find an acceptable solution. Our objective here is to create the conditions so we can restart the second potline and rehire the people with whom are regrettably had to part company in December.
 Okay, moving on down the slide. In October, at the same call, we spoke to you about the operating configurations at each of our U.S. plants, each plant's product portfolio and their cost structures. And we told you our objective was to achieve a structure in the current commodity environment in which all our plants are at least break-even.
 We also told you our Board had no interest in using cash to fund unprofitable operations. During the fourth quarter the work to achieve this status was in process. As a reminder the Hawesville potlines were curtailed by the end of October and the cost structure action taken by mid-November.
 At Mt. Holly, the potline was curtailed and the personnel actions occurred, obviously, in the month of December. Based upon this the results for the fourth quarter came right in line with our expectations. Cash flow, we thought, was also very good for the environment and Rick will take you through the details of the financial results in just a couple of minutes.
 Once again, our objective was to get each of our U.S. plants to at worst a cash flow break-even in the current environment. And as Rick will detail for you, our 2016 plan shows we've exceeded this goal, we've bettered this goal. You'll see that our consolidated cash flow break even, that's net-net cash flow after CapEx interest after everything, is at an LME below $1,450 a ton. Now of course we need to execute against this plan but we're optimistic we can do it.
 In addition the company's financial profile remains strong. Leverage is very manageable, with no near-term maturities, as you know, and no maintenance covenants and liquidity remains very good. Thus, bottom line, we think the strategy as a whole remains well intact. It's pretty straightforward.
 We're going to preserve the cost structure to remain at worst cash flow-neutral in the current environment. This includes preserving the ability to make modest investments in growing and improving the businesses. I'll talk about that in just a couple of minutes.
 We'll obviously continue to be opportunistic with regard to any external opportunities that might present themselves. Our ultimate goal here is pretty straightforward, and that's to position the company to reward share owners when the environment turns.
 And with that, I'll turn it over to Shelly to talk about the industry.

 Chinese aluminum projects continue, despite existing overcapacity, and we expect to see supply from China well in excess of internal demand requirements again in 2016. As Mike noted, we continue to believe that this is a direct result of unfair trade practices and illegal government subsidies.

This dynamic should be supportive of higher regional premiums but the potential for Chinese aluminum producers to continue or accelerate expansion projects remains an overhang on the broader market.
 In 2015, global aluminum demand grew at a year-over-year rate of 4%, driven by 3% consumption growth in North America and 7% in China. This healthy demand growth was overshadowed by a 6% global production increase. Almost 90% of that increase came from China, which brought on nearly 3 million net tons of aluminum in 2015. Overall we saw global surplus of 1.2 million tons last year, which was entirely driven by Chinese oversupply. In 2016 the global aluminum market is expected to be reasonably well balanced with a large surplus in China resulting in exports even in excess of the record levels set in 2015. Okay, just a couple of quick comments on the alumina market before I hand it back to Mike.

Rick Dillion,  Century Aluminum Company - EVP, CFO: Thanks, Mike.
 If we turn to slide seven of the presentation I'll provide some details on our financial performance for the fourth quarter.
 Our net sales were down 16% from third quarter, reflecting unfavorable market conditions and lower sales volumes due primarily to the curtailment activities. Looking at the market impact on a two month lag basis the average cash LME price was down 9% and the midwest transaction price was down 10% during the quarter. Realized prices in the U.S. were 6%.
 For Iceland, the all-in two month lag LME and European duty paid premium decreased approximately 10% in the fourth quarter, consistent with the decline in realized prices. On a consolidated basis global shipments were down 8% in the fourth quarter of 2015 versus the third quarter. North American shipments were down approximately 18,000 tons, driven by the decision to further curtail Hawesville operations in October and reduce Mt. Holly operations by 50% in December.
 Sebree shipments were up 8,000 pounds, partially offsetting the impact of curtailment actions on the North American totals. The increase in shipments at Sebree reflects increased production during the quarter as well as the sell-through of existing inventories. We'll discuss the positive impact this had on working capital and cash generation in a few minutes.
 Turning first to our operating profit for the quarter, we are reporting an adjusted EBITDA loss this quarter of $28 million, a decrease of $3 million when compared to the $25 million loss reported in the third quarter. The adjustments to EBITDA include $4 million in costs related to the curtailment of operations at Hawesville and Mt. Holly, a non-cash post retirement benefit gain from the same activities, as well as a non-cash adjustment to the carrying value of our inventories.
 Lower all-in pricing including the impact of a declining LME, declining regional premiums and net of the impact of the LME on our power and certain alumina contracts, all combined to reduce EBITDA by $28 million during the fourth quarter of 2015. The market impact on our top line was partially offset by lower raw material costs of approximately $14 million including the realized benefit of lower aluminum costs as we work down inventory levels.
 In addition, favorable power and natural gas costs at our North American operations added another $5 million to EBITDA in the fourth quarter. As a result of curtailment actions and given the unfavorable pricing environment, net lower sales volume for the quarter resulted in a benefit to EBITDA of approximately $6 million.
 In summary, lower market prices during the quarter partially offset by lower raw material and power costs drove the net $3 million decrease in EBITDA during the fourth quarter resulted in an adjusted loss per share of $0.53, a decrease of $0.05 from the $0.48 lost per share reported in the third quarter of 2015. As you will note, in our reconciliation of adjusted earnings per share in the appendix we also recorded an impairment on our BHH investment, a carbon end note and cathode venture located in China.,
 Late in 2015 we completed the expansion of our (inaudible) carbon anode facility to 145,000 tons. While completing this expansion we decided to pursue an exit strategy from our investment in BHH. And as a result of this activity, determined that the carrying value of this investment was impaired, resulting in a non-cash charge of approximately $12 million, which has been excluded in this determination of adjusted earnings per share.
 In addition we finalized our purchase accounting for the Mt. Holly acquisition during the quarter and recorded a $5 million true-up of depreciation, which has also been excluded from the determination of adjusted net income and earnings per share for the quarter and the fiscal year.
 Moving on to liquidity. There are no outstanding borrowings under our revolver other than the letters of credit. As noted in our release, as of the end of the year our available liquidity was at $200 million, consist of $115 million in cash and $85 million of net availability under our revolving credit facilities. As a reminder these facilities are secured by both accounts receivable and inventories, thus the reduction in availability on the revolvers is reflective of the significant cash generation from accounts receivable collections and inventory reductions during the quarter as you can see in the working capital column, if we turn to slide eight.
 Cash decreased during the quarter by only $8 million as the $45 million in cash from working capital almost fully offset the EBITDA loss, capital spending, taxes, interest and cash curtailments costs incurred during the quarter. If we can now move on to slide nine, I'll take you through the company's full year performance. Total shipments for the year were up 6%, reflecting the impact of a full year of ownership of Mt. Kevin McCarthy,  Kayne Anderson Energy Development Company - President, CEO: Thanks, Monique, and good afternoon, everybody. Thank you for joining us today for our third quarter earnings call.
  As we typically do on these calls, I'll start today with a review of the market conditions for the MLP sector and the broader energy markets before discussing the performance of our portfolio in more detail. Then, Terry Hart will discuss our financial performance and guidance before we open up our line to your questions. With that, let's turn to a review of market conditions.
  Our third quarter was impacted by the extreme volatility in the overall financial markets as well as the MLP market. As I'll review in more detail on this call, despite this volatility we believe that the operating fundamentals for the MLP sector remain intact and that current MLP valuations are very attractive.
  There really was no shortage of factors weighing on the markets during the quarter, including the health of the global economy, the potential for a double-dip recession, the US debt ceiling stalemate, the US credit downgrade, and concerns over European debt.
  The resulting volatility was quite dramatic. From mid July through the end of August, we saw 11 out of 34 trading days in which the S&P 500 swung by plus or minus 2%. During the quarter, the S&P 500 was down 9.4%, but that hardly tells the story considering that the market fell almost 17% from late July to early August and then recovered 9% from the August 8th lows to quarter end.
  Relative to this broader market, MLP has held up relatively well during the quarter as the MLP Index fell only 3.4%. While MLP has outperformed the S&P by 600 basis points, their performance was also quite volatile during the quarter. The MLP Index fell by 16% during a four-week period from mid July to early August before recovering 12% to close the quarter.
  Since quarter end, volatility has remained high. MLPs fell 4.2% in September and were down another 2.7% in the first three days of October. Since then, MLPs have recovered nicely and are now up almost 6% for the month. Since the start of our fiscal year, MLPs have generated a total return of 4.4% as of last Friday.
  As I mentioned in my opening remarks, despite this increased volatility we continue to believe that the fundamentals in the MLP space are very positive. One of the best measures of this, in our opinion, is distribution growth trends.
  During the quarter, 39 MLPs announced an increase in their quarterly distribution, compared to 35 in each of the past two quarters. The average annualized increase also grew to 6.3%, compared to 5.6% in the prior quarter.
  MLPs have just kicked off their distribution announcements for the third quarter, and the quarter is off to a very good start. As of yesterday, seven of the eight MLPs that had announced distribution increases were at an annualized rate of 9.2%. Kayne Anderson expects 2011 distribution growth for this space to be around 6% and we expect distributions to grow by a similar amount in 2012.
  As we've discussed on prior calls, the midstream asset build-out that's required for these unconventional shale plays is what's driving much of this growth and we believe that MLPs will benefit from the development of these reserves for quite some time.
  Turning now to MLP valuations, we believe the current MLP valuations are very attractive. The group has an average yield of 6.6%, which is 439 basis points greater than the 10-year Treasury bonds. That's well above the historical average at 219 basis points. When compared to investment grade bonds, the story is similar. MLPs yield 99 basis points more than BBB bonds, which is much higher than the historical average of 11 basis points.
  Turning the comparison to other high-yielding equity securities, MLP yields compare favorably to the yields on REITs, which are 3.8%, and utilities, at 4.2%. And of course, the current yield only tells part of the valuation story for MLPs. With a strong track record of growing distributions, we believe the yield plus growth, or total return, story for MLPs is exceptionally strong.
  In an interest rate environment that's expected to be low for an extended period of time, we believe that MLPs' expected total returns in the low double digits should be very attractive to investors.
  We typically provide an update on the M&A and capital markets for MLPs during our quarterly calls. Both were relatively quiet during the quarter as market volatility reduced the pace of deals. Of note, the bidding war between Williams and Energy Transfer to acquire Southern Union is continuing with the resolution expected in the next couple of months. There were several drop-down transactions during the quarter, including deals by El Paso and Sunoco.
  Yesterday, the midstream space got a lot more interesting with two large M&A transactions. The first, the Kinder/El Paso deal, is really a transformational deal for the industry. The second deal, which involves Energy Transfer's sale of its propane business to AmeriGas, was also an important step for ETP to position itself ahead of this (inaudible).
  Capital markets deals in the third quarter were much slower than the previous two quarters, but MLP balance sheets remain in very good shape. There were three MLP IPOs during the first part of the quarter, and the backlog of IPOs is quite large with nine deals in registration.
  Of note, this backlog includes three upstream companies and several non-traditional industries. Given the market volatility over the last several months, we think it will be a challenge for many of these names to access the public markets.
  Turning to the energy markets, prices during the quarter were also very volatile as energy prices tended to trade in lock-step with other asset classes, especially during steep equity market sell-offs. I really can't recall a period where the price of oil has been so strongly correlated with the stock market on a daily basis.
  WTI crude oil, which traded near $100.00 per barrel in late July, fell to a low of $79.00 per barrel in August before rebounding roughly $10.00 by quarter end. Since early September, WTI has traded in the range of $75.00 to $90.00 a barrel; it is currently trading near $87.00 per barrel.
  We continue to see large price discounts for West Texas Intermediate compared to Brent crude. This discount is primarily due to insufficient pipeline capacity to transport growing oil supplies primarily from Canada and from the Bakken shale from Cushing south to the Gulf Coast.
  This differential, which widened to a record high of $26.00 per barrel in August, benefits the mid-continent refiners as well as certain MLPs with crude oil gatherings, storage, and transportation assets.
  Not surprisingly, we've seen several MLPs announce projects to build new pipeline capacity to alleviate this bottleneck. We believe that increasing oil production from unconventional sources like the Bakken is going to create tremendous opportunities for MLPs for many years to come.
  In the natural gas market, prices trended lower throughout most of the quarter in spite of demand that boosted by warmer than normal summer weather in much of the country. The principal reason for the decline was the unprecedented increase in supply as the result of rising shale production. While these low prices hurt natural gas producers, these prices have been driven by excess supply, which actually helps the midstream MLPs.
  Shale gas production continues to grow in spite of the low prices, really for two reasons. First, many producers have contractual incentives to drill in order to hold leases or to meet investment obligations. Other producers have a strong economic incentive to aggressively develop shales that are rich in natural gas liquids.
  As a result, many analysts are becoming increasingly bearish on natural gas prices for 2012 and don't see gas prices recovering to normalized levels to before 2013 or 2014. I'd like to emphasize that midstream MLPs with natural gas gathering assets are benefitting from this increased production levels. Additionally, midstream MLPs with natural gas processing and NGL fractionation assets are benefitting from the price differential between natural gas liquids and natural gas.
  Now, let me turn to the performance of our portfolio. KED's share price increased by 6.1% during the quarter, compared to a decrease of 3.4% for the MLP Index. KED's adjusted NAV, our measure of the fund's total returns, performed slightly better than the MLP market as KED's adjusted NAV decreased 1.8% during the quarter, compared to a total return on the MLP Index of negative 1.9%.
  As of August 31, our investments consisted of 24% private MLPs and other private equity, 59% public MLPs, and 17% energy company debt. While the totals by investment category are little changed since the end of last quarter, we did take advantage of the market volatility during the quarter to rotate a portion of the fund's public MLPs and quoted debt holdings. During the month of August alone, we rotated approximately 10% of our MLP portfolio.
  While we hate volatility, as long as we have it we're going to take advantage of it by swapping MLPs that have been disproportionately hurt for those that have traded relatively well. There was an unusual amount of opportunities to swap out of one MLP into another MLP that had similar asset quality, similar yield, but a much greater growth rate.
  Our private investment portfolio is little changed from May 31, consisting primarily of our investments in Direct Fuels, VantaCore, and ProPetro. At 24% of portfolio, KED is underweighted in private investments compared to our target portfolio, but, as we had pointed out last quarter, this is due to the successful monetization of our investment in International Resource Partners in April and our decision to deploy those proceeds on a temporary basis into public MLPs until we find attractive private investments.
  During the quarter, we have stepped up our efforts to source new private investments and have evaluated several opportunities, some of which are still under active discussion. As we said last quarter, however, we're going to be very selective in evaluating new private opportunities and we haven't established a timetable for making such investments.
  Now I'd like to share a little bit more details about our three largest private investments. Our largest private holding is our investment in Direct Fuels, a private MLP which operates a specialty refining and terminalling business in the D-FW area.
  Direct Fuels had a very strong performance during the second quarter as it focused on its core transmix refining and fuel terminalling business. Direct Fuels successfully renewed several key transmix supply contracts during the quarter and added a significant contract with a new supplier.
  The partnership also continues to benefit from its exposure to the refining crack spread, which is the difference between the price of transmix it purchases and the price of refined products it produces. The partnership is exposed to the crack spread because some of its transmix supply is priced off WTI crude oil.
  This spread continues to trade at historically high levels because of the discounted value of WTI versus Brent and other light switch crudes that I mentioned before. These high spreads have created an opportunity for Direct Fuels to convert much of its crack spread exposure to longer term, fixed margin contracts. In these contracts, it purchases transmix based on a formula that is tied to the price of the refined products that it produces.
  On October 1, Direct Fuels successfully converted one of the largest of such contracts at an attractive margin, thereby reducing the partnership's exposure to commodity prices going forward. While this will lower results in the short-term, we believe that any moves that reduce the earnings volatility will benefit the partnership in the long-term.
  For the second consecutive quarter, we received the full cash distribution on all of our Direct Fuels preferred and common units. Going forward, we expect that Direct Fuels will continue to pay full cash distribution on its preferred units, and we also project that the partnership will continue to pay the full $0.45 per unit on its common units for the next several quarters based on the strength of its transmix business. On a longer-term basis, we believe that $0.40 per common unit is sustainable based on more normalized market conditions.
  As of August 31, we kept the valuation of our Direct Fuels units unchanged at $13.00 per unit as weakness in the comparable public valuations offset the continued strong performance in the transmix business.
  As a reminder, we increased the valuation of Direct Fuels by 30% at the end of the prior quarter, reflecting the resumption of cash distributions and the deleveraging upon the sale of its biodiesel business.
  Next, VantaCore, our second largest private investment, is a private MLP in the aggregates, mining, and asphalt business. VantaCore's operations include its Winn/McIntosh business in Clarksville, Tennessee and Southern Aggregates business near Baton Rouge, Louisiana.
  During the quarter, VantaCore added another location to its portfolio by closing on the purchase of an operating quarry in Kentucky, which is approximately 15 miles north of its Winn quarry in Clarksville, Tennessee. KED purchased $1.9 million of Class B preferred units to help finance this acquisition, and we expect this acquisition to be immediately accretive to the partnership.
  As we mentioned last quarter, VantaCore's performance during 2011 has been well below expectations. This trend continued in the latest quarter as demand for aggregates was lower than forecast, particularly in the commercial and residential construction markets. VantaCore is clearly feeling the impact of the slowing economic recovery and the resulting impact on the construction market.
  In terms of the factors that are within the partnership's control, we continue to see selective improvements in operating efficiencies and we continue to focus on cost controls. Since August, VantaCore has also seen prices for its products increase in both Tennessee and Louisiana markets, which is a very encouraging sign.
  VantaCore's board of directors, including Ron Logan, who is our representative on the board, continued to closely monitor performance and set direction for the partnership as VantaCore navigates through this challenging marketing environment.
  In early September, the board initiated a significant restructuring of executive management responsibilities, which we believe will keep the partnership focused on the right priorities. As part of this restructuring, Irik Sevin, one of the partnership's founders, will no longer be part of the executive team but will continue to serve as a consultant to the board of directors.
  As we anticipated on our last quarterly call, VantaCore's ability to pay cash distributions was severely limited this quarter by certain financial tests in its senior credit agreement. In August, we received a partial cash distribution of $0.04 per unit on our common and preferred, and we received the balance of VantaCore's minimum quarterly distribution in the form of additional preferred A units.
  The cash component of the distribution was lower than expected due to the results of the second quarter. The preferred units, which we received, are equivalent to the common units in respect to distributions but are senior to the common units in liquidation with a liquidation preference of $17.50 per unit.
  We expect VantaCore to continue to pay a portion of the distribution in the form of (inaudible) units over the next several quarters. Over the next four quarter, we estimate that VantaCore will pay approximately 40% to 50% of its MQD in cash with the remainder paid in additional preferred units. I would also remind you that the amount of cash versus preferred units will depend on quarterly variations which tend to fluctuate seasonally.
  As of August 31, we reduced our valuation of VantaCore common units by $2.25, to $9.50 per common unit. This was based on VantaCore's financial results as well as weaker valuation for comparable public firms and the prospects for a slower recovery in the construction market.
  I'd also like to update you briefly on our third largest investment, ProPetro, which is an oil field service Company where we own a combination of debt and equity. Results at ProPetro continue to be very good, with August results setting a monthly record for the Company.
  Through the first eight months of 2011, ProPetro has generated $25 million of EBITDA, more than double the results for 2010. Strong performance in the Company's pressure pumping business continues to drive these results.
  The Company has added two fleets of pressure pumping equipment this year and expects to add two more fleets in November and December. We expect the Company's financial results to continue at record levels for the remainder of the year and believe the Company is poised for very strong results in 2012.
  Our August 31 valuation for our investment in ProPetro is $17 million, up slightly from the prior quarter, as a result of the PIK interest on the term C note held by the fund. Of note, our august 31 valuation did not reflect the record August results which were substantially higher than the projected results we had at that date.
  For more details on our guidance and our financial performance, I'll now turn the call over to Terry Hart, our Chief Financial Officer.
