During the quarter, asset level performance for KED sectors was negative. The total return of the public MLPs in our portfolio was negative 2.2%, which slightly underperformed the MLP Index's total return of negative 1.9%. The total return of the private MLPs in our portfolio was negative 0.9% due to VantaCore's performance during the period.
  Our debt portfolio, including ProPetro, had a total return of negative 0.6%, outperforming the Bank of America, Merrill Lynch, High Yield Energy Index, which had a total return of negative 1.5%.
  Our stock price performed very well during the quarter, benefitting from the second quarter increase in our dividend from $0.31 per share to $0.38 per share, which we announced on June 30. The day after the announcement, our share price was up 7.8%. Since then, our shares have continued to outperform MLPs and the broader market.
  For the quarter, our share price increased 6.1%, compared to a decrease of 9.4% for the S&P 500 and a decrease of 3.4% for the MLP Index. Additionally, the gap between our share price and NAV has continued to narrow over the last several quarters.
  Turning now to our results of operations. Investment income totaled $2.9 million for the quarter. We received $4.5 million of cash dividends and distributions, of which $2.9 million was treated as a return of capital during the period.
  In the third quarter, we increased our return of capital estimate by $0.3 million based on 2010 tax reporting information from our portfolio of investments. During the quarter, the Company received $1.3 million of interest income, of which $0.4 million was paid-in-kind interest from ProPetro. We also received $0.8 million of paid-in-kind dividends, of which $0.6 million was from VantaCore. These paid-in-kind dividends are not included in investment income, but are reflected as an unrealized gain.
  Operating expenses, including management fees and interest expense, were $2.4 million. And during the quarter, we had $2.3 million in after-tax realized gains and $7.3 million in after-tax unrealized losses.
  During the quarter, our net distributable income beat the midpoint of our guidance range of $0.39 to $0.40 per share by over 7%. The increase was primarily due to Direct Fuels paying $0.45 per common unit, compared to our project of $0.37 per unit. On October 5, we declared our distribution of $0.38 per share, which was unchanged from last quarter. This distribution will be paid on October 28.
  On October 14, we had $69 million borrowed under our revolving credit facility, which represented 56.8% of our borrowing base and 62.1% of our quoted borrowing base. The pricing on our borrowing base is LIBOR plus 2% as long as our borrowings are less than the borrowing base attributable to quoted securities.
  Now, turning to our guidance. As of August 31, we increased our estimate of income tax payments, primarily associated with the sale of IRP, to $21.2 million from $19 million, which was our estimate at May 31. The primary reason for our increase was additional realized gains generated during the third quarter. We paid $14.1 million in federal and state income taxes during August and were able to defer $7.1 million of tax payments, which we'll pay in November.
  Our guidance is pro forma for the $7.1 million in estimated tax payments and assumes that all of these payments will be funded through the sale of traded debt securities in our portfolio. We estimate that the pro forma portfolio will generate dividends, distributions, and interest income of approximately $6.6 million in the next quarter.
  This estimate includes a cash distribution of $0.45 per common unit of Direct Fuels, is expected to pay on $0.475 per common and class A preferred units or $800,000 in paid-in-kind distributions from VantaCore, and $400,000 in paid-in-kind interest from ProPetro.
  Our guidance does not reflect any of the changes in cash distributions made by MLPs or changes in interest rates since August 31, and our guidance is not a projection of investment income on a GAAP basis since it includes PIK distributions and it excludes the impacts of return on capital.
  Let's now turn to our estimates of interest expense and operating expenses. Based on our projected borrowings of $70 million under our revolving credit facility, we estimate cash interest expense to be approximately $390,000 per quarter, assuming a LIBOR rate of 0.22% and a spread of 2%. We estimate our management fees to be approximately $1.3 million per quarter and other operating expenses to be approximately $480,000 per quarter.
  Based on these estimates and assumptions, our net distributable income is projected to be approximately $0.415 to $0.425 per share in the fourth quarter. This guidance reflects our expectation for the distribution amounts we expect to receive from Direct Fuels and VantaCore during the next quarter.
  Our net distributable income in the fourth quarter is projected to be greater than our current dividend of $0.38 per share, but we feel this level of payout is prudent and sustainable under a variety of different events that could occur at our three largest private investments. We will reassess our dividend guidance as we have more clarity regarding these potential future events.
  Now I'd like to turn the call back over to Kevin.

Steve Parks,  STR - SVP, CFO: Thank you, Anissa. Good morning. Welcome to Questar Corporation’s third quarter 2004 teleconference and webcast. We’ve got a lot of ground to cover this morning. First, I’ll review our third quarter financial results and some of the key drivers. Questar earnings jumped 29 percent year to year for the third quarter. Higher earnings from gas and oil exploration and production and gas gathering activities offset a larger seasonal loss in our Utility Questar Gas. 
 Following my comments, Keith Rattie, Questar’s Chairman, President and CEO, will discuss our 2005 outlook. Chuck Stanley, President and CEO of our Questar Market Resources subsidiary, and Alan Allred, President and CEO of our Regulated Pipeline and Gas Distribution subsidiaries, are also here to help answer your questions, following our prepared remarks. 
 Later today we’ll make a transcript available on our website at Questar.com. 
 In our earnings release Tuesday we raised our 2004 earnings guidance to $2.55 to $2.65 per share from the previous $2.45 to $2.60 per share. In addition, we gave initial 2005 earnings guidance of $3.25 to $3.45 per diluted share, which excludes one-time items. Please note this correction. We based our 2005 guidance on the October 18 forward strip, not on the October 25th strip as improperly stated in our earnings release. 
 Forward gas prices on October 18 were about 50 cents lower than the prices a week later on October 25. 
 Our remarks today contain forward-looking statements about the future operations and expectations of Questar. These statements are made in good faith. We believe they are reasonable representations of the Company’s expected performance at this time. Actual results, of course, may vary from our stated expectations and projections, due to a variety of factors that are described in our Form 10-K and 10-Q filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. 
 Now here are the key drivers behind our 29 percent improvement in the third quarter 2004 earnings. Net income from the company’s exploration and production and other nonregulated businesses rose 36 percent, to $37.2 million in third-quarter 2004, compared with the year-earlier period. 
 QMR subsidiary, Questar E&P, grew production 10 percent, including an 18 percent increase from our mid-continent operations. Questar E&P’s Pinedale production rose 34 percent year to year, with 30 more producing wells than a year earlier. Pinedale continues to be one of the major stories in the US E&P sector. Our net income of course also benefited from strong prices, including an average realized natural gas price of $4.07 per Mcf during the quarter. 
 We hedged about 76 percent of third quarter 2004 production, at an average price of $3.99 per Mcf, net to the well. We hedged to lock in acceptable returns on invested capital and to reduce commodity-price risk. In a rising environment we left money on the table. Hedging reduced revenues by $23.6 million in the third quarter. 
 Our Wexpro subsidiary, which develops and produces cost-of-service reserves for our gas distribution company, reported 12 percent higher earnings in third-quarter 2004. Wexpro earns an unlevered after-tax return of about 19 percent on its net investment. Wexpro is benefiting from both a growing investment base and higher prices for oil and NGLs. Keith will talk more about new growth opportunities for Wexpro in just a minute. 
 Earnings from Questar Gas Management, our gathering-and-processing-services business, rose 60 percent, to $4.8 million in third-quarter 2004, on the strength of a 15 percent increase in volumes and a 10 percent increase in revenue per decatherm. We saw strong growth in Pinedale production and gathering for third parties in Utah. 
 Finally, Questar Pipeline earnings were 2 percent higher in the third quarter than a year earlier. A 7 percent increase in revenues was partially offset by higher operating costs. Questar Gas, our gas distribution utility, incurred a seasonal $9.8 million loss in the 2004 quarter, versus an $8.3 million loss in the 2003 period. The higher loss was due to higher costs for depreciation and operating and maintenance expenses. 
 Now before I finish, I want to mention that last week our board approved a $587.1 million capital budget for 2005. Questar Market Resources’ share is $376 million, Questar Pipeline $102 million, Questar Gas $78 million, and Corporate and Other $31 million. That 31 million includes $25 million for as-yet unidentified projects in our operating subsidiaries. The budget is based on a 30-well per-year Pinedale drilling program. We will ask the board to increase the budget if the BLM approves our request for year-round drilling at Pinedale. 
 Now, I’ll turn the microphone over to Keith Rattie.

Keith Rattie,  STR - Chairman, President, CEO: Good morning, everyone. The central theme of our call today is that Questar is capitalizing on both commodity-price fundamentals and organic growth potential in our E&P business. Last week we reviewed our five-year plan with our Board of Directors. I'm going to give you the highlights of that in a moment, but first I want to make one more comment on and try to help clear up the confusion on our guidance for next year. 
 As we noted in our press release, we estimate that 2005 earnings will range from $3.25 to $3.45 per share next year. That guidance was based on the forward strip on October the 18th, not October 25th as stated in the press release. As Steve noted, the strip on October the 25th was about 50 cents higher than it was on October the 18th. One more piece of information to give you some sensitivity on our earnings next year; a 10-cent change in NYMEX translates into about a 2-cent per share change in EPS. Hopefully that's going to clear things up. 
 Now let me give you the highlights on our board meeting. A few years ago investors described Questar as a utility with an E&P business. Today, we’re a growing E&P company that also owns a utility. The utility today generates less than 15 percent of our net income, and we expect that share to decline over the rest of this decade. 
 We believe we can grow production with the drill bit at about 10 percent per year over the next few years, and that’s driven not just by Pinedale, but also our growing prospect inventory elsewhere in the Rockies and the Mid-continent. 
 We think we run our business in a way that differentiates us from some (indiscernible) E&P companies. We’ve driven a focus on returns into our culture. Today and for the foreseeable future, we think we can deliver higher risk-adjusted returns by reinvesting in our E&P business. 
 We will continue to hedge to protect returns, cash flow and earnings. Please note that we have significant probable and possible reserves potential on our acreage. Over the past several months we’ve done a lot of work to quantify this potential. Our independent reserves consultants are now reviewing this work and we’re going to give you more information on this early next year. 
 Steve mentioned Wexpro. Wexpro has the potential to grow its investment base, and therefore, net income at high single digit rates over the remainder of this decade. Wexpro has identified $400 to $500 million of future investment opportunities on its acreage. 
 Our gathering-and-processing-services business, as you no doubt have noticed, has grown at a compound rate above 20 percent over the last five years and we believe it has the potential to grow at about 10 percent over the next several years. That’s because today, over 3 trillion cubic feet of reserves are contractually dedicated to our gathering and processing systems in the Green River and Uinta basins. 
 Our regulated companies, plus our pipeline, plus our gas will play a role. They provide stable earnings with low to mid-single-digit growth potential. They pay most of our dividend, and support our credit ratings. 
 We gave a detailed breakdown of our third-quarter and year-to-date operating results in our press release on Tuesday. Let me touch on the highlights. You’ll note that we grew gas and oil-equivalent production about 12 percent in the first nine months of 2004. Also note that we expect 2004 gas and oil-equivalent production to exceed 102 bcf equivalent, and that will be up about 10 percent from 2003. Just as a reminder, when we give production results, we exclude Wexpro. 
 In the Rockies, Pinedale production grew 73 percent in the first nine months of this year compared to the same period a year ago. Uinta Basin production declined 17 percent in the first nine months of 2004. But the important trend here is that third-quarter 2004 production was about 3 percent higher than average first-half 2004 production. In short, we overcame decline with ongoing development drilling. And we expect production in 2005 to be higher than 2004. 
 Another trend to watch – Rockies legacy production, which includes all Rockies E&P activities except Pinedale, the Uinta Basin and Wexpro, rose 9 percent in the first nine months of 2004 compared to a year ago. Still another trend to watch – We grew Mid-continent production 16 percent in the first nine months. We obviously can’t sustain this rate of growth, but our experienced Mid-continent team keeps finding new opportunities on our existing leaseholds. 
 We summarized our cost structure in a table at the end of our press release for those who focus as we do on margins, so I won’t repeat that here other than to reiterate that our goal is to maintain a cost structure that ensures acceptable returns at a $3.50 NYMEX price. 
 Let me turn now to our production forecast for 2005, and developments at Pinedale. I’ll comment on several promising new plays in our E&P business, and then give an update on Clay Basin and the Questar Gas dispute. 
 For 2005, we estimate that natural gas and oil-equivalent production, again, excluding Wexpro, could range from 112 to 114 bcf equivalent, about 10 percent higher than 2004 – and there’s upside in this number. We base this guidance on a 30-well drilling program at Pinedale next year. If the BLM approves our request for year-round access, we intend to drill and complete 42 wells at Pinedale next year. And with a 42-well program, our 2005 production could range from 115 to 117 bcf equivalent. A 42-well program would add about $.08 per share to 2005 EPS, but the real impact of year-round access will be apparent in 2006 and beyond. We’re expecting a BLM decision sometime in the first half of November. 
 You’ll note from our press release that we recently acquired new federal leases on over 2,000 acres adjacent to our existing Pinedale acreage. This new Pinedale acreage may add up to 32 new low-risk 20-acre drilling locations to our current 430-well inventory, and there’s further upside depending on drilling results. Questar E&P, QEP, has a 100 percent working interest in these new leases. Now several groups have appealed these leases, but we believe these appeals are without merit, because this acreage was previously evaluated under the original Pinedale Environmental Impact Statement. 
 We noted in our press release that our deep exploratory well at Pinedale is behind schedule. We spudded this well in mid-July after a two-month delay due to sage-grouse activity in the area. Since then the drilling pace has been beset by chronic mechanical problems with the rig and poor performance of the inexperienced crews. 
 To illustrate, our “on-bottom” time – and that’s the percentage of time that the drill bit is actually grinding away at the bottom of the hole. On-bottom time has been a little over 50 percent. This compares to the 75 to 80 percent on-bottom time we typically get from better rigs and crews. We’re now almost down to the intermediate casing point at the bottom of the Mesaverde, which is at about 14,200 feet. Once there we’ll suspend operations, remove the rig, and resume next spring with another contractor and rig. 
 Elsewhere in the Rockies, we like what we see with our latest well in our ongoing evaluation of deep potential below the Wasatch Formation on our Uinta Basin acreage. We recently completed a 12,850-foot well targeting the Blackhawk and Mancos formations. Chuck can give you more details in Q&A, but the key point here is that there’s significant gas potential below the Wasatch. And we’re making progress in our effort to figure out how to exploit this potential. 
 Also in the Uinta Basin, we continue our pursuit of bypassed oil in the Green River Formation, which lies above our core Wasatch gas play. After decades of both primary and secondary development, less than 15 percent of the 600 million barrels of original oil in place has been recovered on our 100 percent Red Wash acreage. Our Green River team believes that horizontal drilling is the key to improved recovery of this bypassed oil. We gave them some capital earlier this year to test their beliefs. And during the quarter, we completed two horizontal wells with average initial production of 150 barrels per day per well, again, on 100 percent acreage south of the Red Wash unit. 
 We’ve also been quietly accumulating acreage in the Uinta Basin. Over the past couple years we’ve added over 15,000 net acres to our Uinta Basin leasehold. There are numerous additional locations. Let me give you one example. We recently drilled and logged a promising well at our Flat Rock prospect, about 35 miles south of our core Wasatch gas play. You can ask Chuck for more color during Q&A. 
 I also draw your attention, noted in our press release, to our recent acquisition of 2,400 net acres in the Wamsutter area of southwestern Wyoming, which will add over 50 new locations to our low-risk development-drilling inventory. The target here is the Almond and Mesaverde formations with reserves averaging 1-2 bcf equivalent per well. 
 Now over the past couple of years you’ve heard us speak in general terms about opportunities on our Rockies legacy properties. Obviously for competitive reasons we remain reluctant to provide a lot of detail, but we’ve given you some examples today. The acquisition of new acreage at Pinedale, in the Flat Rock area of the Uinta Basin, and in the Wamsutter area of the Green River Basin are examples of what we consider our “three yards and a cloud of dust” approach to E&P growth. 
 Perhaps the highlight of the year for Questar has been strong production growth in the Mid-continent. So far this year our Tulsa Division has drilled and completed 17 wells in our ongoing infill development program in the Elm Grove Field in northwest Louisiana. They currently plan to drill another 24 wells in 2005. 
 Our Tulsa division has also drilled 34 wells this year in our Hartshorne coalbed-methane play in the Arkoma basin in eastern Oklahoma. These wells have average reserves of about .5 bcf. They IP at more than one-half million cubic feet per day, with average drilling and completion costs of about $450,000 per well. A reminder, a key feature of this play is that these wells produce immediately after we turn them to sales. We don’t have to wait for the wells to dewater and they don’t make much water. 
 Our Oklahoma City division, which manages our activities in western and central Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle, also keeps finding ways to offset decline and generate modest production and reserves growth from our acreage in the Anadarko Basin. To give you an example, using Oklahoma’s forcepooling rules, our Oklahoma City team scrapped their way up from an initial working interest of only 1 percent, to about a 33 percent in a Roger Mills County, Oklahoma, prospect we call the Hartman. They drilled the Hartman and turned it to sales in June with an initial production of about 8 million cubic feet per day. Then they fraced the well in July and the rate jumped to 14 million cubic feet per day. This well has made over 1.4 bcf gross in its first four months and is currently producing over 7 million cubic feet per day.

Recall that we had taken pressure surveys in April that indicated a potential disparity of up to 11 bcf between the current book volumes of cushion gas in the reservoir and the volume of cushion gas implied by those pressure surveys. At this point we haven’t resolved the apparent disparity. And this could even prove to be a false alarm. But we have narrowed the list of possible explanations. 
 We’ve thoroughly reviewed the operating history of the Clay Basin field going back decades. So far we haven’t found any obvious explanation for the disparity. We haven’t found any evidence of any significant migration of gas out of the reservoir – and that’s important. We haven’t found any evidence of any significant subsurface leaks in any of our wells or from any of our surface facilities – and that’s important. We haven’t found any busts in our accounting records, and that, of course, is important. 
 We have confirmed that the disparity first appears in the mid-1990s, after Questar increased the working capacity of the reservoir. The working capacity, as you know, is the amount of gas injected and withdrawn each year. This fact might be significant, because when we began shoving more working gas into the reservoir, again, in the mid-1990’s, we may have pushed some gas out into areas of the reservoir that are ineffective – gas that’s still in the reservoir, but not detectable with short-duration-pressure surveys that we take and possibly not producible within the typical range of storage operation.

The bottom line here is we need more data before we can answer those questions, and it may be months or possibly even years before we have the data we need. Again, because the short-duration pressure surveys that we use to measure the volume of gas in the reservoir are not precise, we’re going to need to take more surveys at both the beginning and the end of the withdrawal season. We’re also going to need data on how the reservoir performs this winter on withdrawal. So we’ll keep you posted. 
 Finally, let me update you on the gas-processing debacle in Utah. On August 30th, as you know, the Utah PSC reversed its earlier orders and instructed our utility, Questar Gas, to refund about $29 million in previously recovered gas processing costs, previously recovered in rates over a five-year period ending in May. The PSC ruled that Questar Gas had failed to prove that the Company had acted prudently back in the 1990s when they decided to manage an emerging gas-heat-content problem by contracting with affiliate Questar Pipeline for processing services. 
 Now the PSC order had no material impact on 2004 earnings, because we’d previously accrued for the full $29 million amount. But the PSC has forced us to manage heat content without compensating us for that service. Processing remains the lowest cost option for doing this, so we can’t avoid these costs by shutting the plant down or doing something different. We’re on track to have another good year in 2005, and I hope as you’ve heard from our call today, we feel pretty optimistic about our growth potential over the longer-term. And with that, we’ll be glad to take your questions.

 Role of Questar Pipeline and Questar Gas, our regulated businesses are still a key part of our value proposition, which is to offer investors a lower risk play on the strong fundamentals of natural gas. The E&P business obviously is in the limelight today. That’s were we get the best risk-adjusted returns. We’re getting superior risk-adjusted returns as well in our gathering and processing business, driven by what we’ve referred to in the past as our hub (ph) strategy. 
 I would also point out that the value of having regulated companies was evident for us in 2002, at a time when commodity prices, particularly in the Rockies, tanked. Our regulated companies provided very important support. We don’t often talk about it in the context of regulation, but Wexpro provides stable earnings with solid double digit growth earns a 19 percent, after tax unlevered return and as I mentioned earlier, we have a very substantial base inventory of identified growth opportunities, something in the neighborhood of $400, $500 million, over the next several years. 
 As for the fundamentals for the Pipeline business, there are plusses and minuses here. Obviously, the Rockies Region production is growing. Regional market is small. Only about 20 percent of the gas that gets produced in the Rockies gets consumed in the Rockies. The rest has to move out of the region on export pipelines. A lot more investment in pipelines is going to be needed over the next decade as Rockies production grows. 
 However, we have seen a deterioration of the risked return ratio, or relationship in the Pipeline business. The Pipeline business has been significantly deregulated over the last two decades. Pipelines today are not the monopolies they once were, but nonetheless, returns remain capped at levels allowed ROEs in the 10 to 12 percent range. 
 When we are out competing with other major pipeline companies in this region, we slug it out for the opportunity to build new pipe. Increasingly, the producers are driving the bus as far as new investment. Producers are the ones that are stepping up in the Rockies to hold the capacity and to underwrite new pipelines with long-term contracts. However, we’ve seen recently in one very significant example, what the producer is asking the pipeline developer to do is to amortize the investment, reflecting its rates and amortization of the investment over 30 to 35 years, but they’re only willing to sign a 5-year contract. 
 And when we look at the potential in supply in the out years, we see rising recontracting risk. As long as that continues to be the case, adhering to our rigid, risk-adjusted return focus, we see that creates a lot of uncertainty about whether or not we are going to be able to play and be a significant participant in the growth of the Pipeline business. 
 Turning to the utility, Questar Gas has currently allowed returns about 11.2 percent. That’s average for utilities across the country. But as you will note, it’s been a long time since Questar Gas has consistently earned its allowed return. We’ve dealt with some of the underlying causes of under earning, dealt, for example, in our last rate case, with the historical test year issue, but we continue to have these repeated events. The latest, of course, being the gas processing dispute, which undermines returns.

Today, we have about we’re sending out about 780,000 bills to residents, commercial customers, businesses here in Utah, Wyoming and Idaho. That customer base grows by about $20,000 per year.  This concludes the operational update, and I will, as usual, leave the floor to CFO, David Tønne, to provide his perspective on the financial events in the second quarter. David, the floor is yours.

David Torvik Tønne,  Aker BP ASA - CFO: Thank you, Karl, and good morning, everyone.
 The second quarter has been a quarter of high activity and strong performance, not only operationally, but also financially. Increasing realized prices, cost discipline and low cash taxes contributed to a high operational cash flow. With project execution and capital spend in line with our plans, this translated into a strong free cash flow and a further deleveraging of our balance sheet.
 In parallel, this quarter, we have taken several proactive steps to further strengthen our financial position by extending debt maturities and diversifying our sources of funding. In combination, this further improves our ability to continue delivering on all our 3 capital allocation priorities as a pure-play E&P company in a market environment with high volatility and uncertainty.
 Now if I zoom in on the second quarter results, our net production in the quarter was 199,000 barrels of oil equivalents per day. The reduction from Q1 was mainly driven by the planned maintenance activities that Karl has already covered. Then due to a small underlift, sold volumes ended at 195,000 barrels per day or 17.8 million barrels in total.
 The realized crude price ended at $68.7 per barrel, in line with the average Brent dated in the period. Adjusting for NGL, our average liquids price was $66.9 per barrel, up 11% from Q1. Including gas, the realized average hydrocarbon price was $63.4, up approximately 13%. And consequently, we report a total income of $1.124 billion for the second quarter.
 Given the high activity level across several assets in the quarter, I'm glad to see that we were able to maintain productivity and cost discipline. Production costs related to oil and gas sold in the quarter amounted to $158 million, down 10% from Q1. Cost per produced unit amounted to $9 per barrel. The increase from Q1 was driven by lower production, as the underlying cost of operations was actually down quarter-on-quarter by $6 million or roughly 5%. For the first half of 2021, the average production cost per barrel was $8.8, in line with the full year guidance of $8.5 to $9.
 If we take a look at the other main P&L items and subtract both production costs of $158 million and other operating expenses of $9 million from total income, we get an EBITDAX of $957 million. Exploration expenses amounted to $102 million, of which $62 million was field evaluation costs, with almost 2/3 being the NOAKA project. NOAKA is now in its final stages before concept selection, and once it has been formally passed this key milestone, costs related to the project will be mostly categorized as CapEx. We had $16 million in dry well costs in the quarter, mainly related to the Equinor-operated Shenzhou well in the Barents Sea.
 Depreciation was $240 million or $13.3 per barrel. The small increase in depreciation rate from Q1 is driven by a change in the mix of production from the various fields. Net financial expenses were $62 million and included $24 million in costs related to an early redemption of a $750 million bond. Furthermore, net currency gains in the quarter were $37 million, where $22 million was related to a newly issued euro bond of EUR 750 million. I will come back to both these transactions later in my presentation.
 Summing this, this gives us a profit before tax of $552 million, up 10% from the first quarter. Tax expenses amounted to $399 million, which means an effective tax rate for the quarter of approximately 72%. Net profit in the quarter then ended at $154 million or $0.43 per share, up 21% from Q1. With stronger prices, cost discipline, no cash taxes and a positive contribution from working capital changes, the growth in operating cash flow was even higher than the growth in net profit.
 Operating cash flow in the second quarter ended at $1.108 billion, up 23% from Q1. Then investments, including payments on lease debt, amounted to $511 million across the various spend categories, with CapEx being over 75%. Investments increased with roughly 50% quarter-on-quarter, in line with our spending plan for the full year.
 Free cash flow before financing was $597 million, an increase of 7% compared to Q1. As already mentioned, during the quarter, we redeemed our last callable bond and issued a new bond in euros with a lower coupon. Net cash flow from these activities amounted to $132 million. Dividends paid in the quarter was $112.5 million. And interest paid and other finance items was $33 million. We then ended the quarter with a cash balance of $975 million, an increase of $583 million from end of Q1.
 In addition to the fairly large change in cash on the balance sheet, there are 2 other things worth highlighting. On the left-hand side, property, plant and equipment increased by $238 million. We had additions of $457 million, where investments at Valhall and Hod made up roughly 45%; and the 4 assets, Alvheim, Skarv, Ula and Johan Sverdrup, made up roughly 50%, with between 10% and 15% of the investment each.
 On the right-hand side, other current liabilities increased with $245 million. A key driver for this is the higher license-related liabilities which is typically caused by accruals for project work that has not yet been invoiced. An increase like this is something that we typically see when we increase project activity and investment spend like we have done from the first to the second quarter, and this has a positive effect on working capital. We would then typically see the opposite effect if activity is reduced.
 Although there is only a minor change in bonds and bank debt on the balance sheet, the underlying changes are quite material as we, in the second quarter, have continued our journey of optimizing the capital structure. The specific activities executed can be summarized in 3 main elements. Firstly, as I noted in our first quarter presentation, in April, we amended and extended the maturity of our working capital facility from 2022 to 2024, with the option to further extend to 2026. In addition, we utilized the remaining option on the liquidity facility to extend the maturity from 2025 to 2026. Both facilities are currently undrawn with a commitment fee of 35% of the applicable margin. With a weighted margin of 1.1%, the commitment fee today that we pay is less than 0.4%. These debt facilities provide significant financial flexibility, supporting both our organic investment program and enable us to react quickly to potential inorganic opportunities that may arise.
 The second activity is that we, in May, issued an inaugural euro bond of EUR 750 million. This has now opened up a new source of capital for us providing additional funding optionalities for the years to come. The bond issue attracted high demand and was significantly oversubscribed. This allowed us to price inside our existing U.S. yield curve and at a record low coupon of 1.125%.
 The third activity is that we have redeemed our last outstanding callable U.S. high-yield bond. This $750 million bond was issued back in 2019 and was originally maturing in 2024 with a coupon of 4.75%. By amending our bank facilities, retiring all debt and issuing new longer-dated bonds in euros, we have added optionality through new sources of funding, reduced our financing costs and extended our debt maturity profile. Following these transactions, our average drawn debt maturity is over 7 years. Our first maturity is $500 million in 2025, and we only have $1 billion of debt in total maturing before 2029.
 The results of the very strong cash flow generation and the refinancing activities are that at the end of the second quarter, net interest-bearing debt, excluding IFRS 16 leasing, have been reduced from Q1 with roughly $500 million, down to $2.6 billion. Leverage has been reduced down to 0.85x EBITDAX, and our available liquidity remains industry-leading, ending the quarter at $4.4 billion. This unique financial flexibility puts us in a very good position to deliver on our capital allocation priorities of maintaining financial capacity while we invest in profitable growth, and continuously return value back to our shareholders across various oil price scenarios the next decade.
 I'm also happy to see that the strong operational performance, combined with a more constructive price realization, means that we are now again moving into a taxpaying position. For the fiscal year 2021, we have now fixed the first 3 tax installments payable in Q3 and Q4 at $100 million and $200 million, respectively. As you can see from this slide, the size of installments in the second half of 2021 corresponds roughly to the $65 scenario, indicated for payments in Q1 and Q2 of 2022. This indicates that the assumed average Brent price for the full year 2021 used at fixing the first 3 installments in the second half of 2021 is roughly $65 Brent, using an exchange rate of NOK 8.5. This also means that if we end up in the $70 scenario for the full year 2021 indicated on the slide, the first 3 installments are a bit too low and will result in a catch-up effect in the Q1 and Q2 next year.
 Now to round off my presentation, I will, as always, walk you through the key guiding parameters for 2021. In short, we keep all our guiding parameters unchanged from our capital markets update in February and as also reiterated at our Q1 presentation. Production in the second quarter was, as expected, lower than the guided full year average due to planned maintenance. The large planned maintenance program impacting production in 2021 is now behind us. Year-to-date production is 210,400, and we expect production for the full year to end somewhere between 210,000 and 220,000 barrels of oil equivalents per day. Capital spend year-to-date is roughly $1 billion, and our project activity is progressing as planned.
 Abandonment activity is mostly done for the year, but CapEx activity will still be ramping up with, for example, several production wells being drilled at Alvheim and Hod towards the end of the year. In addition, spending on NOAKA will be categorized as CapEx after the concept selection in late Q3. Production cost of $8.8 per barrel year-to-date is, as already mentioned, in line with plan, and we keep the guidance between $8.5 and $9.
 Lastly, our proposed dividend of $450 million for 2021 remains unchanged, and the Board of Directors has resolved to pay a quarterly dividend of $112.5 million later in July.
 I will now leave the word back to Karl for some concluding remarks before we move on to the Q&A session. Thank you.

The package with an estimated proved reserves of 40 Bcfe of at year end 2006 is comprised of approximately 60% shelf and 40% onshore assets. We have retained Petrie Parkman, contacted potential purchasers and have had a data room opened for the last few weeks. We are encouraged by the significant interest in this package and recent announcements of deals of this type involving Gulf of Mexico assets. Proceeds from the asset divestiture will be used to pay down debt.
  Additionally, the Board authorized a hedging program designed to mitigate commodity risk with new positions in place for the second half of 2007, full-year 2008 and the first half of 2009. Implementation of the program is going well and since April 1 we have achieved average floors for gas around 685 per mmBTU and $55 per barrel of oil with no increased volume risk to the Company during the hurricane season.
  With our tender offers and refinancing of our debt completed and asset divestiture and hedging programs underway, we look forward to focusing our attention on our core business.

  Revenue for the first quarter 2007 was $108.5 million, slightly down compared to first quarter 2006 revenues of $109.2 million. As part of the previously mentioned final settlement from Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, we received a cash settlement of $92.9 million during the first quarter, generating $9.1 million in additional business interruption recovery, and a gain on insurance recoveries of $8.1 million for a total of $17.2 million.
  As Rick mentioned earlier, first quarter production averaged 25,982 barrels of oil equivalent per day. That was comprised of 9,244 barrels of oil, and 101.4 million cubic feet of natural gas per day. On the oil/gas split, oil represented 36% and natural gas represented 64% of total production.
  Price realizations were lower in the quarter versus the same period a year ago, averaging $53.31 per barrel of oil and $7.09 per MCF for natural gas. Those prices represent decreases of 10 and 15%, respectively, over first-quarter 2006 price realizations of $59.16 per barrel of oil and $8.30 per MCF of natural gas.
  Through the first quarter, our hedging contracts qualified for cash flow hedge accounting treatment, and commodity prices are stated net of hedging impact. However, effective April 1, we have elected to discontinue hedge accounting as a result of the implementation of our new hedging program, which uses derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting. The likely effect of the discontinuation will be earnings volatility, as periodic changes in fair value of these derivatives will be reflected through a reporting gain or loss related to these contracts on our statement of operations.
  As Rick mentioned, we have new hedges in place for the second half of 2007 through the first half of 2009. The program is designed to hedge a significant portion of production, up to a maximum of 75% of the forecasted annual proved production. The program to date is comprised of zero-cost collars, put options, and the gas contract during the third quarter of 2007 with collared pricing secured without deliverability risk to the Company. We have now completed the 2007 part of the hedge program, with the updated hedging schedule being on our website in the investor relations section.
  I will now turn to expenses in the quarter. Lease operating expense for the quarter was $16.8 million excluding transportation charges, or $7.16 per barrel of oil equivalent.   Depreciation, depletion and amortization was $47.9 million for the quarter, or $20.49 per BOE, in line with our guidance range of $19 to $22 per BOE.

  Net interest expense for the quarter was $6.6 million, which is an increase from $4.8 million in the same quarter of 2006, but below our guidance range of 7 to $7.5 million. With the asset divestiture proceeds earmarked for the paydown of our bank facility, and the flexibility for an early repayment of our senior floating-rate notes, we're targeting a debt to total capitalization ratio of 50% within three years.

Tony Alexander,  FirstEnergy - President & CEO: Thanks, Jonathan. Good morning, everyone. At least there wasn't much traffic this morning getting here; given everything else that is going on in this town. You see the safe harbor statement. Take a few minutes to review that, if you would. You know we start every one of these off with a quick review of that requirement.
 The agenda is fairly straightforward. I am going to give you a quick overview of FirstEnergy, what is going on in Ohio with respect to the transition to market based generation rates, as well as in Pennsylvania, and then I will switch a little bit and talk a little bit about how we are maximizing the value of our generation fleet, hedging our commodity exposure and talk a little bit about our financial flexibility.
 If you think about FirstEnergy from an overview standpoint it is basically we have an integrated approach to our operations of both a regulated component which consists of seven regulated utilities, about the fifth largest in the United States based on customers. We serve in Ohio, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Our competitive operations runs about 14,000 megawatts of capacity. It is a separate SEC registrant. Both sides of the business are really focused on the fundamentals of particularly as we make this transition in Ohio and Pennsylvania.
 Let's talk a little bit about what is going on in Ohio. I seem to get a lot of questions on that, although we are in the middle of a process, which makes it very difficult to tell you exactly how it is going to end up, which is what you really want to know. But if you think about what we've done in Ohio which we have two plans on file, one called an ESP on our electric security plan, that would establish prices and provide stability to customers over a two-year period with an option to the Commission essentially to have a third year at stated prices. We also have a market rate option, which is the comparison model against the ESP. If you think about the plan and the way the process works the Commission will evaluate our ESP; in the aggregate including all of its terms they believe it is more favorable than the market rate option; it will under the statute it would accept the electric security plan. If not, they would use the market rate option as the means for establishing pricing in the state of Ohio.
 If we talk about our electric security plan or ESP, it is a pretty comprehensive plan. It includes not only generation, but also transmission and distribution pricing over the two-year timeframe 2009 and 2010, as well as 2011. The price increases are fairly predictable, 5, 4, roughly 6% over that time frame. The generation prices, as you can see on the chart, are again relatively fixed. There are some re-openers as you go in time. Then the main, these are the prices; and in order to accomplish the percentage increases there will be generation deferrals in the magnitudes laid out on this chart over this time frame.
 Like I said it is a pretty comprehensive plan, has a lot of parts to it. One of them is we would no longer charge in the Cleveland Electric Illuminating Company service territory, a regulatory transition charge for the RTC. That will result in a write-off of about $485 million. Like I said earlier, we resolved the distribution rate cases that we have pending, revived for increased distribution revenue. It provides for recovery of prior deferrals and establishes new deferrals, as well as recovery mechanisms for those new deferrals at specific times.
 The generation supply is going to be provided by FirstEnergy Solutions, and they have committed under this arrangement to increase their generation supply by about 1000 megawatts over this time frame, as well as to help support the utility's efforts to re-mediate and reclaim old, essentially old generating facilities and manufactured gas sites that are still owned by the utilities but yet need to be reclaimed and remediated.
 The timeline is, as you can see on this chart, we would expect an order some time prior to the end of this year, so rates can go into effect on January 1 of 2009. The market rate option is the alternative to the ESP. And again, it is to secure the provider of last resort, default service obligation effective January 1, 2009 assuming the Commission does not accept the electric security plan. It is a competitive bidding process is what we have proposed, a slice of system kind of approach. There would be an independent manager to assure transparency of the bidding and affiliates of FirstEnergy would be allowed to bid.
 It is essentially a power supply pass-through kind of arrangement. Although underneath the competitive bid obviously the customers will be assured of a fixed price for the period of the bid. We plan and proposed kind of a staggered process that would mitigate wholesale market volatility. And essentially what we would do is acquire because of the time, essentially a 100% of supply for 2009, about two thirds of the supply for 2010, and about one third of the supply for 2011. Then that would continue to roll each year so that you are buying one third of the supply every year from that point on.
 We would also in the future propose to do the bidding over more than one day, probably two or three times during a year in order to get more levelized pricing over the time frame so it is not affected by pricing that might be in existence at any one point in time. The Commission has this case in front of them now. I understand that this week we closed the hearings. That's probably in some sort of briefing schedule that I don't know about, but it is public record of some type. You can find out. But I would expect them to reach a decision within the time frame that they have as indicated here on the chart.
 Let's talk about Pennsylvania a little bit. Again, transition in Pennsylvania from Met-Ed and Penelec. Two of our subsidiaries in Pennsylvania scheduled to take place on January 1, 2011. Our Pennsylvania Power subsidiary is already at generation prices are already established pursuant to competitive  the competitive market. They no longer have the POLR obligations that Met-Ed and Penelec have. There is legislation pending; we all know about it. There is a lot of moving parts in Pennsylvania right now, and I think at this point we are just going to have to wait and see how this process continues to evolve.
 There is a lot of emphasis in Pennsylvania, as there should be as you make these transitions, on energy efficiency, conservation, renewable energy requirements, ways to mitigate the transition between and handle the transition between, moving from fixed prices, particularly fixed prices like in Pennsylvania that haven't changed in 15 or 20 years, to competitive market prices.
 In Ohio as example we are using phase-in to accomplish much of that as you saw in our earlier presentation. So we will just have to wait and see. There are a few days left in this session and then a couple years before we actually get to the competitive market in that state.
 When we talk about the rest of the business, getting out from under the regulatory space at this point because obviously those are two parts of what is going on at FirstEnergy, and two very important parts moving our generation supply to the competitive marketplace, particularly since most of you know we have about a 27,000 megawatt load and only a 14,000 megawatts of capacity. So being relieved of that POLR obligation, matching so that we can match better our supply with our customers will be important going forward.
 And as we look to what the company is going to be doing going forward, start talking about how we are going to expand our generation fleet. What are the options we have to continue to grow our business? Beyond these transitions? As you know, we have started several years ago mining our asset initiative, which is basically trying to get as much out of our existing fleet as possible through efficiency, through new equipment and essentially making it run stronger.
 We've added 447 megawatts through this type of additions in the last couple of years. We have scheduled to add another 300 or so, so about 770 megawatts over the last three or four years or six years, about the size of a major generating plant. Nobody is even known that it has really happened. Easy to manage, capital controlled, making your units more efficient at this point is a much more effective way for us to grow our generation fleet.
 We've also recently purchased the Fremont Natural Gas plant. In total it is about a 700 megawatt combined cycle facility. It is expected to be in service by the end of 2009. Renewable energy will also be part of our portfolio going forward. We already have in place 145 megawatts of capacity. We have scheduled another 70 online before the end of this year, and we will continue to look for opportunities for wind and other renewable energy to meet the requirements of both Ohio and Pennsylvania going forward.
 We also look to maximize the value of our generation through appropriate hedging. Coal, coal transportation, nuclear, emission allowance positions are all significantly closed through the 2010 timeframe. We do have rising fuel costs. We've talked about this before. We expect about $200 million in increased fuel costs in 2008 and a similar number in 2009. Brought about by different parts of the fuel cycle but nevertheless, about the same magnitude in each of those two years. In order to better utilize our generating facility and match our fuel choices with our fleet in order to maximize margin we use something called "fuel flex" in which we are blending coals almost real time in our bunkers. So that we can maximize revenues and time them as close as possible to changing prices in the marketplace.
 One of the other things we have recently undertaken, and that is the strategic investment we made in the Signal Peak mine, formerly called the Bull Mountain mine in eastern Montana. This mine ultimately will produce between 12 million to 14 million tons. It sits on about 440 million tons of reserves at this point. Our equity investment will be about $125 million. We will own 45%. We have in place a 15-year coal agreement and we have concurrent rail arrangements and agreements so that the Bull Mountain coal can be effectively utilized at our facilities, primarily along Lake Erie, but also it can be delivered to our facilities on the Ohio River.
 When you look at this particular supply, we believe it will be operational in the types of tonnage that we are looking for in about 2010. We will take about 7.5 million tons of this coal to our facilities. We expect the remaining coal to be placed into the market and sold. Some international likely, but not yet fixed on that as to exactly what markets we will attempt to penetrate with the excess coal that is produced at this mine. From our perspective it has a significantly higher heat rate, BTU content is 10,300 versus 8,800, which is what we typically have been using. 8,800 is powder river basin coal, which is what Bull Mountain will substitute for at our facilities. It will give us somewhere between 170 and 200 megawatts of additional capacity. Quite frankly, we are quite pleased with what we have seen from the coal and its characteristics at this point. It has some environmental advantages. Again, which will match well with our existing fleet.
 When you look at FirstEnergy I still believe that we have a very attractive risk reward opportunity. We are managing the transition to competitive markets in both Ohio and Pennsylvania. We are focused on maximizing the generation value of our fleet and maximizing that. We have earnings and cash flow growth from our competitive business. We are focused on the fundamentals over the next several years. We do not have a large capital spend other than what it will take to complete our environmental projects that are scheduled and so we are very focused on the fundamentals of our business. We are achieving operational excellence, and we have the financial flexibility to maximize the benefits to our shareholders in the future.
 My time is almost up. Thank you very much for your investment and your interest in FirstEnergy. I guess I might turn it over to Paul and we will take your questions at the end of the session.

Mike Morris,  AEP Ohio - CEO: The point that is really important here is the legal requirement that the commission has to test the ESP against the market rate option. And I don't think there is any question for AEP Ohio that the market rates would have to fall through the floor before the proposal that we put in front of them as an ESP would be less advantageous for the customers, which again is the legal requirement.
 You heard us say this before and I don't want to make a big deal out of it, but Ohio is a very unique state; it is a state that believes wholeheartedly in the implementation of the laws. The Ohio Supreme Court which for us is the jurisdiction of first review of any orders issued by the commission has been straight as an arrow on the notion of not creating law or interpreting law but simply applying the law as it is.
 So the whole notion of you put in an ESP and its gets wrinkled beyond recognition, we all have very strong legal rights to say, hey, wait a second, the ESP we filed was legally better off than the market rate option that could have been implemented. And to Tony's point, you have a couple of opportunities. You can reject and refile or you can reject and go to a market rate option. Tony is exactly right that if you choose that, then there is never a road back to ESP land, constructively put together by the legislature. But nonetheless, the law in Ohio will be filed, will be followed I should say.
 So we feel comfortable as does Tony that we are well below what a market rate option might yield for our customers over that horizon and have every reason to believe that the balanced filing we've put in front of the commission has a high probability of being accepted. Now if you had the Office of Consumer Council here or the Ohio Manufacturer Association here, they would probably give you a different view. If you had the Ohio Manufacturer Association here and they said all three of us including Cincinnati all four of us intended to give electricity for free to the manufacturers in Ohio, they would still have something to complain about here.
 That is part of the nature of what we do, it is the business that we are in. I understand that. If I am [Tim Timken], I don't like $21 energy. I would rather have $12 energy or $8 energy. But none of those pork chops are around anymore.

 We achieved strong growth from our Healthcare/Life Sciences, Communications and Aerospace and Defense market sectors with Communications strengthening significantly within the quarter. We were able to achieve these results despite a highly constrained supply chain market that is limiting revenue upside ability.
 We produced GAAP EPS of $0.79 for the fiscal third-quarter, including $0.14 of stock-based compensation expense, a result that was slightly below the midpoint of our guidance range. Our operating margin of 4.5%, while still best among our peer group, was below our expectations for the quarter. Product mix was most significant factor that contributed to the lower than expected margins.
 We delivered higher revenue than anticipated associated with new program ramps; a critical stage of the product lifecycle but requires increased investment. Concurrently, volumes of more mature higher-margin products were slightly down in the quarter.
 In addition, we experienced operational inefficiencies due to supply chain constraints as we continue to prioritize actions and investments towards those necessary to drive customer success. We expect the margin pressure to be temporary as the products become more mature and we gain efficiencies.
 Return on invested capital was a healthy 15.9%. This represents an economic return of 640 basis points above our weighted average cost of capital, well above our 500 basis point goal.
 Next I will highlight a few significant accomplishments within the fiscal third quarter. Our teams delivered quarterly manufacturing wins of $202 million, another solid outcome positioning us for continued growth. In addition, our funnel of qualified manufacturing opportunities increased over the prior quarter to $2.7 billion.
 Our exclusive focus on mid to low volume high complexity markets and passion for delivering customer service excellence is resonating with current and prospective customers. Further, our teams booked a record $38 million of engineering solutions wins and increased the engineering funnel to record levels. We are optimistic we will continue to excel with this differentiated service offering as we develop leading-edge products which will transition into Plexus manufacturing.
 We continue to make good progress in our revised capital allocation strategy initially announced on February 20, 2018. As of the end of the fiscal third-quarter, we have repatriated over $380 million from the APAC region.  During the fiscal third quarter we refinanced $150 million of the maturing $175 million of senior notes at a reduced interest rate. We anticipate the reduced share count and lower interest expense will contribute to meaningful EPS leverage in fiscal 2019.
 Advancing to our guidance for the fiscal fourth quarter of 2018 on slide 4, we expect our revenue growth trajectory to continue due to our strong wins performance and improved end markets. As a result we are establishing revenue guidance of $735 million to $775 million.
 The midpoint of our guidance range suggests we'll deliver approximately 4% sequential revenue growth and greater than 12% revenue growth from the fiscal fourth quarter of 2017.

Neil A. Hansen,  Exxon Mobil Corporation - VP of IR & Secretary: All right. Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to our first quarter earnings call. We appreciate your participation and continued interest in ExxonMobil. This is Neil Hansen, Vice President of Investor Relations. Joining me on the call today is Jack Williams. Jack is a Senior Vice President and member of the Management Committee with responsibilities for the projects organization and the Downstream and Chemical business lines.
 After I review the quarterly financial and operating performance, Jack will provide his perspectives on the quarter and give updates on the significant progress made in a number of key areas across the business that will generate accretive value for our shareholders. Following Jack's remarks, we'll be happy to take your questions.
 Our comments this morning will reference the slides available on the Investors section of our website. I'd also like to draw your attention to the cautionary statement on Slide 2 and the supplemental information at the end of the presentation.
 Moving to Slide 3. I'll now highlight our first quarter financial performance. Over the past few month, we made excellent progress on our growth projects with several key final investment decisions and continued exploration success. We also remain on track with plans to increase production in the Permian Basin to 1 million oil equivalent barrels per day by 2024. In fact, growth in the Permian during the quarter supported a 5% year-over-year increase in liquids volumes.
 The first quarter was also characterized by solid operating performance including the successful execution of scheduled maintenance across a number of our downstream facilities. The impressive progress in the first quarter was achieved in a margin environment that for both the Downstream and Chemical business lines was extremely challenging.
 In addition, North American crude differentials narrowed significantly, eliminating the large arbitrage opportunities that our logistics allowed us to capture in the fourth quarter. So while the fundamentals and demand growth that underpin our investments remain strong, near-term supply and demand imbalances pressured margins, in fact, in the Downstream, the lowest levels we've seen in the last decade.
 Earnings per share for the quarter were $0.55, including a negative $0.04 per share impact from asset impairments. All in all, the results were in line with our expectations given the margin environment we experienced during the quarter.
 I'll now go through a more detailed view of developments since the fourth quarter, starting first with the Upstream. Average crude oil prices were lower than the fourth quarter with Brent down $4.56 and WTI down $4.22. However, despite the decline in crude markers, ExxonMobil's liquids realizations increased by $2.32 driven by improved Western Canadian differentials. Gas realizations on the other hand were down in the first quarter consistent with crude-linked LNG pricing lag and a $0.50 decline in Henry Hub pricing. Production in the Permian averaged 226,000 oil equivalent barrels per day, an increase of 19% relative to the fourth quarter and more than double the average production we saw in the first quarter of last year.
 Exploration success continued offshore Guyana with 3 additional discoveries since the beginning of the year. In February, we announced discoveries at the Tilapia and Haimara wells, and the Yellowtail well, which we announced last week, marked our 13th discovery on the Stabroek block. These discoveries add to the previously announced estimated recoverable resource of approximately 5.5 billion oil equivalent barrels.
 We also discovered a major natural gas reservoir with the Glaucus well in Cyprus, made a final investment decision to proceed with development of the Golden Pass LNG project and made significant progress on another key project in our LNG portfolio with the signing of a gas agreement with the PNG government to support the Papua LNG expansion.
 In the Downstream, industry refining margins weakened due primarily to excess gasoline supply. As I mentioned, North American differentials narrowed in the first quarter with increased takeaway capacity in the Permian and production curtailments in Western Canada. From an operational standpoint, we successfully completed a heavy slate of scheduled maintenance, in part to prepare for the upcoming IMO 2020 sulfur spec change.
 We announced final investment decisions for the Singapore resid upgrade project, the Fawley hydrofiner and the light crude expansion project in Beaumont. These advantaged investments will increase our capacity to produce higher-value products, including ultra-low sulfur fuels and Group II premium lubricant base stocks.
 Although fundamentals remained strong in the Chemical business, margins were challenged during the first quarter, with supply length from recent industry capacity additions pressuring realizations. Supported by continued demand growth, our volumes in the Chemical business increased by 100,000 tons. We also progressed a polyethylene expansion at Beaumont, which is on track to start up in the third quarter, and we funded 3 major olefin derivative projects on the U.S. Gulf Coast.
 Moving to Slide 5 for an overview of Upstream volumes. Production in the first quarter of 2019 was 4 million oil equivalent barrels per day, in line with the production in the fourth quarter of last year. Again, production in the Permian increased by 36,000 oil equivalent barrels per day, a 19% increase, bringing total production in the Permian to 226,000 oil equivalent barrels per day in the first quarter. This impressive growth was more than offset by lower Kearl output and natural fuel decline.
 Looking at first quarter production relative to the same period of last year shown on the bottom left chart, liquids volumes increased 5%. Growth of 126,000 oil equivalent barrels per day in the Permian drove volumes higher. The absence of the PNG earthquake and lower maintenance in Canada and Qatar also contributed to an increase in volumes. Warmer weather in Europe led to lower seasonal gas demand, but again overall, volumes were higher by more than 90,000 oil equivalent barrels per day compared to the first quarter of last year.
 Moving to Slide 6 and a review of first quarter results compared to the fourth quarter of 2018. First quarter earnings of $2.4 billion were down $3.7 billion. Upstream earnings were down approximately $400 million driven by the impact of fewer sales days in the quarter, higher maintenance in downtime, notably at Gorgon, and the absence of various onetime items that impacted our fourth quarter results.
 Downstream earnings decreased by $3 billion, with several factors contributing to the lower results: narrowed North American differentials, lower industry margins, the absence of fourth quarter asset sales in Germany and Italy and derivative impacts. And I'll provide more details on these drivers on upcoming slides.
 Finally, Chemical earnings were lower by $200 million primarily driven by the absence of a favorable non-U. S. tax item in the fourth quarter, and Chemical margins remained under pressure with recent industry capacity additions.
 Turning to Slide 7, I'll expand on the business drivers that impacted our Downstream results, again relative to the fourth quarter. Downstream results for the first quarter were a loss of $256 million, a decrease of $3 billion compared to the fourth quarter of last year driven by the absence of the Germany retail and Augusta refinery asset sales and unfavorable margin impacts of approximately $2 billion. These unfavorable margin impacts are in line with the drivers that we previously communicated with the largest impact due to narrowing crude differentials, again mainly in Western Canada, that resulted in about half of the unfavorable margin impact.
 In addition, industry refining margins were lower driven by excess gasoline supply and a tightened clean-dirty product spread. Finally, the absence of favorable mark-to-market derivative impacts in the fourth quarter, which were the result of a declining oil price environment, combined with the unfavorable impact in the first quarter as a result of a rising oil price environment, resulted in a negative book margin impact of more than $600 million quarter-on-quarter.
 On Slide 8, I'll provide a more detailed view of the current margin environment in the Downstream. The chart on the left of the page plots industry refining margins over time and clearly shows that the industry is inherently volatile. In the first quarter, industry refining margins were among the lowest we've seen in the last 10 years. Low conversion margins were relatively strong supported by fuel oil and distillate. However, high conversion margins were challenged, weak gasoline, naphtha and LPG crack spreads. High refinery utilization drove oversupply of these products.
 Slide 9 provides some additional perspective on the current chemical margin environment, and again, the chart on the upper left there shows the amount of polyethylene capacity added by year since 2009 compared to the annual growth in demand over that same period. Chemical demand remains strong and is expected to grow at approximately 3% per year or 1.2x global GDP. However, recent capacity additions have outpaced demand, depressing global PE margins, as shown on the bottom left chart. On the U.S. Gulf Coast alone, the industry has added nearly 5 million tons of capacity since 2017, in great part to capture the advantage of low-cost ethane feedstock. As a result, polyethylene margins have declined by approximately 45% since 2015, reflecting the cyclical nature of the Chemical business.
 Moving to Slide 10, which provides a review of our cash profile for the first quarter. First quarter earnings when adjusted for depreciation expense and changes in working capital yielded $8.3 billion in cash flow from operating activities. We experienced a $1.3 billion working capital release during the quarter. This was mostly offset  this is mostly due to higher seasonal payables balances, which were primarily tax related, and an inventory release in the Downstream. This occurred as we drew product inventories booked prior to plant maintenance turnarounds. Other noncash items had a negative impact of approximately $1 billion, which most notably included the reinvestment of equity company earnings as part of the Tengiz Expansion project.
 First quarter additions to PP&E were $5.9 billion driven primarily by increased activity in the Permian Basin. Total capital expenditures were $6.9 billion, in line with the 2019 CapEx guidance that we provided at Investor Day in March.
 Earlier this week, the Board of Directors declared a second quarter cash dividend of $0.87 per share, representing a 6% increase from last quarter and marking our 37th consecutive year of per-share dividend growth. Gross debt increased by approximately $3 billion in the quarter, and cash ended the quarter at $4.6 billion.
 Now before I turn it over to Jack, let me provide a few observations regarding the second quarter. In the Upstream, we expect lower gas volumes driven by seasonal demand, and I'll provide a little more detail on this on the next slide. In the Downstream, we expect industry refining margins to recover with higher seasonal gasoline demand and heavier industry maintenance, which is common this time of the year. North American crude differentials however are anticipated to remain near first quarter 2019 levels. Scheduled maintenance in the second quarter in the Downstream will be similar to what we experienced in the first quarter.
 Chemical margins are expected to remain under pressure as the market continues to work through supply length from recent capacity additions. And like the Downstream, scheduled maintenance in the Chemical business in the second quarter will be significant, and I'll provide some additional details on scheduled maintenance in a few slides.
 But first, let me provide some more detail on seasonal gas demand on Slide 12. The chart on the left there shows the negative impacts we typically experience from lower gas demand in Europe in the second quarter. As you know, gas demand is highly seasonal and driven by weather. Second quarter gas demand is on average 200,000 oil equivalent barrels per day lower than the first quarter of the year, and we expect a similar trend to occur this year.
 Turning to Slide 13, I'll provide some perspectives on our second quarter outlook for Downstream and Chemical scheduled maintenance. As we previously communicated, scheduled maintenance in the Downstream in 2019 will be higher than normal and again partly in preparation for IMO 2020. We expect the impact from scheduled maintenance in the second quarter to be broadly in line with what we experienced in the first quarter. The estimated earnings impact for the second quarter for the Downstream is shown on the upper left chart.
 In the Chemical business, again shown on the bottom left chart, and as I indicated, we expect to see significant scheduled maintenance, with the impact in the second quarter similar to the amount we saw in the entire second half of 2018.
 Hopefully, that provides you with some helpful perspectives on key drivers of our expected performance for the upcoming second quarter. At this time, I'd like to hand it over to Jack.
